The total paid-up capital of the five is £60,473,352, and the amount of the average holding works out at £219.

As to the directors, they hold their posts in a fiduciary capacity, and on the whole it may be said that they are selected and confirmed in their posts because they are not only trusted by the shareholders of the banks, but their integrity is unknowledged by numberless depositors and borrowers.

The effect of nationalising these banks would be to buy out the tens of thousands of shareholders—and with what object? It would change the ownership by this very large number, whose average holding is only £210, for ownership by the State, and it would presumably change control by the directors, who may be regarded as experts, for control by one or more Government Departments, and ultimately by the Cabinet of the day. A Cabinet is not, and never will be, composed of men who know the highly specialised business of banking. Still less is a Cabinet ever likely to understand the difficult business of lending to suitable borrowers of varied character reasonable amounts for sound business transactions of every kind, with as little risk of loss as may be avoided by prudent and well-informed direction and management.

The change in ownership of bank stock needs to be made as little or no difference to the policy to be pursued. A change in bank policy could only be secured through the directorate. Nationalisation may mean a transfer of control by the directors, who are actuated by commercial and financial principles only, to control either by politicians, who direct bank policy for political purposes, or by persons appointed by, but with no instructions from, the Government of the day. In the latter case the present directors or men who have similar knowledge and are of similar integrity would have to be appointed or reappointed to direct the banks.

The change, indeed, to what is called nationalisation of the banks appears, therefore, to be unnecessary, and if it is to be a change to political direction it might become corrupt, and would be very dangerous. Certainly nothing can be gained by turning the ownership of the banks over from their large numbers of proprietors, with comparatively small holdings, to the State, whether the State is to be represented by Bank Commissioners, or a Government Department, or a Committee of the Cabinet or a Committee of the House of Commons.—Yours

London, April 23. WALTER HUNGTMAN

headline: WHAT COULD BE DONE.
text:
"Wake up, Agriculture" movement is in progress.

Few people have an idea of the vast importance of the egg trade. During the twelve months ending December 31 last week, imported from abroad over 20,000,000 long hundreds (that is, 120's), of a value of more than £15,500,000. In addition to this, we imported more than £2,500,000 worth of dried and liquid eggs; writes Mr. E. T. Brown, the "Westminster Gazette" poultry expert, and lecturer at the Royal Agricultural College, Cirencester, in the news. paper named

The home crop of eggs—those produced in this country—were valued at about £14,000,000, which brings the total quantity of eggs consumed in this country in a single year to well over £30,000,000.

"When it is remembered that the total annual wheat crop of Great Britain amounts only to £18,000,000, the importance of the poultry industry may be realised." "We could easily produce all the eggs required in this country, and thus divert great sums of money at present flowing into the pockets of our foreign rivals into the pockets of our own farmers and smallholders."

"At the moment there is not one hen per acre of cultivated land; the number could be increased fourfold without the displacement of any other class of live stock.

But farmers and smallholders must be given some encouragement. With eggs at a shilling a dozen, or less than the cost of production, it is not likely that our people will extend their flocks.

To this end the Government should do as the South African and other Governments are doing, and that is to advance money to farmers and smallholders on the security of eggs in storage.

"Bankers are always willing to advance money to traders against warehouse receipts. Why should not the Government—or even some of our more progressive banks adopt a similar plan for the encouragement of poultry farming?

headline: PORTUGUESE CONSULAR FEES. / JLAVY DOCUMENTARY CHANGES.
text: Shipping agents are finding it difficult to explain to their clients why charges for legalisation of documents are heavy for goods consigned to Lisbon, Oporto, Madeira, and Portuguese Africa. These charges add to the prices which are eventually paid by consumers at final destinations before taking into consideration the import duties which must be paid at ports of discharge. To legalise invoices, etc., at the consular office concerned in Liverpool, for instance, a fee is charged equivalent to 4 per cent. of the invoice value of the goods. In the case of consignments valued at less than £25 a minimum fee is charged amounting to anything from 4 per cent. to 6 per cent. Shipments to Spain are treated at their Consular offices quite differently, as a standard fee of considerably less than ten shillings is fixed for legalisation of documents on goods consigned to Spain, Canary Islands, Spanish Morocco, etc., irrespective of the value of the goods. The increase in the case of Portugal (from one half per cent. to 1 per cent. and then to 4 per cent.) has been brought about during the last two years, and amounts to a serious burden on trade. Compared with the above figures freight and insurance charges are comparatively low, being.50s,.per freight ton to Lisbon (less 5s. for carpets) and.30s. to Madeira for freight, and about 12s. 6d. per cent. for insurance effected on textiles with full cover.

headline: RESTRICTION
text:
"In influential quarters it is held that the time has come for the removal of restrictions on rubber output. There is a keen public interest in the subject in these days of universal motors and the innumerable other manufactures in which rubber is used. No man is better qualified to lead the discussion than Sir George Beharrell, managing director of the Dunlop Rubber Company, who raises vital questions," says the "Daily News," and in an article published in that newspaper Sir George Beharrell forcibly states

With stocks short and supplies, in part, artificially controlled, the position is dangerous to any manufacturer who would attempt to visualise a programme of manufacture some time ahead. Moreover, it is comparatively easy to restrict rubber supplies, but it is rather more difficult to bring about a reverse operation, as the provision of additional rubber requires, say, seven years of preparation.

It is not unreasonable to assume that to meet some sudden development large supplies of rubber might be needed in the near future, but that on account of the policy pursued in the last few years adequate supplies would not be forthcoming. Hence substitutes would perforce be found, and consumption of rubber suffer a serious set-back.

"No one will deny that there is slowly increasing demand for rubber. Many countries which before the war were large consumers are beginning to re-enter the world's markets. With their currencies on a more stable basis they are striving their utmost to increase their foreign trade."

Against this, we find a very considerable reduction in stocks. It may perhaps be urged in defence of this policy that the demand is

America, which is the largest user of rubber in the world and therefore the chief sufferer, may perhaps some day decide upon a course which will eventually leave those who at present control our rubber policy plenty of spare time in which to regret their action.

headline: COMMERCE / LAND SLUMP
text:
A recent remarkable full of land prices in suburbs of Tokyo has taken pluco, and has occasioned much worry to the real estate companies which, through propaganda and manipulation in past years have artificially raised the prices for land. The high cost of living and the shortage of dwelling houses in the city limits of Tokyo in recent years has caused a rapid development of adjoining rural districts of Tokyo and farms and forests were sold in many places for residential quarters. Many real estate companies, "such as the Hackone Land and Building Company and Tokyo Land Tenement House Company, purchased large tracts of land in suburbs at cheap prices and sold them to those who intended to live in the "suburban districts. This tendency was the more remarkable after the great earthquake and fire of 1923, when people who lost their dwellings sought refuge in the suburbs, and the residential quarters were expanded with great rapidity. More than 150,000 houses are reported to have been built in these few years in Tokyo's suburbs, most of which were erected after the earthquake and fire. The purchase of large jobs of land and the erection of tenentent houses were undertaken by these real estate companies through speculation in anticipation that Tokyo's resident land quarters would be entirely removed to suburbs.

When the boom broke, the firms raised the land prices through artificial measures and mining people were induced to purchase land at high prices. A set-back started last year in economic circles and this caused active sales in houses and lands in city limits of Tokyo. Good lots of land were sold at cheaper prices. This has told severely upon the business of these land companies who intended to reap profit in the sales of suburban lands and there are few persons seeking to buy land in suburbs under the prevailing high prices. Consequently, these companies are now in an awkward position financially as no sales of suburb lands are being made at present. At the same time the land prices are falling precipitously not only in Tokyo city but also in the suburbs and the actual land prices for transaction are 60 per cent, cheaper than those named by these real estate firms. Even in Shibuya, Meguro, Kahata, Yodobushi, Tsebukuro, Mejiro, and other adjoining towns which are comparatively convenient in point of transportation and cheaper in daily living, land prices are very low and at almost half of the price which prevailed right after the September

Authorities on German finance writing in the European financial Press have lately been indulging in much speculation as to how last year's 2,700,000,000 marks excess of imports has been paid for. It is pointed out that the report of the Reichsbank for 1924 refers to the success of its credit restriction policy, which compelled persons who need to cash to realise on their commodities and their hoards of exchange. It has been semi-officially stated that at least 700 million marks' worth of foreign banknotes went abroad last year as a result of the Reichsbank policy, and that 1,800 million marks in foreign bills had also to be melted. These, together with the foreign loans and credits, variously estimated at from 1,400 millions to 2,000 millions, created a fund from 4,000 to 4,500 million marks, so that, after providing for the payment of the excess of imports, there remained a large balance with which gold and exchange for the Reichsbank were acquired. The Darmstaedter and National Bank, in the report for 1924, refers to this subject as follows:—

The balance of foreign payments for the year 1924 is extremely unfavourable; and shows an excess of imports over exports of 2,750,000,000 marks. It is true that the conversion, in connection with the stabilisation of our currency, of sums held abroad or at home in foreign currency has helped us to counteract the effect of this deficit, and we have even been able by the help of the credits granted from abroad, after the issue of the Dawes loan, greatly to increase our holdings of foreign exchange. But this cannot deceive us with regard to the seriousness of the situation created by our taking up some 2,000,000,000 gold marks as short-term foreign credits in 1924. headline: MANY YÁCANT NOW.
text: According to the latest investigation made by the Tokyo Prefectural Government, vacant houses are increasing daily in Tokyo suburbs and there are now 75,000 such houses throughout the suburban districts of Tokyo. The Dojinkai, an organisation for tenement houses under subsidy of the Tokyo prefectural authorities recently erected 4,000 houses in the suburbs and more than 3,000 of these houses are left vacant despite the cheap rentals. The authorities concerned are now discussing measures to fill these vacant houses.

headline: AND FINANCE. / SHIPBUILDING / THE GERMAN YARDS:
text:
Some interesting details concerning the Deutsche Werft, the German shipyard which secured the much-discussed contract for the Furness With ships, are given in a message from the "M.G.C." correspondent at Berlin. The concern was founded in 1918 from very important German industrial groups—namely, the Gute Hoffnungshuttle, the A.E.G., and the Hamburg-Amerika Line. During the last year of the war and the following year the company built large shipyards on the Elbe and installed by far the most modern equipment in Germany. By its close connection with its associated organisations the company is not only able to work at low costs by effecting economies at every point in the complex process of production, but is in a position to make use of very important patents. For steam engines the Deutsche Werft have at their disposal the patents of the Gute Hoffnungschutte, for steam turbines the patents of the A.E.G., while for Diesel engines they are the German licensees of Burmeister and Wain, Copenhagen. Actually the yard was constructed and equipped during the depreciation period and, amongst others, this factor has contributed a good deal to low construction costs. The gold mark balance sheet has not been published yet, but the following assets in the balance sheet drawn up at December 31, 1923, may be noted. The figures are given in billion marks, and we may take one billion marks as equal to one gold mark.
Machines and equipment3,913,875
Stocks733,256
Cash in hand and with
The paid-up capital amounted to 60 million paper marks and debentures issued in 1920 to the extent of 30 million paper marks are outstanding. At the end of 1923 the company was employing some 7,000 people. Important as the advantages of being constructed when the mark was on its downward course are, more important in the competitive power of the Deutsche Werft is its close inter-relations with other industries and its modern equipment. The British yards may not be able to make such an imposing showing in their inter-relation with feeding industries, but in technique and traditional skill this country still holds the lead. In the long run price will prove the ruling factor in the acceptance of shipbuilding tenders, but, as Mr. Lawrence Holt points out in a letter to the "Liverpool Post and Mercury," those who are ready to pay 10 per cent. more for a ship built in one of our good yards are probably wise in their generation. Mr. Holt has just returned from a visit to ten shipyards on the Continent, and the reasons he gives for the ability of Germany to build cheaper ships than our own yards are lower wages, universality of piecework, longer hours, no restriction on the use of labour-saving machines, no demarcation obstacles between trades, no redundant labour, and keener work by management and workers. In the light of these observations of a prominent shipowner there hardly seems an unanswerable case for the artificial stimulation of our shipbuilding industry by means of a subsidy, which would tend to remove an effective incentive towards the reorganisation of our yards and the modernisation of their plant.

headline: LESS FISH EATEN.
text:
That people are.eating less fish is a race disclosed by a five-years' review of the sea fisheries issued by the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries.

According to the report the average yearly consumption per head fell from 41½ lbs. for the period 1907-1910 to 88½ lbs. in 1920-1923. "It is clean," adds the report, "that fish as presented to the consumer is not sufficiently attractive to be given a permanent position as a principal item in the menu; and that if the home market is to expand it is essential to educate the consumers to the dietetic value of good fresh fish, and at the same time ensure that supplies of such fish, at prices which will enable it to compete with all classes of meat are continuously available."

There are mystery, thrills and suspense in abundance in "Red Lights," which opened a four days engagement at the World Theatre yesterday. It would be unfair to those who see the picture later to give the plot in detail, but it is a story of a young girl, Ruth Carson, the abducted daughter of a railroad maguate, whose identity is at last discovered. This discovery begins a series of strange and mysterious warnings of imminent death. Her lover, John Blake, calls on his friend, the crime deflector to protect the girl. Passage is engaged to Chicago on the Continent, at Limited but the mysterious warnings and strange happenings (including a murder, the baffling appearance of balls of red light in the car) continue to take place. The story comes to a climax when the rear car of the Limited is uncoupled from the train while it is going up a steep grade over the mountains and dashes madly down hill towards the second section of the train. Catastrophe is averted only because the switch is turned and the rear car is shunted off on a blind siding. Here the mysteries are solved and the villains punished. "It is an annoying portrait," said the angry father. "You have not done my daughter justice." "Sir," said the artist, "it is not justice she needs, but mercy."

headline: TITN FINANOIER'S DEATH
text:
The mining industry in both Cornwall and Nigeria has lost an ardent supporter by the death, after a long illness, of Mr. Oliver Wetliered, whose appointments included the chairmanship of the Cornish Chamber of Mines, and the deputy-chairmanship of the Nigerian Chamber of Mines. He was also chairman of the Dolcoath, Geevor, and Rayfield companies. "It was through Mr. Wethered that outside capital was found for the old Dolcoath tin mine, Cornwall, when it became a limited liability concern in 1805. That new capital gave the mine a fresh lease of life, during which it paid numerous dividends."

The Geevor mine, which was being worked on a very small scale when it was taken over and financed by Mr. Wethered, is now producing at the rate of over 500 tons black tin per annum.

Capital was also found by Mr. Wethered for a number of Nigerian tin-mining undertakings.

headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE. / LONDON'S MEAT BILL
text: Interesting details about London's annual meat bill, which, as shown by supplies to the Central Markets, reached a value £36,500,000 last year, are contained in the report for 1924 of the clerk and superintendent of the Smithfield Markets, Mr. H. G. W. Millman. Last year was a record for the markets, the total supplies (including poultry and provisions) amounting to 480,520 tons, which exceeded anything hitherto reached in the previous fifty-six years' history of the market. It is estimated that the live stock killed to furnish this food consisted of:

parent_headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE. / LONDON'S MEAT BILL
text: The total value of all commodities of £36,500,000 was in excess of the figure for the previous year by £1,500,000; this being attributed to the increase in supplies and the wholesale values of all classes of produce, except fresh-killed mutton and pork. One fact which emerges is that London's taste for mutton is decreasing at the expense of beef. Of the total supplies beef formed 55.2 per cent, mutton 27.8, and pork and bacon 10.5. In 1913 the ratio of mutton to beef was 3.9 per cent. higher.

headline: LESS BRITISH PRODUCE. / EIGHTY PER CENT FROM ARROAD
text:
How dependent the people of London, say 8,000,000 consumers, are upon the Central Markets for their meat was shown by the quantity distributed through the markets during the year—a quantity sufficient to provide each week a mixed-ration of beef, mutton, and pork of 38.7oz per head, viz., beef 22.9 oz, mutton 11.5oz, and pork 4.3oz; and how not only the public but meat traders rely upon overseas sources of supply, Colonial and foreign, was further shown by the fact that of the 38.7oz, the quantity of British-bred meats marketed was just sufficient to form 7.5oz per head, viz., beef 3.9 oz, mutton 2oz, and pork 1.6oz weekly. The value of the weekly list of retail prices, the issue of which was commenced last November, is commented upon. The list (states the superintendent) forms a price indicator, not only for London, but other parts of the country. It only embraces best quality meats—ewe mutton is not included—and if the people pay more, then they either lack the shopping or marketing sense, are indifferent, or require extra services which justify the retailer charging higher prices. Sections of the retail trade, who were critical, now help in a task which is generally conceded to be in the interests of all sections of the public from producer to consumer. The issue of the retail list should continue, for it affords the public information, and any appreciable fall in wholesale values, or rise, as the case may be, can be adjusted weekly in favour of or against the bearer of all charges—the consumer. The average of the wholesale prices of Scotch sides of beef during 1924 was about 19.2 per cent above the average prices of other classes of fresh killed beef. Scotch and English mutton prices were lower than the year before, with the advantage in favour of the former, and realised 13.4 per cent higher values than other fresh mutton supplies—mostly Dutch, 72.3 per cent more than New Zealand mutton, and 100 per cent more than mutton from Australia and Argentina. Scotch and English lamb prices for 1924 were somewhat in favour of the home country. Chilled and frozen meat supplies from all sources totalled 317,994 tons. Of the total imports—900,808 tons—of beef, mutton, and lamb into the United Kingdom during the year 36.3 per cent. passed through the market for distribution, this being an increase of 1.2 per cent on 1923.

headline: LONDON ASSURANCE. / MARINE INSURANCE RESULTS.
text:
The earlier underwriting accounts of the year gave, it seems, a pretty good index of the state of affairs in marine insurance. The others are merely following on the same track. Of those published in the last week or two the London Assurance, it is true, transfers to profit an amount of £64,000, of which under £40,000 was earned in interest on funds. But that leaves in reserve only £1,000,000, against premiums last year totalling £1,122,000. The premium income of the London Assurance is particularly high, since before the war the annual premiums amounted only to around £400,000.

None of the other companies is so ambitious either as regards premiums or transfers to profit. The Alliance Assurance have put their interest receipts of £45,000 to profit, and on a premium income last year of £510,000 find their reserve a little less than at the end of 1923 at £1,008,000. The Royal Exchange Assurance are keeping their interest receipts in the underwriting account, and even so, on an increased premium income of £635,500, have only managed to increase their reserve by £40,000. It now stands at £792,000. The Phoenix Assurance is another company writing over £1,000,000 in premiums. The account is remarkable for the depletion of the reserve by over £400,000, notwithstanding that the first-year claims settlements for 1924 are rather lower than the average. The claims settled for previous years, totalling nearly £900,000, are very high, and, it would seem, another such year would seriously disturb the account.

headline: FIRST DIVDEND SINCE 1912.
text:
After going dividendless since August 1912, holders of the 6 percent. Cumulative Preference shares of the La Plata Electric Tramways are at last to receive a small return on their investment, the company now announcing the payment of 3 per cent.

In December 1919 the Debenture stockholders agreed to a postponement of the payment of £10,421, representing interest outstanding on January 1, 1920, until January 1, 1923, and Deferred Interest warrants were issued in respect of this amount.

Those warrants were paid off at their due date, thus paving the way for a resumption of Preference dividends.

headline: NEW ZEALAND. / THE LANCASHIRE COTTON
text: It is interesting to learn that Mr. Elmsille, H.M. Trade Commissioner in New Zealand, considers that the Lancashire cotton trade is doing as well as ever it did so far as New Zealand is concerned, and, in fact, is showing gradual signs of development. He avers that the enthusiasm for British goods is such that purchasers will give up to 20 per cent more in order to obtain British-made in preference to foreign products. America and Japan, it is true, are doing their utmost to exploit the market, but Mr. Elmsille believes they are not making any headway, and in the matter of motor-cars and agricultural and dairying machinery in particular there is still considerable scope for the exporter in Great Britain.

headline: BRITISH SOAP.
text:
Not only is the soap consumed in the United Kingdom lower in price and higher in quality than that of any other country, but as a natural result the United Kingdom enjoys a larger export trade in soap to neutral markets of the world that of the total exports of soap of any other three nations added together," said Lord Leverhulme at the annual meeting of Lever Brothers.

Speaking of the present high taxation of Great Britain, he said that against this inequality the British taxpayer gained the advantage of the high standard of exchange. British credit had been maintained, and of the two evils high taxation or low rate of exchange we had chosen wisely in preferring high taxation. But, all the same, he added, British trade and commerce were staggering under this heavy burden.

headline: THE PHILIPPINES
text:
The overseas trade of the Philippines for April, 1925, showed an increase of more than P5,000,000 over the trade for the corresponding month in 1924, the figures being P43,143,944 and P38,078,333, respectively, according to a complete compilation of trade accounts made public by the statistical division of the bureau of customs. The balance of trade was in favour of the Philippines by more than P11,000,000, according to the report, the exports of the country for April, 1925, amounting to P27,197,764 as against P15,946,176 worth of imports during the same period.

The United States as usual obtained the lion's share of the Philippine trade for the month under review, the import and export trade with that country amounting to P29,425,893, or more than half the total. Of this sum, P20,906,862 represented the value of Philippine products that went to the United States during that month and the rest, imports from that country into the Philippines.

With Great Britain, the Philippines overseas trade for April, 1925, was valued at P2,902,877, of which P1,916,829 represented the value of exports. Trade with China went over the two-million peso mark, but the Philippine exports for last month amounted to only a little over P500,000. The same was true of the export trade with Japan, the products sent to that country amounting to over P800,000 which was less than the imports from the island empire. The total trade with Japan for April, 1925, was P2,145,775.

headline: ANGLO-PERSIAN IN TH2
text: Sir Charles Greenway, who has recently returned from Buenos Aires, is reported to have said that he was greatly impressed with the markable progress of that country, but was disappointed by the attitude adopted by the Argentine Government towards foreign capital engaged in the oil fields. The trouble is that some of the lands in the Comodoro Rivadavia field which the Anglo-Persian had acquired, and on which a producing well had been brought in have been included within the limits of the enlarged national oil reserve formed by the Argentine Government. The claims of the Anglo-Persian, which would appear to be strong, have been ignored. The Argentine Government has committed itself to a policy of intensive oil development by the State. The Budget for 1925 includes an appropriation for an increased drilling campaign the construction of further storage tanks, and the purchase of another tank steamship. On its oil operations in 1924 the Government claims to have made a surplus of three million pesos. This has probably counted against Sir Charles Greenway.

headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE. / UNEMPLOYMENT / MATTER
text: And furthermore, it is equally important to realise that at the present time unemployment is largely a problem of a few special industries—coal mining and the so-called construction industries in particular. It the figures of unemployment in these special industries are deducted from the general total and allowance made for the 400,000 unemployable, there remains a figure which is not greatly above the normal. Here, again, this consideration does not detract in the least from the importance of the general problem, but it should lead us to see in a truer perspective. The truth is that just as people were too optimistic a year or two ago, there is a danger that at the present time they may fall into the opposite error. In a country such as our own quick recovery after the effort of the last ten years is not to be expected—and it is in just those industries which were most affected by that effort that unemployment is now abnormal. Let us keep this steadily in mind when we come to consider emergency measures.

"Cash on delivery" seems to be coming at last. It may mean much to British agriculture or very little, according to the scale of charges. England differs from most others in not having to seek any export market for its agricultural produce. In consequence, there is no sufficient incentive to co-operation among farmers for the purpose of marketing, which abroad includes the organisation of transport. Here, every farmer likes to sell independently if he can; preferably at the neighbouring market town. His stuff goes to the big cities, through the hands of a host of middlemen, which accounts for the much advertised disparity between what the producer gets and the consumer pays. At the same time a large trade is done direct, especially by small-holders, who contrive to deliver small consignments of butter, eggs, etc., to their personal acquaintances in town, on credit. This trade is severely restricted by the high rates of the parcels post. Cash on delivery might stimulate small-holdings enormously, but only if the rates are considerably reduced.

headline: THIRD-CLASS LINERS.
text: The White Star Line has placed its third-class steamer Vedic on the Australian run and it remains to be seen how well she will succeed. After the war there was quite a boom in steamers carrying third-class passengers only, in anticipation of a big increase in the emigrant trade, but the Dillingham Restriction Act in the United States put an end to most of these hopes, and most third-class travellers prefer to travel in a three-class ship whose name is a "household word." That was on the North Atlantic; it remains to be seen whether the same feeling holds in the Australian trade or whether the very concrete advantage of having the whole ship to themselves will outweigh this purely psychological consideration in the minds of the travellers. The Atlantic Transport Line, it will be remembered, has over come the difficulty by transforming its big third-class ship into a tourist vessel at reasonable prices and looks like risking a success of it; but such a tourist trade could not be hoped for to Abuatu

headline: SHIPBUILDING PRICES
text: With regard to the statement in the House of Commons recently that shipbuilding material has been sold by British works to Continental shipbuilders at 30s. per ton below the price ruling at home, the Press Association has authority from the British works in question to state that the actual difference in the price was merely 2s. 9d. per ton between the price delivered to the Dutch shipyard (which is on the coast and in a position to take the material free alongside yard) and the price delivered to shipbuilders on the north-east, const. The British quotation for these ships was stated to be £12,000 per ship above the Dutch. The tonnage of plates and sections in each ship is about 3,000. Thus the difference in the cost of the plates and sections accounts for only £412 per ship against the £12,000 above referred to. It will be remembered in connection with the ships recently placed by the Furness Company with a German shipbuilding concern that the difference between the British price per ship and the German was -tated by Sir Frederick Lewis to be no less than £60,000. These were similar sized bonds to the above. Consequently, if the plates and sections had been delivered free of charge this would not have bridged one-half the difference. It is not to the manufacturer of plates and sections that shipbuilders should look for relief in costs. Slopbuilders would be the first to admit that the prices of steel plates and sections, which are now at about 30 per cent, above pre-war prices, are cheaper in comparison than any other substantial item in their present costs.

headline: KRAMERY
text: The Maypole. Dairy repout for the year 1924 is a disappointing one. At £218,341, the net profit is less than half last year's £439,793, which, in turn, was some £34,000 lower than that for 1922. The result is that the holders of the 21,583,000 deferred shares of 2s. each receive no dividend, whereas for 1923 an interim dividend of 3d. per share was paid on the deferred capital. In that year, however, the Board found it necessary to provide out of the reserve a sum of £250,000, or very nearly the amount paid in deferred dividend, to write off losses incurred in the West African business, so that if the fact be taken into account that last year no such draft was necessary the comparison with the previous period becomes somewhat less unfavourable. Out of the present profits £10,000 is, in fact, placed to reserve and £10,000 to income tax reserve, as against only one appropriation of £10,000 last year, and after providing for the preference and preferred ordinary dividends there remains £137,387 to be carried forward, as against £49,576 brought in. The cash position is not a very strong one, but the directors say that during the second half of last year trading showed considerable improvement, and that they have every reason to anticipate a return to more normal conditions, in the current year.

headline: BLUE / RECKITTS 250,000) FOR EMPLOYEES
text: The shareholders of Rockitt and Sons, of Hull, who are manufacturers of starch, etc., approved of £80,000 being distributed among the employees as a prosperity bonus. This works out at 1s. 6d in the pound on salaries and wages, plus an extra allowance according to the number of years' service. The shares in the appropriation—which is £25,000 larger than that made a year ago—are 5,000 persons in Hull and 1,000 elsewhere. The meeting also agreed to a final dividend of 1s. 9d. per share on the ordinary, making 4s., or 20 per cent., for the year, as against 171 per cent. for 1923. The report stated that the sales of the company's products continued to expand, and last year's profits were the largest it had ever made. It was decided to transfer £282,532 to the reserve, making that fund £1,500,000, and £248,080 was carried forward.

The Board of Trade's import and export returns for March make cotton manufacturing and the production of machinery appear to be highly prosperous industries. That, however, is only because the comparisons are with the trade done in a time of great depression. Cotton yarns and manufactures total nearly £10 millions, which is an increase of £3,108,000 on the corresponding month of 1924 and £4,426,000 on 1923. Three things have to be remembered, however—the first that the Egyptian cotton was about 1s.6d. per pound dearer during part of the month, although American was about 3d. per pound cheaper, the second that a large part of the exports represented orders received before Christmas, when trade was better, and the third that, even with the aid of these old orders, the mills spinning American cotton were as to rule only running 35 hours a week, where they were running at all, large numbers of operatives being on the dole. Proportionately, the machinery trade's figures look better still, with an increase of £954,000, the total being £4,172,000, but if we turn to the 1021 returns we find that the corresponding amount then was nearly £7,300,000. The coal trade, on the other hand, shows a decline of £1,883,000 from 1924 and £4,261,000 from 1923, the comparison being with a time when the French occupation of the Ruhr had caused the dislocation of the coal industry there. Last month Germany only received from the United Kingdom 336,000 tons, or barely more than half the amount last year, and little more than one-sixth of that in 1923. French demand has also fallen off materially, though not so stiffly as German.

Mr. Briggs, retiring president of the Manchester Wholesale Provision Association, suggests that the Government compel all imported butter to be packed in 56lb. boxes, instead of in tubs.

He points out that, until recently, Continental butter fetched 8d, a lb. more than New Zealand's best, though there was no differences in value, and says that traders explain the difference in price as due solely to the women of certain districts, who do not believe they are getting their money's worth unless they see the butter ladled out of tubs, and always think the best butter comes in tubs. It is impossible to change these old-established habits.

Mr. Briggs adds that New Zealand cannot ship butter in tubs owing to freight charges and the difficulties of stowing.

headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE
text:
HELP FOR RUHR PRODUCERS

A blow aimed at the British coal industry, which has been threatening for some time, has fallen at last. It is officially announced today that the German railways have finally decided to reduce the tariff on all coal transported from German mines to German ports. Shipments to Hamburg are to enjoy a reduction of 30 per cent. of the present tariff, shipments to Bremen 15 per cent, and Shipments to Emden 12 per cent.

headline: RUHR OUTPUT.
text:
All these ports and other North Sea ports receive the Ruhr output. Correspondingly proportional reductions will be made on shipments to Baltic ports from the Silesian mines.

This measure is merely the final move in a great scheme, which has been long on the horizon, to create gigantic trust, embracing the coal, iron, steel and shipbuilding industries; and protecting them from foreign competition, especially English competition.

Similar tariff reductions are already operative for iron, steel, and shipbuilding parts from German factories to the yards.

The tariff reduction on Ruhr cost is obviously directed at British coal, which hitherto came within the radius of most German North Sea ports, on account of the cheaper transport by sea. The Germans will now be able to extend their radius in order to exclude the English market.

A result of the agreement reached recently is that practically all the Ruhr mines are now syndicated so as to be able to control their prices according to the price of foreign coal.

headline: A LARGE RETURN
text: The Birmingham Small Arms Company further improved its position in the financial year which ended in January last, and, for the first times since 1921, the directors are able to recommend a dividend on the ordinary shares. The rate proposed is 5 per cent. less tax—the same as that for the eighteen months to January, 1921, except that the latter was free of tax. The profit reported now is £305,320, and, with £131,027 brought forward, there is £435,347 available. Interest at 6½ per cent. on the 12-year notes for £2,500,000 issued in 1920 and the preference and ordinary dividends will apparently require an aggregate of £250,200, and £177,147—an increase of $46,000—will be carried forward. For 1923-24 notes interest absorbed £125,260, and the preference dividend (which has been paid continuously during the depression) £24,044.

headline: CANADIAN TRADE / SOME INTERESTING ITEMS.
text: A considerable quantity of alfalfa seed produced in Algeria last year was sold to United States dealers, indicating the demand for northern grown seed. It is estimated that over a quarter of a million pounds were sold altogether. Algeria seed growers also sold 100,000 pounds of Timothy seed.

headline: ST. JOHN'S NEW FOUND LAND.
text: The sensor's kill of the Newfoundland sealing fleet amounted to approximately 127,000 seals, which is considered fair in comparison with other years. Tenvessels were engaged in the hunt this year. One vessel was destroyed and this tended to lower the combined catch of the fleet.

headline: OTTAWA, ONTARIO.
text:
Civil aviation in Canada has developed rapidly in the past two years. Actual flying time increased from 188,008 hours in 1923 to 294,778 hours in 1924, according to the report on civil aviation which has just been issued by the Department of National Defence. More than 9,000 persons were carried in aircraft in Canada last year, while in the previous year there were 5,324 persons carried. Exclusive of the Royal Canadian Air Force, 32 licences were issued for aircraft operation, while the total licensed personnel qualified to take part in civil flying was 201

Canada's exports of non-ferrous metals have risen from a value of $42,000,000 in the twelve months ending February 28, 1923, to $88,000,000 in the year ending February 28, 1925, according to a report published by the Department of Mines. Gold finds in northern Ontario account for a large proportion of this increase, and the new finds this spring indicate that it will not be long before Canada is mining more gold in a year than the United States.

Approximately 2,000,000 motor vehicles entered Canada during 1924, as compared with 1,250,000 in 1923, according to a report issued by the Canadian Parks Branch of the Federal Government. The increase in cars entered for a period longer than one day during 1924 was 32 per cent of the 1923 entries and 105 per cent of the 1922 entries.

Egg exports from Alberta increased 33 per cent during 1923, compared with the year previous, according to a report of the Provincial Department of Agriculture. Three years ago Alberta was almost entirely an importing province with respect to eggs, but last year it exported more than 60,000 cases, or 133 carloads.

headline: MONTREAL, QUEBEC.
text:
Shipments and manufactures of paper from Canada during the year ended March 31, 1925, amounted in value to $90,041,910, an increase of about $3,000,000 over the year previous, according to Government reports. The United States was, the heaviest buyer, accounting for approximately 80 per cent of the total exports. The United Kingdom also purchased large quantities of Canadian paper, while smaller shipments were dispatched to countries in all parts of the world.

According to Canadian official returns, the exports of live cattle to Britain during 1924 amounted to 79,435 head, as compared with 56,672 head in 1923. Exports to the United States were 97,847 cattle, 35,178 calves and 18,745 sheep, as compared with 96,873 cattle, 24,074 calves and 28,748 sheep in 1923.

headline: THE SHIPBUILDING POSITION.
text:
The influence which is being exerted by the oil engine on the shipbuilding industry throughout the world is strikingly illustrated in an analysis published by "The Motor Ship." The countries in which an improvement in shipbuilding is shown, compared with a year ago, are those where motor ship construction is proceeding proportionately more rapidly than elsewhere. In the United Kingdom the tonnage of ships now being built is 300,000 less than in April, 1924, and the percentage of motor ships to steamers is 45. In Germany, Holland, Italy, Denmark and Sweden more work is in progress than was the case a year ago, and in these countries collectively 75 per cent. of the vessels now being constructed are to be equipped with oil engines.

It is, however, satisfactory to add that the largest marine Diesel engine yet built has just been completed in Harland and Wolff's Belfast works. This is a 10,000 h.p. unit and is one of two sets for installation in the Royal Mail Steam Packet Co's 22,000-ton passenger liner "Asturias".

headline: COMMERCE AND / HALL & HOLTZ
text:
HANGHAI FIRM'S POSITION.

The interest taken in the meeting of Hall & Holtz, Ltd., is evidenced by the fact that just under twenty thousand shares out of a total of 26,000 shares were represented by those in attendance, and it may be stated in this connection that the list of shareholders in this company is a very extended one.

The balance sheet presented to the meeting, signed by Mr. E Barraclough, secretary and accountant, and Messrs. Seth Mancell and McLure, auditors, showed a debit balance at profit and loss of $8,781.32, debentures outstanding of something under three hundred thousand dollars, and over half a million due to the Hongkong & Shanghai Bank. On the asset side land and buildings were listed at over eight hundred thousand dollars and stock in hand was listed at more than six hundred thousand. The sundry debtors account stands at over a hundred thousand.

The following are the main points in the address to the assembled shareholders made by the Chairman, Mr. L. W. Hutton:

headline: INCREASED TURNOVER.
text:
The turnover on the year's working, notwithstanding, a discount of $10 per cent. for cash purchases and a discount of 10% to shareholders was increased by over $88,000—whilst the overdraft which last year stood at $740,902 stood at $563,254 at the end of the year. Leaving out the amount realised by the sale of the Soochow Road property this meant a reduction during the past year of $82,643. The overdraft to day stood at $481,685, showing a still further reduction. The directors consider this is highly satisfactory, especially as during the past three months such reduction had been the result of purely normal trading, without resort to cheap sales or the sacrificing of stock. This reduction in overdraft meant a considerable saving in bank interest.

Expense account showed a decrease of $18,500,—sundry creditors showed a small increase, but bills payable showed a decrease of over $5,000, and yet were substantially represented by goods in transit, (over $10,000).

All ascertainable liabilities had been taken into consideration in the accounts. Depreciation had been amply provided for, on all permanent assets, that on buildings having been written off against Property Reserve. Doubtless due to the 10% being allowed off cash purchases, Sundry debtors showed a substantial reduction, nearly $27,000 as compared with last year. With regard to stock on hand, this showed a decrease of close upon $100,000, and at least so far as the head office is concerned, stocks were clean and represented a fair value.

Considerable difficulty was experienced with the bakery department during the year but by alterations in the staff, a great saving in cost of production had been made. At the end of January, upon expiration of his agreement, the secretary Mr. G. H. Bartlett tendered his resignation, which had been accepted with regret, Mr. Barraclough, the accountant, had been appointed to the dual position of secretary and accountant, which appointment meant a saving to the company financially. More efficient service was obtained through combining the two positions.

headline: MR. CUMINE'S CRITICISMS
text:
Mr. H. M. Curnine in rather extended remarks, criticized the accounts from the point of view that they did not give the shareholders an idea of how the losses were being incurred—for instance was it worth while continuing the outport branches? As regards Shanghai, the Company had premises at the corner of the two busiest and most important thoroughfares in Shanghai, and yet the Company would not have been able to pay rent on the premises they occupy if they had to pay rent for them, instead of owning them.

Mr. Cumine then remarked that the statement of the profit and loss account showing a loss of $8,781.32 did not disclose the real situation. For one thing, the credit balance of last year of $7,894.02 had disappeared. Therefore, that meant that it had to be included in the losses. As regards the book value of the land, this had been raised by $263,690.63, taking advantage of the figures in the recent reassessment. Practically this same amount had been set down as a general reserve fund and from this $100,401.63 had been deducted as an amount written off stock, although the then Chairman at the meeting last year had stated that the value of the stock in hand was considerably below cost. This was a matter, said Mr. Cumine, which required further explanation. The actual loss for the year, Mr. Cumine contended, was really $117,077.87.

This is more than 20 per cent of our capital," exclaimed Mr. Cumine. "We cannot afford to allow this to continue. We have not been earning anything for many years. Our capital is dead to us. It is high time to save the founding ship."

Mr. Moller, the Chairman last year, said he agreed with some of Mr. Cumine's remarks, but he was not in favor of a suggestion made by Mr. Cumine that a committee of investigation should be appointed. He felt sure that the directors would only be too glad to give any shareholder every facility to inspect the accounts and would welcome suggestions. Mr. Hutton remarked that that was certainly the case. Mr. Cumine then proposed a resolution that the accounts be not accepted, and the meeting to be adjourned, the eventual idea being to convene an extraordinary meeting at which a committee of three or five shareholders to investigate the accounts and take suggestions should be appointed. As previously mentioned this was lost on a show of hands and also on a poll.
The accounts were then formally passed, Mr. W.S. King was re-elected a director, and Messrs. Seth, Mancel and Mc-Eure were appointed additors.
The Chairman in ringing the meeting to a close citerated that directors were always glad to give facilities to shareholders to inspect the accounts and invited suggestions.

headline: BANK SHARES.
text: In a letter to the “Times” on the question of the nationalisation of banking, which is again being urged in certain quarters, Mr. Walter Runciman gave figures showing how widely banking shares are held by investors in Britain. The paid-up capital of the “Big Five” English banks is £60½ million, and there are no less than 275,400 shareholders, giving an average no-final shareholding of only £219 5s. These figures are a strong argument against the agitation for handing over the business of banking in Britain to the State. The revival of the discussion of this topic has had no effect whatever upon the market prices of banking shares, which during the recent uncertainty in markets have remained remarkably steady. The shares of the Midland Bank, for example, stand at a figure which gives a yield of just under 5 per cent., and although this is a special case, since rights attach to the shares for subscription to a new issue below market price, the quotations for the shares of the four other large banks are such that the yields obtainable are relatively low. Possibly the reason is that higher dividends are anticipated for the current year. It is certainly highly improbable that dividends will be reduced, and if the volume of loans and advances continues to expand at its present rate and conditions in the money market remain favourable, an expansion in banking profits will no doubt be shown at the end of the year.

headline: WEEKS AND CO.
text:
Speaking at the meeting of Weeks and Co., Ltd., the Chairman, Mr. T. E. Trudman expressed regret that the year's working had again resulted in loss. Conditions of trade similar to those in the preceding year had again prevailed, and while the gross gain on the turnover was practically the same, they had to reduce selling prices in many instances to a very low margin to move the stock. Added to this, they had to face the writing down of a lot of stock in the Hankow branch which had been accumulated by the recent manager. The cause for writing down was not that the stocks has deteriorated or was in any way bad; in the contrary the bulk was of excellent quality and in perfect condition, but it had to be brought down to present day valuation and below, in order to enable the company to reduce the quantity to a normal figure. The action thus taken would place the Hankow branch in a position to sell at keenly cut prices. In Shanghai stocks are in excellent condition and stood at present day market value.

The trade working expenses, Mr. Trueman explained, were less than for the preceding year due in the main to the smaller charge for interest, by the gradual reduction of the overdraft—a satisfactory feature. Interest charges were a heavy item and this was due of course to the fact that the trading capital had only been increased by $36,410 since 1903, (the other $200,000 having been used entirely in the purchase of their property), while the turnover had increased by 150 per cent. and the stock had increased proportionately. This meant that interest was being paid to the Bank instead of dividends to the shareholders as would have been the case if the company had adequate capital.

All assets, said Mr. Trueman, appear in the balance sheet at much below their intrinsic or market value.

The 1924 assessed value of the Shanghai land was nearly Tls. 120,000.00 (Tls: 119,785.66) more than book value of the land building.

The Bank overdraft was $33,705.67 less than last year and $93,778.04 less than the combined overdraft and debentures in 1923, while sundry creditors stood at $1,185.18 more.

Mr. Trueman then referred to a letter from a Shareholder which asked the directors to give the shareholders some indication as to the future prospects of the company. "Shareholders need have no fear as to the financial stability of the company," said Mr. Trueman. "From the balance sheet you will see stocks in Shanghai and Hankow more than balance the bank overdraft while assessed value of the land without buildings more than covers the share issue by almost a lack of dollars."

headline: POOR DIVIDEND PROSPECTS
text: The disconcerting part is the fact that we have paid no dividends for the past two years. This apart from trade depression is in fact due, as I have already mentioned, to interest going to the Bank in lieu of to shareholders, due to our inadequate capital. To reduce the capital of a Company, is a relatively easy matter, but to increase our capital at the present time is not so. We have had this matter under consideration for some time and this is all I can say at present to you. With regard to future prospects I think I can quite safely say that you will not receive next year such a bad report, but until trade revived and the public are spending money more freely, added to our lack of capital already referred to, the prospects of a dividend are not too good. The accounts were favourably passed.

headline: SOAP.
text: For the year to the end of November last the Warrington soap company of Joseph Crosfield and Sons—all the ordinary shares in which are held by Lever Bros.—made a profit of £384,063, against £331,269 earned in the previous year, and £330,937 in the year to November 30, 1922. headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE. / RESEARCH RESULTS
text:
The Belfast linen trade is experiencing severe depression, but the results achieved by the Linen Research Association are regarded as so hopeful that it has been decided to prolong the society's five years' probationary period for another five years. It has been recommended by the Committee of Inspection that an upkeep of £15,000 per year will henceforth be necessary; and the Scientific and Industrial Research Department will make a grant till 1929 of £21,000, the Northern Ireland Government will donate £10,000, leaving £35,000 to be subscribed by the Irish, Scotch, and English linen manufacturing concerns forming the Association.

A plentiful and cheap supply of raw material is essential to every industry, and in its development of the "J.WS," pedigree flux seed, which promises a 200 per cent greater and better spinning fibre product, the Linen Research Association has probably fulfilled its greatest achievement. From a single pickle of this seed, evolved by minute selection and breeding, Dr. J. Vargas Eyre, Director of Research at the Linen Institute, has been able to report a bulk now available of 20 tons. Continental linen activity now tends to make hopes of future foreign flax supplies both costly and precarious. Simultaneously the acreage under flax in Northern Ireland has dwindled during the last 30 or 40 years from 200,000 acres to 40,000. Happily the work carried on at the Research Institute, near Belfast, gives every hope that flax growing will in future be more remunerative to the home farmer, and this is imperative if "cultivation is to be maintained at an adequate level.

headline: FRASER'S WEEKLY REPORT

headline: THE RUBBER POSITION. / SOME UNCOMFORTABLE
text: It may confidently be expected that, for the quarter beginning on May 1, the amount of rubber exportable from the East Indies under the Stevenson Scheme will be raised to 65 per cent of the standard output, the increase of 10 per cent being the maximum that can be made in any quarter. Meanwhile the rubber situation has one or two uncomfortable aspects. Stocks in London have declined continuously, for some months, and it is doubtful whether even now the price of rubber, which has certainly increased steadily during the current quarter, adequately reflects the strong statistical position of the commodity: this can perhaps be attributed in part to the hand-to-mouth buying policy adopted by American consumers. It is certain, however, that consumption has increased and is increasing, and there is now a strong demand for "spot" and "near" rubber. In some quarters there are fears that a shortage will develop within a few months, but the restriction scheme is not so rigid as to preclude adjustment in face of such a contingency. If fears of a scarcity become acute, prices will rise to such an extent that it will be profitable for producers to pay the extra tax levied on exports above the prevailing quota, though necessarily it would take some time for these increased supplies to be forthcoming. With the price of rubber at its present level, however, and with the prospects of a good demand, it would appear that the time is propitious for considering the abandonment of the scheme, now that it has served its purpose. Probably the existence of the scheme has induced a cautious attitude in the minds of investors, so that the shares of rubber plantations have not benefited as much as might have been expected from the state of the commodity market. It appears that the restriction of exports has increased not only the overhead expenses of the plantations but also the working costs per pound, and, in consequence, the financial condition of most of the companies has not improved very greatly. This perhaps may account for the disappointing condition of the market for rubber shares at the present time.

headline: INSURANCE NOTES. / LEG L AND GENERAL
text:
Although the past year was an uneventful one for the Legal and General Assurance Society, yet it marked a real and solid step in the progress of the affairs of this very efficiently controlled office. In the Life department the number of policies issued during the twelve months was 5,308, compared with 5,141 in the previous period, and the gross sums assured were thus brought up from £2,135,868 to £3,506,717, and new premiums from £157,177 to £201,362. Deferred annuities were granted for £35,137 per annum. In contrast with £30,085 per annum for 1923. After deducting the amount of business placed with re-insurance offices, the total sum assured amounted to £3,087,317, compared with £2,941,868, while new premiums totalled £189,863, compared with £150,056. Although the total of net assurances is not a record, it compares very favourably with that of 1919, which was the boom year, while as regards the gross figures, they constituted a record, with the exception of 1909.

The general fund is really of secondary importance, but last year new premiums of £10,801 were secured, compared with £11,450 in 1923. Thus, combining the results of the two branches, the total number of policies issued was 5,387; the gross sums assured were £3,725,804; the net assurances, £3,306,404; and gross new premiums, £212,163; and net new premiums, £200,664. The total net premium income in the two sections was £1,433,834, compared with £1,376,740, while expenses amounted to 14.24 per cent. of the net premium income, which compares with 1451 per cent. twelve months ago

As regards claims, those in the Life branch were somewhat higher, the figure of £822,376, comparing with £711,175. Death claims absorbed £551,891 against £446,022. At the same time this must be regarded as quite favourable, since the total claims only amounted to 712 per cent. of expectation and the number of deaths 61.2 per cent. of expectation. The net premium income from the fire and accident business amounted to £209,700, being an increase of £9,776, attributable to £2,588 in the fire fund and £7,388 in the accident fund, which may be regarded as satisfactory.

The result of operations was that the total premium income from all the departments was £1,643,624, compared with £1,576,754, and the total was equal to the total funds were increased by £936,292 to a total of £16,577,663, and total assets amounted to £16,758,026. The market value of securities was £328,259 in excess of the book value.

headline: P. I. LUMBER. / QUALITY SAID TO BE OBJECTIONABLE,
text:
The lumber industry in the Philippine Islands is threatened by numerous complaints received by local dealors from buyers of Philippine wood in foreign countries. For the last few months, the quality of Philippine lumber had been considerably reduced by the destructive insects which attack the wood prepared for shipment abroad.

The precarious state of Philippine wood may be attributed to the lack of sufficient inspection, it is said. Because of the absence of enough personnel, the forest bureau cannot assign inspectors to examine every piece of lumber shipped to other countries. In many instances, there are lumber shipments which were never inspected at all, it was declared.

The situation explains the decline in the popularity of Philippine wood in some countries. Australian lumber, manufacturers recently returned a consignment of lumber to Manila because the quality is so poor that it cannot be sold in the market.

Director Fischer of the bureau of forestry declared that unless the government set aside an increase in the appropriation for the services of more lumber inspectors little or nothing would be accomplished to improve the lumber production.

The Philippine lumber prices had been considerably high in the last few years. The revenue entering the government from the sale of wood could be doubled if the yield is only improved. It seems, however, said one dealer, that there will be a slump in the lumber market if the yield should remain unimproved.

Another important factor which must be considered, it is pointed out, is the safeguarding of the prestige the Philippine wood has in most foreign markets. In China, Japan, and in the United States, the reputation of Philippine wood is high.

headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE. / CANADIAN TRADE
text:
CONSIDERABLE GAIN SHOWN.

Ottawa, April 28.—Business in Canada is holding its own very well, proof of this being seen in the latest statistical material.

Bank clearings for last week were $67,000,000 higher than for the corresponding month last year, an increase of nearly 28 per cent. The increases were quite general, for 27 out of 29 cities reported them.

It is especially noteworthy that that every city in the east reporting had an increase, those in the case of Toronto and Montreal being $20,000,000 higher.

The March bulletin of the Labour Department shows the percentage of employment to have been approximately the same as during the corresponding month last year, or, if anything, slightly better.

In the manufacturing industries there has been pronounced recovery during the last month, their staffs having been increased by nearly 11,000 workers.

The largest gains were in iron and steel, notably in vehicle and rolling mills, and in lumber, clay, glass, and stone, pulp and paper and rubber works. The improvement reported a year ago was much less extensive, while on April 1, 1923, there were large reductions in personnel.

Pig Iron production during March was 69,932 long tons, or more than the combined output during the first two months of the year. The foregoing information dispels some of the gloom that some are all too prone to depict.

The International Paper Company has awarded contracts for the extensions to its plant at Three Rivers, which will bring its total capacity up to 700 tons of newsprint a day. Eight machines will be operated when the new plant is complete. When in full operation it will produce enough newsprint every minute to cover more than two acres of ground or enough every day to make nearly 4,000,000 24-page newspaper, of standard size: Wayagamack News, Ltd, has made an issue of $1,500,000 6½ per cent bonds, a portion of the proceeds to be used in the building of its 200-ton newsprint mill.

The erratic action of the grain exchanges continues to be a source of anxiety to legitimate dealers and farmers. The latter especially are complaining, for while the existing price is good, they think that it is really much below the figure warranted by the world's crop situation. Seeding operations in the west are going forward rapidly, and, indeed, in some parts the wheat is appearing above the ground.

The following are the estimated acreages that will be shown to wheat in the Canadian west this year: Manitoba, 2,643,000 acres: Saskatchewan, 8,555,183 acres; Alberta, 2,721,689 acres.

Saskatchewan shows an increase over the acreage of last year. The grain inspections in western Canada during the eight months ended March were 187,798 cars, this number for such a period having been exceeded only four times in the history of the country.

Of these 106,555 cars were on Canadian Pacific lines and 81,243 on other roads. During March, exports of wheat were 4,422,528 bushels, as compared with 13,466,100 during the corresponding month last year, the value being $7,755.194, as compared with $13,603,222.

headline: CANADIAN BOND ISSUES.
text:
Exports of wheat flour during the month were 1,385,240 barrels, or 12,570 less than during March, 1924; the value was $10,972,554, as compared with $7,122,602. Exports of wheat flour during the eight months ended March were valued at $53,106,873, an increase of $8,742,441 over the corresponding months of the last crop year.

A number of Canadian Government bond issues are being placed in New York, the most important of these, during the last week, having been that of the Province of Ontario, which sold $20,000,000 of 37½ per cent one and two-year Treasury bonds to a United States syndicate, the price being 98.65. The proceeds are for maturing issues. The sales of Canadian bonds to the United States so far this year run close to $100,000,000.

Rumours that a merger of Canadian biscuit-making firms is in sight have not been confirmed by actual developments, but the re-organisation of the oldest of these corporations, the Christie-Brown Company of Toronto-is announced with considerable infusion of American capital, which is being accompanied by the presence of three American directors on the board. An offering of $1,000,000 of preferred stock has been taken by a Canadian American syndicate. Canadian financial opinion is much interested in the approach of sterling to par. Its strength has also been reflected in the movement of the Canadian dollar to par in New York during the last week. It is expected that the United Kingdom will soon return to the gold standard, which means that Canada will do likewise, though such action on Canada's part will not be hurried.

The return of the United Kingdom and Canada to the gold standard should have a beneficial effect on the export trade of the United States for its proportion as their currencies approach to a purity in the United States the stronger becomes their purchasing power there.

Trade settlements between Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States taking a triangular form, the movement of these currencies is of much interest in this country.

headline: LABOUR BANKS. / NEW ERA BETWEEN CAPITAL AND LABOUR.
text:
San Francisco, California, April 22.—The development of labour banks, conservatively operated for productive purposes only, and the increasing participation of wage earners in investments, are seen by Don D. Lescohier, associate professor of economics, University of Wisconsin, as the salients of a new alignment between capital and labour.

Speaking before the Commonwealth Club of California, Dr. Lescobier pictured the labour union as decadent, and the advent of the open shop or so-called American plan, as "indicating labour's changing attitude on collective bargaining.

Founding of the Mount Vernon Bank in Washington, D.C., in 1920, by the International Association of Machinists, started a new movement in the history of American labour, the speaker said. The Railroad Brotherhood's chain of branch banks, keyed to the main bank in Cleveland, capitalized at $28,000,000, is a subsequent development, one of many that has thrown a large part of $7,000,000,000 of wage earners' savings into labour a new modus of action. Dr. Lescohier continued:

This may sound very theoretical but it is quite the reverse, forecasting a happier relationship between employer and employee. Among patrons of the new Federation Bank in New York on the first day were 200 manufacturers, and merchants, persons who had never held a union card. They were there because a new bank had been opened at a convenient location. And these banks differ from capitalist banks only in that they are co-operatively owned by labour unions, that they will make loans to business men only for productive enterprises which give employment to manual labour, limit dividends and distribute all earnings in excess of 10 per cent. to their depositors.

headline: MONEY BELONGS TO / STOCKHOLDERS.
text:
A new theory is evolving. About thirteen-fourteenths of the bank funds of the United States, used by the banks to make loans, belong to the depositors rather than to the stockholders. The labour banks maintain that this fact entitles the depositors to a part of the profits. Not charity but justice underlies the dividend to depositors. The depositor's dividend also has proved to be good business. It has reduced depositors' interest costs on borrowed deposits and made it worth their while to trade with the labour bank.

I believe American labour is crossing the threshold of a new epoch. Wage earners, depending in the past on earnings only are now being encouraged to draw an income from invested capital. The railroad engineers have established five investment banks which is a step toward the participation of labour in industrial management and control.

No economic development in the world to-day is so full of promise as the entry of organized labour into the mobilized saving power of workmen, employed through safe and intelligent managed investment, will lift the whole relationship between capital and labour to a higher plane. It will be a bridge to better understanding on both sides. It will teach labour the problems and risks of capital; and it will teach capital more common sense in its dealings with labour.
It has been said that an insurance company is not firmly established until the income has reached £100,000 per annum.—Mr. J. J. Kershaw (Mutual Property Insurance Co.).

headline: STANDARD QIL
text:
THE POSITION IN BRITAIN.

The Anglo-Standard Oil entente, is being carried a stage further by the purchase of control of the British Mexican Petroleum Company by the new Standard Oil subsidiary — Pan-American Eastern Petroleum Company. The British Mexican is the fuel oil bunkering company formed in 1919 by Lord Iaverforth and other shipping interests in conjunction with Mr. Doheny, and it now controls the Agwl Petroleum Corporation, as well as a petrol distributing concern, the Redline Motor Spirit Company.

The Standard Oil of Indiana thus obtains a foothold in the British petrol market and fuel oil bunkering facilities at all the principal British ports. It is expected that it will also take over Lord Inverforth's interest in the Lago Corporation, which is now the second largest shipper of oil from Venezuela.

It should be appreciated that the Anglo-American Oil Company will have no connection with the British companies to be controlled by Standard Oil of Indiana. The Anglo-American is a subsidiary of the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey, and Standard Oil companies have a habit of working independently in the same markets.

headline: PHILIPPINE HATS / INDUSTRY PICKING UP.

headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE / CUNARD LINE. / AMERICAN EXPRESS SERVICE.
text:
The experiment of the Cunard Line of so arranging their timetable that the incoming mail-ships can call at Plymouth, Cherbourg, and Southampton all in the one day certainly seems a success as far as it has gone, judging from the first few sallings only. But this promise only holds good in the winter, when ships travelling by the short route can fit in the call's conveniently and still land their passengers in London or Paris at a reasonable hour. When they have to go farther south on account of icebergs, however, it will be found that this does not apply.

Unfortunately, it is just this summer season that the first call in England is wanted as many people complain that the Cherbourg call coming first persuades many American visitors to see France before they come on to England, with the result that they have done all their shopping in Paris and spent very much less in this country than would otherwise be the case.

In the meantime we have got n very considerably accelerated mail service between London and New York, and that is something to be grateful for. Before the war the Germans learnt that the extra half-knot could be just as troublesome as it could be advantageous.

headline: FREIGHT FALL
text: The general level of British shipping freights fell in March to the lowest point touched since August, 1923, according to the Chamber of Shipping index number published by "The Statist." The March index, at 26.08, is 935 per cent lower than for February, and 1886 per cent lower than for March, 1924. The time charter rate, in which a fall of 4.37 per cent was recorded in February, fell another 1.56 per cent in March. Freights are now virtually at the pre-war level, as if the average for 1913 is taken at 100, the average for March, 1925, is 105.5. Virtually all routes contributed to the March decline, the heaviest falls occurring in the Red Sea, Arabia, and India group, Java to United Kingdom-Continent, Australia to United Kingdom, Argentine, Uruguay, &c. to United Kingdom-Continent, and United States to United Kingdom groups.

headline: IDLE SHIPPING.
text: Quarterly returns of the amount of shipping laid up Idle at the principal ports of Great Britain and Ireland on April 1, compiled by the Chamber of Shipping, show that as compared with January 1, last, there was a decrease of 95,190 tons net, or 19.5 percent; and compared with a year ago a decrease of 17,303 tons, or 42 per cent Theports at which there have been the largest decreases as compared with the beginning of the year are: Bristol, with a decline of 12,000 tons; Cardiff, 13,000 tons; Liverpool, 46,200 tons; London Docks, 36,800 tons; and Glasgow, 14,500 tons. On the other hand, increases are recorded at Dartmouth, 4,000 tons; Hull, 6,000 tons; London River, 7,000 tons; Manchester, 6,000 tons; Newcastle, 13,000 tons; and Southampton, 8,750 tons. The total for English ports has decreased by 63,800 tons net; that for Scottish ports by 25,600 tons; and that for Irish ports by 5,800 tons net.

headline: COTTON.
text: American cotton "prices have been unsettled, but influences of weakening character have predominated at the close of the week and values have lost more ground. The report of Messrs J. F. Hutton and Co., Ltd.'s weekly statistics, shewing that the visible supply of American has decreased by 222,000 bales on the week to 2,969,000 bales against a reduction of only 82,000 bales to 1,882,000 bales last year attracted bullish support. Trade demand has also been more active. At Liverpool spot sales have increased substantially owing to a revival of Continental buying. Speculative selling has, however, proved stronger than these factors owing to generally favourable crop news. It is believed, indeed, that a fairly extensive short interest has been created. If this is the case it may prove to be a strong influence in a reversal of sentiment should either the crop outlook or trading demand. shew any unexpected development, as the present situation has already been discounted by a fall of 1½d per lb. Egyptian prices have been firmer. In the Manchester market there has been a fair volume of enquiry of a very varied nature, but the easier tendency of cotton values has effectively checked enterprise on the part of most buyers. A moderate turnover, composed almost wholly of small lines, has been arranged, but the larger lots which have been under negotiation are apparently held up pending some further indication as to the course of values. In American yarns there has been an improved demand for fine and also coarse couts; prices are irregular and ¼d to ¼d per lb. lower. For Egyptians there has been a fairly good enquiry but transactions have been disappointing and prices are 1d per lb. down. India has bought some good lots of drooties, also shirtings, light whites and miscellaneous styles, and enquiry for the finer makes has been more in evidence. For China a few shirtings and dyed goods have been sold. A moderate business has been arranged for the Near East and Africa. The Home trade, Persia and South America have also bought sundry styles.

headline: SMYRNA CLAIMS
text:
INSURANCE COMPANY WINS.

London, May 2.—The test case on which depends enormous claims against various insurance companies, brought by the American Tobacco Company against the Guardian Assurance Company, was decided in the Court of Appeal yesterday against the American Tobacco Company. The company sued to recover £168,000, the result of loss sustained in the destruction of Smyrna on September 19, 1922, when the Turks evicted the Greeks.

The insurers refused payment on the ground that the losses incurred were war risks, and not ordinary fire risks. The total Smyrna losses were estimated at £20,000,000, of which a considerable percentage was covered by fire risks, which are now held to be void. The present decision confirms the decisions already rendered by the French and Italian courts.
