headline: THE CHINA MAIL. / JAPAN'S BANK DEFECTS.
text:
Yukinori Aoshino, Managing Director of the Kushimg Bank, in the Taiyo (Sun) states:

The bankers of Japan have many defects and shortcomings. It is not my present purpose to point them out one by one. I only intend to trace out the origin of the defects, shortcomings and errors, connected with the banking business with a view to certifying them.

The principal cause is too many banks, which is liable to occasion unnecessary composition. In consequence, various forms of viciousness have resulted. I hold that the amalgamation of numerous small banks on a comprehensive scale as the most commendable means for the prevention of further viciousness. The Finance authorities are fully aware of the advisability of this plan, but its realisation is by no means easy.

The question will naturally be asked whether this improvement of the bank organization is impossible: A negative reply to this question would be a mistake. As for me, I would rather say that, if the bankers be fully alive to the necessity of mutual confidence and co-operation, improvement of conditions and the rectification of errors are possible, even if the organisation remains as it is at present. One of the most glaring errors is that bankers are utterly ignorant of the credit of their customers, and that they thus advance funds to business men of doubtful credit. At present, a business man has connections with several banks. As long as such a condition prevails, bankers will not be in a position to ascertain the credit of their customers.

It is desirable that bankers should extend uniform treatment to all customers, but this is not practicable. I suggest in this connect-

headline: LIVING COSTS. / SYMPTOMS OF INFLATION
text:
The cost-of-living figure, which indicates the purchasing power of our money, is shown to have fallen appreciably during the month of March. On February 25, it was 97 per cent. above pre-war; on April 1 it was 75 per cent., says the Daily Chronicle.

Though seasonal cheapening of eggs and milk counts for something in this, we are probably justified in assigning a definite influence to the raising of the Bank Rate. The justification of that criticised step was that, apart from any question of the American exchange, commodity prices, were slowly but steadily rising in this country, i.e., the purchasing power of money was falling.

"In other words, there were the initial symptoms of inflation. The raising of the Bunk Rate was calculated to correct them, and appears to have done so. But the process needs careful watching, lest it go too far. With trade as it is, we are in no position to embark on an active deflationary policy."

To those not fully acquainted with the Company, it may be explained that the chief business is the disposing of and acquiring small lots of shares for the interests of clients. The Company also negotiates the transfer of houses, land and property as will have been noticed by its various offers in the local Press. As the majority of investors are able only to purchase in small lots and as these small lots do not interest the ordinary broker of Hongkong the consequence was, that until the formation of the Small Investors in Hongkong, nearly three years ago, the investor in small shares—and this means the average person—had no broker or firm specialising in meeting his or her needs. To cater specially for the small investor the Company was commenced and it has had the pleasure of serving innumerable clients since that time with such satisfaction that many of the Company's clients have been the means of introducing also from one to five new clients. The present clientele, therefore, has largely grown from introductions made by original clients; pleased investors satisfied with the service rendered.

headline: HONGKONG COMPANY'S FACILITIES:
text: "When the Small Investors' Share and Real Estate Company (Hongkong) was started last year, it filled a long-felt want, and some interesting particulars are forwarded to us to show the public support received. The first month's gross business amounted to $170,000, all cash business. This is small compared with the business's to the old established sharebrok's do, but it is sufficient to indicate that the Company fulfils a real need and that it has the confidence of the public. The Company will shortly observe its first anniversary. While it was primarily formed for the convenience of small investors, local and out-port, it is in a position to handle the affairs of larger investors with the same facility, promptitude and service. The Company, furthermore, will accept commissions to dispose of, or acquire, land, buildings; or rent same, for the benefit of clients. No fee is charged for consultation, but on the contrary, prospective clients are welcome, whether business results or not. For shares the clients merely give the usual local fee, irrespective of the number of shares negotiated. A free daily list giving particulars of local shares will be sent to foreigners and Chinese alike upon application at the Company's office, 8, Des Vaux Road, or P.O. Box 484, Hongkong. headline: Great Increase.
text: Since the above appeared in the "South China Morning Post" on February 8, 1924, we understand the Company's volume of business transactions for a recent month amounted to $245,000 and the number of clients has increased 400 per cent.; a fair proportion of these are in Macao. There are still a good number of investors for whom the Company has not yet been privileged to act. With the object of obtaining a larger proportion of these investors a local-limited company is now in the process of negotiation to be known as the Small Investors' Shares Real Estate Co., Ltd. The limited company will follow the procedure adopted by the old company for the last three years except that certain small lots of shares will be purchased for the Company's own holdings from a variety of sound local companies yielding satisfactory dividends and bonus. These profits will be collected by the Company and in turn paid over to shareholders. The great advantage of such a system is that instead of an individual buying a particular share which may not yield satisfactory returns he will, as a shareholder of the Small Investors' obtain dividends from the majority of companies in which the firm have invested. In other words all his eggs will not be in one basket so that if one particular basket drops he will still (given a hundred baskets) be 99 per cent. to the good. This method is long tried and successful as is proved by the success of investment companies in Britain. Moreover such companies are able to furnish unbiased reports, reference to any particular share, held by its shareholders and it is the intention of the Small Investors to furnish such reports.

headline: Branch in Macao.
text: An office will also be opened in Macao as a good proportion of the Company's clients are in the neighbouring colony, and it is the Companys intention to furnish reliable quotations from the Hongkong office by telegram daily. At present, share lists arrive in Macao from Hongkong a day late and, apart from this delay, it will be readily appreciated by prospective shareholders there that cabled quotations transmitted from Hongkong will be of great satisfaction and will enable a client to obtain, in selling or buying, a substantial difference to his profit. Local shareholders will naturally, by doing business with the Company, be helping their own interests as the brokerage fees they pay for the acquiring or disposal of shares will eventually be returned to them in the form of dividends and bonus.

headline: COMMERCE AND FINANCE. / GRAVE TRADE OUTLOOK.
text:
He had always been an optimist, said Sir Robert Horne, K.C., M.P., speaking at Reading, but to-day it seemed to him that we had arrived at a period when it would be folly if we did not face the facts, however unpleasant they might be. Looking at some of the staple industries of the country, he could find no glimmer of light.

Over the whole field of the great coal industry, he continued, there was no factor which gave reason to hope that there was going to be any immediate revival of prosperity. In the steel trade, the situation was becoming worse instead of better. In regard to shipbuilding, everyone knew of the great orders which had been going to shipyards in Holland and Germany instead of to British shipyards. A friend of his, who had just returned from Holland, told him of one particular yard in which ten ships were being built, nine of them for British owners. (Shame.) "Only last week," said Sir Robert, "my services were sought by two very large and important shipbuilders in this country to try to obtain some arrangement by which there would be brought to their idle yards a great contract which is being given out at the present time for eight ships to carry refrigerated meat from South America. The disparity between their tender and that of the foreign tender was in the region of £20,000 to £30,000 per ship, and their tender was based upon figures which involved absolutely no profit to the British shipbuilder. It was put in at actual cost. Ulimately they were prepared to build these ships at a loss, and made an offer to that effect, but it was still very many thousands of pounds above the offer of the Continental shipbuilder."

They had got, concluded Sir Robert Horne, to bring the facts of the situation home to the minds of the people in order that they might get such co-operation in the work of the country as had never been seen in the past. This was no time for people to be going about urging combinations of workmen to bring the work of the country to a standstill. That could only end for everybody in disaster. The only hope for the country and the people was that they should work together in amity and goodwill.

headline: FOOCHOW SHIPPING / THE TEA EXPORT TRADE.
text:
Ocean-going steamers call at Foochow principally in connection with the tea export trade. They stop generally at the Pagoda Anchorage, the channel further up being too shallow, although dredging operations in this section of the Min River are now in progress. According to the Foochow Customs, Report for 1923, 1,526 ocean-going steamers entered and cleared the port in addition to 76 sailing vessels. The total tonnage of the year aggregated 1,483,442 tons, of which 564,178 tons were contributed by Chinese, 381,236 tons by Japanese and 369,968 tons by British shipping. Foochow is also an important centre for coastal shipping. There are four companies keeping regular sailing schedules between Foochow and Shanghai and other northern port. Several foreign firms are also engaged in coastal shipping, their sailings being confined to ports near Foochow including Chuan-chow, Hinghwa, Wenchow, and certain ports in Formosa, Junk traffic in the Min River has been badly interfered with lately by bandit activities, The frequent commandeering of boats and pressing of men into military service by the local military leaders have terrified the boat men and oftentimes caused complete suspension of junk traffic on the river. Fukien officials are now fully alive to the necessity of affording due protection to the boatmen in order to keep the traffic on the river in normal condition. A shipping bureau has been organised at Foochow to give guarantees to the junks against commandeering. The Bureau collects a toll from all the passing junks, which are divided into five classes according to their size and the value of the cargo they carry. In addition to this levy, each junk is required to register itself with the shipping bureau by paying a registration fee of $5. When a junk has paid these levies, the officials will guarantee its immunity from commandeering. A British merchant recently established a transportation company in Foochow. The fleet of junks owned by the company are engaged principally in carrying cargo from the hinterland to the coast either for others or on the company's own account. headline: £10,000,000 LOAN PLAN.
text:
WHAT EAST AFRICA NEEDS FOR TRANSPORT.

A £10,000,000 Government guaranteed loan for the development of transport in East Africa is the outstanding recommendation of the East Africa Commission; whose report has been issued.

The Commission, consisting of three members of Parliament, Mr. W. Ormsby-Gore, M.P. (Conservative), chairman; Mr. P. C. Linfield (Liberal); and Major A. G. Church (Labour), spent three months in the various territories last year. They consider that the further economic development of both native and non-native production is dependent on the early provision of increased transport facilities, and, in particular, on new railway construction.

They, therefore, propose a Bill; authorising the issue of a loan for the amount stated.

The demand made on the British taxpayer would, it is argued, be more than counter-balanced by indirect benefits of increased trade and production within the Empire. Approximately half the capital sum would be spent. If Great Britain on rails, bridging material, rolling stock, etc.

For Kenya, the Commission recommends the establishment of a Trust Board, in which all native lands should be vested. Mr. Linfield, in a supplementary memorandum, proposes a series of Trust Boards.

Stress is laid upon the duty of the Government to develop agricultural efficiency in all native areas.

Mr. Linfield's memorandum contains but several interesting points. One is his recommendation that the tax collected in each native area, instead of going into the central treasury, should be expended in part on direct services in the area

More far-reaching is his suggestion that an Imperial Development Board should be set up, to which a fixed sum would be paid annually from the Imperial Exchequer. He mentions £3,000,000 a year for a period of ten or fifteen years. By the end of that time the Board would have a steady revenue from interest and repayments, and eventually it would become independent of any further Exchequer grants.

headline: BRIFISH CAPITAL IN CANADA. / RAILWAY CHIEF'S ADVICE.
text: Mr. E. W. Beatty, President of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, addressing the Quebec division of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, emphasised the importance of encouraging the investment of British capital in Canada. The British investor, he said, both on patriotic and national grounds, would, under proper conditions, prefer this country to any other portion of the world, but Canadians should not create the impression that this was not a country in which honest investments were given proper protection. "Whatever we may do to encourage the introduction of capital, we should see that it is entitled to such a measure of just protection as will place the burden of failure, if failure ensues, on its own administration, and not upon the country's fiscal political policies." Mr. Beatty's reference follows the publication of British Press comment on the Canadian railway situation.

headline: LEVER'S
text:
News of Lord Leverhulme's death caused a slight decline in the shares of Lever Brothers, not because of any apprehension over the future of the business, but because it was feared that the deceased peer's shares might come on the market. This is not to happen.

Lord Leverhulme, a few years ago, made the necessary arrangements for the future conduct of "Lever's," and the constitution of this huge business is unlikely, for the present, to be affected by his death.

Just 30 years ago Lever Brothers was turned into a public company with a capital of £1,500,000. So rapidly has the business grown that to-day the issued capital totals £56,627,546. Last year's profits amounted to £5,476,000. The shares largely held by the public are the 7 and 8 per cent. Preference issues.

text:
An interesting appointment which has just been made by the E stern Telegraph Co., is reported by the “China Express and Telegraph” Mr. J. C. Denison-Pender, in addition to being joint manager of the Eastern Telegraph Co., has become its Vice-Chairman as well as Vice-Chairman of the Eastern Extension Australasia and China Telegraph Co., of which he is already a director.

The son of the present chairman of the company and grandson of Sir John Pender, one of the pioneers of the cable industry, to whose firm belief in the future of the submarine telegraph, this country owes its pre-eminence in the underseas communications of the globe, Mr. J. C. Denison-Pender may be said to have been born for the exalted position he now holds. He first saw the light in 1882, and is the third generation of his family to be virtually at the head of the Great Eastern group of cable companies. Educated at Eton, it is to his credit that he is gifted with practical knowledge, beginning from the lowest rung, which few men enjoying such early advantages can boast.

He joined the Eastern Co. as a young man, and went through the telegraphists' hard school in the ordinary way. Then he roughed it at sea for three years on cable ships, taking part in extensive cable-laying operations, and finishing the training for the position he now holds by serving in all the big departments of the Eastern Co.

Although an intensely busy man, he yet found time for relaxation in politics. From 1915 to 1918 he represented Newmarket Division in the House of Commons, and also sent for one of the Wandsworth Divisions from 1918 till the Labour Party came into possession in 1922. He also represented St. Pancras, on the London County Council for nearly ten years.

headline: CONTRACTS WE LOSE.
text:
A novel suggestion for stimulating British shipbuilding and shipping industries was made at Jarrow at the launching of a collier for the South Metropolitan Gas Co. by Mr. G. F. Mulherion. He said: "There are many reasons why foreign shipbuilders should undercut British builders, but the way the Government allows British money to go abroad while British workmer are starving is another question.

"In my opinion it is a question whether import duties should not be imposed on ships built abroad rather than allow money to go on contracts abroad which could do so much good at home... It may strike the German mind that if they were to spend £50,000,000 a year they could ruin the industries of this country."

headline: COPRA DEMAND. / REACTION IN MARKET NOTED AS SUPPLY DIMINISHES.
text:
A reaction in the wholesale copra market in Manila as reflected by the renewed demand in the United States for coconut oil, coupled with the approaching rainy season when copra drying by sun will be a slow and tedious process, is expected to come at any time, according to the markets section of the bureau of commerce and industry.

Copra and coconut oil, both in domestic and foreign trading, have continued weak and featureless, little attention being given by local producers and dealers.

Now that the demand is growing again, values of copra and coconut oil will naturally increase, it is explained. Reports from New York stated that American soap men have just entered the market for coconut oil, despite the campaign to credit coconut products in the western states. This change in the oil market, it was observed, has had favourable reflection in the local coconut oil and copra trading. Co-operating for the development of the coconut industry in the islands, W. L. Brooke, chemist of the bureau of science, has recently determined in a study made at Nagcarlan, Laguna, the weights of the component parts of the coconut. It was found that about 37.54 per cent., by the weight of the coconut is represented by the husk, 25.45 per cent., by the meat (parcel), 17.69 per cent., by shell, 14.08 per cent., by water, 3.61 per cent., by parings, and 1.82 per cent., by steami g loss.

headline: STRIKE MALADY
text:
2 p.m. to 4 p.m.

It is possible to add to established optimism by regarding conditions as they are at the moment in the light of a sickness. There have been the symptoms, then the outbreak leading either to a crisis or a quick suppression; and in the case of the former to convalescence and complete recovery. This view indicates that a resumption of normal Hongkong life is merely a matter of time. This being so the continuation of marking time in strict measure, if it needs not to be urged, can lose nothing by being emphasised. The community has been given a distinct, direct and clear lead by H. E. the Governor. For this let us give due credit. In addition the recognised leading foreign firms and institutions have nobly ridden the storm. No praise can be too lavish in commenting on the arrangements so promptly initiated and so efficiently maintained. It is in the main due to this happy triumph of maintaining the supply of essential service that really matters — the supply of food — that the spirit of equanimity is so strongly evident to which has to be added the knowledge that the Colony has had a pistol placed at its head which, probably to the surprise of those who have held it has misfired. Attention has been diverted to Canton and to the happenings there. As in Hongkong, so in Canton! There is no case to answer and nothing of which to be ashamed. The spirited action of the British Com

sul there has won commendation by its absolute fearlessness and its insistence on the truth. Blood-shed is to be deplored but those who resort to it must expect reprisals. All this but skims the cream of the present situation behind which the evil of anti-foreignism backed by the worst forces of Bolshevism lurk. The simile of sickness suffices for the time being. The disease has spread, but the doctors have the case well in hand and the time seems rapidly drawing in sight when the patient arriving at convalescence will sit up and take n'urishment—of common sense.

headline: Prolixity.
text: Lord Oxford is responsible for the reference to an American orator that “he was like a train of fifteen cars and only one passenger.” And England’s orator of good English comments—“That is prolixity.” The quotation comes very apt after a glance at the current issue of that sometimes exciting journal “The Hongkong Government Gazette.” In it is to be found a series of regulations under the caption “Prison Rules.” They are indeed “a train of fifteen-cars and only one passenger.” No fewer than three hundred and thirty-five clauses make up these “Prison Rules” to say nothing of menus of prison fare. Tribute is not paid to the author of this literary masterpiece, Jaded readers of fiction will undoubtedly find something of interest in these pages, and if only on that account, and on that account only a perusal is highly recommended. Clause 177 instructs that “.....the hair of the prisoner shall not be cut closer than may be necessary for the purpose of health and cleanliness.” The scintillating purity and clearness of this instruction like the peace of God, passes all understanding. The Chief Warder has twenty-four clauses devoted to him and of these 22 begin. “The Chief Warder shall.” His job is not exactly “a bobby’s one.” He is not to absent himself from his duties without the permission of the Suparintendent and—and this seems terrible—he “shall endeavour to exercise a sound moral influence over both the officers and prisoners placed under his supervision. He shall restrain by his authority every tendency to oppression or undue harshness on the part of the prison officers, and likewise every tendency to levity, rudeness and insubordination on the part of prisoners, and shall aim to raise the minds of the prison officers to a sense of their responsibility.” If Chief Warders die young we now know the reason..... But space is limited for a further analysis of this momentous piece of official prolixity. If similar productions govern the working of other Government Departments, we can well understand why there is a awareness in performing things.

headline: A LIVELY CROWD / POLICE DISPERSE CROWD CLEARING A WHARF
text:
Large crowds attempted to board the Tung On as she lay alongside the wharf this morning and they became so insistent in their demands that a certain amount of force had to be used by the police in clearing the wharf.

One man, even then, broke away and taking a flying leap, managed to get aboard. The crowd seemed to be under the impression that the boat was leaving at once for Canton but it only went as far as the naval yard where, it is believed supplies for Shameen are to be put on board.

The Tung On, also it is thought, the Sai On and Charles Bardouin will leave later for Canton.

headline: ANTI-FOREIGN STRIKE ENDS (Reuter's Service.) Shanghai June 26th.
text:
This morning's developments terminate the anti-foreign strike in Shanghai, but do not affect the industrial strike which is virtually a boycott aimed principally at the British and Japanese. The Chamber of Commerce last night formally requested the re-opening of the shops and banks of which 70 per cent. acquiesced.

At 9 o'clock crowds in the streets watched the distribution of Chamber of Commerce handbills which were viewed with some suspicion, but in order to ensure the public confidence in them a delegation consisting of the Foreign Commissioner, the Prefect in Chief of the Shanghai-Woosung Constabulary, the Chinese City Magistrate, and representatives of the Chamber of Commerce and federated unions made a procession through the streets in motors bearing flags inscribed "Shops should be opened. The Government takes full responsibility for negotiations." After this the hesitators opened their doors.

headline: STUDENTS' BIG IDEAS
text:
A meeting of the Shanghai Students' Union yesterday afternoon resolved to appeal to the students all over the country to learn the art of war and be ready to fight for their country, to appeal to the patriotism of the militarists and select lecturers to arouse the people and soldiers.

A programme for wide student demonstrations yesterday was largely a fiasco-owing to official prohibitions, while precautions in Shanghai completely frustrated the student activities. Many Volunteers and "Specialists" have been withdrawn from the streets which appear normal this afternoon.

Two Japanese destroyers from Pescadores have gone to Amoy and Canton.

headline: HOPEFUL AUGURY
text:
For the first time since the beginning of the strike the Central Market stalls were manned with a limited number of workers this morning and meat was to be obtained.

This, the Food Controller, Mr. N. L. Smith, told a China Mail representative, is due to the action of the Tung Wah Hospital in placing men at the disposal of the Government. The Government has promised the owners all along that if their men left they would see to the slaughtering and preparation of the animals also the delivering of meat to the market in vans and the owners had replied that it was as much as their lives were worth to allow it to be sold.

The action of the Tung Wah hospital will probably lead to greater confidence, however. The start is only in a small way at present, Mr. Smith informed the China Mail, but there was plenty of beef and pork in stock and the supply in the market he hoped would gradually increase.

Mr. Smith further informed the China Mail that owing to the action of the Tung Wah Hospital in selling rice cheaply the Chinese retailers had this morning been forced to bring their prices down and rice was now to be had at almost below pre-strike cost. Notices were now up at the shops that owing to the price charged by the Tung Wah Hospital the price would be reduced to $7.00 a picul. As much as $14.00 had been charged just recently, said Mr. Smith, which was exorbitant as there was a plentiful supply here.

With regard to firewood, the next most important item in the poor man's budget, as Mr. Smith remarked, it had been found upon inquiry that there was about two months' supply in the Colony. Mr. Harold Seth had been appointed Firewood controller under Mr. Smith and the question was being considered as to whether the Government would have to make purchases elsewhere.

So far he had avoided Government purchase of any supplies, said Mr. Smith.

headline: SHANGHAI POSITION
text:
Shanghai residents arriving here by the P. and O. s.s. Malwa yesterday afternoon expressed surprise that the Colony is so outwardly calm—compared with the more troubled conditions in the North. While the streets in Hongkong have their usual peaceful appearance, apart from the absence of trams and a display of kahki, the streets in Shanghai present an almost warlike aspect, all the shops being shuttered and armoured cars being seen passing to and fro at intervals. There are also large numbers of marines to be seen about the streets. The principal bridges are being guarded by American sailors. Japanese sailors are also in evidence especially in the Honkew district. At night time the motor canteens are to be seen visiting the various point at which the forces are stationed. Shanghai, in short, has settled down to a state of siege. There is a spirit of common endeavour to win through. This spirit is to be seen in a hundred different ways. It manifests itself in the way the public services are being run, no work being too exacting for the many willing volunteers. The spirit of common endeavour is also to be seen in the little acts of kindly help which every person requiring assistance can call upon—indeed such assistance does not need to be sought, it is proffered before it is sought.

The most reassuring feature of the Shanghai situation is the fact that the Shanghai Municipal Council has matters well in hand. The Council consists of men of sound common sense accustomed to dealing with the hard facts of life. They are handling the present trouble in a thoroughly businesslike way. Besides this they have the forces at their disposa to carry their measures into effect, as they are able to call upon a most efficient police force, an exceptionally well organised volunteer corps, and a large number of bluejackets and marines from the ships of the interested powers. Therefore, although Shanghai's Hongkong is not without its share of alarmists, the future can be faced with every confidence in the eventual and final triumph of law and order over the forces of disruption. Hongkong, which is so much better off in many respects, and which must look to Shanghai for an official settlement, can rely upon the problem being handled in the best possible way.

headline: SHAMEEN SHOOTING
text:
Dr. Alexander Baxter, Vice-President of the Canton Christian College, yesterday retracted statements attributed to the seventeen American staff members at the College, in which blame and responsibility for what the statement termed “the merciless and unjustified assault” rests entirely on those who directed the firing from Shameen.

This statement expressed to "our Chinese colleagues, students and friends" deep-felt sympathy and support. The world had been inadequately informed of the Chinese viewpoint, continued the statement, and the signatories were determined to co-operate with the Chinese in the presentation of their case.

The statement attributed to the Shameen troops the firing of the first shots and stated that the parade was proceeding in an orderly manner and was composed largely of students and workmen unarmed and defenceless.

In a statement signed yesterday in the presence of Sir Claude Severn, Mr. W. W. Hornell, Vice President of the Hongkong University, and Mr. A. G. M. Fletcher, Mr. Baxter said that he could not say whether the translation of which the above is an extract was a correct one of what he and his colleagues had signed. The Chinese masters had informed them of the gist of it and had asked that it should be made available at once for publication.

Students from the College had returned after the firing and had stated that their procession had been fired on without firing on their side. They produced blood-stained clothes. Their story was corroborated in every detail by trustworthy members of the Chinese staff and had been accepted, as Dr. Baxter and Dr. Henry the President of the College, had been unable to get to Shameen themselves.

Since this statement had been signed, stated Dr. Baxter, in his retraction yesterday, he had been entirely satisfied from what he had gathered from eyewitnesses that the firing started from the Chinese side. He had not been aware of the fact that the statement had been directed to the American public with the hope that America would do her best to assist China in securing just treatment and in realising her aims to free herself from foreign Imperialism.

headline: HONGKONG AMERICAN'S VIEW
text:
The following letter expressing the opinion of the American community of Hongkong as to the Shameen shooting has been signed by as many members of the American community as could be reached in a short space of time this morning.

The letter is addressed to the Editor of the China Mail and is as follows:—

Sir,— On account of the serious implications and consequences involved in the statement of the American members of the foreign staff of the Canton Christian College as expressed in the resolutions originally printed in the Canton Gazette, we, the undersigned members of the American Community in Hongkong, desire to place on record our emphatic disapproval of the action of the parties concerned, whose entire lack of judgment and restraint at such a time, we consider deplorable.

Although a retraction has been made and published, which places the resolutions originally printed we wish to leave the Hongkong Community in no doubt as to our attitude.

headline: BANKS OPEN / RESTRICTIONS
text:
The Chinese banks opened this morning and although a large amount of business is being done this is chiefly due to the approaching end of the half year.

The “China Mail” understands that the Government has given a verbal guarantee of the removal of the restriction regarding withdrawal of deposits (this will be declared later by proclamation) and the Chinese banks were therefore able to allow depositors to withdraw ad. lib. this morning.

In spite of the absence of restriction, however, there was no run on the banks this morning, A "China Mail" representative who made enquiries at the most important Chinese banks was informed that holders of current accounts were drawing comparatively small sums, although larger perhaps than usual, and the savings banks were also being called upon to a considerable extent. But business was confined almost entirely to small depositors: The opinion was general that the removal of restriction would lead to greater confidence.

Permission has not yet been given the native (as distinct from the Chinese) banks to allow customers to withdraw more than the 10 per cent. and consequently many of them remain closed. It is stated that an arrangement is being come to whereby they will be able to open shortly, however.

"It should be made quite clear that there is no question of insolvency regarding any of the banks temporarily suspended, said a well-known Chinese banking authority to a 'China Mail' representative this morning. They are in the position of having paid out without having got back. They have to pay out in money on deposits, even on fixed deposits (although in the later case it is less interest). There is nothing to cause the least anxiety in their temporary suspension."

headline: POLICE RESERVE WEEK-END DUTY UNDERTAKEN
text:
Over 500 Chinese have been enrolled at the City Hall and have been given work to do in maintaining essential service. Many have expressed willingness to serve in a special place and those to the number of well over a hundred are being sworn in and supplied with uniforms and batons. They are expected to be functioning in a day or so.

The European Police Reserve which outnumbers this in a very large degree owing to the many volunteers who have applied for enrolment at the end of the week, commenced to operate over the week-end-both-on-patrol-work and the guarding of essential points.

headline: H. E. THE GOVERNOR
text:
The following telegram has been received by His Excellency the Governor from the Secretary of State for the Colonies:—

“I have gladly accepted your offer to remain in Colony for the present as I have confidence in your ability to deal with the present difficult situation. I wish to assure you generally of my support and should be glad to know if there are any directions in which you require assistance and what measures you are taking to deal with the situation.”

headline: WOMAN KILLED
text:
A young Chinese woman Chung Ching-tung received a mortal wounds from two men who attacked her as she was selling pork in the Western district yesterday.

The men are reported to have stopped her and asked the price of the pork and on receiving the reply "70 cents per cattle" the alleged attack was made. The woman's most severe wounds were on the head.

Another attack allegedly on the instigation of men concerned in the trade was that on a man who was also engaged in selling pork. This man was seriously injured.

headline: FATAL RUSH
text:
Extraordinary scenes which it is believed have led to the death of a dozen or more Chinese were witnessed alongside the Sai On and Kwong Sai yesterday as they lay in midstream prior to their journey to Canton.

The difficulty which the police have encountered, also the revenue officers who have been giving them a helping hand, in their attempts to maintain order and prevent the crowds from becoming unmanageable has already been reported. This was when the boats filled up as usual from the wharves. In an endeavour to lessen the risk the boats yesterday were ordered midstream and passengers were taken by sampan.

The precipitation into the water of the Chinese who are believed to have lost their lives was partly due to their own eagerness but even more so, to the avarice of the sampan owners who, it is stated by eyewitnesses, were in such a hurry to get away for more boatloads that they brought disaster on themselves and on those they had on board. One sampan containing ten persons turned completely over and on the other, they were seen to re-appear and others are said to have been forced overboard by the crush.

As soon as the Canton boats were full, endeavours were made to prevent further people from getting on board but in the woras of one of the officers who was there "it was impossible, they simply swarmed on board until the ship wouldn't hold any more." The passengers were packed like sardines and in his opinion the danger of suffocation was great, particular as a very large percentage of the passengers were women and children.

in the absence of a return the Special Commissioners made assessments for super-tax of £90,000 for each of the years 1918 to 1921. Notices of assessment were sent to Mr. Whitney in New York; on appeal the Special Commissioners confirmed them, and later they were affirmed by Mr. Justice Rowlatt and by the Court of Appeal. Mr. Whitney then appealed to the House of Lords.

His leading counsel, Sir John Simon, K.C., said he was a non-resident in the United Kingdom in the most absolute sense, and maintained that he was not liable to be charged or assessed to super-tax.

Sir John submitted that a nonresident could be lawfully assessed to super-tax only—if at all—in the name of a trustee, guardian, committee, factor, or agent, and not in his own name; that the Special Commissioners had no power or jurisdiction to serve notices to Mr. Whitney out of the United Kingdom; and that he was not bound to comply.

Lord Dunedin said he did not see how they could get a tax from an absentee except that which was tapped at the source.

Sir John Simon said he did not dispute that the Act might affect a person carrying on business through an agent here. Such a person, though not resident, was represented by his agent. Lord Carson said the question was whether he was within the jurisdiction, and so liable to assessment. Sir Douglas Hogg, K.C. (Attorney General) opened the case for the Crown with submissions that the assessments to super-tax were rightly made upon Mr. Whitney. The fact that a person to whom profits accrued was not resident in the United Kingdom did not affect the chargeability of the profits. Nonresident persons were expressly brought within the scope of income tax in respect of profits arising from sources within the United Kingdom, as was shown in the language of both Schedule D and of Section 41 of the Income Tax Act, 1842.

The topic of conversation continues to be the document said to have been signed by seventeen members of the staff of the Canton Christian College, and the retraction made by the Rev. A. Baxter. It is the manner of the document to which strong exception is taken. There is general agreement with the words of a correspondent to our senior morning contemporary "that it casts serious reflection upon the standard of ability and intelligence of the general body of missionaries, and can be used by opponents to belittle missionaries." And, it may be added, their work. The matter which has caused so much unfavourable comment can only be regarded as an anti-British feeling on the part of those who, by the nature of their calling, should be above any semblance of what may be termed politics, and should be actuated at least by charitable feelings. headline: OUR TRAMS
text:
Significant indeed is the fact of the running this morning of the lower level trams. The moral effect on the Chinese community cannot be denied. It is acting as a tonic. Little knots of people a street corners watch the successful running of the cars with keen interest. The Manager of the Tramway Company, who was noticed in charge of one of the cars, and those who are assisting in this most effective measure of counteracting the action of the men who, of the workers, were the first to "down tools," are to be heartily congratulated on what they are doing. With reasonable care there should be no breakdowns. Those who live in the Eastern portion of the city have now no possible sort of complaint on the ground of effective transport arrangements. In this respect the initiative of the Hotel Co., with its bus service, should not pass without recognition.

Whilst the centre of the town may suggest an air of unreality, it is in other parts that "Business as Usual" may be said to be very much in evidence. This morning coolles were noticed cleaning the tram-lines to make progress of the cars more easy. The motor-break down equipment was seen to be in charge of Chinese. But perhaps best of all, was the sight of the reclamation workers going about their lawful occasions as if nothing unrestless happening.

headline: APPEAL TO LORDS. / U.S. MILLIONAIRE AND SUPER-TAX.
text: Raised for the first time in the House of Lords, questions relative to the position of absentee shareholders in British companies in respect of super-tax were further argued in the case Harry Payne Whitney v. The Commissioners of Inland Revenue. Mr. Whitney, a New York millionaire, and his wife, a daughter of Cornelius Vanderbilt, held shares in a company carrying on business in the United Kingdom. headline: Market Day in Florence.
text:
In the Piazza Signoria they found themselves jammed in a huge, gesticulating, heaving throng, who jostled and swore and laughed. Farmers in heavy red homespun coats, with yellow fur collars turned up to their noses; women with loudly-protesting chickens tucked away under their arms; business men vainly trying to pass, pushing and thrusting with their shoulders; children scrambling in and out or dodging in front of the slowly-moving horses. "E.e.e. yup!" Crack! Crack! "E.e.e. yup!" E-e-e yup." from the impatient drivers. The dusk, when it fell, was a thing of beauty, calm and very translucent. It came to Florence from the outlying hills, from the still more distant mountains. A tinge of afterglow lingered round it, like a smile on a thoughtful face. It cast its spell over people and buildings, mellowing, blending, welding together, melting them into its lovely whole, making them part of itself. The huge crowd still rocked from side to side, but its laughs ter seemed to have grown softer. It was slowly dispersing down the darkening streets, wandering in groups of looks and threes into the neighboring Traitorie. Farmers and their wives climbed into ancient carts, with crates of lowls tucked away under their seats. "Avanti!" Crack! Crack! "Avanti! E.e.e. yup!" The spell of the dusk had lifted. Dogs long imprisoned in the crowd, tacked their freedom. A child began to wait. Some girls, arm in arm, strolled along the Piazza, barcheaded: "The Piazza was gradually finding itself again," stretching its arms in relief. A star came out over the Palazzo Veochio. A truly amazing coincidence but, none the less, true.

A large crowd of strikers have congregated at Sumchun and it is reported that a party of sight-seers, Chinese clerks, still at work but desirous of seeing what things are like on the border, received a rather hostile reception when it became apparent that they were not new recruits. The clerks are said to have contented themselves by watching from British territory whereupon imprecations and threats were hurled at them from across the railway bridge. Revenue Officers at Hongkong whose duties are in the ordinary way confined to in-coming ships are now dealing with ships going out, thus enabling the police to concentrate on in-coming boats. The police have thus been enabled to prevent undesirables from entering the Colony. Interviewed by a Chinese reporter regarding restrictions on money and valuables taken out of the Colony, Mr. Lloyd stated that jewels and diamond rings can be taken out of the Colony by their side passenger. The Chinese banking institutions conducted on the line are carrying on with the line on normal time the time the line is Suzanne's Easy Win.

At Wimbledon for the British Open Lawn Tennis championships the weather was glorious but hot. With two Anglo-French ladies' semi-finals being decided, it was ladies' day. The centre-court spectators were packed like sardines at 1.45 p.m. and there had been a queue since 7 a.m. It was a brilliant scene with multi-coloured parasols and gay, summary toilettes. Five-shilling tickets were selling outside for thirty shillings.

In the ladies' singles semi-final, Miss Joan Fry beat Madame Billout 6-2, 4-6, 6-3.

The 19 year old Miss Fry made her first appearance on the centre-court and received an ovation. Taking the first four games she kept a fine length. Madame Billout netted frequently and double-faulted. The second set was characterised by good rallies. Miss Fry led 8-1 but Madame Billout squared 8-3 and then with a series of amazing side-liners took the set. Madame Billout in the third set played to Miss Fry's backhand but the latter was very sound; Both thereafter concentrated on the baseline but Miss Fry won by her superior speed.

The queen arrived at the start of the Lenglen v. McKane match. In the semi-final of the ladies' singles, Mlle. Suzanne, Lenglen beat Miss K McKane 6-0, 6-0.

Miss McKane only played as well as Mlle. Lenglen permitted her. She was outclassed and was often caught on the wrong foot. Mlle. Lenglen wore a flame coloured bandeau, was at the height of her form, the essence of grace, very speedy and agile; when she came up to the net it was a signal for the end to a rally by a spectacular kill.

In the fourth round of the men's doubles, Borotra and Lacoste (France) beat the Britishers Hunt and Berger 6-3, 6-3, 6-1, thus entering the semi-final.

Also in the fourth round, the Italo-Hungarian combination, De Morpurgo and Dekehrling, beat Randolph Lycett and J. O. Anderson 5-7, 5-7, 6-4, 6-8, 6-8 and thus meet Borotra and Lacoste in the sem-final.

The unaccountable downfall of the Australians was a sensation. They went to pieces after the third set. It was largely the victory of Morpurgo whose service was brilliant, though both Continentals fought very hard for every point. Anderson developed an under-hitting tendency and Lycett was weak in volleying. [J. O. Anderson is one of Australia's best players. R. Lycett is an Australian who has been in the Homeland for some years; he is better at doubles than singles.] In the third round of the men's doubles, Hennessey and Casey (U.S.A.) beat Barclay and Crole Rees (Britain) 8-10, 6-3, 6-3, 6-4. Hennessey and Casey won on hurricane services. Their weakness in other departments was obvious. Hennessey wasted many shots by netting and out driving. Barclay was rock-like in his steadiness and varied his services puzzlingly. Crole Rees was inconsistent overhead.

De Morpurgo and Miss Ryan defeated J. D. B. Spence and Miss Volyer in the third round 6-4, 7-5, the Italian's services were again he dominant factor.

J. Borotra and Mils Langlen entered the semi-final of the mixed doubles, defeating J. Gilbert and Miss McKane 6-1, 6-2.

In the concluding centre court match, Borotra and Susanne Lenglen were not extended. Borotra was marvellous in his speed and terrific smashes at the net where he was almost imposed able to pass. He overhauled Mlle. Lenglen. The holders (Gilbert and Miss McKane) were out-played throughout.

headline: JUSTICE AND FAIRPLAY.
text:
Sir Oracle hath spoken. That oracle is David Z.T. Yui, General Secretary of the National Committee of the Y.M.C.A. for China, who has the temerity to address an open letter to the public dealing with the situation in China and a possible way out of the tangle in which the Chinese students and rioters have got themselves and the Chinese nation.

Montgomery, Ollerton & Co. 10, Des Vœux Road Central.

The letter is not worth repulsion in full. Some of the points therein do not coincide with facts. Some of them raise issues which cannot be settled by means of an "open letter" to the public. Condensed, his plea is merely for a special commission of inquiry to be appointed jointly by the British and Chinese authorities. He praises the Chinese for their "love"

CUBIC YARDS OF EARTH MOVED PER DAY BY OUR STEAM ROYEL EQUIPMENT

"love of fairplay," which should not stand in the way of Chinese being on the Commission. Lastly, he suggests an invitation to "some other fair-minded nationals" to join them on the Commission which he proposes to create.

Evidently Mr. David Z. T. Yui realises that the Chinese students, rioters, and strikers have done China the worst turn for many a long year, and that it is time to do something constructive to stay the rot. That is the impression gained from his penultimate paragraph in his "open letter," which reads as under:—

May we pause for a moment to think of the terrible hardships and sufferings which we are imposing upon ourselves, the amount of self-sacrifices to no good, the real dangers to peace and order not only in the Far East but in the entire world, and the tremendous damage to the international friendships involved? Do we not desire to free us from all these at the earliest possible moment? We believe without doubt that it is altogether within our power either to prolong and aggravate the tense enough situation or to clarify and end it within a very short time. Are we not wise, just, courageous, and large-hearted enough to choose to do the constructive and fundamental and therefore more difficult-ish? That admission from an educated Chinese—“the terrible hardships and sufferings which we are imposing upon ourselves”—is worth noting in any discussion of the situation. Likewise the Chinese gentleman in question believes that it is “without doubt within the power of the Chinese either to prolong and aggravate the tense enough situation or to clarify it and end it within a very short time.” If Mr. David Z. T. Yui would go a step further and endeavour to inculrate some of these rational ideas into his compatriots in Shanghai and Peking, he would be performing a meritorious service for China. Propaganda of this kind is really more required in the big central of China than outside them. Let him get on with the good work in this direction alone, and leave international issues arising out of what he terms “the tragic event” or may go to be senior berwer China and the interested Power in the hours.

The Government in the Lord. If the Prime Minister ever has occasion to demonstrate to one of his young men that none of us is indispensable he need only conduct the Minister concerned to the House of Lords. There, till his recent death, Lord Curzon held undisputed sway and few, if any, members of the Upper House looked for the emergence of a comparable party leader within a few months. The prevailing exception was that it would take two men to fill Lord Curzon's place —Lord Salisbury's almost aggressive virility coupled with the mellowing influence of Lord Balfour. Mr. Baldwin thought otherwise, however, and none who has listened to the Earl of Balfour leading the House of Lords can doubt that his appointment to the senior post, at the age of 77, has been fully justified. I have watched him digest a Foreign Office dossier on a question relating to Persia apparently oblivious of the debating questions addressed to him on the subject; then fold the bundle, grasp it with his coat lapel in characteristic fashion and deliver a reply delightful for the tracery of humour running through it. A day later Lord Balfour was speaking for nearly an hour, again without notes, on the complex problem of European and native in Africa, ending with the announcement of a scheme for the establishment of an Imperial Research Committee to examine questions of Empire development on the lines of the Committee of Imperial Defence with which he himself has had so much to do. Indeed, the new Committee is undoubtedly his own idea and was adopted by the Cabinet as soon as he brought it forward: The Government, therefore, remains well-equipped in the House of Lords.

headline: DELIBERATE ACT. / UNFAITHFUL CHINESE EMPLOYEE / SNATCHER BIRCHED.
text:
A plea for leniency failed before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest at the Central Magistracy this morning as His Worship considered that a Chinese who had fraudulently converted money from his employers to his own use had acted according to a deliberate plan with intent to defraud and not on sudden impulse.

Defendant was employed by a Chinese firm. He pleaded guilty to obtaining $50 by a false chop from the Netherlands India Commercial Bank and to attempting to obtain a further sum of $340 in the same way. On the second occasion the Bank became suspicious, the Police were called in and defendant arrested. His plea was that he needed the money to send to his mother. Sentences of six and three months' hard labour, respectively, were imposed.

Sentence of two months and ten strokes with the birch was meted out to a Chinese, aged 27, who admitted snatching a gold hair pin from a Chinese lady.

headline: MEAT SUPPLIES. / PLENTY OF BEEF IN HAND. / PORK HITCH.
text:
Plenty of beef is to be had today in the local markets but no pork. Upon enquiry of the Food Controller the “China Mail” was informed that the hitch as regarded the selling of pork had not yet been overcome. There was plenty of pork and there was no trouble about killing but the stalls refused to have anything to do with the retailing of it.

The objection to retailing does not, however, apply to hawkers, crowds of whom are to be seen selling meat and vegetables outside the very markets where the embargo seems to be in operation.

headline: COUNTY CRICKET / LATEST RESULTS
text:
Last year the Home country cricket season was spoiled to a considerable extent because the weather did not permit matches to be finished even in three days. This year it appears as if the fashion is being set to complete three-day matches in two days. This morning, more results come through and there was none that could be described as a real surprise.

For reasons which need hardly be explained, the championship table has not been published in the "China Mail" for the best part of a fortnight. To-day the table is given again. It will be seen that Yorkshire have firmly entrenched themselves at the head of affairs and they will take some beating. The "Tykes" were successful in 1922, 1923 and 1924. This season they have exceeded all expectations, so far dropping only four points when Lancashire led them on the first innings. On the other hand, Lancashire—who were tipped by Pelham Warner as the winners this year—Surrey and Middlesex have been taking points from one another.

With Yorkshire's big lead interest is liable to decrease and they will have to lose at least two matches outright to make the competition exciting again.

Since the table was last published, there have been a few changes. Through Surrey losing badly to the champions and Middlesex bringing off a victory over Notts at Trent Bridge, the Oval team drop below the Lord's team. The failure to Middlesex and the loss of first innings points to Lancashire have cost Notts fifth place as Kent move above them.

headline: WORLD CRUISERS
text: A difficult section of an attempted all-round-the-world cruise in a thirty-foot cutter was completed by the arrival in Hong Kong of Captain Otto Prahl and Mr. Emil Euler who left Shanghai on June 7. The boat, which flies the German flag, was bought and fitted out at Shanghai and Captain Prahl, who has spent on it much time and money is determined to accomplish the cruise if at all possible. The occupants of the cutter have had an adventurous time since they left Shanghai and many repairs have had to be effected on the way owing to the ravages of the element. Anchor and chain were lost early in the voyage and when these were replaced a high wind carried away two booms and the chronometer ceased to function. At Swatow a member of the party decided to abandon participation in the project but the other two carried on and experienced very much weather between Swatow and Falking the booms and the uplift and the who may be called the Cinderella's of the competition—have kept at the head of affairs not counting the 'big six' of Home cricket. Essex beat Middlesex at Lord's early in the season and Northamptonshire have been consistent against the weaker fry. Leicestershire and Sussex have disappointed when their 'talent' is reckoned up.

headline: REGISTRATION
text: hitherto responsible for lesser skilled work had been (unknowingly, of course) re-engaged by the police as coolies to relieve the situation at the docks and godowns occasioned a certain amount of resentment. Those upon whom devolves the duty of selection among the crowds of coolies daily congregating at the police headquarters in the hope of being assigned work at the appointed scale of wages consider that they are entitled to more confidence in their ability to select between the good and the bad sheep. Their claim is not without justification in view of their long experience of that particular type of Chinese mentality—a glance at the hands and features and an experienced officer would probably be able to tell at once whether a man was, for instance, a dock hand or a scavenger, coolie. But such methods are after all not infallible, and unless some scheme of registration is introduced there will always be the possibility of strikers from a poorly paid service seeking more remunerative work which in addition guarantees them police protection on the spot. Such a scheme of registration might even be extended to more highly skilled grades of labour for the purpose of distinguishing strikers and workers. Certificates, with photographs of their rightful owners attached, might be deemed impracticable; but something certainly ought to be done to draw a distinguishing line between those who are helping in this time of crisis and those whose presence is but a burden.

It is said that in 1918 a certain Government—Department frequently addressed envelopes to "Lloyd's Coffee House, Royal Exchange, E. C." The Royal Exchange had no obvious connection with an obscure little coffee house, in Great Tower Street, at the end of the 17th century, owned by one Edward Lloyd. Lloyd was a man of remarkable gifts, combining, journalistic ability with commercial enterprise. The result of his life-work is the great institution named after him, which is a byword in our language, and one of the most important insurance undertakings in the world. The cups of coffee sipped by the seventeenth century merchants over their news sheets, have, given place to luncheons in the Captains' Room, and the suggestion that this sanctum should be profaned by the overcrowded clerical staff, made it evident to the Members that Lloyds would have to migrate. As a result the King has just laid the foundation, in Leadenhall Street, of one of the most imposing buildings in the new London which is now rising around us. Designed by Sir Edwin Cooper, it will cost over one million pounds. Lloyds underwriters paid a larger sum for the "Lutine" Bell, which is sounded when news of a shipwreck is received. By an interesting coincidence the name of "Lutine" was brought up last week in an Old Bailey trial. The "Lutine" was captured from the French by Admiral Bacon in 1799, and later was loaned from the Admiralty, and sent, with £1,175,000 in bullion, from Yarmouth Broads to Hamburg. She mysteriously disappeared in the Zuyder Zee. Lloyds underwriters paid up at once, and in less than two weeks, the precious freight was again on its way. Divers have only succeeded in obtaining from the wreck some £30,000, a few cannon, and the famous bell.

headline: DOSSERS' TRIAL
text:
In the Mixed Court before the Chinese Magistrate and the British Assessor, Mr. Fischer, Counsel for Mr. and Mrs. Dosser, applied for at least a fortnight's remand on the grounds that the first charge (of making preparations to commit a hostile action against certain Foreign States) was incomplete and did not specify the countries; likewise the second and third charges were incomplete because no dates were mentioned.

[The'second and third' charges were of possessing literature likely to cause a breach of the peace and menacing the order of the Foreign Settlement.]

The Court replied that the Shanghai Municipal Police was an international body whose duty was to protect all nations. Therefore the objections would be overruled.

Mr. Fischer then challenged the Court's jurisdiction, pointing out that since the Revolution the Consular Body had appointed the Chinese Mixed Court Magistrates and entirely controlled the Mixed Court, consequently the Chinese Government did not recognise the Mixed Court as in Chinese Court; while by the Sino-Russian agreement of October 1924, Soviet citizens in China must be tried by the Chinese Court. Therefore the Mixed Court had no jurisdiction over the Dossers.

The Court again overruled Mr. Fischer's objection, the British Assessor stating that he had the most definite instructions from the Consular body with regard to hearing all Russian cases, criminal and civil.

Mr. Fischer's third plen was that he had not received all relevant documents from the police. The Court replied that the documents which he had not received would not be admitted for hearing to-day.

Inspector Yorke gave evidence of arrest, and described the documents found in the luggage of the accused, also a telegram which Dosser handed to the Captain of the steamship Mantua, informing the Soviet Consul at Shanghai that he was de-tained in Hongkong to be forcibly deported to Shanghai, and adding an urgent request that Peking should be informed. The Captain refused to wireless this message. The hearing was adjourned until Monday.

headline: "LABOUR DUPES."
text: Commenting on Chicherin's attack on Lord Birkenhead a leading article in the "Daily News" remarks that it does not know the value of Chicherin's denials regarding the Communist intervention in China. The main difficulty in the controversy about the question of propaganda is doubt as to how far the Soviets can control it even if they wished to do so. A “Times” leader says that the causes, the extent, and the true character of the movement in China may be broadly ascribed to the contracts of the civilisations of East and West, which the progress of the world has rendered inevitable. A limited but influential class of Chinese, educated on Western lines have become acutely sensible to its existence. Upon this sensibility Bolshevism is playing with its accustomed flexibility. As the British Empire is admittedly the first principal bulwark of historic civilisation against the onslaught of world revolution, it is essential to the survival of Bolshevism that Muscovite politicians should direct the movement in China more particularly against the British, while assuring their Labour dupes in England that the Chinese agitators are revolting against Foreign Imperialism and Foreign Capitalism. The Times says that though the industrial conditions in China are shocking, the real difficulty in the lack of a Government in China able or not have very anxious to enforce reforms in China

At Wimbledon in the British Open Lawn Tennis Championship, the final of the ladies' singles, Mlle. Suzanne Lenglen beat Miss Joan Fry (England) 6-2, 6-0. [Last year Suzanne Lenglen gave up towards the semi-final stage on doctor's orders and Miss K. McKane won in the final. This year Mlle. Lenglen defeated the English lady easily. Miss Joan Fry is one of the younger British players who came to the front this year by virtue of beating Miss McKane in one of the smaller championships before Wimbledon.]

There were extraordinary scenes. The queue since dawn was enormous. The weather was showery. The final was delayed 25 minutes owing to rain.

Miss Fry scored only 22 points. It was remarkable that her hitherto wonderful forehand was made to appear weak though her reputedly weak backhand was very sound. Suzanne was almost motionless and kept her opponent running to and fro on the baseline by superb placing. Miss Fry's wonderful nobility was a feature of the match. She kept up rallies but Mlle. Lenglen eventually made her over-hit and Miss Fry was at her mercy in the second set. The sets occupied 15 and 12 minutes, respectively.

In the semi-final of the ladies' doubles, Mlle. Lenglen (France) and Miss Ryan (U.S.A.) beat Mrs. Beamish and Miss Clarke 6-0, 6-2. [The winners meet Mrs. Bridge

The ladies' doubles match was very tame. Suzanne played with her usual excellence: Mrs. Beamish and Miss Clarke were outclassed.

In the semi-final of the men's doubles, Jean Borotra and R. Lacoste (France) beat De Morpurgo and Kehrlinger 11-9, 7-9, 6-1, 6-1.

This was a fierce battle of volleying with all four at the net. Borotra was once hitting the ball clean through the net; the referee awarded him the point. The fact was not discovered till the end of the game whereupon a new net was erected. Borotra and Kehrling stood out in their play; the former sometimes smashed from the baseline. The pace slowed down after the gruelling first and second sets with the continental pair deteriorating. Lacoste served brilliantly throughout.

It appears that.Borotra's through-the-net shot would have given their opponents the first set as the latter were leading 5-4 and 40-love.

Also in the semi-final of the men's doubles, John Hennessey and Ray Casey (U.S.A.) beat Brugnon and Cochet (France) 7-5, 5-7, 9-7, 6-4. [In America last year, Hennessy beat Borotra, G. L. Patterson and B. I. C. Norton. Casey is somewhat like McLoughlin, the first American tennis "Comet." He is making his debut into international tennis.]

The American v. French match was a ding-dong struggle. The first four games went against the server; thereafter Cassey got into stride with his hurricane service and the games went to 5 all. The second set was almost a repetition of the first. The third set produced brilliant net-play, with racquet to racquet volleying. The fourth set was won from 4 all. Hennessey excelled in his forehand and Cassey in service; the French were superior in overhead work.

headline: Hongkong, Monday, July 6, 1925.
text:
6 a m. to 8.30 a m.

2 p.m. to 3 p.m.

The extension of the cars to Whitty Street—right through the densely-packed Chinese quarter of the city—must be conceded an event—of no slight importance. The tram workers were the first to come out—without giving notice, it is again emphasised—paralysing in a second an arm of service much used by Chinese and foreigners. The limited service begun a week ago has had a moral effect amongst those living in the Wanchai district; and the same is likely to be the case with those living in the central and western district. Foreigners with spare time on their hands, might do worse than take a ride to Whitty Street and back to town. For one thing they will obtain a refreshing and cooling, ride; they will help to fill rather empty cars and encourage the Tramway Co., but above all they will show to those who raise wondering eyes to the sight of passing cars, or stand and smile in a knowing manner, that the foreigner is capable of taking his troubles—his unsought troubles—smilingly.

headline: RED PROTEST. / INCIDENT ON POLISH FRONTIER.
text:
M. Chicherin has sent the Polish Minister a Note protesting against the incidents on the Polono-Soviet frontier, demanding immediate measures on the part of the Polish Government to secure real inviolability of the frontier and the formation of a mixed commission to investigate the incidents.

The Soviet reserves the right to claim indemnity for damage during the alleged attack. The following: "Letter to the Chinese Residents of Hongkong" is sent by a reader who signs himself "An American Friend."

With reference to the above, Warsaw says a Soviet patrol kidnapped a Polish Lieutenant who was on a tour of inspection; two brother officers burned a Russian frontier post as a reprisal; both will be punished and as the Soviet protest—is—couched—in-moderate terms no serious consequences are expected.

A · London cable of July 3 stated:—

Reuter's correspondents from Moscow and Warsaw send conflicting versions regarding the fight on the Russo-Polish frontier between guards on June 28, each accused the other of invading their respective territories. Warsaw correspondent declares thirty Russians were disarmed and interned, whereas Moscow's asserts that the Polish force burned down the Soviet frontier post.

headline: APPEAL TO REASON
text:
LETTER TO CHINESE RESIDENTS

SOME PERTINENT FACTS

You are now living under the fairest government in the world. This is no ill-considered statement and if you have visited other countries and studied their government you must admit its truth. There is no place under the sun where anyone has as much personal liberty as here. You can carry on your life and trade with the minimum of governmental regulation and restriction. You are guaranteed and you receive absolute justice without a suspicion of discrimination on account of race, creed, colour, or condition of life. Your customs and religion are respected without interference of any nature. This colony is administered by a set of men who have made a life study of the science of government; without question they are men of education, probity and sound judgment. They and their predecessors have turned a barren rock into a beautiful healthy spot with a superb system of roadways, excellent sanitation, adequate schools and free hospitals. In all of this you share equally yet taxes are so low that they are comparatively negligible.

And yet you listen to cries of British Imperialism! Fraternalism if you will, paternalism if you must, but not Imperialism in an invidious sense. Do you think you might obtain equal benefits in republics such as France or the United States? Though a citizen of the latter country, I am regretfully forced to tell you that you would not; it is not that the American friendship for China is not sincere, or that you would be discriminated against, but not even its own people have the privileges you receive here. If this be true, what are you doing to assure a continuation of your unique condition? You are alive to the fact that this community cannot exist without trade, principally with South China, and if Bolshevism conquers in Canton, depression will follow here with destitution, misery and want in its wake. The burden will fall on you far more heavily than on the foreigner who can transfer his sphere of activity elsewhere.

There is not a single thing that the Hongkong Government or a member of this community can do to settle the Shanghai or Shameen incidents. The unprovoked walk-out cannot assist the settlement, cannot hasten or retard it. Except for a slight inconvenience to some foreigners, this strike appears to be principally directed against you; surely you must realize that in many ways you are the ultimate losers. The time has come for a show of sanity; a firm courageous word from you will stop this silly procedure at once. The Government has guaranteed you safety and you are convinced that you can trust its guarantee. You know or you can easily find out who these cowardly agitators are you alone can curb their activities; you can kill the silly canards passed among the ignorant here and widely quoted in China. Are you willing to protect your future? Your choice is clear—do you wish peace and prosperity or chaos and penury? Do not listen to hard-brained missionaries; pay no attention to irresponsible, poorly posted politics in America and France.

headline: OBITUARY.
text:
It is with regret that the "China Mail" records the death of Inspector Peter Angus, an efficient and courteous officer, exceedingly popular with his fellow officers and men and well-known and respected by many other than police circles. The respect in which he was held was evidenced by the large attendance at the funeral yesterday afternoon. Death took place early in the morning.

Inspector Angus had been in Hospital for two months and underwent an operation two weeks ago for internal trouble. His condition had given cause for anxiety but the news of his death came as a great shock to many. His age was 51.

The greatest sympathy is felt for Mrs. Angus, daughter, and three sons, a factor which adds even greater poignancy to their bereavement being that arrangements had been made by which the family was to leave for Home very shortly. The deceased's pensionable service was complete a year ago.

The late Inspector Angus was a native of Edinburgh and at the age of 23 he left the Glasgow police for the Hongkong Force. At the time of his death he was Divisional Inspector of the Water Police Station, Tsimshatsui.

The Rev. G. R. Lindsay, of St. Andrew's Church, Kowloon, officiated at the funeral yesterday afternoon when the coffin, draped in the Union Jack, was drawn to the cemetery by a number of police sergeants and followed by large contingents of European, Indian, and Weihaiwei members of the Hongkong Police Force. headline: GOLD MEDAL.
text:
HIGHEST REWARD FOR AMUNDSEN.

Amundsen and his companions have arrived by air from Horten. They were accorded a most enthusiastic welcome. The Polar fliers' aeroplane was escorted to Oslo by five Army and five Navy aeroplanes all of which descended into the harbour to the accompaniment of salutes of the fortress.

A Norwegian cruiser, vessels of the British Naval Squadron now visiting the port and steamers in harbour sirened the people aboard. Crowds ashore cheered, the streets of the city were gaily decorated.

Amundsen and his party received a cordial reception from President Storting, chairman of the Oslo Municipality.

The aviators subsequently drove to the Palace where the King presented Amundsen with a gold medal for a patriotic deed, the highest distinction only held by two living persons.

The other members of the party were decorated with the order of Stoslay.

headline: MR. GODFREY ISAACS
text:
GREAT ORGANISER AND ADMINISTRATOR.

KILLED BY OVERWORK.

Mr. Godfrey Charles Isaacs, whose death, at the age of 59, is announced, was a brother of the Earl of Reading, Viceroy of India, and possessed the same remarkable energy and almost unlimited capacity for work. It was, indeed, his very energy that brought about his death at a comparatively early age, for he died a victim to overwork. The fourth son of Joseph M. Isaacs, the head of a London firm of fruit and ship brokers, he was educated at Eton and at Brussels and Hanover Universities, after which he joined his father's firm. His activities entailed a good deal of Continental travel and he acquired a wide knowledge of foreign affairs and languages, as well as of the intricacies of modern business methods.

After his retirement from the firm, Mr. Isaacs interested himself in business at home and abroad, and his remarkable powers of organisation and administration induced Mr. Marconi in 1910 to offer him the post of managing director of Marconi's Wireless Telephone Company, Limited.

Mr. Isaacs accepted, and under his energetic direction the company rapidly expanded into an organisation of world-wide importance. The signature of contracts with the British Government made it, indeed, in a sense a national institution.

headline: TIRELESS ENERGY
text:
But the evolution and direction of a great commercial undertaking—which brought him many personal triumphs—imposed a strain that could not be borne indefinitely even by a man of his almost tireless energy. He had been in the habit of working 14 hours a day, and during the Great War an additional strain was imposed on him as the directing force of a system of communications of vital importance to Britain and to her Allies.

For years Mr. Isaacs had sacrificed his personal leisure, his recreation—he was a great lover of music—and his health to the keen sense of duty that kept him at his desk, and he confessed that for 43 years he had not taken a holiday.

"G. C. I. was a genius," is the opinion of one who was closely associated with him. But he possessed also that capacity for translating his genius into action which has marked so many of the world's successful men.

For some years his health had been causing anxiety to his friends, and in November last it gave way completely. He resigned the managing directorship of the company and was succeeded by Mr. F.G. Kellaway, a former Postmaster-General.

“I ought to have known what would be the inevitable result,” he said, recalling his strenuous years of work. “If I had allowed myself a proper amount of rest and recreation, and had taken my golf regularly, I believe I could have gone on for a long time. It is a mistake to pursue work to the exclusion of everything else. In all the years I have been in business I have never gone home without a great pile of correspondence to attend to, and even at home urgent telegrams and telephone calls follow me.”

He retired to the country to rest, play golf, and enjoy his favourite hobby, music.

"All I want for the moment is sleep, rest, and peace. I may not be away a year. With sunshine and sleep my restoration to health may be merely a matter of months."

But he had left his rest too late. Mr. Isaacs leaves two sons. Mrs. Isaacs, as Mme. Lea Perelli, was prominent some years ago as an operatic artist. Among other parts she sang Santuzza in "Cavalleria Rusticana" at the London Opera House.
