headline: HOME CRICKET.
text:
ONE BEHIND DR. GRACE.

Many cricket enthusiasts in Hongkong have been arguing, so I am informed, over the number of centuries in first-class cricket standing to the name of J. B. Hobbs, the Surrey professional and All-England player.

On Wednesday this week I stated that his total was 125, which is one behind that of Dr. W. G. Grübe whose record of 126 has stood for some years. This is correct, but the details I gave were wrong. I said that up to the end of last season Hobbs had made 110 three-figure scores in first-class cricket; that he made four more in Australia; and that he put up 11 at Home this season.

Now for, the correct figures. "Wisden's Cricketers' Almanack," says that Hobbs had 110 centuries at the end of the last English season. To a friend who has proved his contention beyond doubt, I am indebted for the following. In the first, second, and third Test Matches in Australia last winter Hobbs made one century in each match. His only other three-figure score in the M.C.C. Tour was made against the Australian Juniors at Sydney which, as my friend points out, "cannot possibly be ranked as first-class." Therefore the total when the present season began was 113. Up to about the end of June Hobbs had made 10 centuries. Since then he knocked up three figures in one of the Gentlemen v. Players matches and the last century was against Kent at Blackheath, the result of which was published last Wednesday. Therefore the total to date for this season is 12. Added to 113, the total becomes 125, which is one behind Dr. Grace's 126. Accordingly Hobbs needs one more century to tie and two to establish a new record.

In this connection another friend has reminded me that Hobbs will put up another record if he gets two more centuries this season. The most hundreds made in one season is 13, a feat accomplished by Mr. C. B. Fry in 1901 by T. Hayward in 1906, and "Pat" Hendren in 1923. As Hobbs already has 12 centuries this season, two more would make his aggregate 14, which would be another record.

For statistic faddists I have also looked up the following:—Hobbs is a batsman who will take all kinds of chances when he has passed a hundred and his side is not in need of runs, and it is not surprising that his name does not appear under many headings in the records. Not including this season he has made four centuries in succession, this being in 1920. Other records up to the end of last season include an opening partnership of 352, with Hayward. for Surrey in 1909—by no means the highest as the best is 554 for Yorkshire in 1898—and another of 323 runs, with Rhodes, against Australia in 1911-12. Hobbs has never scored 3,000 runs in a season, his highest aggregate being 2,827 (in 50 innings) in 1920, nor has he ever topped the Englisha batting averages.

Of those who are still playing, C. P. Mead, the Hampshire professional, has the next highest number of centuries, viz., 80 up to the end of last season. Next come W. G. Quaife with 68, P. A. Perrin 65, F. E. Woolley 63, and J. W. Hearne 56.

W.P.C.

headline: POWERS AND CHINA
dateline: London, July 23. Washington, July 23. London, July 23.
text:
JOINT DECLARATION ON OUTLOOK.

According to the “Daily Telegraph’s” diplomatic correspondent Britain, America and Japan have virtually agreed to the text of a joint declaration dealing with the present outlook in China, re-affirming the readiness of the Powers to assist China to realise her reasonable aspirations and undertaking most sympathetically to consider an early settlement of outstanding issues. It points out that at present the lives and property of foreigners are being threatened and apprehensions are even entertained, in some quarters, lest a movement should materialise to deprive the Powers of their rights under existing treaties. It hoped that such apprehensions are unwarranted, but as long as these disturbing conditions continue, they must necessarily impede the desire of the Powers to express active sympathy with Chinese national aspirations.

Formal acquiescence of the Japanese Government in the American plan on the subject of China has so advanced the negotiations that officials here believe the project will be ratified by all Governments concerned.

headline: HANKOW INCIDENT.
text:
CHINESE ARRANGE. PEACE INTERVIEW.

FIVE POINTS TO SETTLE.

On the initiative of the Chinese authorities an interview took place this morning between the British Consul General and the Commissioner for Foreign Affairs with a view to calming public opinion and securing a local settlement of the Hankow incident.

The Commissioner submitted five points for consideration.

Points 1 and 2 referred to the protection and defence of the Concession. It was agreed, in principle, that a system of cooperation should be devised between the British and Chinese authorities with a view to the Chinese Police and Military supplementing the Concession Police in the event of serious trouble.

Point 3 referred to the compensation for Chinese killed and wounded on June 11 and was reserved.

Point 4, desiring the removal of Messrs. "Butterfield's" Sikh watchmen from the native city, was reserved.

Point 5 required an assurance that there will be no further mal-treatment of Chinese by the Concession Police.

The Consul General expressed willingness to issue warning notices of the necessity to refrain from violence but pointed out that corresponding notices by the Chinese enjoining good behaviour and non-resistance to police authority were desired.

headline: A Chinese Report.
text: Tuchun Hsiao Yiao-nan has telegraphed to Peking suggesting that the first five points of the Hankow incident be discussed at Hankow and the last seven at Peking. The Chief Executive, Tuan Chi-jui, has referred the suggestion to the Foreign Affairs Committee for consideration.

headline: AFTER 42 HOURS.
text:
PROGRESS OF RESCUED

FALSE NATIVE REPORTS.

Various rumours were current during the week as to the fate of the 13-year old Chinese girl who was rescued from the ruins of Po Hing Fong early on Sunday morning after having been entombed for 42 hours.

The vernacular papers stated on Tuesday that the girl died the day after her rescue. According to the report, the cause of death was attributed to the girl having been given too much aerated water and discuits so soon after her enforced starvation, which brought on a swelling of certain organs! This report was later contradicted with an explanation that another girl of the same age died at the Tung Wah Hospital; and that a mistake was made in assuming that it was the rescued girl, Hung Mui, who had died.

Another rumour which had gained currency was that the girl's leg had come into contact with a body had had to be unputtered dying to blood-poisoning setting up

In the account of the rescue which appeared in the "China Mail" on Monday, it was stated that the girl was progressing favourably, and that according to the hospital authorities her injuries were not of a very serious nature. This progress has been maintained as a "China Mail" representative ascertained last evening at the Tung Wah Hospital, where the girl occupies a separate room. The girl's leg was wrapped in bandages, and she stated that she felt great pain in the knee, which was swollen and stiff. The swelling was apparently inevitable after her release as during the period of her imprisonment, a beam, pinned her leg down above the knee and stopped the circulation of blood. This in a way was fortunate, as she would otherwise have bled to death from the wounds in the lower part of the leg.

This girl is of delicate build, and the trials which she had to undergo have rendered her wan and thin. Since her rescue she has been kept on a special diet, and it is hoped that she will gradually regain her strength as she recovers from her injuries.

Put to her it was gathered that she was in total darkness the whole time and very little air found its way into her "prison." She stated that loud sounds of digging and voices reached her from above, and she had been shouting for a long time before she was heard by the workers.

As has been stated in the previous report, the girl's mother was killed in the disaster.

headline: HARBOUR CHASE.
text:
CHARGE AGAINST A BOATMAN.

EUROPEAN'S COMPLAINT.

A Chinese boatman was charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy this morning with using obscene language.

The complainant, Mr. E. L. Stainfield, stated in evidence that he was travelling by the "Star" ferry from Kowloon to Hongkong on Saturday afternoon and in the middle of the harbour the accused used an indecent expression after posting himself at the rear of a passing junk. Witness later engaged a motor boat and in company with his wife and Mr. W. Anderson of the Naval Hospital overhauled the junk near Arsenal Street. Witness stated that the accused jumped into the harbour as soon as he boarded the junk and repeated the expression used.

Accused denied that he used the alleged expression, and explained his fall into the sea by stating that he was assaulted by the complainant and pushed overboard.

The case was adjourned until to-morrow for the examination of other witnesses.

headline: TO-DAY'S WEDDING. / BURLING—HILL
text:
St. John's Cathedral was the scene of a pretty wedding this afternoon, the parties being Miss Gwendoline Hill, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. G. S. Hill, and Mr. W. J. Burling, son of the late Mr. and Mrs. Burling.

The Rev. G. T. Waldegrave officiated.

The bride was given away by her father and looked charmingly in a dress of white satin and ivory silk lace, the veil and orange blossoms. She carried a bouquet of roses.

Her attendants were Miss Gladys Brock and Miss "Doreen Spanton" bridesmaids, who were attired in mauve morocain dresses with hats to match and whose bouquets were also of roses.

The bride's mother wore a dress of nigger brown Paris crepe with silk lace to match and brown hat.

After a reception at the Hong- kong Hotel the happy couple are to leave for Repulse Bay where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's travelling dress is of saxe blue Paris crepe with hat to match.

The presents received were numerous and valuable.

headline: UNANIMOUS DECISIONS. / YESTERDAY'S STRIKE MEETING PACKED
text:
The City Hall was filled to over- flowing yesterday before the hour at which the Community Meeting was due to com- mence and a move was therefore made to the Theatre Royal where here, again, the capacity was taxed to its utmost. The meeting was characterised by absolute unanimity. Governor

The Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak, Chairman, was greeted with loud cheers on rising to address the meeting.

He referred to the fact that this was the second time in less than three years that the (Colony had been called upon to face a strike which was bound to have disastrous economic effects on the Chinese and on ourselves. The workers did not want to strike. The memories and discomforts of the last strike and the non-fulfilment of false promises by the labour unions were too fresh in the memories of most of them to do so. Yet, at the bidding of alien agitatoffs from Cantori and as the result of intimidation they fled in terror and for five weeks we have been dealing with the consequences. The resolutions were proposed not in any spirit of antagonism to our ancient Chinese friends, but with the sincere belief that by the eradication of the Bolsheviks from their midst lies not only the hope of international salvation in all dealings with China but the preservation of her own rights and country from utter destruction. (Applause).

"1. It is recommended that no wages be paid for June to returning strikers and that careful revision of terms and conditions be made upon their re-employment."

No Weakness. In support of this resolution I may state that in the first place the law says it is unnecessary to pay any wages for June, and that you can even recover damages from the servant who has left without warning. In the second place I know—and I think I may fairly say that I am authorised to state—that the principle of the Government institutions throughout the Colony, be it the Civil Government, the Army or Navy, is that no returning striker will be employed unless he is absolutely essential, and that in that case he will only be employed on a lower grade than that at which he left. (Applause.) Far be it from me to advocate a policy of retaliation, but as I have said before, this is the second strike within three years. The settlement of the last strike was responsible for very many servants and employees going out. In the usual British way we were a little soft and a little over-just and generous in the settlement which was made on that occasion, and we hoped it might never occur again. It has occurred again, and without any desire to be vindictive, I think that the Colony ought to see that these strikes cannot recur without the consequences being placed upon those who provoke them. (Applause). I have already stated, and I believe to be a fact, that those who left our employment, were the dupes of a spirit of intrigue which brought them out, and might possibly have brought them out in spite of anything and everything we could have done in this Colony to prevent it. Nevertheless, ladies and gentlemen, I think it is desirable that we should register our feeling upon that point with the spirit certainly of justice and possibly of mercy, but with a little less mercy than we registered last time, because it was abused (Applause).

Mr. W. S. Bailey said: Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen, I have much pleasure in seconding this resolution. These strikers have done their utmost to paralyze our trade. No business or Colony can exist indefinitely without adequate income. The economic losses of both European and Chinese businesses are alike very heavy and must seriously react on staffs employed and on wages paid for some time to come.

There appears no just cause for this strike, the employees having absolutely nothing of which to complain. British firms, especially British shipping firms, the most liberal and generous of employers, distributing yearly thousands of dollars gratuity to employees, together with other benefits—these firms have been discriminated against and all their vessels abandoned while rival vessels under the Chinese flag and paying lower wages have been allowed to run.

Businesses in the Colony, both Chinese and European, have lost money right through this stricken land. and have paid salaries and wages not from profit but from capital, thereby reducing the earnings of these businesses and preventing them, however-willing-they-maybe, from giving employees in future the same liberal terms and gratuities as formerly.

An attempt has been made to starve us out financially by cutting off our sources of income. That attempt has only failed of complete success by the splendid unselfish work of our own people, our own residents of all races, and by the loyal service of the many Chinese workers who have stood so faithfully by us. With such complete unity and cheerful determination as has been shown we could never be beaten, but surely our first duty is to reward those who have so worked for us and not the strikers whose action has so deeply injured both us and them. (Applause).

There may be some who would formerly have dealt even more lawlessly with strikers, but later developments have certainly warranted their adoption of a stronger attitude in this respect. By leaving without notice strikers have dismissed themselves and are liable to forfeiture of a month's pay in lieu of notice and to prosecution, and it would be due to us and due to our loyal employees that returning strikers be dealt with thus strictly according to British law, otherwise there could be no security for future traders or workers of any nationality in the Colony. But justice should be tempered with mercy and we ask only the cancellation of the striker's wages for June, although we cannot forget that the mercy shown by us after the strike of 1922 was apparently mistaken for weakness on our part.

Let us be merciful as expressed by the resolution, but strong and ust. just to ourselves, to our lives and families and to our loyal workers who have so suffered and ill suffer by this strike.

I know ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to support our laws and Government and support the interest of our own people and our loyal helpers by voting unanimously for the resolution. (Applause).

The resolution was carried with enthusiastic unanimity.

headline: Registration.
text:
The following resolution was then before the meeting for consideration:—

"2. This meeting requests the Hongkong Government to cooperate in the establishment of a voluntary system of registration of office employees and domestic servants."

The Chairman briefly stated that he believed in a voluntary system of registration, not a compulsory one which would involve penalties on both sides in certain eventualities.

The Hon. Mr. H. W. Bird said: Mr. Chairman, Ladies and Gentlemen, in rising to second the resolution now before the meeting, I do not for one moment suggest that if the registration of domestic servants becomes an accomplished fact, it will prove to be a panacea for all our troubles, but it is my honest belief that it would be to the general benefit of the community if registration were undertaken on the right lines. We should think of those who are coming after us and endeavour to make this type of so-called strike, where the actual strikers had no grievance, more difficult. Although I do not suggest that such registration would stop strikes, it is my opinion that it would be a partial safeguard. It would be a form of combination on the part of employers to counter the combination of employees, and that is recognized all the world over as equitable. (Applause).

The objections to registration which I have heard expressed, and read of in the papers, do not strike me as very serious. I cannot see why it should cause discontent. All of us have been accustomed ever since the war began, to obtain passports with our photographs in duplicate. We submit without a murmur to the indignity of stating our ages, our physical disabilities, our distinguishing marks (Laughter)—why should Chinese domestics take these matters more to heart than we do? (Applause).

There is in force at the moment compulsory registration for Europeans, by the police authorities, in connection with essential services. All-domestics—at—home have a form of registration under the National Insurance Act. Moreover it is the custom here with a number of the large business concerns to register all their Chinese staff who are in permanent employ. Furthermore, all indentured labour is registered through the S.C.A., and I am told there is never a murmur against it.

As regards finger prints I do not consider that is absolutely necessary. The photograph in duplicate, one on the card to be filed at the Bureau, and the other on the card held by the domestic, is all that would be necessary, and it could be made an offence punishable by a fine for any one to tamper with a registration card.

Because the law has been in- operativa in Ceylon, as we are told, only seems to me to show that it is no longer necessary there, and should such registration become law in this Colony it will probably die a natural death if it is found there is no longer any call for it.

To my mind it is necessary that this registration if carried out should be done by the Government. There is no reason for it to be a financial drag on the Colony, for the fees for registration should far more than pay for the personnel of the office. A registry office run as a private concern does not appeal to me. I have had some experience of such offices, and from the attitude of some of them it would seem that it is to their interest for one to change one's servants as often as possible. (Laughter.)

As regards an employer giving a servant a bad character without due cause, I think it will be found that people are too afraid of the law of libel to make that objection a serious one.

As regards written characters these are useless unless accompanied by a photograph, as one never knows whether the character produced was ever written for the individual who presents it. The ones use dare generally written by a resident who has long since left the Colony, so that there is no means of verifying same.

Ladies and Gentlemen, I am still to be convinced that there is any valid objection to the official registration of servants save the trouble entailed and if it is to the interest of the community that it should be undertaken, then that objection should be over-ruled. With these remarks, Sir, I have much pleasure in seconding the resolution now before the meeting. (Applause).

Mr. J. Russell (Taikoo) and Mr. L. M. Whyte contributed to the discussion, the former suggesting that registration should be arranged by the Residents' Associations. The Chairman said that he did not think there was the slightest hope of legislation being introduced at the present time but if it was proved that there was sufficient interest in voluntary registration the Government might be encouraged to go further with it.

The resolution was then put to the meeting and carried unanimously:

headline: China Business.
text:
Following was the next resolution to be considered:—

That in view of the extremely heavy losses being suffered by all British traders here and in China, present negotiations should be accelerated as much as possible, consistently with retaining all treaty rights, but it is the unanimous opinion of this meeting that no discussion concerning revised customs tariff or extraterritoriality should be begun whilst anti-foreign disturbances or boycotts continue in any part of China or Hongkong.

The Chairman briefly referred to the seriousness of the situation for merchants throughout China, and Mr. J. Owen Hughes, in seconding, attributed the present trouble to forces outside the Colony. Residents of long standing knew full well the worth of the Chinese merchants, and in this trouble it could not be made too clear that we had no quarrel whatsoever with the Chinese. The resolution was carried unanimously.

The fourth resolution read as follows:—

4. That having regard to the recent criticisms in the House of Commons concerning emergency regulations enacted by the Governor in Council to deal with abnormal and threatening conditions, this meeting desires to express the approval of the entire foreign community and all right thinking Chinese, of such regulations as being absolutely necessary under the circumstances, and the entire confidence of the community in the actions of the Governor throughout this crisis, and is of opinion that his firm attitude and strong measures have thus far prevented a serious outbreak of violence.

The Chairman referred to the attacks made by the Labour party at Home on the Emergency Regulations passed by the Hongkong Government, the sacrificing of his home leave by His Excellency the Governor and the measures taken by the Governor-in-Council to deal with the situation. Bolsheviks Elements. The Hon Mr C G Alabaster, in seconding the resolution said that it was only right that because His Excellency at the beginning of the strike informed the community of Hongkong that he and his Government were ready to stand shoulder to shoulder with the law-abiding elements in this Colony, that the law-abiding elements in this Colony should now tell the House of Commons that we stand shoulder to shoulder with him and his Government. (Applause):

Mr. Alabaster referred to the attempts that had been made by an external Government for the utilisation of every anti-foreign element and every Bolshevistic element that could be laid hands on to destroy the very foundations of life and business in the Colony. It was necessary for the Government to counter these measures and the distribution to loyal employees of threatening leaflets, and it was hardly to be wondered at that paid intimidators who had been foiled by the mere introduction of the emergency regulation relating to the imposition of the cat, should telegraph to the Labour Party in London to protest against the cruelty of the Hongkong Government.

Mr. W. H. Bell supported the resolution and it also was carried unanimously.

Following is the fifth resolution then before the Council:—

5. That this meeting desires to point out to the Home Government that the Shameen-Canton question will probably require to be dealt with, separately and in consultation with the Hongkong Government, whose interests are equally vital with those of the Foreign Office in all South China questions, especially as the present Canton Government will probably refuse to recognise any agreement reached with the Central Government in Peking. The situation in Hongkong and South China has been entirely provoked by Bolshevik influence and intrigue and is aggressively Communistic and violently anti-British. This meeting therefore urges His Majesty's Government to take strong and immediate action to protect British lives, property and trade in Hongkong and China by at once increasing the strength of the China Squadron in river gunboats and aircraft-carriers, and that, additionally, a battalion of British troops, should be transferred to Hongkong at the earliest possible moment for use here or in any part of China as emergency requires. Finally, it respectfully urges that His Majesty's Government should immediately inform the de facto Government in Canton that unless it withdraws its support, of the attack upon British interests, that they will be regarded as having entered into a state of hostility with the British Government.

In bringing this resolution forward the Chairman said that the Home Government must recognise that the problems of Canton and Hongkong could not be divorced, and if the Canton problem was referred to Peking without consulting Hongkong, it would be ludicrous. and farcical. (Applause.) The people at Home must realise that though the Shanghai dispute might be settled, the Bolshevik Government of Canton would probable refuse to recognise anything done in Peking. In the settlement Hongkong could not be left out. (Cheers.)

headline: Sir H. Pollock's Views.
text:
Sir Henry Pollock, in second, spoke of the operation in the Colony and in China of the hidden hand of Bolshevism and asked if we were going to allow the interests which had been built up here to be destroyed at the bidding of the Bolshevists. Giving reasons why the Chinese community had confidence in the fairness and protection of the Hongkong Government, the speaker said that the Chinese, from the highest to the lowest, from the richest merchant to the humblest coolie, have a special office, the Secretariat for Chinese Affairs, to which they can send in requests for the removal of any supposed grievances or injustice. Those requests, if in the Chinese language, are translated into English, and in many cases finally reach the Governor in Council; and I can testify personally, as a Member of that Council, of many years standing that the most careful and impartial attention is paid to the representations of all Chinese, however humble their station. Furthermore the Hongkong Government is in constant consultation with the Chinese members of the Legislative Council, who take great pains to ascertain the general feeling of the Chinese Community in this Colony. The periodical large influxes of Chinese with their families into Hongkong in times of disturbance in the neighbouring Republic of China afford yet further proof, if any such be required, of the confidence of the Chinese people in the fairness of protection of our Government. In short, Hongkong is a splendid and wonderful example of the

operation, and of the harmonious working together of the British and Chinese residents under the reign of law and order, which has been maintained here during the past 85 years by civil Servants of the highest integrity and impartiality. Are we going to allow this splendid British Colony which has been built up with such patience and labour and our commerce and credit not only here but all over China to be destroyed at the bidding of Bolsheviks? Are we going, at Bolshevik dictation, to give up the results of the strenuous labour of three generations of our countrymen in this Colony and in Shanghai and other parts of China, the labourers of our Civil Servants, Municipal Councillors, Ministers, Consuls, Commissioners of Customs, merchants and others?

In conclusion, Sir Henry said that it seemed clear that, in default of joint action by the other Powers concerned, the duty rests upon Great Britain, in the interests of civilization and of the national reconstruction of China upon correct lines to take action by herself, if necessity arises.

headline: OUR TELEPHONES. / SIR GEORGE GIBB'S VIFW9.
text:
At the thirty-first ordinary general meeting of the Oriental Telephone and Electric Co., Ltd., on June 19, extended references was made to the recent change in the company's interests in Hongkong. Sir George S. Gibb, the chairman, who recently visited the East, after expressing indebtedness to the Local Advisory Committee of Singapore, under the chairmanship of the Hon. Mr. V. Gibbons, for their useful work and assistance, and referring to the steps to be taken in regard to the introduction of message rates, for which he hoped soon to be able to get Government sanction, said:

I will now pass to the affairs of the China and Japan Telephone Co. These appeared to be in a critical state with the line of due to expire in 1930, and the exchange buildings and equipment so anticipated and, inadequate that it was no longer possible to provide for the growing demand for telephones. The public and the Government were becoming increasingly hostile and instent that something should be done, as previous negotiations had proved quite abortive. Under these circumstances the board decided that I should go to Hongkong to deal with the situation. I arrived there on January 8, and spent 42 days in close negotiation with the Government, the Chamber of Commerce, and a local syndicate headed by Sir Paul Chater, who weq represented in the negotiations by Mr. Tuggart, a man of great ability and experience and reasonable views. In the result we arrived at the agreement, of which the principal terms are summarised in the report now before you, and which is to be submitted for approval to the shareholders of the China company at their meeting to be held after this meeting.

NEW HONGKONG COMPANY. A new company is to be formed and registered in Hongkong with Sir Paul Chater as chairman, and with two nominees of our interests on the directorate, having a capital of five million dollars. We sell to that company our assets and undertaking and stores in Hongkong, free from demonstrive debt, which remains as our liability, as from July 1, 1925, at a dollar price equivalent in sterling to £192,000 at the 48% charge of 2s. 4d. per dollar, plus the value of all stores, and we

get payment in fully-paid shares of the new company of the nominal value of $1,400,000 and the balance in cash. I think that there is no doubt that the new shares, of which the public issue is expected to take place about the end of this month, will be readily subscribed and will soon command a substantial premium. Indeed, I understand that the issue price is to be at 10 per cent. premium.

The new company will undertake the necessary extension and re-equipment of the telephone system and will raise the additional capital required for the purpose, and of course we will have the right to participate in new issues to the extent of our holding, which is equivalent to 28 per cent. of the capital.

Arrangements have been made with the Hongkong Government for the grant of a new licence for a period of 50 years. The rates of charge are fixed at $108 per exchange line, or about 30 per cent. higher than the existing authorised maximum, as a temporary measure. These rates ought to enable the company to pay 10 per cent. dividend from the commencement. But when more capital is spent on the necessary improvements and extensions they will have to be revised, and provision is made for this in the new licence. The basis of future revision is that the rates, which, if not agreed, are to be settled by arbitration, shall always enable the company, after reserving 10 per cent. on the book value of plant and equipment for depreciation and $50,000 for general reserve, to pay 12 per cent. Surplus profits, after payment of 12 per cent. dividend, are to be divided equally, one-half being applied to the payment of extra dividend up to 15 per cent. and the other half to reduction of subscription rates.

It was decided at a meeting of the Sanitary Board yesterday, to close two wells in Cheung Sha Wn, the water from which had been certified insanitary.

Asked by Mr. Wong Kwong-tin how long the wells had been in existence, the Chairman said he supposed for a great many years, probably a century. Mr. Wong Kwong-tin signified his agreement with the closing of the wells providing the standpipes were used.

The interesting statement was made in the course of discussion on another matter that the Board had no power to prevent a Chinese Bank from melting subsidiary coin, which process resulted in sulphur gases penetrating premises above. The Bank could only be approached through the owner of the premises who could be asked to bring pressure to bear on them. It would not be difficult, said the M.O.H., to take steps to carry the gases from the furnaces above the roof. On his proposition it was decided that the Board require the owner of the premises (No. 67, Des Vaux Road) to take steps to prevent the escape of gases in any way except by means of an efficient flue carried above the roof.

headline: PROPOSED CASH GRANT TO / EMPLOYEES.
text:
The management and operating, staff in Hongkong will be transferred to the new company, and we had to consider what to do about pensions for the European members of the staff up to the present time. Some of them have served 14, 15, and 20 years, and you will realise that the pension question is an important matter in connection with service in the East. Most substantial companies have pension or provident funds. It is rather remarkable that the China company did nothing about this in earlier years, as they have for many years paid good dividends. However, we must take things as we find them, and it was not until the year 1923 that the company reserved £2,500 as a nucleus for some pension provision. We have now £5,000 in reserve, which is inadequate as a basis for pension provision in respect of service with the old company if it were merely to be kept and accumulated at interest until the transferred staff retire. The staff have had a very difficult time during the last few years, when the public have been clamouring for telephones which could not be provided owing to lack of accommodation, and some of them had also very hard work in connection with certain valuations that were made a few years ago.

It is only right, therefore, that we should do something for the staff. I ascertained from them that instead of holding up any sum, within the range of practical consideration, to be applied hereafter towards pensions on retirement, they would prefer to get a cash grant which would enable them to subscribe for shares in the new company and thus give them an interest in its promising future.

What we intend, therefore, to submit for the approval and sanction of the shareholders at the China company's meeting is that the reserve of £5,000 shall be utilised, with the addition of £3,000 as a cash grant—that is, a total cash grant of £8,000—for distribution amongst certain members of the staff, the detailed distribution being left to the discretion of the directors. This grant will be in lieu of all pension expectations. I may mention that £500 of the proposed grant is for distribution amongst certain non-European members of the staff who have given long and faithful service in responsible positions.

headline: EXPERTS' VIEWS.
text:
REASONS FOR PO HING FONG DISASTER.

WALL PREVIOUSLY EXAMINED

In the course of his evidence and examination at the resumed enquiry yesterday into the Po Hing Fong "disaster, Mr. A. W. Tickle," Executive Engineer, P.W.D., said that it was his opinion that the cause of the ground was the presence of springs, percolation from the hills above, and aggravation due to heavy rainfalls. The percolation was probably from land south of Caine Road and had probably been going on for some years.

Nothing protected, the site of the new Police Station from a direct fall of rain. From a photograph produced, witness could not show anything protecting it from accumulation of water from Seymour Road, but he knew there was a lateral channel in Hospital Road which would carry an accumulation of water down to the Disinfecting Station. He considered this protection sufficient. As to the site itself he did not suggest that the trenches thereon would hold it watertight. The trenches would take some and the rest would be deflected and go into the Disinfecting Station. He suggested that practically no water would go on the site.

The Hon. Mr. H. T. Creasy, Director of Public Works, was called. He said the question of the position of the new building for No. 8 Police Station was carefully considered and it was decided to erect it. Further back from the retaining wall. This was because the retaining walls were known to be over 20 years old. Careful examination of the walls, particularly the number one wall, the bottom one, was made. No sign of any movement could be found but as an actual precaution it was decided to build further away from the wall. The number one wall was built into solid ground; it was not built and then filled in as some retaining walls were. Behind it was hard isintegrated granite. He examined the site in December, 1923 with the engineer, Mr. Lowick, who pointed cut-all essentials to him. Witness approved the scheme.

headline: Old Cracks.
text:
In reply to the foreman, the Director of Public Works said there were old cracks in the walls but there was then no sign whatever of recent movement. Mr.

Decomposed granite deteriorated slowly under the action of water. Asked if he considered it a good security for building, witness said it was a very usual strata on which buildings were constructed in Hongkong.

Asked if he had complaints as to drainage there, witness said he had heard from Police parts since the heavy rains that Gardens and the roads in the vicinity had been flooded. This was only during heavy rains, and was aggravated by neglect of scavenging.

Capt. Arthur: Would you consider the drainage in that area to be sufficient?—It could be improved.

Witness further said he did consider rebuilding the wall but considered it unnecessary. It would mean building a wall from In Mi Lane 70 feet high which was unnecessary, undesirable and very expensive. There was nothing to show, when he examined the walls, that they were not as good and sound as any retaining wall in the neighbourhood. The new Police Station building would have been no extra thrust on the wall. It was a good wall and well built, but of course the standard of walls nowadays was much higher.

The P.W.D. have taken over the work of excavation and the removal of the remaining debris from the site of the collapse. Digging operations yesterday were carried out by coolies under police supervision without anything of value or further bodies being taken from the ruins.

headline: BORDER INCIDENT.
text:
WOMEN KITILED BY LABOUR

OFFICIAL RIPONT.

boatlord of Chinese women by a Chinese Labour picket stationed on the borders is that two women were killed and two drowned. The report is by the Assistant Superintendent of Police, New Territories, to the Captain Superintendent of Police, and is as follows: "Many and various stories have been circulated regarding the incident, the last information received by me and reported to you being to the effect that one woman only was shot. This information, as reported, appeared to be correct but, having caused further enquiry to be made, I find that the real facts are as follows:

About 3 a.m., July 16, 1925, eight Chinese women went to Man Kam To Ferry, from Heung Sai, Chinese Territory, with the object of crossing over into British Territory. The reason for their crossing at that hour was to carry away some baskets of icepets which had, the previous evening, been conveyed to the British side of the river and there left.

The woman, on arriving at the river, went and untied the ferry boat which was moored on the Chinese side of the river. Some of them got into the boat and others were engaged in pushing the boat off when they were hailed by a Labour picket and ordered to return.

The women refused to obey the order, whereupon the picket fired, killing instantaneously one woman and mortally wounding another. The latter was subsequently carried to Heang, Sai village, by her daughter (also in the party and who escaped uninjured), and there died. Two other women jumped into the river and were drowned, their bodies having not yet been recovered. The remaining women, three in number, were arrested by the picket and sent next day to Canton. They were subsequently released, one woman returning to Heung Sai on July 20, 1925, and the two others on July 22, 1925.

The women all came from Heung Sai, Chinese Territory, the description of them being as follows:—

— Name... unknown. Wife of Cheng Xwan, Heung Sai village. Shot and instantaneous-by-killed.

2.—Surnamed Wong, Wife of Cheng Kwan, Heung Sai village. Did at Heung Sai. 3.—Kwan-Mui-daughter of No. 2. Escaped uninjured. Carried her mother back to Heung Sai.

4.—Name unknown. Wife of Cheung Chui, Heung Sai village. Jumped into the river and was drowned.

5.--Ah Kit, daughter of Cheung Chui, Heung Sai village. Jumped into the river and was drowned.

Name unknown. Wife of Cheung Cheuk-wan, Henng Sai village. Taken prisoner to Canton and released and returned to Heung Sai. July 20, 1925.

7.—Name unknown, Wife of Cheung Pak-chun, Heung Sai. Taken prisoner to Canton and released and returned to Heung Sai. July 22. 1925.

3.—Name unknown. Wifs of Cheung Yam, Heng Sai. Taken prisoner to Canton and released and returned to Heng Sai, July 22, 1926.

(Sd.) W. G. GrrnABD.

headline: EDUCATION IN CHINA
text:
WHAT OF THI FUTURE?

Sermon preached by the Rev. W. T. Featherstone, M.A., Headmaster of the Diocesan Boys' School Hongkong, at St. John's Cathedral, Hongkong, on Sunday, June 28, 1925, on Education in China.

1.--The Advantages inherent in the Chinese system of Education.

3.—The Future of Chinese Education.

The Advantages (1) State Education.—The old system of education in China is the oldest system of Government Education known to history. The schools described under the early feudal period B.C. 2357-1122 were state schools. Of these earliest ages Prof. James Legge says Education was state conducted. The importance of generally instructing the people was acknowledged even before Confucius 550 B.C. It is said in the Book of Rites B.C. 1200 "That for the purposes of education among the ancients, villages had their schools, districts their academies, department their colleges and principalities their universities. This, so far as we know, was altogether superior to what obtained among the Jews, Persians and Syrians of the same period. If we may depend upon these records the schools continued to be supported by the state from the Shang dynasty B.C. 1766 to A.D. 706.

headline: Chinese Classics.
text:
(2) The second advantage was the Uniform Curriculum—based upon the Chinese Classics.

When the Chinese records become entirely historical we find that the multiplication table, Arithmetic, Geometry, the Knowledge of the properties of the right angled triangle and the elements of trigonometry were studied. Instruments for calculations, sundials, and instruments for measuring distances were in use. But the principle course of study in the early curriculum was probably the Chinese Classics.

Confucius B. C. 551-478 made a Compilation of the Chinese Classics which have been used from that day to this and very probably used before that date. We have an impressive testimony to the high estimate in which they were held in the fact that when the schools ceased to be supported by the Government in A. D. 706 the Classical course of study had such a hold upon the people that the private schools continued to teach them as faithfully as the Government Schools. It is difficult to overestimate the value of a uniform Curriculum accepted by every school in the nation, for about 3,000 years in creating uniform type of civilisation.

(3) The third advantage was its Democratic Character. Wu Wang, the Founder of the Chow Dynasty 1122 B.C. ordered that in admitting students to degree no distinction should be made between high and low, rich and poor. His son and heir began his education in a village school. Vacations of 45 days were ordered in order that the land might be prepared for cultivation thus allowing students to assist in Agriculture etc. It was also democratic in the appointment of scholars to public officers.

headline: Practical Character.
text:
(4) The fourth advantage was its practical Character — While the Chinese have deemed a knowledge of Reading, etc. desirable, yet they have not deemed it essential to send to school a boy who was destined to work on a farm or in a shop. Consequently the overwhelming mass of the Chinese are almost destitute of any scholastic training. This does not imply that the common people have no education whatever. Professor Parker writes—“We talk about—“Jack” being a handy man he is nothing to the Chinese. The visual exceptions excepted every Chinese knows the time without a watch; can, at a pinch buy, prepare and cook his own food; wash, patch, if not make clothes; judge the weather; till fields, carry a pole, and its load, indicate the North, manceuvre a punt, sail a boat, catch fish, saddle a horse, tackle animals, walk or ride long distances, sleep anywhere at any moment, take no exercise whatever for any length of time—do anything, go anywhere.” We can see the practical side of education in the small boys working as apprentice craftsmen, painting, working in banks as money changers, etc. Moreover, such training was under the supervision of parents; it was and is often now a common life in the open with small opportunity for vice masters and workmen eat together and discuss problems; all these combined keep the number of degenerates down, result in the

more general spread of knowledge than would seem possible among an illiterate people and leads to a comparatively high level of efficiency in the art of earning a living and maintaining the existing civilisation. Thus there are four advantages in the old system, it was State Education, it was uniform, democratic and practical.

headline: The Dangers:
text:
1.—Its Private Nature.—In A, D. 706 there was a serious revolution in Chinese Education. An imperial Edict stated that in future the salaries of the teachers would be paid by the pupils and not by the State. The Government controlled education after it ceased to support it. Private education, generally speaking, is more narrow than State Education, it lessens the respect for the teacher, it makes the teacher subject to the student and the hired man of his patrons; thus it is often commercial and for personal gain.

2.—Corruption.—Early in the Christian era a proclamation was made saying that all persons who gave 177 lbs. of rice towards a Famine. Fund would receive a Literary Degree; later no less than three ranks of degrees could be bought; later still only those who held literary degrees could hold political office. This sale of degrees and offices has continued to a greater or less extent down to the present day and has been one of the prime causes of political corruption in China. There was bound to be official corruption because officials had to recoup their purchase money.

3.—The third danger is the inherent conservatism of Chinese Education. Education with its training in Classical literature and its reverence for institutions which are old, and, with its knowledge of the failure of countless reform schemes, tends, in general to timidity and conservatism. The schools of Egypt rejected Moses, the Schools of Greece rejected Socrates, the Schools of the Scribes and Pharisees rejected Jesus and Paul, the Universities of Europe opposed the Reformation, the leaders of the Church of Rome forced Galileo to recant, the Universities of France opposed the French Revolution, the University of Oxford rejected Methodism but nursed the reactionary Anglo-Catholic movement.

headline: Aristocracy Of Learning.
text:
But in no other country has education been so conservative a force as in China. And the exclusive exaltation of the learned class which created an aristocracy of learning has been much more subtle, insidious and far reaching and full of corruption than for example, the aristocracy of blood in Europe and the rising aristocracy of wealth in America. Thus we see four advantages and three dangers. I suppose it is the dangers of which we are thinking most to-day, the system of Private Education which has bad discipline and corruption, and the inherent conservation which produces stupidity and timidity. In these Strikes we see all these things.

Now let us briefly consider the Future of Chinese Education.

To do so we first of all require an insight or knowledge of its history.

Let me mention a few facts. In A.D. 100 the Chinese knew of the procession of the equinoxes. In A.D. 301 Sun spots were observed.

In B.C. 540 the Chinese had a fair knowledge of Botany, medicine and human anatomy.

In A.D. 286 the Caesarian operation was performed. In the 12th Century inoculation

In or about 926 A.D. the Chinese Classics were printed, that is five hundred years before the Bible was printed.

Between the years 1644 and 1900 China got into touch with the West and during the last hundred years education was more widely diffused. The Jesuits gave excellent scientific training and the Protestants and the Roman Catholics opened Public Schools in many parts of China. Since the Chino-Japanese War in 1894 and the Boxer Uprising in 1900 there has been a great impetus to foreign learning.

In 1901 an Imperial Decree was issued about founding Universities, Schools and Village Schools; unfortunately this Decree had no results and existed on paper only.

In 1905 and 1912 Commissions on Education were appointed. Since 1905 the Education of the Chinese was taken over, nominally, by the Government. From A.D. 706 to A.D. 1905 China had relied on Private Schools.

To-day in China you will find several millions of Scholars in a large number of Private Schools in which, generally speaking, there is a great lack of discipline; secondly, there are about one and a half millions of scholars in the Chinese Government. Schools where there is liable to be�

very often the Teachers' salaries are from three to nine months overdue; and thirdly there are about 350,000 students in Protestant and Roman Catholic Schools.

Those figures are all approximate figures and cannot be regarded as exact. This short review furnishes us with some basis for a forecast of the future development of Education in China.

(1) The future Education will undoubtedly be supported by the Government, it will be democratic and should be practical. While Classical Education tends to a timid conservatism, Education with inspiration has produced such reformers as Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Plato, Paul, Luther, Calvin, Knox, Bacon, Newton, Galileo, and Darwin, and those men of strong personality have received their discipline at the great seats of learning. The hope of China's future rests upon the adoption, gradually, of the opportunity of universal Education maintained partly at Government expense and partly by fees or Scholarships. The fees need only be very small for poor people. In England and America and in the Far East a great mistake has been made during the last fifty years of giving Education too cheaply. Too much has been given for nothing, consequently there has been lack of respect and loss of discipline. The Education in China above all things should be practical; it need not be compulsory. I would advocate a system of part-time schools where a scholar who is doing work could attend for a short time daily. A prospective farmer should not be forced to spend the whole of his time within the four walls of a classroom. Ricsha coolies should not be forced to become cheap clerks, poor people who sleep out of door under verandahs in the hot weather should not be compelled to sleep in stuffy cubicles for the good of their health. We should remember that people are generally much happier if they are left alone and not dragooned so much.

headline: The Second Hope.
text:
The second hope is the introduction of Western learning.

Western learning is at hand, a mental revolution is already in progress; but along with Western Science China must preserve the universal industrial training of her children.

The third hope and by far the largest hope for China is in religious and Christian education. With regard to religion it has been said that the Teachings of Confucius are a Providential preparation of China for Christianity even as were the Greek and Roman Ethics and the teachings of the Old Testament. So we ought to encourage a respect for China's Classics along with a knowledge of our own Religion. This religion of ours, its idealism, its purity, its hardness in that it is hard to live up to its ideals, its strength, discipline and spirit is what it wants to-day.

The almost hopeless mess in which China is to-day is due to the lack of discipline and the corruption in the home, in the school and in politics. For example, small boys are petted and pampered and often for fear of losing face, upheld against the master or quietly removed to another school for promotion to a higher class or to a class with a higher name or to a school called a College,—a mild form of corruption; and thus indiscipline and corruption are encouraged. With all charity I would say that it would appear that the greatest need to-day in China is a Father on earth as well as a Father in heaven who, with resolution and kindness without any semblance of bullying, and that has been our attitude in the past, will show no weakness, no hesitation and no doubt.

Let us pray that there will be no need for any very extraordinary measures and let us, calmly and strongly see to it that we, by our example in big and small things will help these three hopes of Universal Education, of the practical introduction of Western Education and of Christian Education.

It is connected with the Jewish Pentecost, not only in the historical date of its origin but in idea, the Jewish festival being one of thanks for the first-fruits of the earth, the Christian for the first-fruits of the Spirit. In the middle ages the Whitsun services were marked by many curious customs. Among these were the letting down of a dove from the roof into the church, the dropping of balls of fire, rose-leaves and the like. Whitsun is one of the Scottish quarter days, and though the Church festival is movable, the legal date was fixed for the 15th day of May by an act of 1693. Whitmonday, which, with the Sunday itself, was the occasion of the greatest of all the medieval church ales, was made an English Bank Holiday by an act passed on the 25th of May, 1871. So that is why we enjoy a holiday in Hongkong today.

text: To-day is Whitmonday and a holiday. Why? According to that greatest of all reference books, the Encyclopaedia Britannica, Whitsunday, "one of the principal feasts of the Christian Church," is celebrated on the fiftieth day after Easter to commemorate the descent of the Holy Spirit on the Disciple. headline: Child Labour.
text:
It would be interesting to know what has been the moral effect upon the Chinese in introducing ameliorative measures of reform connected with the labour of children in factories in the Colony. The report for 1924 of the Secretariat for Chinese Affairs in this respect, makes pleasant reading. There was some protest when legislation was urged. It would upset the Chinese; it would interfere with production, wages, household affairs, etc., etc. The result has been nothing of the sort. Three hundred children in factories work in safe and pleasant surroundings, in reasonable hours. The great fact is that a considerable number are prevented from doing so until a reasonable year of discretion has been reached. Incidentally this particular report is an interesting evidence of Chinese industrialism in the Colony. There are 28 factories in Hongkong and Kowloon—a fairly large number of seems—given over to the production of such things as knitting, glass, and fireworks. These factories, but illustrate once again the versatility and ability of the Chinese. Those in charge of them are to be congratulated on an evident willingness to promote the construction affecting work in

One result of the Great War has been the abolition of fixed alliances. These, at one time were a common feature of European and international politics. France and Britain allied; Italy and Germany also; then Japan and Britain. The expiry of the latter treaty and its non-renewal seem definitely to have set the seal on alliances generally. This is all to the good. An alliance of two great powers tended to create suspicion and misunderstanding—and worst of all, jealousy. If anything the League of Nations would have an influence contrary to the creation of alliances. In that body could be discussed questions likely to lead to disruption and war and to find a way to lasting peace. The work of the League can be and is being supplemented, by treaties of a peaceful nature. Thus the latest memorandum of the British Government to France dwells on the necessity of suitable arbitration treaties supplementing the Rhine security pact with a view to guaranteeing the peace of other parts of Europe. Here is further evidence of the "come, let us reason together" policy. At this rate we shall soon be realising that the pen and tongue are mightier than the sword.

headline: Deport Them.
text: Portugal has set an example in the matter of dealing with bomb throwers and insurrectionaries generally. A number of these misguided people have been placed on board a cruiser and are now on their way to Portuguese Guineu—“far, far away.” Hongkong's idea of deportation consists in sending undesirables—principally beggars—to Canton which is not “far, far away.” With steamer fares at cut-throat, competitive prices, a return to the happy hunting ground of the beggar is simplicity itself. Why not fix on some other place to which to send these people? A dumping process of such a nature, faithfully and ceaselessly carried out, would have its own moral effect. Swatow, Amoy, Foochow, might be tried as experiments. Caution the next batch of beggars that a reappearance means exile to other and more distant places than Canton, and some good is likely to accrue. Whilst the nuisance is said to be abating as a result of the efforts recently initiated and maintained, there is a suspicion that when the official back is turned, the beggar, in all his dirt and deformity will be back again.

headline: SHREDS AND PATCHES.
text: The Whitsun Whitsun Mysteries were Monday. acted at Chester, seven or eight on each day during the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday in Whitsun week. The drapers, for instance, exhibited the "Creation," the tanners took the "Fall of Lucifer;" the water-carriers of the Dee reproduced the "Deluge;" the cooks had the "Harrowing of Hell." The performers were carried from one station to another by means of a movable scaffold, a huge and ponderous machine mounted on wheels, gaily decorated with flags, and divided into two compartments, the upper of which formed the stage, and the lower, defended from vulgar curiosity by coarse canvas draperies, answered the purposes of the green-room. The performers began at the Abbey gates, where they were witnessed by the high dignitaries of the Church; they then proceeded to the High Cross, where the Mayor and the civic magnates were assembled; and so on, through the city, until their motley history of God and His dealings with man had been played out. The production of these pageants was costly; each mystery has been set down at fifteen or twenty pounds, present money. The dresses were obtained from the churches, until this practice being denounced as scandalous, the guilds had then to provide the costume and other properties.

headline: A FALLACY. That Moths Eat Clothes.
text:
This fallacy is somewhat akin to the one that a thaw bursis the water-pipes, for when a thaw comes, then also comes the inconvenience of burst water-pipes. Similarly, when the clothes are taken out and found moth-eaten, and moths fly from them, the too-ready conclusion is that the moths have eaten them. What occurs is this: The clothes' moths lay eggs on suitable materials, these eggs develop into larvae or grubs, which eat the clothes. The larvae then change into pupae, each forming a tiny cocoon (similar to that of a silkworm) for itself, and after some time the cycle of changes is completed by moths emerging from these cocoons, which may be found among clothes that have been badly moth-eaten. So we see that the moths which fly out on the clothes being disturbed are quite innocent of the harm that has been done up to that time; but if left, they will of course lay eggs, and the resulting larvae will start operations at once.

An entomological friend told us a very amusing experience of his illustrating this fallacy. He gets

his friends to collect moths and butterflies for him, and on calling one day at the house of a fair collector, she showed him a very fine living specimen of the Emperor-moth (Saturala pavonia minor), which she had caught for him. Not knowing how to kill it, she had kept it alive for several days, and, moreover, out of the kindness of her gentle heart, she had fed it. On being asked what she had fed it on, she replied ingeniously, "Oh, I gave it a bit of old rag to eat!"

Some moths do not eat anything, as they have a sufficient store of nutrient to enable them to fulfil their mission in life, after which they die young. Others sip the nectar from flowers, and it is the flowers which open at night that are most strongly scented for the purpose of attracting the moths by their sense of smell, that of sight being useless in the dark.

headline: PLAIN ENGLISH.
text:
At one of the London police- courts the other day a gentleman was charged with drunkenness. What entitles his case to honour- able mention is his defence. A doctor went into the box and swore that "his condition was due to spastic paraplegia." Yet the magistrate was not satisfied. He replied, all too curtily, "What is that?" Possibly he thought there was some confusion: that spastic paraplegia was a phrase devised to test the power of speech of one suspected of inebriety, for which purpose, indeed, it seems worthy of the attention of the medical profession. Possibly he suspected a misunderstanding — for to the mere layman it would seem that spastic paraplegia ought to mean some sort of drawn or contracted paralysis. But it is ever rash to assume that men of science use their technical terms to mean what the words ought to mean. According to the testifying doctor, spastic paraplegia really means "acute nervous exhaustion." Then, said the disgusted cadi, "Why not use plain English?" When the doctor explained that it was "not the custom," the cadi exhorted him to change that custom, complaining that "the medical profession has received sufficient hints from the legal profession as to what is the proper thing to do and they will not take notice." There speaks the bitterness of the man who has had to wrestle with experts in the witness-box. But we depreciate any attempt to make one profession the censor of another. With all respect to the magistrate, we must point out that the doctor's might turn upon him. There is a legal jargon as well as a medical jargon, and the physician may protest that his Greek-like quite as good as the tarrist's Latin. In fact, when some of us did not

some of them reasonably formed, some of them superfluous, perverted, obscure. "Such esoteric vocabularies are always being built up among people who have intercourse and interests a little apart from the rest of the world. Many families have their private slang. Each generation of undergraduates invents some of its own. Any popular game acquires, decade after decade, a mass of peculiar phrases devised by the players of the period. "W. G." knew not the googly, nor Arthur Shrewsbury the cow-shot. Some of these terms are needed to express new things, many of them are mere decorations of language. Even the most learned of the professions and the most austere of the sciences are not exempt from the common human instinct to be decorative in speech. It does not please the expert to call a common phenomenon by a name which common men never heard of. When he has discovered a new fact or invented a new theory he loves to give it a name worthy of his own ingenuity. In general he feels that his dignity is enhanced by talking in a jargon which nobody else uses, as the Meteorological Office derives an exquisite satisfaction from reporting the weather in terms of millibars. Let us not blame him. We encourage him continually. We like our experts to be incomprehensible. When we consult our specialist, we want him to talk in words we never heard before. If he used plain English he would be as disappointing as if he said there was nothing the matter with us. We know at the back of our minds that neither the cause nor the cure of anything is revealed by giving it a name derived more or less estimates from the Greek language. headline: “CHINA MAIL” SPORTS PAGE. / VOLUNTEER
text:
FIRST MEETING A SUCCESS.

The Hongkong Volunteer Defence Corps held their first annual athletic sports meeting on the ground of the Hongkong Football Club at Happy Valley yesterday afternoon, the events being watched with much interest by a large gathering of spectators in the stand despite the counter attraction on the race course. The initial meeting was in every way a success, both in number of entries and in the performances of the competitors.

Among those present were His Excellency Sir Edward Stubbs, who was accompanied by Capt. R. Neville (A.D.C.) and Mr. T. J. Gaisford-St. Lawrence (Private Secretary), His Excellency Major General C. C. Luard, and Commodore A. J. B. Stirling, R.N.

Points were awarded for first, second and third places in the competition for the inter-unit Challenge Cup presented by L.L. Col. L. G. Bird, D.S.O., the Corps Commandant. The units taking part were the Artillery Company, Engineer Company, Mounted Infantry, Armoured Cars, Machine Gun Platoon, Infantry Company, Scottish Company, and Reserves. The Infantry Company won the Cup with 39 points, the Scottish Company being second with 29 points, and the Engineer Company being third with 15 points.

A. Mair, of the Scottish Company, was the outstanding competitor in the long distance races, winning the half mile, one mile and three mile races, and also making a very strenuous effort in the relay race in which he was the last runner twice round the track. D. D. Urquhart, the first runner for the Infantry Company, gave a good lead to his side, and Howell coming in last got home with Mair following behind after he had made up the greater part of the deficit.

G. P. Lammert amassed points for the Infantry Company by winning the 100, 220 and 440 yards races and securing a third place in the long jump.

J. Watson of the Engineers and A. K. Mackenzie of the Scottish did well for their respective units.

Two teams from the Hongkong Police tried conclusions with the H.M.S. Durban and the R.G.A. in exhibition tugs-of-war. In the first encounter the heavy Police team easily pulled over the sailors in two straight pulls. The R.G.A. had a hard fight, securing only one pull in three.

Races for bandsmen and the coolie workmen had special interest to those lining the ropes.

The band of the 5/2nd Punjabi Regiment, under the baton of Mr. L. Larter, gave selections.

His Excellency the Governor gave away the prizes and was given three cheers on the call of the Corps Commandment.

At the first hearing of the Coroner's inquest, the sister of the murdered girl identified her as Grace Blackaller and said she had been the youngest daughter of their father, John Blackaller, who was dead. headline: BASEBALL / PRACTICE GAME TO-MORROW.
text:
The Hongkong Baseball Club has arranged a practice game to be played on the Happy Valley Diamond at 4 p.m. to-morrow, with the team of the U.S.S. Sacramento now in port.

The U.S.S. Sacramento is reported to have good material this season, but have been handicapped by lack of opportunity for practice.

A close game should result and, as this practice game will indicate the possibilities of the local Club, it is hoped that a good crowd will turn out to support the boys. Thursday evenings have been allotted to the nine of the H.K.V.D.C. for practice regularly.

headline: CHOPPER ATTACK
text: A Chinese living at 99 Battery Street, Yaumati, assaulted two women inmates with a chopper and inflicted serious injuries early yesterday morning. After the assault the man jumped from the second floor to the street and was picked up in an unconscious condition. All three were taken to hospital. It is believed that the man had become mentally deranged.

Sir Hall Caine writes to the "Sunday Times" as follows: Sir, —May I claim a little of your space to call the attention of the public to the evil effects of a pernicious practice which is becoming lamentably common in our Courts of Law—I mean the practice of introducing, to the injury of justice and the public conscience, matters that are utterly irrelevant to the issues being tried? A particularly flagrant example of this legal libertinism has just been reported from a London Coroner's Court, and while fully aware of the limitations of my knowledge as a layman, I cannot resist the desire to give expression to my indignation of what I consider a shameful and cruel scene.

headline: THE CORONER'S ACTION

But the irrelevant statement of the mother that her husband, on his deathbed, had asked another person to undertake the guardianship of the child, was found to be untrue, and at the second hearing of the Coroner's inquest this matter, which had nothing to do with the murder, took precedence of all others. First, the sister was recalled to withdraw her statement that the murdered girl had been the youngest daughter of their father, and to say that she had been, in fact, the illegitimate child of their mother, born several years after their father's death. Then the mother was recalled to say that it was not true, as she had said at the previous hearing, that her husband, on his deathbed, had asked another man to take care of the child, inasmuch as he was dead before the child was born. Then a third woman, acting under some obscure and apparently unnatural impulse, was called to say that she was the widow of an entirely independent person, also dead, and that he, not John Blackaller, had been the father of the murdered girl. Then the Coroner himself told the mother of the grave consequences that might have befallen her if, before taking the verdict of the jury, he had not adopted the lenient course of allowing her to correct a false statement she had made on oath concerning the parentage of her child.

headline: INHUMAN, STUPID, USELESS.
text: I confess that my heart tingles with shame to its utmost depths at the thought of this juhuman, stupid, and useless scene in a British Court of Law. I think first of that most miserable mother, against whose character nothing else, so far as I know, has been said, having the dark secret of her lapse of sixteen years before, which she had made a vain and futile and mistaken but pardonable effort to conceal, dragged out of her own mouth in open court, in the tragic hour of her agony, after the shocking murder of her child; and I see her, in her confusion and degradation, stammering out her conflicting replies to relentless questions which served no purpose of justice that the present jury had, for so much as a moment, to take into account. I think next of the dead girl, who may never have known of the shadow over her birth, having it exposed to public view on the first day after her dishonoured death. I think of the Coroner, the representative, for the moment, of the public conscience, warning the tortured mother of the possible penalty of an offence, that of perjury, which, serious as it is, no Public Prosecutor with a sense of legal necessity, and no Home Secretary with a particle of humanity, would have attempted to punish, where it had done nothing to disturb justice and need never have become known. And last, but by no means least I think not only of the cruelty but also of the palpable injustice of the reading in Court of that egregious and mendicious letter which, by manifest implication, cast a slur on the character of the murdered child, and contributed to create an atmosphere favourable to her possible murderer.

headline: A PERNICIOUS PRACTICE.
text: Is it not time that this pernicious practice of introducing at trial matters that are totally irrelevant to the issues being tried, should be most rigorously suppressed? It is not in Coroners' Courts only that the practice prevails. Some recent cases in the High Courts appear to laymen, like myself, to have offered shameful examples of the lengths to which it can go in wrecking personal reputations and corrupting the public mind, without promoting the cause of justice. We have heard a great deal lately, from prominent lawyers, about the duty of putting an end to blackmail by the bravs course of challenging it in the public courts, but persons not wanting in moral courage will rightly reply that before such advice can be of much avail the prosecutor must have some assurance that he will be strucually protected by the judges from the legal muck-taking which too often is late his disbonoured the proceedings it our Courts of law.

headline: Gentlemen—The King!
text:
If there is a fixed pomp about the ceremony of observing the King's birthday, it is but to remind us of the majesty that hedges in the office of kingship. It has been so from time immemorial. The ritual of the observance does not however cloak the inherent simplicity and grandeur of the kingly office. Kings

..... are like stars—they rise, they set, they have The worship of the world.

But if they have not the worship of their own people set and securely fixed in affection, and devotion, they are as nothing worth. It is in the hearts of the people of Britain that the King indeed reigns by right of a conquest, simple, and unaffected, achieved with no apparent effort, but with that spirit that understands, appreciates, and enters into the lives of subjects with a perfect understanding of their own peculiar difficulties and desires. To-day's celebrations will certainly take on a distinction of their own. His Majesty has but recently recovered from an illness that but reminds us that even Kings are human and must pay tribute to the unseen. The King's birthday this year comes at a time when the heir-apparent has concluded a visit to the South African Dominion of the Crown that has been triumphal in its progress and the results of which are as apparent as later on they will be real. A younger son also returns from a visit to another part of the empire, whilst a sailor prince of still younger years remains abroad to cement the feeling that exists between the reigning house and the people of a great empire. Kings have no response; the poet Shelley tells us. Very true is this of our own King, so far as it indicates no shirking of duties, and no lack of interest in all that pertains to the welfare of his subjects. Hongkong, no less than other parts of a far-lung Empire, voices its own royalty and affection in its utterance of the simple but sincere line.

To the Communist Party must be assigned the sensation of the moment. To have smuggled into Britain two of its most noted continental leaders to attend a Conference at Glasgow, in defiance of the Government's restriction, speaks itself of the strength of the movement, and the power and determination of those who control it. How this feat of smuggling has been done, will doubtless soon be revealed. That smuggling into Britain has been going on of Communists generally has been known for sometime. It is alleged that the whole weight of the second International has been transferred from Germany to England. Not only are the Bolsheviks sending their own countrymen to Britain, but they are pressing into their service people who arrive from America travelling with United States passports. It has been found that these people are Russians naturalised as United States subjects. The incident under review is perhaps the most direct challenge which has been made to British authority—an authority which distinctly ordered that no foreign Communist was to be allowed admittance to the country to attend the Glasgow Conference. The Communist peril is directed at undermining the Constitution of the British Empire — at all costs. These "costs" include red revolution which the heart and soul of the Empire detests and is determined to subdue. Nowhere under the sun is there a more just constitution than that under which British subjects live. There is freedom and liberty for all and right means of redressing known grievances. It is not likely that the present Government will sit down lightly in face of the challenge now issued to it. It may be childish to think that a Home Secretary in his own person can stop a British revolution by preventing the Communists of different countries from meeting; but it is not childish to believe that a Home Secretary with a free Government behind him—and better still a free people—will effectively take measures to stop any undermining of such a Constitution as the British people possess, by means of anarchy. It looks very much as if the British Communist Party at any rate has voluntarily committed suicide.

headline: THAT "D——D INDIA HOUSE."
text: An unusual Charles Lamb centenary was celebrated by a distinguished company at dinner at the Inner Temple Hall recently under the chair-manship of Mr. Augustine Birrell, writes the London corres.
