Trouble has broken out on the island of Samos where insurgents have seized government buildings, arrested officials, released prisoners

from the jails, and looted the contents of the State coffers amounting to nearly a million drachma.

Whether the movement is political or more net of banditry on the part of two notorious influential Summan brignnds, the brothers Vafiades, is not yet clear, but it is known the leaders are demanding the resignation of the Greek Government and fresh elections, though this may be more cannotflage.

The Government is determined speedily to crush the outbreak and has despatched a naval squadron to surround the island pending the arrival of the troops.

headline: LATEST POSITION.
text:
Officials, soldiers and gen- darmes from Samos who have arrived at the neighbouring island of Chios report that the insurgents number 450 men armed with captured rifles.

The landing of troops at Samos is momentarily expected.

It is semi-officially stated that armed bands from the interior teck possession of Samos with the object of ejecting the Greek officials and securing a reduction in taxes. They threaten to proclaim Samos an independent principality unless their demands are satisfied.

headline: COTTON NEEDS. / VIENNA CONGRESS VIEWS.
text:
The international "cotton congress has passed a resolution expressing the opinion that the world's statistical position in cotton is such as to warrant an extension of cotton growing wherever feasible on commercial bases; urging the governments of all countries where cotton can be produced advantageously to stimulate development of cotton growing by increasing the cultivated area; creating efficient transport; recogning the construction of irrigation and drainage works such as are being undertaken in the Sudan and India which are the proper means of bringing about an increased supply of cotton; and fervently hoping that all governments will decide on similar works where it is shown the cotton crop will be considerably increased by means of irrigation.

At the final sitting of the cotton conference the chairman, M. Buhler, of Switzerland, referred to irrigation proceeding in India and Sudan and declared that was the best way the Governments could extend cotton growing. He added that the high price of the American product, which was likely to continue, was injuring the welfare of the industry.

headline: SYRIANS
text:
KINGSTON, JAMAICA, June 7. The Governor, Sir Samuel Wilson, is going to England on June 8 for two months leave of absence on medical grounds.

He will discuss with the Secretary of Colonies, Mr. L. M. S. Amery, among other matters, alien immigration which was discussed by the legislature recently, when it was declared Jamaica would be ruined unless steps were taken to prevent further immigration of Chinese and Syrians.

King Victor Emmanuel III. is 55 years of age. He succeeded to the throne in 1900, on the assassination of his father, King Humbert. He married in 1896 Princess Helene of Montenegro.

King Victor took a prominent part in the relief of victims at Messina after the 1908 earthquake.

He is industrious, amiable, and well read.

He led his nation to join the cause of the Allies in the spring of 1915 amid great enthusiasm. His eldest daughter, Princess Yolanda, married Count Calvi di Bergolo, on April 9, 1923.

In May, King George and Queen Mary visited Rome. The King of Italy and the Queen visited London, May, 1924.

headline: HOT TO COLD.
text: The great heat wave which for a week past has made life almost unbearable, suddenly broke yesterday on the eastern senboard. Fatalities from the heat wave and storms totalled about 350. Meanwhile the heat wave continues in the west and middle west.

headline: LEAGUE FINANCE.
text:
TOO MUCH MONEY ON HEALTH.

The Council of the League of Nations opened to-day. Mr. Austen Chamberlain urged economy by the health section whose expenditure was 1,000,000 francs in 1925 compared with 700,000 in 1924.

The Council decided to refer the subject to the next Assembly of the League in September.

headline: GERMAN COLONIES.
text:

headline: STINNES-MILLIONS.
text:
BANKS TO RESCUE.

Reports that one of the Hugo Stines companies is being reorganized recall one of the most remarkable careers in modern industry.

Stinnes, Jr., takes over the general direction, while three banking experts will join the supervisory board for maritime transport and overseas trade.

It is understood that the big banks have guaranteed financial support to the extent of 44,000,-000 reichsmarks. The foreign credits of the firm have still a considerable time to run.

Last week's cables stated that the big banks with the co-operation of the Reichsbank are coming to the rescue of the Stinnes trust with 40,000,000 marks to prevent the complete collapse of the organisation which has encountered a financial crisis allegedly owing to taking up too many short term credits which it has been unable to meet upon maturity.

Hugo Stinnes who died on April 10 of last year was the wealthiest and most influential man in Germany. In 1897 his father, a mineowner, left him a fortune of 9,000,000 gold marks (£450,000). His own fortune just before the war is said to have been 40,000,000 of gold marks. His fortune at the time of his death was estimated at more than 1,000,000,000 of paper marks. In the war Stinnes was the chief contractor for war material, especially iron and steel.

Stinnes owned nearly all the German canal and river steamship lines and a big proportion of German transmarine steamship conpany shares. Together with half a dozen other industrial magnates he controlled nearly all the factories and natural resources of the Rhineland and Ruhr Valley. Several of the finest German hotels were his.

At the time of his death Stinnes group controlled the greater part of Germany's coal, iron and steel supply. The greatest of the Stinnes combines was the Rhine-Elbe Union which produced 16,000,000 tons of coal yearly and owned innumerable smelting and steel works.

When his father was alive, Hugo Stinnes Jr., the eldest of the four sons, who inherits much of his father's acumen, was required to attend every important conference his parent held. Stinnes did this on the theory that if he should die suddenly his eldest son should know what was going on and be qualified to step into the breach.

text:
FRENCH ADVANCE POSTS RETREAT.

The French advance posts at some points have fallen back in good order.

Enemy efforts to perelrate the French lines south of Wergha have been beaten off with heavy losses.

All the prominent Moslems of Fez visited the wounded soldiers to whom they brought many gifts. A collection made in the Arab quarters yielded within some hours 15,000 francs, which the natives handed over to the French authorities in order that the money should be distributed among the wounded of every religion. General Lynutey is receiving from all parts of Morocco messages congratulating and thanking the troops.

SEVENTHEN MEN FACING

Sturgis, Kentucky, June 9. It now appears that seventeen miners may be entombed by an explosion in the West Kentucky Coal Co.'s mine and there is practically no hope of rescuing them alive.

headline: SPEED TESTS
text:
BABIES" COMPLETE CIRCUIT.

Thirty-five out of thirty-eight airmen who participated in the fifth and last circuit of the round Germany flight up to the present have returned to the Tempelhof Aerodrome. The winners of the competition will not be announced for a fortnight.

The fastest speed of the last circuit was attained by Baumer with a 60-h.p. Wright machine of 488 minutes. Two babies completed this circuit in sixteen hours. Loerzer will probably be the winner of the under 40-h.p. class as he has flown the greatest mileage, although he was not able to complete the last circuit through a forced landing.

headline: SOVIET ENEMIES.
text:
THREE DEATH SENTENCES SUSPENDED.

MOSCOW June, 9.

The execution of General Belavin, M. Ivaroff and Madame Kizeczkovska has been suspended. [The Kieff Military Tribunal concluded on June 6, the trial of the members of an anti-Soviet organisation called “Russia for the Russians,” headed by an ex-Tsarist General Belavin, who is accused of military espionage on behalf of Poland. General Belavin and M. Ivancoff, who was an official on the Staff of the Ukrainian Red Army and a woman intermediary, Nina Kizeczkovska, were sentenced to death. Twelve others were variously imprisoned and one acquitted. General Belavin is alleged to have described himself as the ideological enemy of the Soviet and to have admitted the charge.]

The Air Chief Marshal, Sir Hugh M. Trenchard, addressing the Cambridge University Aeronautical Society, said: "Although the Empire is peculiarly and geographically fitted for an air war, surpassing in that respect any other country, I would like to abolish the atmosphere, because the horror and devastation of air warfare outbalances the benefits of civil air services.

headline: EARLIER CABLES.
text: Later information concerning the proposed Security Pact shows the intention to make it absolutely of a bilateral and mutual character, Britain's contribution to the agis of the League of Nations being a guarantee of the existing Rhine frontiers against aggression both from France and from Germany. headline: LORD DERBY'S VIEWS.
text:
Lord Derby speaking at the luncheon given by the Association of France and Great Britain referred to the agreement between M. Briand and Mr. Chamberlain regarding the security pact, and declared that it was absolutely indispensable that France and Britain should cooperate, for if they stood apart it was good-bye to the peace of the world and safety for France and Britain.

Lord Derby added that at the present moment there existed in Britain greater friendship and love for France than had ever been known in their histories and the expression of that feeling was best shown in the Briand-Chamberlain agreement.

headline: LACK OF FUNDS.
text:
GERMAN INDUSTRY'S TROUBLES.1

SHIPYARDS CLOSE.

BERLIN; June 10.

The financial difficulties of German industrialists are reflected in the all round slump in industrial securities on the Bourse.

It is reported that several concerns are faced with a similar position to that of the Stinnes concern and have been forced to throw their holdings into the market.

The offerings are so heavy that securities are not being absorbed even at low prices.

A typical case is provided by the Reiherstieg-shipyards at Hamburg closing down in spite of big orders on account of the lack of fund with which to carry on.

A message from Wezzin states that owing to enemy pressure which resulted in many penetrations of the French line along the Wadizess, the French command decided precautionarily to remove the civilian population of Wezzin to the south. The evacuation was carried out very calmly.

Moscow, June 10.—An aerial expedition consisting of six aeroplanes, including — four — constructed — in Russia, left this morning for Peking in the presence of thousands of people including members of the government. Many other aeroplanes escorted the expedition on the first stage of the journey, the object of which is to survey an air route across Siberia by may of the Gold desert to China. It successful is proposed to form a Soviet Chinese company to establish permanent communication between Burma and China by this route.

headline: SAFER FLYING. / HANDLEY-PAGE AMAZES THE

While A. G. H. The experts were astonished to see the new-comer like a drunken sky-rocket, perform every evolution calculated to end in disaster. He flew tail down and repeated stalling only resulted in the aeroplane slowly sinking horizontally to the ground.

Mr. F. Handley-Page disclosed to the special representative of "The Sun" that the machine was fitted with his new patent "slotted wing," which he proposes shortly to demonstrate in Australia, and which he is also fitting to numerous British commercial and Air.Force craft.

Fokker was the first to congratulate the Air Force test pilot, Bulman, after which Fokker and Bulman proceeded to take part in a thrilling aerial hovering contest.

Bulman, in a half gale, appeared to drift backwards without losing height.

text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail.)

Sir,—I thought it well to call the attention of such of your readers as are thinking of returning permanently to England to a practice of the British Revenue Authorities which may give them considerable trouble.

In a recent instance with which I have been dealing, a public servant invalidated home, was repaid a large sum to which he was entitled from the Official Staff Provident Fund accumulated over a number of years. The Crown Agents, however, by instructions from the British Revenue Authorities, deducted full tax at 4/6d, on this sum when it was paid to my client in England and it was only after a very drastic correspondence with the Revenue Authorities that the amount was refunded in full.

In my opinion such a sum paid to a man who through residence abroad, was never liable to British tax at all throughout the period of the accrual of the fund, is not assessable to British tax, merely because it happened to be paid to him on his arrival in England. In this particular instance, however, my client had not actually become technically resident in England and so the matter was beyond dispute.

To avoid this difficulty, might I suggest that it would be prudent to have any such sum paid over before departure to England as all. But

is actually deducted in the arbitrary fashion indicated above, this should not be submitted to, as in most cases it will probably be found that the Revenue have no right to any such deduction where a fund has been accumulated wholly abroad by a person not subject to British Tax.

The primitive motives maintained halls of justice and temples, the shrines of their shurk gods, poison gods and other deities, and observed a rigorous code. The "Paba" of forbidden net, was violated upon the pinnel of death. The women were not allowed to eat with the men, in fact separate ovens even were used to cool the food of each.

The kings, priests and medicine men exerted absolute control over their subjects, and even the mention of the royal title demanded that the native prostrate himself. They believed they could pray an enemy to death. Infanticide was openly practised, and human sacrifices were not unknown. In their worship they observed a ritual similar to ancient Palestine. Later when whaling ships visited the islands and trades exchanged runs for sandal wood, the natives observed that the white men did not seem to soft from violating the "Tabu," and from that time the influence of the idols and priest began to wane. The arrival of Americans missionaries in 1810 furthered the enlightenment, and the natives accepted Christianity, gracefully. However, many of the old superstitions remain to this day.

He put an end to inter-tribal warfare by invading the island of Ona-upon which Honolulu is located—and forcing the army of Kalankupule over the 1,200-foot precipice of Pali to their destruction. King "Kal" escaped, but was found later hiding in a cave and was offered as a sacrifice to the war-god. This event was followed by many years of peace, but always under the nience of foreign invasion. At one period the Russian flag was raised upon one of the islands. At another, the Bélgians tried to establish sovereignty. In 1848 the islands were ceded to Great Britain, but restored to monarchy by Admiral Thomas the same year. In 1849, the King finally tired of the demands of foreign powers entered into a treaty with the United States. Kalakana was elected king in 1874, and upon his death in 1891 Liluokalani was proclaimed queen, and after a short but tempestuous reign, during which she was tried for treason, a provisional government was created. In 1808, precipitated by the military necessity of our War with Spain, the Islands were finally annexed to the United States. The naval base at Pearl Harbor was established, and the islands provided with important army posts.

headline: Beautiful Scenery.
text: The scenery of the islands is distinctly mountainous, with serrated peaks, softened to velvet effect by the luxuriant verdure in different shades of green to the very summits. The view from the famous "Pali" is one of the most inspiring to be found in the wide world. Beautiful valleys, sugar cane fields and pineapple plantations, the regularity of their rows due to the custom of setting out plants through the holes of specially prepared paper, to preserve the moisture in the soil and protect the young plants from too much rain—the "Liquid Sunshine" which is said to fall in one island "eight days a week." Beyond the valley lie the coral sand beaches and the opalescent sea with its wonderful jade, sapphire and malachite colouring. Even the fish are in rainbow colours, one of the smallest being known as the "Humuhumunukunuku-puoa"—making up in name what he lacks in size.

The gorgeous Royal Ponciana, its flaming red bloom contrasting sharply with the "Golden Shower" of nearby Aenigins. The "Pride of India," with its mist of lavender; Flamboyant hibiscus everywhere, Ie-Ie evines with their yellow "Candles" surrounded by whorls of scramlet leaves. The Lehue tree with its shower of pink blooms. Giant fern trees, the Apo-Ape, the Kukui and Roa tree, the Algaraba and weird Hau Tree and the gobelin Bayan. The mysterious sword plants and ghostly night blooming cereus. The pungent ginger flowers, and more delicate Ylang-Ylang, Stepehinotis and Plumaria ningle in creating a heavy increase in the air. Palms in great variety, fenthery Australian Pines, great olusters of bamboo, banana, breadfruit, avocades, mangoes and paw-paw, guava, oranges and limes, growing in private gardens as well as upon the plantations. A garden spot indeed, the "Tula," disintegrated laveroals of the soil that responds munificently to the frequent showers—more sprinkles of "Dry rain," inevitably terminating in rainbows, and upon moonlight nights that mystic phenomena of the South Sen Isles, the Lunar rainbow with its delicate pastel primatic rays.

text: Kilnuen, with its crater six miles in circumference, of most recent activity, is located on a slope of Mona Loa four thousand feet above the sea, but nearly ten thousand feet below the summit. Mona Ken, a few miles distant, enjoys the distinction of being the highest island mountain in the world, and while snow capped, is girded by a tropical forest at its base. "Hulemaunau"—"The House of Ever-losting Fire," is within the crater of Kiluea, and at night the trees of crimson blue, purple, orange and green, with her and there fountains of blood red, with great plumes of yellow sulphur smoke present a scene suggestive of Danto's Inferno. The fumes of sulphur are strong, but as Mark Twain cleverly commented, not unpleasant to the sinner. Tourists search picture post-cards in the fursures of the crater as Souvenirs of their visits. During the Mixed Court trial of alleged rioters in Shanghai a Chinese physician gave evidence that the students were not shot in the back.

A Chinese physician's testimony that the student rioters killed at the Louza station on May 30 were not shot in the back, and the admission of a missionary, who saw the shooting that under the circumstances the police action was inevitable, were the outstanding incidents in the hearing of 19 students charged with participation in the riots in the International Mixed Court before Mr. Jacobs, American Assessor, and Magistrate Kwan. Forty-six students were scheduled to appear, but 27 forfeited bail ranging from $10 to $100.

Dr. O. Fischer watched the case on behalf of the Chinese Commissioner of Foreign Affairs. Mr. E. T. Maitland, police prosecutor, conducted the case against the accused, one of whom was defended by the Chinese lawyer, Mr. Ho Fei. In the afternoon Dr. H. C. Mei was called in to defend some of the students.

The evidence was most important in correcting statements which have been made repeatedly not only by agitators but even by the Peking Government in notes directed to the "Legations. Dr. H. C. Chen, a Chinese physician attached to the Woosung Road police hospital, contradicted the unsupported statements which have been circulated throughout China and in foreign countries that the students were shot in the back. Dr. Chen examined seven of the slain men when they were brought into the hospital after the riots of Saturday and Monday.

Dr. Chen said one of the victims was wounded in the left scapule, the second in the chest, a third in the right side, a fourth in the neck, a fifth in the right shoulder, a sixth in the chest and the left shoulder-blade, and the seventh in the left eye and skull.

The Chinese physician added that any wounds which might have been received in the backs of other wounded men might easily have been received while turning around to beckon the rioters to come on.

Mr. Harry "Westnidge, a Szechwan missionary attached to the China Inland Mission, who has lived for 15 years in China, in giving the evidence, upheld the necessity of the shooting. Near the Town Hall the mob were striking the foreign police with their fists, and witness particularly noticed how forbearing the police were in endeavouring to maintain order. When they were being overwhelmed and had to protect their lives he saw one Sikh policeman draw his baton while the foreign officers drew their canes.

"I noticed," continued Mr. Westnidge, "that when the police had their backs turned to any of the attackers the mob seemed to gather more courage. Crowds from the side street began to flow into Nanking Road. The side of the tram car held up in the vicinity assisted the police in their manœuvres to make a more hurried return to the station. The crowd ran on the other side of the tram in an endeavour to intercept the police, and were by this time rushing forward from all direc

Geneva, June 15.—General Habibullah, the Persian delegate, withdrew from the arms conference owing to the adoption of articles dealing with the supervision of the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman which Persia considers derogatory to her sovereign rights and dignity. —Reuter.

tions to the Louza police station. I rather feared what would take place, and suddenly heard the shooting. The police seemed to be inside the entrance, and appeared to come out to meet the throng.

Asked what would have happened if the police had not then opened fire the witness replied:

“I am used to Chinese crowds, and at first this one appeared to be simply the grinning ‘look sees.’ They appeared to be a lot of boys who never expected to run into so serious a matter. I think the students started out without ever dreaming of so serious an ending. If the police had hesitated a moment they would have been trampled down unquestionably.

Cross-examined by the Chinese lawyer as to what nationality he was the witness replied that he was born in England, but that in Szechwan he was called a China-man. After the shooting occurred he rendered assistance to the wounded. The surging mass were yelling so much that he only heard the sound of the shots.

Witness in answer to a question put to him replied by asking the Chinese lawyer if he realised what the students were doing at the time when “they were yelling and screaming and rushing at the police station from three directions in a mixed mob.”

Asked if he would have shot, he replied to the Magistrate that "he would have hated to as a missionary, but that as an officer of the law there was no option. If it had been a foreign crowd at home we would have got the same. I believe that the students were looking for trouble, and not the police."

Witness told the court that some of the older students he saw in the street appeared to be the leaders, and that one man who ran along the side streets shouting and waving a flag appeared to be acting as a warner and a collector of the crowd. Inspector Everson then elaborated the evidence he gave at the inquest, describing how the mob had “made a blind rush at the gates.” When the mob were within six feet of the police he gave the order to fire. The crowd in the opinion of the witness were by no means composed all of students, and by the look of most of them they appeared to be loafers.

The afternoon session was occupied until 6.15 in hearing the evidence of the other foreign police who drove the crowd back to Wing On's and were then attacked near the Town Hall. The case was adjourned, bail being granted to all the accused.

London, June 15.—The considerable anticipations of the Budget duty are reflected in the trade returns for last month, the imports of silk goods totalling fourteen million yards, as contrasted with eight/and a half millions for April. Goods under the category of the McKenna duties, excluding motor cars, tofalled £1,000,000, compared with £580,000.—Reuter.

Brussels, June 15.—In an effort to solve the crisis which has deprived the country of a Cabinet for nearly three months, the King summoned a conference of the Catholic leaders Vaudevyvere, the Socialist Vandervelde and the Liberal Masson. He urged the subordination of party considerations to the need of forming stable government.—Reuter. INDIA'S LEAD.

In the House of Commons, replying to Mr. J. S. Wardlaw Milne (Conservative) with regard to conditions of labour in Japanese cotton mills at Osaka compared with mills at Bombay, Lord Winterton, Under Secretary of State for India, said he had been informed that the legal maximum working hours under the Japanese factory act were twelve a day but this need not be strictly adhered to in factories employing only male operatives over fifteen years of age. Women usually worked between 10 and 12 hours a day and were employed at night. The amendment act of 1921 reducing the legal maximum for women to eleven hours daily and prohibiting night work of women was not being enforced at present. The legal maxima in India were sixty hours a week, eleven daily for adults and six daily for children under fifteen years of age. Night work for women was prohibited.

headline: RAILWAY MAGNATE.
text:
The death has occurred of Mr. Julius Kruttschnitt, ex-Chairman of the Southern Pacific Railroad Company.

[Mr. Kruttschnitt, who was born in New Orleans in 1854, was connected with railways all his life, being resident engineer in charge of construction as far back as 1878 and rising to be General Manager of the Southern Pacific Company's Atlantic lines in 1885, ultimately becoming director and chairman of the whole concern. He was also a director of the Western Union Telegraph Company and similar concerns.]

headline: MEXICO'S DIGNITY
text:
Although the statement of President Calles, like that of Mr. Kellogg, was directed to the Press and the statements were therefore not an exchange between the two governments, some officials are astonished at Mr. Calles' using the words "insults" and "threats against the sovereignty of Mexico," although it is recalled that Mr. Kellogg's statement was uncommonly blunt. Behind Mr. Kellogg's statement lies a wealth of information in regard to the conduct of Mexican affairs, including the seizure of American property by so-called agrarians.

London, June 15.—The suggestion of a conference with the Peking Government and representatives of the provinces interested in foreign trade, is made by Sir John Jordan in a letter to the "Times," wherein he cites past examples of successful Anglo-Chinese co-operation as an indication of the prospects of reconciling conflicting interests and claims.—Router.

London, June 15.—The proceeds of the sale of Dunlop debentures have been principally devoted to redeeming higher interest-bearing debentures shortly maturing, holders of which have first option on the new issue.—Reuter.

The light-tower, which is round, built of steel, and painted white, is situated on the small island at the eastern end of Talutao Island, and is 28 feet in height from base to lantern vane.

headline: FAIRY GODFATHER OF SUSSEX VILLAGE.
text:
Telcombe, the capital village of the wild and rolling downs, owes its happiness, its prosperity and its very isolated beauty to the efforts of one man. It is, indeed, the One-Man Arcadia.

Mr. Ambrose Gerham, bachelor, gentleman farmer, keen sportsman, rider to hounds and, above all, lover of children, is the embodiment of the fairly godfather and the hail-fellow-well-met. Nothing happens in Telcombe unless Mr. Gorhaz is behind it. Few people come to Telcombe who are not made welcome by Mr. Gorhaz.

Mr. Gorham renovates the church; Mr. Gorham educates the children; Mr. Gorham has the children taught to dance the beautiful measures of the countryside; Mr. Gorham has the hedges trimmed the fences painted white, the cottages kept in repair, the lanes kept sound and neat; Mr. Gorham employs practically the entire male population of the little village, and there is a wonderful content existing.

The One and Only Danish Beer on the Market

But his most notable achievement, surely, was when he decided to preserve Telcombe just as it is—a typical village of the Downs; set deep between the wind swept hills, its houses and cottages clustered about the 12th century church.

There is no shop in Telscombe, but the village is well served. There is no policeman, there is no public house, though the institute possesses a licence; there are no lunatics or paupers.

Such is the pride of Mr. Gorham in these facts that some years ago he had a Christmas card designed setting forth the village virtues. Telscombe is a good place to live in. Mr. Gorham has made it his hobby, and he has achieved the making people happy.

headline: OUTLOOK GRAVER.
text:
The situation is unchanged. The removal of negotiations from Shanghai to Peking has not caused any outward excitement.

It is reported that the Japanese have handed in a Note of protest as regards the affair at Kiukiang; on June 18, but both the Chinese and Japanese authorities are maintaining complete secrecy.

The Union of Labour, Commerce and Education, which came into being in consequence, of the events of May 30, have decided to insist on the continuation of the strike of shops, despite the decision reached at the meeting of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce, which decided that the banks should re-open on Sunday.

headline: Terror Gang.
text:
The students yesterday terrorised the shopkeepers, bankers, and members of the Chamber of Commerce in connection with the decision to re-open the banks and shops to-day.

Two special meetings were held in the Chamber yesterday, at which the extremists contended that foreigners would view the re-opening as a sign of weakening. The business members pointed out that the closing of the banks and shops was not materially affecting the foreigners but was causing tremendous Chinese losses, instancing that enormous supplies of tea and cocoons were piling up in Shanghai, which were at present unfinanceable and not movable.

Yesterday morning the meeting resolved to postpone the opening until June 24. Last night's wholly rescinded the resolution of June 19, and resolved to postpone settlement day until the end of the lunar month, namely July 21.

headline: Chairman Attacked.
text:
During the discussions, the extremists bitterly attacked Yu Ya-ching, the Chairman of the Chamber of Commerce, charging him with having received $500,000 from the Imperialists to re-open the banks and shops.

Yu Ya-ching vehemently denied this. He hurried to Shanghai from Peking, and since worked day and night in the interests of China and her people. He had not influenced the voting, and he had sufficient money for his few remaining years on this earth.

The attack on Yu Ya-ching silenced other solid business men, and the rescission was carried by a huge majority.

While a definite split between the business members, and the extremists has not occurred, each group is attempting to justify itself, and the outcome will depend largely on the attitude of the Chinese Government.

headline: More Bluster.
text: Delegates, representing 48 colleges, met at the Law College this morning. They sent a deputation to interview the Foreign Minister and War Minister, this afternoon, demanding severance of diplomatic relations with Britain and the impeachment of the Hankow Tupan. The situation, however, at least outwardly, is becoming quiet. There are no signs of the boycott or strike. Numerous students have left for their homes during the past week.

text:
A message from Chungking yesterday, states that after student agitators worked up popular excitement, rioters on the 17th. attacked foreign customs, employés and assaulted Britons on the streets, though none were seriously hurt. Meanwhile a demonstration occurred at the British Consulate, where the rioters-threatened-the-consular Chinese stuff. The Consul, thereupon, requested the city commandant to furnish a consular guard and restore order. As there was no response, the Consul evacuated the Consulate and went aboard a gunboat.

He sent messages to all Britons, advising them quickly to assemble on the gunboat. The community, on June 18, found accommodation at the riverside, under the protection of gunboats where they are remaining. Order has

been restored in the city, but excitement has not subsided. It is unsafe for foreigners to appear in the streets, though no danger is apprehended under present circumstances. The British Consulate is damaged to an extent unknown, and troops are now guarding it. At Chungking, as at many other centres the rivalries of the militarists have proved an important factor in the situation. Leaders, who are inclined to restore order feared popular ill-will and held aloof at a critical period.

The Foreign Office Note, in reply to the Powers' note regarding the riots against foreign sentiment in China, states that the accounts of different incidents given therein are not in accord with the local Chinese authorities' reports.

The Note gives a lengthy Chinese version of the recent occurrences. It says the Hankow British Volunteers suddenly opened fire on an entirely unarmed crowd and the British authorities should assume full responsibility for their violent action.

At Kiukiang, during an altercation between the police and a small number of workmen, fire suddenly broke out at the Taiwan Bank. During the confusion at the time of putting out the fire slight damage was "caused" to sundry articles in the British and Japanese Consulates. Such damage was accidental. Regarding the killing of a British subject at Shanghai, the Note says that he was outside the Settlement, where the Municipality has built roads without China's consent. The motives of the criminals have not been ascertained. It is regrettable for the above reasons that the incident occurred.

headline: Peking "Stands Firm."
text:
The Note goes on to say that with the exception of the killing of a British subject at Shanghai all the incidents happened as a result of failure to obtain a prompt and fair settlement of the Shanghai case.

There never existed any anti-foreign tendency.

Since the Shanghai occurrence, the Government has issued mandates ordering the people to exercise self-restraint, and has instructed the provincial authorities to maintain order. In view of the present circumstances, the Government hope the Ministers of the Powers will promptly settle the Shanghai case, then the present indignation will be appeased and- excitement subside. The Note, in conclusion, declares "I declare the stand I have taken in the previous protests will be insisted upon."

headline: The Chinese View.
text:
Responding to the diplomatic commission's statement, the Chinese delegation have issued a statement in which they express the belief that a permanent basis of settlement could only be achieved by solving certain questions which have been sources of misunderstanding between the Chinese and foreigners in Shanghai, including the rendition of the Mixed Court, the amelioration of conditions of labourers and the participation of Chinese ratepayers in the Municipal Council.

These points were presented at the first meeting when it was intended to apply for authority to discuss them. But, at the subsequent two meetings, the commission evinced a desire to shift onto the Chinese authorities, the responsibility for indirect causes which led up to the shooting. The commission further stated that not having authority to deal with questions of an international nature it must leave immediately for Peking. The conference was thus brought to an end: The Chinese delegation much regrets that its sincere efforts hitherto have failed to bring about a satisfactory solution.

The statement is signed by Messrs. Tsai Ting-kan, Cheng Chien and Tseng Tsung-chien.

headline: Need For Prayer.
text: At the annual meeting of the conference of British Missionary Societies, a resolution was passed recording the conviction that an urgent need exists for prayerful study of various movements underlying the present situation in China. The Conference considers that the true solution can only be found by mutual confidence and conciliation resulting from a patient and sympathetic investigation of the difficulties with which China at present is confronted as a nation.

headline: From Afar: EDINBURGH, June 20.
text:
Over a thousand delegates, representing sixty countries, attended the opening of the World Women's Christian Temperance Convention. The Conference opened with a devotional session, at which delegates from South Africa, Australia, Denmark Canada, India and China gave short addresses.

Miss Tinling from Shanghai said that in the present trouble the Chinese should not be blamed for the effects of Bolshevik influence. The rest of the world was threatened with the same changes. The Chinese were only doing what mobs do elsewhere.

headline: Shanghai Position.
text:
Shanghai is quiet, but there is no cessation of anti-foreigo propaganda. The decision to reopen the banks and shops is favourably affecting the general situation; but merely reflects the necessity of the Chinese to end the phase of the situation causing them much severer losses and inconvenience than foreigners.

The shipping strike, which is a strong anti-foreign weapon, is not weakening. Strikers are beginning to kidnap Japanese employees who are taken to Chapei, robbed and beaten and only released on payment of money and promises to quit employment.

A wireless from Chinkiang says the strikers have resolved that coal will not be sold to British or Japanese.

No danger is now apprehended t Anking.

At Swatow anti-foreign demonstrations continue.

At Foochow an anti-Japanese boycott has been decided upon but no date has been fixed.

Ample Strike Funds.

The extremists are not concerned in the deadlock, for sufficient funds for strike purposes continue to flow in from China and abroad.

The strikers' programme includes a huge demonstration in the native city to-morrow, which together with the growing activities of organised bands of ruffians, is giving rise to additional precautions. Chang Hsue Liang is bringing a second brigade to Shanghai of Fengtien soldiers and is taking up strategic positions in the vicinity of the native city.

The vernacular papers all published Mr. Chamberlain's speech, some commenting on it as nonsense, and others treating it impartially.

headline: Chungking Situation.
text:
The position here is improving. Foreigners are remaining across the river. The other Yangtze ports, and Peking and Tientsin are quiet. The Chinese Delegation has been ordered to Peking.

Message From The Pope.

The University professors recently solicited the Pope's support in the Shanghai affair. The Pope empowered Mon-signor Constantini, the Apostolic Delegate to China, to signify his sympathy with the great Chinese people and keenly deploring the shedding of fraternal blood and praying that concord and order would soon be restored in a spirit of mutual understanding, according to the principles of justice, equity, and Christian charity.

headline: Fengtien Troops Mutiny.
text: The 3rd Fengtien Regiment mutinied at Chensin, on the Peking Mukden line, damaging the station. The gendarmerie commandant of a neighbouring town has sent a detachment to round up the multi-neers.

headline: Outroges Continue. SHANGHAI Tura
text:
The strikers yesterday afternoon attacked the wharf coolies coaling the Blue Funnel liner Pootung. Messrs. Butterfield and Swire's assistant compradore, intervening, aroused the ire of the strikers who set upon him and chased him to the river-side, where failing to reach a sampah, he fell in and was drowned.

A Briton, Mr. Moalem, a driver of the Volunteer Machine Gun Co., was going home in uniform last night by way of Lord Lane when he was struck between the shoulders and the neck with a meatchopper. He was seriously wounded and taken to Hospital.

[A message received later in correction of the foregoing states that it was the younger brother of the Holt's Wharf compradore who was killed, not Messrs. Butterfield & Swire's compradore]

No damage resulted from the wharf incident which was quickly over. A British warship is protecting the wharf to-day.

Mr. Moalem is progressing satisfactorily.

headline: China Replies to Powers. PEKING June 21
text:
Replying at last to the Powers' note, China maintains her original attitude that nearly all the trouble is due to the conflagration at Shanghai for which the Powers are responsible.

The communication adds that the death of Mr. MacKenzie on June 146, occurred outside the Settlement where the Municipality had built roads without the consent of China.

headline: CHINESE
text:
EXTRAORDINARY INCIDENT

About a hundred young Chinese invaded the Chinese legation this evening, overpowered the porter, cut the telephone wires, locked the doors and gained admission to the private room of the Chinese Minister, whom they threatened with violence and forced him to sign a series of documents, including a proclamation assuring the Chinese people that he sympathised with the struggle against the foreign Imperialists. The police have made one

The police have made one rest.

headline: KOWLOON WEDDING.
text:
The Rosary Church, Kowloon, was the scene of a pretty wedding yesterday; the parties being Frederico Muria Gutierrez, only son of Mrs. Milvinin of Shanghai, and Margaret Frances, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. F. H. Barnes of 3 Lyemun Villas, Kowloon.

The bride was given away by her father and was tastefully attired in white georgette with silver trimmings. Her two attendants the Misses Annie and Agnes' Barnes, wore dresses of mauve crepe morocain and pink crepe morocain respectively and the bride's mother was dressed in beige crepe morocain.

The ceremony was conducted by the Rev. Father G. M. Spada and Mr. A. A. R. Botelho and Mr. J. W. Barnes were the bridegroom's sponsors. Mr. O. Baptista was at the organ and suitable solos were rendered by Mr. E. G. Aquino.

The reception held at the Club de Recreio was largely attended and after receiving the congratulations there of many friends the happy couple left for Repulse Bay. Next week, they are to leave by the Empress of Asia for Shanghai.

Paris, June 21.—The "Petit Parisien's Berlin correspondent reports that the British Charge d'Affairs called on Herr Stresemann and emphasised the importance the British Government attaches to the proposals in the French note in regard to security. He declared the note formed the best possible starting point in the negotiations between Germany and the Allies.—Reuter.

Rome, June 20.—The Chamber by 274 votes to 42 adopted a Bill relating to the dismissal of State officials. The Minister of Justice said officials will be asked to embrace the Fascist faith. No official could feel offended, thereat. The law would only affect small groups of would-be politicians who infested the Ministries. An amendment to exclude magistrates from the scope of the law was defeated, Signor Mussolini declaring that the purification of all departments was imperative. No exceptions could be made.—Reuter.

headline: 一
text: Berne, June 20.—With regard to the British and Dutch gold standard measures, the Board of the National Bank states it must maintain the Swiss exchange rate between gold points and the dollar rate. Furthermore the exportation of gold must be facilitated, in this sense, namely, general authorisation of export of unworked gold, must be granted insofar as applicants are able to prove they had imported a like quantity.—Renter.

headline: Santiago de Chile. June
text:
Santiago de Chile, June 21.—In order to stop Soviet propaganda in Chile the Government has ordered that the Russian ship Vorovsky shall not be allowed to enter Chilean ports.—Reuter's American Service.

Moecow, June 21.—The Russian Batic fleet made for the open sea this morning for manoeuvres, with Admiral Frunze abroad a battleship.

Paris, June 20. The Main announces 20 arrests in Paris and the provinces in pursuance of the measures of suppression of Communist propaganda in regard to Morocco. M. Painlevo will early raise a question in the Chamber raising Parliamentary immunity in respect to two Communist leaders, who are deputies, to enable prosecution.

Tangiers, June 20th—situation in the Western Spanish Zone is becoming serious. The Rif contingents are concentrating at various points along the Court Torcan Larache line.—Reuter.

headline: MRS. LANGTRY.
text:
THE DUKE AND THE WATER-LILIES.

"In The Days I Knew" by Lady de Bathe or Mrs. Langtry (to give her the name by which the London of her glorious youth knew her so well) provides here a wealth of good stories and interesting recollections of the great figures in the social world.

Hers is a most entertaining book. Almost from the hour of her first appearance in England as a young bride she became the vogue and was photographed, painted, and worshipped for her extraordinary beauty. The eighth Duke, of Devonshire, who was not usually susceptible on my admiring the lovely coloured water-lilies reposing in marble pools, drenched his clothes pulling them out as an offering, as also the gorgeous liveries of the footmen into whose arms he flung them, and who strewed our brougham with such quantities of the dripping blossoms as to make the latter conveyance rather molster than was convenient.

Simplicity was the note of Mrs. Langtry's life in her first season: Through all this procession of opera, dinners, and balls I wore, extraordinary as it may sound to members of my sex, my one black evening gown, the creation of Mme. Nicole, the fashionable dress-maker of St. Heliers, Jersey.

headline: MET THE PRINCE.
text:
The black frock became the rage, and so with everything she wore:

One morning I twisted a piece of black velvet into a toque, stuck a quill through it, and went to Sandown Park. A few days later this turban appeared in every milliner's window labelled "The langtry Hat." It was very embarrassing and it had all come about so suddenly that I was bewildered.

At her first meeting with King Edward, then Prince of Wales, she says:

I was immensely interested in watching the Prince, and soon realised that, while good-natured and pleasant to everyone, he preserved his dignity admirably; in fact I decided that he would have been a brave man who even at this little intimate supper-party, attempted a familiarity with him. His affability to servants was well known to all who entertained him.

Queen Victoria appears to have looked askance at her. A portrait of her was bought by Prince Leopold, who hung it over his bed in Buckingham Palace, where it remained until one day when he was ill, the Queen went to see him. She evidently did not approve, for I was told she then and there took it down, standing on a chair to do so.

headline: DONKEY IN BED.
text:
With various Princes she indulged in amusing pranks. Thus at a friend's house at Cowes:

One night a donkey was hoisted to the bedroom of the son of the house as a surprise for him—a proceeding in which both the aforesaid Princes took part. I believe they dressed him up and put him in bed, though how to keep him there must have puzzled them.

She tells a charming story of Disraeli:

He remarked quizzically, "What can I do for you?" As it happened to be just before the Ascot Races—a meeting where women like to wear fresh, beautiful frocks, I answered jokingly, "Four new gowns for Ascot," on which he laughed, patted my hand, and said: "You are a sensible young woman. Many a woman would have been made duchess in her own right."

An amusing passage in these lively memoirs is where she tells of an attempt to dye her hair raven black, at the advice of the Austrian Crown Prince Rudolph:

It met with enthusiastic approval on the part of the artist who had achieved the innovation. But, alas! after several washings it became yellow again, with the added glory of heliotrope-zebra-like streaks. The Viennese dye had only worked partially.

headline: LIFE IN CHINA.
text:
MR. BALDWIN REVIEWS SITUATION

GERMANY AND THE LEAGUE.

Mr. Stanley Baldwin, the Premier, addressed fifty thousand Lancashire and Cheshire Unions at Lord Derby's residence at knowsley Park. He said that the host satisfactory feature of the foreign outlooks was the evident desire of Germany to continue negotiations with both Britain and France. He wished that Germany would enter the League of Nations very soon, when existing problems, notably disarmament, would assume a new and better aspect.

headline: OVERSEAS TRADE.
text: Mr. Baldwin continued that the chief factor in checking the growth of Britain's overseas trade was the great increase in productive and distributive costs. We were threatened with a conflict between the coal-owners and miners, each with a very strong case, but all the time the financial position of the industry was getting worse. These conflicts must be lifted on to a new plane by both masters and men. He hoped that the negotiations which were about to be resumed would result in carrying on an harassed industry over a year or two till it would be easier to negotiate permanent settlements.

headline: CHINA'S CHRONIC TROUBLE
text:
Discussing foreign affairs, Mr. Baldwin referred to the disunion and confusion in China, which amounted to little short of inarchy. Some of the unrest is somet候 from sources which, if not checked, will make the unrest chronic and anarchy universal. We have long been deeply interested in the prosperity of China. While we have profited by her prosperity we have contributed thereto materially. We have definite responsibilities for the security of British life and property in China, which we are determined to discharge with energy and firmness. It is our duty to have the unfortunate collision at Shanghai thoroughly investigated and see that impartial justice is done. It is impossible for us to deal with that incident by ourselves. We are in consultation with other nations to secure an agreement as to the best method of proceeding, but we must go further yet. WASHINGTON TREATY.

Mr. Baldwin said the Powers three years ago, agreed with China at Washington that efforts should be made to readjust some of the provisions of the old Treaties now out of date. Complications had incurred and both sides had drifted too long without action. "I am glad to say that the cause of the delay does not rest with us. The Washington Treaties have now been ratified. We shall be only too glad to appoint delegates to push on the work of the conference with China and discuss and settle the questions at issue when once the present unhappy incident is closed and normal conditions are restored. There should and will be no delay in considering, with sympathy and generosity, the legitimate requirements of China as regards the future conduct of the trade on her borders and the administration of those areas where our people enjoy the privilege and responsibilities of trade."

headline: SERIOUS FLOODS.
text:
NORTH CHINA RIVERS HISING.

Owing to the tremendous rains of the race three days, during which upwards of fifteen inches of rain has fallen, serious floods are feared in various parts of Chihli. Rivers are breaking the banks and dykes, causing serious damage. Up to the present no drowning has been reported in the vicinity of Peking.

headline: Korean Casualties.
text:
The following official figures in connection with the Korean floods have been published: drowned 436; missing, 215; refugees 101,431

London, July 26th. At a conference of the World Federation of Education, Association of Edinburgh yesterday, Scholars, Hums, speaking on belief of the Russimaches, declared that the East and West would never be united without Russian Association, Doctor Tai, Chancellor of the Peking University, said that China now clearly recognized that the regeneration of her ancient civilisation would be a reality if the rising generation could be educated on new lines.—Reuter.

headline: BOYCOTT DENIED. / SHANGHAI CHAMBER'S DESIRES
text:
SPEEDY SETTLEMENT

The Chinese General Chamber of Commerce denies that it has decided on a British and Japanese boycott.

The Chinese General Committee of Commerce has requested Reuter to deny the report in the local Press to the effect that the Vice-Chairman of the Chamber, at a meeting last Sunday, announced that goods purchased after June 30 from British and Japanese sources would be seized and confiscated after discovery by the students and that the boycott should be maintained for a year. The Chamber states that the report is unfounded, as the meeting was convened exclusively to discuss steps to urge the Chairman, Yu Yah-ching, not to retire. Hostile foreign criticisms have here been aroused and various retaliatory measures are proposed in letters to the foreign Press, all calculated to do harm to Chinese and foreign relations. This Chamber wishes all foreign business men to understand that no action of an illegal nature has been or will be contemplated by the Board of Directors, whose only hope is that a speedy settlement on the lines of international justice of the May 30 affair, may be effected and the moral support of the foreign friends of China abroad is earnestly solicited and will be heartily appreciated.

headline: Wharf Coolies Resume.
text: The majority of the wharf coolies have resumed. Many indignation meetings are being held as the result of the closing down of the Labour Unions. Agitators accused the Fengtien General of accepting foreign bribes. A female speaker endorsed the suggestion that efforts to compel the General to modify his policy should be made.

headline: SECURITY PACT. / FOREIGN SECRETARY'S SPEECH.
text:
British interest in the settled Continental situation, was emphasised by Mr. Austen Chamberlain at Birmingham. The Foreign Secretary expressed a little disappointment at the character of the German Reply with regard to the mutual pact, as it would involve a continuance of written communications instead of a personal conference to hammer out the agreement. Nevertheless he recognised the German desire to advance their own proposals. He was hopeful of a settlement of the question, which would remove a sense of fear of renewed peril and afford sensible relief throughout the world.

It must not be supposed that we have no interest in the relations of our neighbours, in their security or in the peace of Europe. Some people objected to our giving any form of guarantee regarding the existing French and Belgian and German boundaries, but the sanctity of those frontiers was the groundwork of our own protection. We had it in our power, by associating ourselves as guarantors of that peaceful settlement, to give a measure of confidence to France, Belgium and Germany, which they would never find in any instrument to which we were not the parties.

Swamps off, July 25.--It is stated that President Coolidge will not sneqion any attempt to revise the Warf Art at the next Congress, as here of the opinion that tampering with will create general uncertainty, reacting undivourably on business. --Reuter's American Service.

Newer cabs from Tokyo state that the newspaper's "Asahi's" two aeroplanes, proceeding to London's Moscow, left that city at 9 u.m. on July 25 amid roms of "Banzai." The places arrived at Osaka at 11:30 a.m. and left for Taichiirai at 9:50 a.m. on July 25, but returned to Osaka owing to engine trouble at a due to restart today.

headline: RUBBER BOOM. / REQUEST TO MODIFY RESTRICTION.
text: A manifesto emphasising the adverse effect to their interests of the legislative restrictions of rubber exports from Malaya and Ceylon has been signed by the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, the Royal Automobile Club, the Commercial Motor Users' Association, and the British Cycle and Motor Cycle Manufacturers' and Traders' Union. The manifesto points out the enormous increase in the prices of crude rubber for immediate delivery and says that approximately six million cycle and motor users in Britain are paying and will continue to pay the price during the present restriction; describes the scheme as too inelastic to adjust the supplies with the necessary rapidity to prevent the maintenance of an abnormal price, and urges that it is the Government's duty to modify the scheme.

headline: AMERICAN DIFFICULTIES.
text: Mr. Kellogg (Secretary of State) has cabled to Ambassador Houghton describing "for his information" the difficulties facing the American manufacturers owing to the rise in the price of rubber. Similar representations are reported, to have been forwarded through the British Embassy at Washington.

headline: CLOTHES AND CLIMATE.
text:
A PROBLEM IMPOSSIBLE OI SOLUTION.

Lecturing at the Royal Institution on The Effects of Climate on the Circulation, Professor Joseph Burcroft, said that science may perhaps never be able to give reliable advice to the user of clothes as to how he should clothe himself.

Burgerot, said that sciences may perhaps never be able to give reliable advice to the user of clothes as to how he should clothe himself. The difficulty, he said, lay in the fact that the problem was so complicated. The question as to whether a funnel, silk, or cotton should be worn next the skin depended partly on climate, partly on the variability of the persons concerned, and partly on the change in their constitution from time to time, so that it was difficult to establish any real scientific basis for clothing. He believed that the British climate was too bad for it to be possible to vary clothing adequately to meet it. His own view was that experience was the best guide. Mankind had not changed so greatly in its habits during the last few generations that the experience of its fathers and grandfathers was not valuable. Peking, July 25.—It is semi-officially reported that hostilities have broken out at Yenping, Fukien, between Tu Hsing-pang, the self-styled head of the People's Army, and Tupan Chow Yin-jen. The latter is reported to have asked for assistance from Sun Chuan-fang, who is sending troops to the Fukien border.—Renter.

headline: A NEW BURRIS.
text:
The first instalment of a series of hitherto unpublished letters written by the late Mr. Walter H. Page during his American Embassage in London, and now obtained from the private files of the late President Wilson, appears in the June issue of "The World."

In a letter dated February 22, 1914, Mr. Page declared that the feeling was strong in this country that the United States Government wished to prohibit European financial adventurers from exploiting Central and South America because we wish to exploit them ourselves!" "Men who have looked on at the parcelling out of the world and have taken part in it don't all at once think of the people that dwell on a land before they think of the land itself," the letter continued. "This is one interesting test of the great distance that the Old World thought is behind our thought in all matters of popular welfare. I am constantly surprised to discover how far ahead of them we have travelled.

"I told the German Ambassador (Prince Lichnowsky) here the other night that we wished no more territory, and didn't want Mexico as a (free gift of the gods. He looked at me—a mere glimpse of one one hundredth of a second—and I saw this flit across his mind: 'You are a consummate liar or an impossible idiot.' In this kingdom the Tories do not understand the vocabulary that the Liberals use, and the Liberals wouldn't understand our democratic vocabulary. They have no idea of our notion of freeing men."

HISTORIC THE GOVERNMENT. Writing on May 1, 1014, Mr. Page described a conversation which he had at dinner with "a remarkable old lady, the daughter of one earl and the wife of another," who was "full of the notion that a democracy was necessarily vulgar and venal." "This old Tory notion of the corruption of the United States," Mr. Page's letter proceeded, "crops up oftener than you would think, and there lurks in it a sort of aristocratic hope that it will yet fail. But this is not an active anti-American feeling. It is rather a social resentment of the success of a democratic order of society. It is, I am sure, becoming more and more merely a subject of historical-interest—a curious survival that has no important meaning now."

Of a conversation with a Welsh bishop, who spoke "with shame and grief and horror of the wicked effort to disestablish 'God's Holy Church' in Wales and thus strike the first blow, towards the dethronement of his most gracious Majesty himself, Mr. Page wrote: "I swear he almost persuaded me to be a Tory." He continued:

"When the appeal is made in the name of English history and of your vision of this conquering race sending its soldiers and sailors and bishops and adventurers to blazo ways for civilisation on all sens and continents, it was that sort of an appeal that almost persuaded me to be a 'Tory'—till I got out in the open air and drove over the bridge to Westminster Hall, where, at 11.30 at night, the political partners of the bishops were hectoring and insulting the Government in a way that ought to have put the Tower in commission again."

"They use this historic appeal—they use everything—to cling to their privileges, often you feel with all sincerity. They are English history; they are England; they are the Empire; and they point to all the strength and glory of the past to prove it—for all the world exactly as our own tariff nabobs used to point to every good thing in our land as of their bringing, and as Wall Street used to prove that the prosperity of Yuda Dam in Arizona was of Wall Street's creation."

Nobility not "played out." "In our country," continued Mr. Page, "there is nothing noble or convincing in the beneficiaries of civilize: as a role, they are more sponges, with no more moral quality than sponges. Here they are in many respects the finest flower of British civilisation. Physically they are remarkable. The noble families of this kingdom have practised engenies pretty well for centuries. Now and then there's a dirty duke's (I know one who is the biggest liar in England) now and then a noble lord marries a chos girl or gambles away his ancestral vectrals. But, after all, they are few.

"The race isn't degenerating: I imagine that the noblemen of this generation on this island include more first-class men than those of any preceding generation. The error they make is to conclude that they owe their vitality to their special privilages. If you look at the House of Commons, the Opposition believes show more men of chity, of good mettle, of individual power than they. Governments you have they have every adornment of newspaper rights in the House of Commons and stock in the same reservation."

idea, more or less popular

in the United States, that they are playing out, is wholly wrong. What the future has in store is something like this—with the gradual conquest of liberal ideas over privilege, they gradually move forward—many younger sons move forward very fast, and they'll remain the rulers of the world till we accumulate money enough to take our turn at the wheel. There isn't going to be any such New Zealand as Macaulay predicted, and London Bridge will be open to traffic. I imagine, when Gabriel blows his trumpets. headline: “YOU STOLE IT!” / WOMAN ACCUSES D'ANNUNZIO.
text:
VILLA AT LAKE OARDA.

"You (d'Annunzio) stole it from the widow of Thode, the German art critic, who is the rightful owner. I will call on your fellow authors in Europe and America to condemn you by a universal pro-test," writes the Danish author, Madame Karin Michaelis, says the Paris correspondent of the "Weekly Dispatch." The letter is arousing a sensation in literary circles. She is accusing Gabriele d'Annunzio, the Italian poet, of stealing a beautiful villa on the shore of Lake Garda, with its extensive grounds, valuable tapestries and pictures. The villa before the war belonged to Thode. D'Annunzio, declares that he legitimately purchased it. Mme. Michaelis replies that the Italian Government sequestrated the villa during the war, and subsequently decided that it be conditionally returned to Thode, who died in 1921. When his widow called on d'Annunzio, who was living in the villa, says Mme. Michaelis, he avoided seeing her, but wrote promising to endeavour to get the property restored to her. D'Annunzio afterwards paid 10,000 lire to the Italian authorities in order to retain possession of the villa. Mme. Michaelis declares that even this small sum was derived from the sale of pictures that the villa contained.

headline: MITATION “CLOUDS.” / METHOD OF TRAINING PILOTS.
text:
The loss of the sense of balance which is suffered by aeroplane pilots when flying within clouds or fog can now be imitated exactly by a particularly ingenious contrivance. This contrivance will enable pilots to continue their navigational training during clear summer weather.

A hood, similar to the hood of a peril-regulator, is fitted in front of the pilot's cockpit. The instructor, who occupies the observer's seat immediately behind, draws the hood back over the pilot's head directly he believes that a safe height has been attained. The pilot is then seated in a miniature dark room for the hood is fitted so as to exclude all light. Small electric bulbs glow upon his instrument and permit him to read the compass, altimeter, airspeed indicator, turn indicator, revolution counter, and "bubble" (a transverse spirit level). By these instruments he must set his course and fly perhaps 100 miles without sight of the outside world.

headline: GOLD & SILVER FLOWERS and HAIR ORNAMENTS / KING IN CITY.
text:
SPEECH ON ROMANCE OF COMMERCE.

HINTH OF THE NEW LLOYD'S

London.

The King, who was accompanied by the Queen and Prince Henry, inaugurated another chapter in the history of commercial London when, in the presence of 3,000 business men, he laid the foundation stone of the great £1,500,000 building which is to arise in Leudenhall Street as the new Lloyd's.

Replying to the address presented on behalf of the Corporation of Lloyd's. His Majesty said:—

I have been impressed, as everyone must be, by the extraordinary and romantic history of Lloyd's, and by its evolution from an ordinary seventeenth-century coffeehouse to the great public and international institution familiar to us all.

Cromwell said that no one rises so high as he who does not know whither he is going, and this has held good in our organisations as well as in men.

"You have also referred with legitimate pride to the traditional honour and integrity upon which the greatness of Lloyd's is founded. The history of the Corporation is the embodiment of the highest qualities of British commerce.

"Lloyd's policy has never been a one-sided pursuit of gain, but a combination of keenness and efficiency in business with a real and deep public spirit.

headline: AS IN 1793, SO IN 1014
text:
It is not a mere coincidence that we owe the institution of our life-boat service to Lloyd's, or that our National Gallery began with the pictures collected by a famous chairman of your body.

There is one branch of your work which calls for special reference, and all the more so because you have modestly foreborne to make the least alusion to it yourselves the inestimable services which Lloyd's has rendered to the country in war time.

Throughout the long wars of the Revolutionary period, Lloyd's was constantly able to supply the Admiralty with valuable information as to the safety of commerce, the presence of hostile cruisers in the Channel, or the loss of merchant vessels through enemy action, and took a most active interest in the adoption and better organisation of the convoy system.

In similar circumstances in our own day, the Lloyd's of 1914 rose again to the situation and displayed the same loyalty and public spirit as in 1793.

“The State largely depended on the machinery of Lloyd's for reports, received through its agents and other channels, which contributed to the safety of British shipping and British cargoes of indispensable value to the welfare of the country.

headline: WORLD-WIDE INFLUENCE.
text:
"It would however, give an imperfect view of the scope and effect of your work were no mention made of its international character; your world-wide organisations and influence have always been at the disposal of all maritime peoples who are in peace and unity with the British Empire."

Remembering the history of your Corporation and its record of services to Great Britain and the whole world, we confidently hope for still greater things from that expansion and development—the outcome of today's inauguration.

Even without the assurance in your address, your fellow country-men proudly recognise that you are conscious of your great inheritance and traditions and determined to hand on these to future generations.

"I pray that the blessing of God may rest upon the Corporation of Lloyd's. May your new home write the continual growth in your work prosperity, and well-carned honor!"

headline: SHANGHAI APPROVES / MURDER DONE?
text:
SEQUEL TO HECTIC NIGHT.

HONGKONG'S FIGHTING STRIKE MEASURES.

SIMILAR POLICY REQUESTED:

MILLIONAIRE AND POLICEMAN.

The emergency measures adopted in Hongkong for dealing with strikers have aroused the ire of the Labourites at Home, but judging from editorial articles and the correspondence columns in the Shanghai newspapers, they are looked upon as the very thing for bringing the Chinese involved to their senses.

Donald Parsons, a millionaire member of the Stock Exchange, was celebrating so industriously amongst the cabarets that a policeman had to see him home.

Parsons invited the policeman inside, and the officer later retired with the members of the household, only to be awakened by the smell of smoke. He quickly phoned for firemen, who failed to arrive before Parsons and his son Vivian had been burned to death. The police are investigating what promises to become an amazing murder mystery, committed right under the policeman's eyes, even though they were closed.

"We adhere to our opinion that, if the strike can die a natural death, it had better be allowed to do so. If it can be broken by means of passive resistance, there will be the less heart-burning and bitterness afterwards. And if General Shing will act up to the threat of his own proclamations, put down the unions and suppress the intimidation, the workers would go back to their work with alacrity. Welcome news was received last night that he had caused six agitators to be arrested and there are other indications that his forbearance is reaching its limit. It needs only that he should shoot one intimidator, to make the rest understand that their game is up. But if he does not take action on resolute lines, then it will become necessary for the Settlement authorities to do so. Already it begins to be felt by persons in a position of responsibility that the strike and boycott can only be ended by a display of force. And if that line is reluctantly decided upon, there are plenty of ways in which it can be adopted. Why, for example, should the Settlement continue; by means of volunteer labour replacing the strikers, to supply water and light to Chapel, the headquarters of the strike? And why should the Chinese workmen who will not allow their fellows to work—every office probably knows whom it has to thank for this among its own former employees—be permitted to reside in the Settlement free to carry on their silent terrorization? As for those convicted in the Mixed Court, we cannot unfortunately use the "cat" but there are plenty of other more appropriate punishments for them, as Hongkong has shown.

The putting of agitators to "useful if unpleasant duties" in connection with the sanitation of the Colony has particularly met with approval as a fitting punishment, also the campaign conducted against intimidators and the banishment of idlers.

"One of our correspondents to day has obtained some extremely interesting information as regards Hongkong's way of dealing with strikers and intimidators, writes the North China Daily News." A good deal more might be told, but the censorship imposed in Hongkong is very strict and since the Government of the Colony does not wish to let out such information by the usual channels, we have no wish to defeat its policy by divulging what has been obtained from travellers. In a word, however, it may be said that the strike in Hongkong is being fought; not just played with; and the results of this were seen a day or two ago in the brief telegram saying that the volunteers for essential services had been demobilized, implying that regular labour was now available.

And yet another correspondent details a number of measures which might be taken to break the boycott. The answer to Mr. Sowerby is that a week ago things may have been different from what they are to-day. In point of fact they were. At that time it appeared that the strike funds were running out and that General Shing Shi-lien's proclamations might be expected to have an effect on the intimidators. With regard to the latter we have been waiting patiently. It is difficult to belliave that a man in General Shing's position can speak so plainly as he has done and not give effect to his words. Surely he must "lose face" by falling to do so to an extent far worse than any unpopularity he might earn with the riff-raff by acting sternly in defence of law and order. headline: RETURN BOUT? / DUPRE AND JIM CARTLIDGE. / LATEST NEWS.
text:
Andre Dupre (ex-featherweight champion of France) is coming back to Hongkong and a return bout with C. P. O. Jim Cartlidge (undefeated Imperial Services champion and lightweight beltholder of the Colony) is practically certain.

Mr. J. Brook, the popular manager of the Hongkong Boxing Association, has received a cable that Dupre is returning here by the P. & O. S.S. Nagoya. Mr. T. G. Bennett, the enthusiastic hon. secretary and treasurer of the Association, has lost no time in making a start with the preparations for another big fight. Dupre, on his arrival, will undergo a special course of training under Staff Sergt. Hunt, the well-known physical culturist and gymnast.

Cartlidge will train at his old quarters at the Kowloon British School.

No date has yet been fixed for the bout, but doubtless this awaits the actual arrival of Dupre on the scene.

It is understood that Dupre has now arrived in the Colony and that hopes exist of bringing the men together on June 18

headline: NEW CHAMPION.
text:
WORLD'S CRUISER WEIGHT TITLE

MCTIGUE DEFEATED.

SPLENDID RALLY IN LAST ROUND.

Paul Berlenbach has been given decision over Mike McTigue, in light-heavyweight boxing championship of the world.

By defeating McTigue, Berlenbach becomes the fourth holder of the world's light-heavyweight title in three years.

Berlenbach was most aggressive. He repeatedly forced McTigue to the ropes and was boring in with hard rights and lefts but McTigue covered up and dodged causing Berlenbach frequently to miss. Nevertheless, Berlenbach landed in number of solid punches, cutting McTigue's eyes and mouth.

McTigue rallied gamely in the final round and took the offensive but the judges had no difficulty in awarding Berlenbach the decision.
The defeated champion.

headline: MILITARY BOXING
text:
SURREYS' PLATOON

"Tommies" Do Well

Bouts of three two-minute rounds under Service conditions were the order of things at Murray Barracks on Saturday night when the semi-finals and finals of the Surrey Regiment's platoon boxing tournament for the Montague Bates Cup were decided.

The three days' sport in the "Montague Bates" Platoon Boxing Tournament proved a success in every way, and those who went to witness the semi-finals and finals last night were treated to a display which was quite creditable in the realm of army boxing.

The best bout was easily the final of the bantamweight between Pte. Baxter and Drm. Simpson. Both men gave a splendid exhibition of clean boxing.

One bout in the semi-final of the flyweight and two in the welter-weights were not fought, one of the contentants in each case being indisposed, thus providing a walk-over for the others into the final. However, the latter gave exhibition fights with others who filled the gap.

Five out of the seven final events went the full distance, Owing to a misunderstanding in the awarding of points for the Cup, an adjustment had to be made, the results at the conclusion being as follows:—Drums and Signals, total points 10; Machine Guns (Right Section), total points 8½.

Results:—

headline: LADIES' GOLF / LLNESSEOYER

After several months' absence from the game through illness, Miss Cecil Leitch returned to competitive golf when at Moor Park the annual tournament among the Medical, Legal, Parliamentary, and United Services ladies' golfing associations was decided.

Miss Leitch led the first named association, who secured the trophy in 1928 and 1924, but, although she won both her games and her side was successful in the semi-final against the Parliamentary team, United Services took the shield by defeating Medical in the afternoon by 7 games to 2. A feature of the morning play, when Medical beat Parliamentary by 7 to 1 (a player being absent from either side), and United Services beat Legal by 5 to 4, was the contrast in the short game of the two sisters, Miss Cecil and Miss Edith Leitch. headline: RACE MEETING. / GOOD DIVIDENDS:
text:
Except in the most important race of the day, good fields were sent out for the various events of the card on Saturday—the first day of the Whitsuntide extra meeting which continues this afternoon. A drizzle now and then did not dampen the enthusiasm of the spectators who attended. Racing honours were evenly distributed but Mr. Pollock rode three winners in five attempts. H.E. the Governor (Sir R. E. Stubbs): accompanied by his A.D.C. (Captain R. Neville, R.M.L.I.) and Private Secretary (Mr. T. J. Galsford St. Lawrence) arrived in time to led in his pony, Gaudie, which ran third in the opening event; this race was won by Lady Severn's Jambu (the griffin's second victory) and the Hon. Sir Claud Severn was also present. It is interesting to note that Hailsham, who finished between Jambu and Gaudie, was once the property of Captain Neville.
