headline: BRIGHTER BANKS / ARMCHAIRS AND BOOKS FOR CLIENTS.
text:
Banks are to be made brighter. Ordinary people usually leave banking premises as quickly as they can. They are oppressed by the melancholy opulence. Now this is to be changed, and the Midland Bank, Limited, will go down to banking history as pioneers.

To make their clients feel thoroughly at home they have opened a reading and writing-room and a ladies' rest-room at their handsome new branch in Piccadilly.

The step is one which will be welcomed by business men. In the beautifully panelled reading and writing room, furnished in the early Georgian style, customers can transact business, write letters, or pass a quiet hour in reading.

"Ample facilities are available in the shape of literature," the bank announces. At one end "of the room is a counter where officials will attend to the requirements of clients.

The ladies' room is decorated in green and gold, the walls are of plaster panelling, while the general design; "electrolier and furniture are all early Georgian.

This “reform” bank stands on the site of the old Vestry Hall of St. James, and is so built that it makes an admirable foil to Wren's church, which the master builder himself considered one of his best contrived churches. A notable feature of the bank is a magnificent Georgian ceiling designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens.

To mark the opening the Midland Bank, Limited, have published a quaintly-bound and illustrated brochure, Landmarks in Piccadilly, for which type purchased in 1672 by Bishop Fell for the Oxford University Press has been used.

headline: ALL RED.
text:
The Chiefs of Gambia expressed themselves when they closed their address to the Prince of Wales with the words, "We are black. We cannot speak or write English, but we are English." I am reminded (says an "Evening Standard" writer) of a story told me by a friend who happened to be in the East at the time of Queen Victoria's death. Going to the memorial service on that occasion he met a Chinese acquaintance, of whom he asked why he was there.

The yellow-skinned British subject replied, "You English—me English. Both alike—All red inside."

headline: THE QUEEN'S DOLLS'
text: Lord Stevenson said that the Queen's Dolls House at Wembley made £38,764, and had been visited by 1,617,556 people. I wonder how many of these visitors really saw the Dolls House (says an "Evening Standard" writer.) For my part, each time I made the circle I became more anxious to be allowed to get up close and spend an hour examining the amazing details. As most visitors probably felt likewise, the moral is that the magnificent total could still further be increased if it may time.

headline: A "NATIONAL JOKE"
text:
DEFENCE OF THE ALBERT MEMORIAL.

For some time I have felt rather sorry for the Albert Memorial, writes Kathleen O'Brien in the Daily Chronicle. From being a National Monument it has somehow passed into a National Joke. Now I find it quite reasonable to joke about a solemn thing that everyone else takes seriously. But to joke about a solemn thing that everyone else jokes about, too... no, that is sheer bullying. I am suddenly and perversely moved to pity. I find I must instantly take its part. It was in this spirit of compassion that I went and had a close look at the Albert Memorial.

headline: A DETAILED STUDY.
text:
You know, there are things about the Albert Memorial, if you honestly look for them. For one thing, to see it properly you stand with your back to the Albert Hall, so that the enormous posters announcing contiguously a performance of the "Dream of Gerontius" and a puglistic bout between Bert Hammerjaw and Kid Basheye are temporarily powerless to inflict their yellow pain. Wherefore the site of the Memorial at least must command our respect. Then let us look (as the guidebooks say) at the figure groups seated at the four outer corners of the base.

Who is this dauntless woman seated on a ferocious bull, with no more sign of nervousness than if she were riding down the Strand on a bus? Ha! Europa, of course. The Big Four are seated at her feet—no, not that Big Four; these are, obviously, Britannia with her trident, Italia with her lyre and palette, France and Germany—er—by the way which is France, and which Germany? One has a book and the other a sword, but that is little to go by. Neither can you go by their faces, for in feature and expression the might be twin sisters, which I am nearly sure is incorrect. However, let us not be fussy fussy about details.

headline: THE INTREPID LADY
text:
Next, America. America, intrepid lady, rides on a bison, with its head down; as if about to butt something. Another intrepid lady, one of America's daughters, is hitting the bison on the head with a nasty-looking stick. "I'll learn you to butt my mother!" she is saying. A man at her side has set down rather suddenly on an astonished lion, which he has completely flattened out. Its claws dangle helplessly in the air. Another standing lady, with a lamb's fleece over her shoulder, offers a bunch of, I think, rhubarb, to an indignant man in a hat and nearly nothing else, who is rightly refusing it. He is holding a rifle in readiness in case his wife offers him rhubarb any more.

Africa comes next. Egypt sensibly rides a camel, which, though possibly old-fashioned, is a far more reliable-steed than these new-fangled bulls and bisons. Near her is a wise man with a note-book in his hand, a kind of hassocky thing—or is it a bale of merchandise? And is his book the Precepts of Ptah-Hatep or a cash account book? Beside the camel a rather "school-marry" person shakes her, finger at a negro who is making faces at her behind Egypt's back. Don't do that, you naughty, rude boy!" she says severely, "after all the pains I've had educating you, too!"

And last, Asia. An elephant nearly as large as the lady who is seated on him has rather ignobly collapsed. You see it is not only the weight of his rider that oppresses him. There is a conquering young man with a far-away expression leaning against the elephant's ribs and sticking the point of his shield into the elephant's side, regardless of the pain he must be inflicting on that dumb, faithful creature. Round the other side a visionary is seated rupt in dreamy contemplation, with his foot very near the elephant's tail. I consider it a great tribute to the remarkable powers of concentration possessed by the visionary that he can retain that serene, placid expression with a justly irritated elephant well within kicking distance. I couldn't.

GREAT MEN'S GRIEVANCES. Now consider the marble relievos of great men at the hasement of the memorial.

Homer, at the centre, touches his lyre, to which listen Dante, on the one hand, and Shakespeare, his tunic trimmed with the now fashionable row of buttons on the other. Pythagoras is saying to Virgil in a disgusted voice, "Just look here! They've only put half of me in! But I suppose you can't expect a nation of shopkeepers to appreciate philosophy!" A little further along, Haydn searches a newspaper anxiously, to know what came home in the 3.30. Purcell closes his ears, with dignity, on an altercation over a document between Tallis and Lawes. Michael Angelo, tired of standing, leans on Raphacl's chair. "Might let me sit down for a bit!" he grumbles, "I don't know what these young people are coming to!" headline: IN CHINESE EYES. / GENERAL HSU ON LONDON
text:
In a signed article in the Daily Express General S. T. Hsu, head of the Chinese Mission, now in London to study our economic and political institutions, expresses his admiration of the ladies of London and of the limbs of the law who control the street traffic. The former he describes as "like lotus petals swaying in the wind," and the latter as "marvellous fellows."

London, he says, is to me such an incomprehensible multitude of people that I am overwhelmed by her enormity. I have been in your mighty capital for so little time that my impressions will not yet form themselves. But in my journeyings through her wide, open streets I have cast an eye on her beautiful ladies, her smart guardians of her law, her traffic extraordinary, and some of her marvellous buildings, and these have pleased me. Not yet have I had the honour of pausing in front of the Cenotaph, but I hope soon to be accorded the privilege of placing a wreath of flowers on the tomb of your illustrious dead.

I consider the ladies of London are elegantly attired, of most graceful carriage, and that their demeanour is quiet and modest. As they walk they look like lotus petals swaying in the wind. In China we say that the beauty of a pure and good woman shines like the beauty of a pearl, and that the grace of her carriage and her movements is heavenment. I think of this when I see the wives and daughters and sisters of London citizens, so beautiful, so modest, so full of grace.

Unhappily, it has not been my inestimable joy to meet and hold discourse with these fair daughters of the West, but from my observations I can see that many of them are also highly accomplished and of a great knowledge. It is said that they are as fortunate in the world of commerce as in the smaller world of the household to which in ancient times they were dedicated. Here they are different from my women, who still give an undivided attention to the homes of their husbands.

It is my invariable custom to study the relation of women to society, nor I consider that they exercise a wide influence on politics. These eminent, highly-born men who are so fortunate as to have cultured wives who are intellectual companions and intelligent help-meets to them and good mothers to their children are blessed indeed.

headline: WAKEFULNESS
text:
For your policeman I have nothing but praise. He is a marvellous fellow, for he does nothing at all! And yet I know that it is he who has made the London traffic the orderly, docile organism it is. He only seems to do nothing. Actually it is that white-gloved hand of his that has accomplished everything. I can appreciate perfectly the difficulty of regulating such a big and tremendous traffic. It is a pity and a shame to say so, but during the last four or five years since I have left the city the traffic control in Peking has become worse than before.

Your streets impress me with their cleanliness London is said to be a city of fog and grime. Yet everywhere I see bright, shining cleanliness, and—at this time—marvellous splashes of green. The parks, the quiet, dignified little squares, and the trees in the yards of the ancient churches all make London green and beautiful to me.

I went in a motor-car to Aldershot, where I was entertained to luncheon by Lady Chetwode, the honourable wife of the general commanding your troops in that town. Her home was a pattern of gentle grace and kindly dignity, and she a pattern of hospitality.

As we moved along in the motor-car, through your country roads, I was profoundly moved by that quality of the English spring of which our travellers have so often spoken. It was like the gentle waking-up of the earth child after the slumber of the long, dark winter months.

All about me in your mighty capital I can feel the tradition of centuries, but it possesses also that same spirit of wakefulness which I observed in the country, and which must make it for ever completely different from the slumberous age-old cities of the Orient.

headline: “CHINA MAIL” SPORTS PAGI / CHEFOO SPORTS.
text:
The C.I.M. Preparatory Sports were to have been held on May 13, but on account of rain had to be postponed till Friday, June 15, when a large crowd of fellow scholars from the higher schools, parents and friends were present to watch the kiddies run, and to enjoy the fun.

Messrs. George Andrew and G. P. Welch acted as judges, and Mrs. Knight very kindly distributed the prizes to the happy, little winners.

The events this year were as varied as usual, including besides the 100 yards dash and high and long jumps, such races as a blind man's race and a catch-the-train race, which together with a rather unusual obstacle race, caused roars of amusement from the on-lookers.

Harold Graham was the proud recipient of the pennant awarded to the boy in the Upper School who secures the most points of the afternoon. He won the long run, 100 yards and potato race, and was second in the catch-the-train race; his team also won the team race.

There have been a couple of cricket matches. between the Cricket Club and the School since I last wrote, in both of which the boys were victorious.

In the first, on May 16, the Schoolboys batted first and had scored 90 before they were all out, Ford contributing 36, and Hazeland 34, before he retired to give the rest of the side a chance to bat as the time was limited. Messrs. Grubb and Dowglass both bowled well, the former securing 5 wickets for 29 runs and the latter 4 for 22. When the men went in to bat they were quickly disposed of for the low score of 29, Colin Ford securing 6 wickets for 18 runs.

In the second game on May 30, the _Cricket Club_ put up a much better show. The School won, the toss, but elected to field, and the Club had passed the century before they were all out. Mr. Matson made a good 29, Mr. Smart 15, and Mr. Ray Eckford 20 not out, the total score being 103. Best secured 3 wickets for 22 runs, and Hazeland 4 for 22. Hazeland and Ford opened for the boys and carried the score to 67 before Hazeland was bowled by Mr. R. Eckford. The boys' batting collapsed after Ford was dismissed, second wicket down with the score standing at 94, but when stumps were drawn they had passed the Club's total having made 120 for 8 wickets down.

Oxford University's team against Middlesex on May 2 was J. L. Guise, C. H. Taylor, T. B. Raikes, E. P. Hewetson, G. E. B. Abell, J. V. Richardson I. J. Collins, E. R. T. Holmes, W. N. McBride, L. R. Serrurier, and C. L. D. Fawcus. Three Oxford men turned out for Middlesex, viz., J. O. Butterworth, J. B. Wheatley and Lord Dunglass.

headline: TENNIS
text:
ANOTHER LIST FIRST TEN.

ENGLAND BEHIND

Why does Great Britain lag behind in the acquirement of world's lawn tennis honours? A. Wallis Myers suggests in his editorial foreword to "Ayres Lawn Tennis Almanack, 1925," that we have neglected the art of the game in a craze for competition. We hold more tournaments than any other country, and we produce fewer players of outstanding ability. America has no handicap events at its chief tournaments—entry to which is by invitation only—nor does it encourage mixed doubles play, believing that both are inclined to reduce the speed of the game.

The editor of this admirable year book—a long-way-the-best that is published on the game, of which it furnishes a complete record at 2s. 6d.—classes the first ten players in the world thus:—1, W. O. Tilden; 2, Vincent Richards (both U.S.A.); 3, J. O. Anderson (Australia); 4, W. M. Johnston (U.S.A.); 5, R. Lacoste, 6, J. Borotra (both France); 7, H. Kinsey (U.S.A.); 8, G. L. Patterson (Australia); 9, H. Cochet (France); 10, M. Alonso (Spain). So England has not one in the first-ten!

headline: QUIET SATURDAY.
text:
While any unrest which existed throughout the French Concession yesterday was due principally to the activities of unorganised loiterers and would-be looters, the condition to-day of the areas under foreign protection would suggest that even these had ceased all efforts to resist the determined resolve on the part of the authorities to maintain peace and order at all costs.

Like yesterday this morning opened quietly following an uneventful night. No incident to mar the present quiet situation presented itself at any point in the International or French Settlements throughout the forenoon and it is almost safe to predict that the rainfall which commenced this afternoon will have a staying effect upon any contemplated outbreak or demonstration scheduled to take place as part of the programme of the strike-leaders and anti-foreign propagandists.

Yesterday drew to a close with success, for the most part, on the side of the agitators. From all parts of the compass reports were received that additional labourers had joined the ranks of the idle. By nightfall the number of workers of all classes who had stopped work amounted to something over 200,000 and this number was swelled almost hourly. While this was to be deplored it was certainly gratifying to note that almost without an exceptional instance, the servants, labourers or professional employees who finally agreed to quit did so solely through intimidation. The activities of the strike leaders were broadcast and relentless. Backed up by misleading. Communist propaganda, ill-advice and distorted viewpoints acquired through contact with nationals and literature from countries which have sunk beneath the social plane through adopting similar methods, the local Bolsheviks yesterday pursued their programme of social and business upheaval throughout the length and breadth of the city.

Frenchtown Involved. As we reported in our last night's issue, Frenchtown succumbed to the agitators after having remained aloof from all disorders for a period of several days.

The same methods employed to bring about this condition as in the International Settlements though fortunately no blood was shed. Shopekeepers, market-vendors, public servants and houseboys were all approached in the same sly, menacing manner and in a great many departments the workers agreed to follow the instructions of the intimidators. Shops of all descriptions closed their doors as ordered but, with even an eye for business, pigeon-holes and side entrances remained open for the use of customers. The public services of the French Concession have not been as fiercely approached as those within the settlement.

Why They Must Go.

A number of our staff who lives in one of the smaller hotels, yesterday noon came across a very good example of the manner in which this strike is being managed. On his floor there is an ancient coolie, probably well over 77 years old, a typical specimen of the lower classes of old China, totally ignorant, but thoroughly imbued with the idea that in every hour of the day, without consideration for himself, he must obey implicitly every order of those he regards as born to be his superiors. headline: Polka Blamed
dateline: Tokyo, June 10. Kiot Trial. SHANGHAI, June 10.
text:
The Chinese Legation, instructed by Peking, this morning issued a statement blaming the foreign constables for firing without a warning. The statement denies any anti-alien or pro-Bolshevik complexion and accuses the Shanghai Municipal Council of traducing the friendly relations between China and the Powers to conceal its own faults.

At the trial to-day the American assessor announced the admissibility of documents containing Bolshevist Literature which the police seized at Shanghai University and which was not admitted yesterday.

Inspector Everson, who ordered the firing on May 30 described the circumstances and said that the crowd was absolutely uncontrollable for three minutes before the firing. The squad consisted of eleven Sikhs, twelve Chinese and two foreigners.

The Chinese Magistrate asked whether firing at the legs would have been effective.

Witness replied that such would be contrary to the instructions which were only to fire as a last resource and then to shoot to kill. He had to obey those orders. The defence called Sidney Anderson, an American Methodist missionary.

Witness said that he did not see any resistance either by the crowd or by the arrested men. The crowd were only blocking the street and cheering. They shouted something like "Hurrah" and were quite manageable. Their object was apparently a sympathetic movement in favour of the imprisoned students. He guessed that about fifty or a hundred shots were fired, and considered the police absolutely unjustified in firing.

Cross-examined, he said he could not see the people in front of the crowd at the time of the shooting. He could not understand what they were shouting. He admitted that the police were too few to hold back the crowd. Doctor Cline, a Methodist Missioner, and ex-President of Soochew University, gave evidence similar to Mr. Anderson's. The hearing was adjourned until tomorrow.

Dr. Cline is also an American. Seaman's Strike. SHANGHAI. June 10

headline: LAOK ON GOVERNMENT PROVISION.
text:
The Director of Education was questioned at yesterday's Education Board meeting, over which he presided, as to the number of private schools that had been started in the Colony during recent years and members expressed the opinion that the Government was not doing as much as it might do in the matter of providing educational facilities for a growing population. Mr. Wylie criticised the Government in that there was only one Government School for Chinese in Kowloon.

The discussion arose out of answers to questions which Mr. Li Forster had given notice of, these being that 126 new private schools had been registered in the Colony during the last three years; that 103 had given up and that "the teachers at such schools were not forced to attain to a fixed standard.

There were schools of many types, said the Chairman referring to the absence of a fixed standard for teachers. Some of them were performing a very useful work while others only gave a smattering of education for the benefit of workmen or servants. The suitability of the teacher was, however, always considered before a school was admitted to registration and no Government grant was given before a certain standard of efficiency was attained. There was supervision of them by the Government at least once a year.

Mr. Alves asked what was being taught in the schools and Mr. Wylie replied that so far as the Department was concerned they had no means of telling. "I think," Mr. Wylie added, "these schools should be done away with altogether and that the Government should provide schools to take their places."

Mr. Forster said that it did seem on the face of it, that the Government had not made adequate educational provision during the last ten years, for the expansion of the Colony. His whole point in asking the questions was to show that these private schools had come into existence as a result of a demand which was not being met by the Government and he felt that perhaps they were exploiting the community. Several voluntary schools had gone in for expansion but the only development on the part of Government Schools appeared to be that in connection with Sayingpun School which would only supply sufficient places for the present scholars. Schools run by religious bodies were cheaper from the Government point of view than if they had to maintain them solely, and it might be that the Government was getting education too cheaply. The voluntary system was not adequate to deal with the situation and it was because of that these night schools had sprung up run on a commercial basis.

The Chairman remarked that the Government could not hope to provide sufficient schools to take the places of all the private schools and it would be a pity for voluntary effort entirely to be swamped.

Rev. T. W. Pearce attributed the present exceptional demand for schools to the troubled state of China resulting in people coming to Hongkong. Perhaps when China returned to normal again some of these difficulties would disappear.

Mr. Wylie congratulated Dr. Pearce on his optimism in expecting to see China return to normal again.

Rev. T. W. Pearce: It might certainly be a suitable subject for discussion. (Laughter).

Mr. Wylie asked questions relating to the provision or lack of provision of educational facilities for Kowloon in the course of the meeting. Was there any hope of the Government erecting more schools there at an early date? he asked.

The Chairman replied that he could not say definitely. They had sites for two more schools and he was hoping that sufficient money and labour would be available to make a start shortly.

Mr. Wylie pointed out that there was no Government Girls' School on the Peninsula. The only boys' school, too, was at Yaumadi and even at that distance they were having to turn pupils away. The meeting closed with a reference by Mr. Wylie to the technical classes in Kowloon. Could the Chairman give any information regarding them?

The Chairman said that he had not received the report in time and it had not yet been circulated.

headline: SLAVE OF DESIRE. / A WORLD THEATRE ATTRACTION.
text:
The management of the World Theatre announce that they are to show a special production called "The Slave of Desires" from to-day. It is a wonderful picturization of Honore de Balzac's immortal story "Magic Skin" and has been brought to the screen in a most lavish manner. It deals with a young man, penniless and disconsolate, strolling along the banks of the Seine, bent on ending his life in its dirty waters. As he walks along, he comes upon a shop of a dealer in antiques, and goes in, hoping to sell the scarab on his watch chain—the last relics of the gifts given him by his father. The old shop-keeper becomes very much excited when Raphael shows him the scarab. He tells the astonished Raphael that his scarab is the key to the skin and that he is now entitled to this "magic skin." An inscription in Sanscrit on the skin tells of its power to grant every wish to his owner, but with each wish the skin will shrink. The days of the owner are measured by the size of the skin.

To test this talisman, Raphael utters the first wish which enters his head—that he has a riotous good time with some of his old companions. The Antiquarian reminds him to the effect that such wishes will have upon his life. As he rushes out of his shop, he meets some of his old friends on their way to a banquet, and joins them. At the banquet he meets an old friend, Emile, to whom he tells his story. He establishes himself in a sumputous home. One night, he accidentally meets Pauline whom he does not recognize in her fine clothes. She tells him that her father has returned from Russia laden with jewels. She has always loved Raphael and he now realizes that it is Pauline whom he has already cared. The skin grows smaller and smaller, Raphael, terrified by his ever-nearing death, shuts himself up and will allow no one to see him. He even gives up Pauline for he fears that he cannot marry her with this curse upon him. How Raphael and Pauline reunite is told in a wonderful and interesting manner. In "Slave of Desire," Balzac plumbed the depths of human life and suffering. Its great theme, world old, and ever new, is that no matter how long overdue, we eventually pay the full price for evil committed in this world. Around the "Magic Skin" the great author has woven a story with the genius of which he alone was capable.

headline: JACKIE COOGAN. / QUEEN'S THEATRE ENTERPRISE.
text:
Jackie Coogan and a great circus are coming to town. Jackie will realize the dream of nearly every boy—young as six or old as sixty—and will be the star of a glittering, gorgeous, mammoth aggregation of the world's most marvellous wonders. Though he will be seen first as a very humble and a very forlorn young lad selling ice-cream, lemonade and peanuts to occupants of the "big-top" of Daly's greatest show on earth.

The name of the lavish picture which will be shown at the Queen's Theatre to-morrow is "Circus Days." It is a very free and liberal transcription for the screen taken from James Otis' ever popular story for boys (and girls, too) "Toby Tyler," which story has been current and popular for two generations and bids fair to endure unto the classic age.

Barbara Tenant will be seen as Toby's harassed mother; Claire McDowell will appear as Martha, the somewhat soured aunt of the hero; Russell Simpson takes the part of Uncle Eben Holt; Cesare Gravini, who made a big hit with his performance of the role of the aged violinist with Jackie in "Daddy," will portray another endearing role, that of clown; Peaches Jackson will be adorable as the tiny equestrianne star of the big show; Sam De Grasse assumes the role of the harsh Mr. Lord, owner of the circus concessions; De Witt Jennings is Mr. Daly, the shrewd and none too kindly owner of the show and Nellis Lane and William Barlow will appear respectively as they really are, the fattest woman and the jeanest man in the world.

And he clinched the position so far as Great Britain is concerned by stating that it is intended to seek a solution of the difficulties in a conciliatory spirit, whilst insisting on the maintenance of law and order in the foreign Settlement.

The bitterest partisan of the anti-foreign movement in China can find little to complain of in a policy of the kind enunciated by Mr. Ronald McNeill. If there is the slightest defect in the treaties between China and the Powers the foreign diplomats on the spot may be trusted to bring such to the notice of their respective Governments with a view to revision. But it is not the place of interested outsiders—if the phrase be permitted—to make those treaty rights a bone of contention between China and the subjects of the Powers. The best possible proof of the equity of those treaty rights in the foreign-Settlement is to be found in the fact that nearly two million Chinese are content to live therein and enjoy the solid protection that these afford in preference to the shadowy and fleeting protection of the Chinese in their own distinct territory. Why is it that these two million Chinese have not "packed up" long ago and gone to live under the Chinese flag and not under the flags of the foreign Powers? The answer is obvious—life would not be worth living for the very reasons that have been cited above as the causes of the present disturbances: the lack of a strong Central Government, destructive wars and the irritation caused by petty local rulers. Furthermore, on the score of industrial conditions, these may not be exactly perfect, but even in the Japanese cotton mills they "are the equal or superior to anything in China." Wherein, then, can the treaty rights of foreigners be inimical to the well-being of China? Until the Bolshevik intrusion in Chinese affairs, precious little was heard of those treaty rights being inimical. The best brains of the Chinese themselves made China a party to such treaty rights, and they in their day never conceived any idea of repealing them either by conciliation, or by propaganda, or by violence. Why, then, should the Chinese leaders of today harken to the evil counsels of outsiders whose interests are certainly not the interests of China? Until China rests out those evil spirits in her midst regains her former confidence in the Powers.

headline: NOT INIMICAL
text:
Once again attention has been directed in the House of Commons to the campaign "by those interested" against the Treaty rights of foreigners which are alleged to be inimical to the well-being of China. That is not only a mere shibboleth, the constant reiteration of which is becoming wearisome, but it is a gross perversion of the truth. The statement by Mr. Ronald McNeill was made in the course of a reply to a number of questions regarding the Shanghai trouble, when the Under Secretary for Foreign Affairs expressed the opinion that the origin of the disturbances was owing to the lack of a strong Central Government, destructive wars, and irritation of the Chinese with petty local rulers, resulting in discontent. Furthermore, he pointed out that industrial conditions hardly operated at all as part of the cause of the troubles, and he called attention to the very striking fact that the strike began

The day is past when there can be any truth in the allegation that the foreigners are only out to exploit the Chinese with a ruthless disregard for the ethics of business morality. To-day the foreigners are as convinced as the Chinese themselves that a peaceful and tranquil and settled China is not only the best in the interests of China herself but also the best in the interests of the Far East, commercially, socially, and educationally. headline: Traffic Sense.
parent_headline: QUALITY STYLE AND CHARACTER STYLE $3850 PRICE $22.50
text: The Chinese generally are accused of lacking what is known as a traffic sense. It would be interesting to know how far past and present authorities have helped to make the absence of that sense more pronounced. The earlier Governments had probably no idea of the expansion that was to take place later. They jogged along a day at a time and narrow and rural roads were the rule and not the exception and sufficed for the number of residents and the mode of traffic then in vogue. Those in charged during the last decade must be accused of a lack of foresight. And even to-day that lack seems much in evidence. Legacies from early days are still in evidence. Quite a number of roads can be indicated where there is either no side-walk for the pedestrian, or so little of one as to make walking on it no attraction at all. The pedestrian—European as well as Chinese — cannot be blamed if he or she clings to the moderate spaciousness of the middle or near middle, portion of a road. The attempt to dislodge either from it has failed as is clearly proved by the failure of the Captain Superintendent of Police to get pedestrians to keep to the sidewalks. Evidence of the Government's lack of foresight is shown in the number of times new roads have been widened to make room for motor traffic. All along it has been motor traffic first—others not at all. A walk along the Praya East reclamation bears this out. For a considerable portion of it there is no room for the pedestrian at all. The space is there but in the main it is given over to temporary buildings, some verging to the edge of what was once a sidewalk. It is useless expecting people to keep to the left, or right, if no opportunities are available for so doing. The wonder is that there is not a daily list of accidents. This must be ascribed to that Providence said to watch over drunks and fools; certainly not to the Government.

But the dreadful thing is that, although his doctor has really ordered him "out of a house in which he is overcrowded," the miners are told, "He is now a plutocrat; you should turn him out." No wonder that in anguish of soul he appeals to his miners. "Now what am I to do?" But in our dull bourgeois, why we could suggest one or two medientive things which he might do. He might cease to cry out so loud every time he is hurt. He might train himself to believe that he is, after all, much as other men are. He might abstain from making speeches which proclaim that everybody who enjoys a comfortable income, everybody who is as well off as he is, is a brutal capitalist grinding the faces of the poor. For until he practises that form of self-control it is very probable that the attacks which he delivers on people who live as he does will be directed by his faithful followers to his own address.

ICE CREAM. grow on trees in the backyard of America. A report of the discovery by experts of the Depart- partment of Agriculture of cherimoyas, or "vegetable ice cream trees," growing in Ecuador, has attracted attention in Wall Street, which is the part of New York in which ideas and money ultimately meet, and if it should succeed in making any mouths water there, it may easily stimulate a correspondent flow of capital. It should appeal at once to the soda fountain seneschals, of course, for it is said to combine in each mouthful the flavours of bananas, pineapples and strawberries. An attempt to send the fruits to New York and Paris was made several years ago, the Ecuadorian Consul-General in New York says, but the trip was too long to avoid losing the flavour, and the cotton packing required to keep the very soft skin intact made them too expensive. It ought to be possible, however, the Consul believes, to grow the trees from their small nuts at least in the warmer parts of the United States. After a little acclimatization, of course, the trees will probably be crossed with wheat and the ice cream cone industry established on a permanent basis.

headline: CREASED TROUSERS.
text: The passionate loyalty of the Labour party to their leader, we learn with surprise and regret, draws the line somewhere—draws it, in fact, at Mr. MacDonald's trousers, remarks the "Daily Telegraph" (London.) This would seem a domestic matter best settled at one of those happy gatherings of the party in which the followers, going into secret session, tell the leaders how to behave. But Mr. Ramsay MacDonald's is one of those sensitive souls which cannot bear to suffer without a cry; and he has never been so affecting as upon his trousers. It appears that certain ignoble creatures in the ranks of Labour have cast it up against Mr. MacDonald that his trousers are too elegant. We do not know how to express our emotions about this, but if we may say so without offence, we are surprised and horrified. Conscious of virtue, he might well have disdained such slander. But his gentle nature could not bear it. He had to tell the miners of Cymmer the whole history of those trousers. It is an affecting story, perhaps a little too pitiful for a May Day festival, but glowing with him, interest. On his recent holiday Mr. MacDonald took out an old pair of trousers and found when he put them on they had a beautiful crease. He happened to be photographed in these. It was then said that he had deserted the workers because the crease in his trousers showed that he was getting far too respectable. But this is not all. All another time he went into most respectable company.

By those people who think that all possible types of human character have a right to full and frank portrayal, Mr. Maugham's very full and frank delineation of Charles Townsend and Kitty Fane will be not merely accepted, but admired. Quite recently it has been under water owing to the flooded condition of the Thames. Runnymede is a meadow by the side of the road, from which one catches a glimpse of Windsor Castle. Magna Charta Island lies in the midst of the stream. The barons are said to have been camped on the meadow and the King on the north side of the river, and the delegates of the contending parties met on the island to discuss the "protocol." It is generally believed that the King placed his seal on the document which is usually regarded as the foundation of English liberaties in a pavilion erected on Runnymede. headline: MONEYLENDERS.
text:
Only occasionally is Hongkong aroused to the fact that the Colony has in its midst those who lend money at varying high rates of interest. No advertisements appear in the local Press, and residents' letter boxes never contain envelopes with circulars offering big and little sums "on note of hand only." Local moneylenders carry on their labours quietly. No spacious offices house them and no brass plates record their habitation. Occasionally it has been necessary to reduce the rate of interest they charge, thanks to the "interference" of a Judge of the court when, on occasion, cases of a moneylending nature have been heard. If there were no borrowers it follows there would be no lenders. The former are so either through thriftlessness or by reason of some misfortune which they have been unable to avoid. At Home an attempt is being made to curtail the activities of moneylenders—especially those of the vampire class—and to make the calling less a menace than it is to large numbers of unfortunate people, and to "get at" those who, principally in poor and slum areas, simply batten on people. The main feature of the proposed legislation is that it is exacted that "interest charged in respect of the sum actually lent and exceeding twenty pounds per centum per annum shall be deemed to be excessive and the irriscoretion shall be deemed to be harsh and unconscionable." There are

including one which prohibits any newspaper from inserting a moneylending announcement. This proposed Amending Bill will, if time is given for its consideration in Parliament, pass into law; in which case the Hongkong Government might well adopt some of its provisions, particularly those relating to the rate of interest to be charged in any transaction.

headline: Chinese Waste.
text: The incredible wastage going on almost continually at Canton, and the wasteful happenings at Shanghai must for ever explode the theory that the Chinese are thriftful or even careful. There is in fact a considerable amount of economic and other wastage daily taking place in the country. And this is confirmed by the American Commercial Attache at Shanghai who from his own particular coign is able to speak with authority. The Attache's main contention is that China's largest waste is due to a lack of adequate transportation, Labour has been cited as cheap in China; yet it is possible to import wheat from America and sell it at a cheaper rate than is the same produce from the Hwei Valley to Hankow a few hundred miles away, simply because transportation charges are so excessive. One of the many suggestions made for the use of the Boxer Indemnity Funds was that part of it should be used for the making of roads. The suggestion came from a Chinese body showing that at least in one direction the need for roads, and with it a system of road transportation is recognised. There are other instances of waste. In Hongkong the observer is struck with what seems to him the numbers of men it seems necessary to have in Chinese stores of the smallest kind and the overloading of houses by the number of servants made necessary by the one man one job system which prevails. There is also the system of false independence that prevails, shown in sudden derelictions from duty and the desire to use such double-edged weapons as the boycott and the strike at any odd moment—resulting in harmful wastage. Of militarism all over the country little need be said. The wastage from this in man and money is enormous. Some day, and that soon, the great mass of Chinese will have their eyes opened to the need there is for reform. When that time comes, attention will be directed not so much on the alleged imperialism and misdeeds of foreigners, but on the active misdeeds of these of the Chinese people who have it in their power as effect reforms but have made no move to put them into operation.

headline: Education in China.
text: Tsing Hua College, Peking, is a result of the return of the Boxer Indemnity on the part of America. It may thus be called an evidence of goodwill. Those conducting it might be expected to manage it with this fact in mind. It cannot be said to be conscientiously controlled if the following, which has been given wide publicity and has, so far not been contradicted, is true. In brief it is that in April the College was visited by M. Kamkhan, the Soviet Ambassador, who addressed the students on the evils of Imperialism and Western Capitalism, and urged them to struggle against world Imperialism, Doubtless there are evils connected with certain forms of Imperialism and Western Capitalism—evils which the most ardent Imperialist and Capitalist would willingly abolish—evils, of which it will do the intelligent no harm to be told. But such evils need to be explained by a fair-minded person and not by one whose statements are likely to be of the worst possible kind with the worst possible effect. This particular instance illustrates the type of gratitude that has sprung up in certain Chinese quarters for the facilities for education so generously and wholeheartedly given by foreigners. It illustrates further the difficulty of reaching right and lasting settlements. It may almost be true to say that the Chinese student class is more sinned against than sining, thanks to the baleful influence that has been cast over them for some considerable time.

headline: A THOUGHT FOR SUNDAY.
text:
"I will make them joyful in My House of Prayer."

The spare attendance at so many of our churches on Sundays—though neither minister nor little band of regular worshippers appears to suspect its true cause—is perhaps almost wholly due to the dour and dismal character of the services as therein conducted.

Of course one expects a quiet, reverential atmosphere in all places of public worship. But this is not necessarily incompatible with the joyfulness that God plainly tells us it is. His will to see in His House of Prayer. The waters of all true joy run deep, and their very stillness shows their depth.

But before minister and worshippers in any of God's Houses of Prayer can bring the magic touch of what the old psalm calls "the joy of salvation" into their services, and so radiate broadcast through the world the one spirit that will attract the many hungering for it, they must learn what is the real, the only source of joyfulness in all religious life. It is the thing Christ meant when He said, "By this shall all men know that ye are My disciples, if ye have love one to another." A community of people not alone outwardly professing the Christian Faith, but manifestly bearing the true Christ-like love for one another, can no more exist in a busy centre of human life without drawing the spiritually hungry ones to them, than a magnet can fail to find the steel filings hidden in this dust.

headline: UP THE MEKONG
text:
The long, slow way is the over-ture to the Angkor drama, the quiet preparation for overpowering scenes.

If Angkor Vat and its group were accessible to the tourist loafer at Suigon, if one could take a ricsha or a gharri from the qual or the public gardens, and in a few minutes reach the ruins and hastily scumble over their bordering terraces—one of the world's greatest wonders might fall to thrill the souls of such hasty audience. With consummate art of progress the approach is prepared. After the heat and noise of the French city of Suigon, the deck of a river steamer is a refuge of cool repose. We awoke to Mytho, the first stop. Mytho which seemed only a pierful of chattering Annamites, baskets of green cocoanuts, bananas, pineapples—all against a park-like background of tropic trees splashed with bongainvillea. From that on, one floats all through the fragment day on a wide, wide river of yellow water, while gradually wise, mild nature changes the finiered traveller into a tropic idler.

Such a river as it is, the Mekong, slow, wide, keeping itself muddy by constantly licking off the day of rice paddies, with no banks higher than the trade of the brown children who play at its edge. But traced on the map, it runs right away free of the French Protectorate and finds its independent way through taxifying gorges in China, gorges which are created only by perilous wires on which the most hazardous of people hang during the crossing of the canyon from off the cliff. Further away still this indomitable river has its source—in impenetrable Tibet, whose melting snows provide its first floods.

This is not all of its tricks. It grows so low in the dry season as to cause even a sampan to look to its plumb-line, while during the summer rains it rises to the point of inundation. The effect of this is to make it desirable to visit Angkor between November and January. Flat, flat, all is flat. "It is just like the savannahs of Florida," another Bike aloud to nobody, ferretting the world with his pismatics. The sky line is made of palms, nothing but palms. One thinks of the Bible, of the open of "Aida," of "Enoch Arden," and one lies down to pleasant dreams at siesta time.

All day, and all the long languous evening, it is the river. Delicious monotony of scene. Every native hut is like every other native hut, a bamboo bird-cage set high on stilts.

Around each native hut is a banana grove, a bunch of those poetic utilitarians, the cocoanut palms, and around the holes of these the naked brown babies play hide-and-seek with the passing boats. And between each house are the wide stretches of the rice, paddies. It is interesting to know that Khmer civilisation followed the coegree of rice. Where it grow, there also grow the intellectual progress of the mysterious race which famed and faded. headline: LADY GOLFER.
text:
U. S. CHAMPION

Of the American lady golfer now seeking honours in Britain, George W. Greenwood writes:—

Miss Collett's golfing career commenced at the age of fourteen, and two years ago she gained one of the desires of her life by winning the United States championship, having in the meantime captured State championships in almost every part of the American Continent. She was taught by Aloe Smith, a brother of Macdonald Smith, and has also received valuable assistance from Hagen and Sarazen. Miss Collett carries a veritable forest of clubs—five wooden clubs and a regular armour of iron—but only a fayoured few are given a chance of justifying their existence. Like most first-class American golfers, Miss Collett dispenses with the formalities of address: the clubhead is placed to the ball, there follows one small movement, and the swing is started. It is an object-lesson in economy of physical and nervous effort.

When I first set eyes on Miss Collett I was reminded of Mr. Bobby Jones, who wastes no time in perpainions; he walks up to the ball, puts the club down, and without any further preliminaries the swing commences. It is an admirable scheme if you can't do it, because it tends to less confusion of mind, the great obstacle to all progress in golf. I do not think there can be any doubt that Miss. Collett is the best American lady golfer who have yet seen. The wooden club play is particularly good, both as regards length and acorney. This can severely be said of her iron shots, which are inclined to be a little "flabby" because she swings at the ball instead of hitting at it. In this respect there is a marked difference between Miss Collett and Miss Wethered. The latter attacks the ball as if she means business, who the American girl gives the impress on that she is afraid to hurt it.

headline: LADY SUSPENDED.

HOME GOLF UNION'S ACTION.

The Ladies' Golf Union in Great Britain has suspended for three years a lady who returned an incorrectly marked card.

Leading players and sports-women say that cases of women cheating are very rare, and that women are just as good sports as men.

The consensus of 'opinion regarding the Ladies' Golf Union's drastic action in suspending for three years a lady member of the Dorset Club, for returning an incorrectly marked card, is that it will be a timely warning that adherence to the rules is growing woefully tax.

One critic says: "It is a terrible warning, but the players are constantly incurring penalties of which they are entirely ignorant."

"Cheating at golf is not usually done out of a desire for dishonest gain, but for the sake of vanity, enabling a player to boost of the lowness of his, or her, store. It is an unpleasant thing to say, but the unanimous opinion is that women in all games are not as strictly accurate at scoring as men, who are more accustomed to take beatings cheerfully."

It is understood that the students have decided to postpone their one-day strike until June 25. According to Chinese unofficial reports, the Catholic church at Klafeng was burned down yesterday, and one Italian priest was killed.

It is persistently reported this evening that the Foreign Minister, Shen Juai-lin, has gone into hiding, fearing that the students will persist in extreme demands to which he cannot agree.

headline: TWO LIVES LOST. / LAST
text:
Although it has materially solved the serious problem of water supply, last night's deluge has left a trail of disaster, two lives having been lost, shops flooded and roads closed as a result of landslides.

The two lives lost were through the collapse of the retaining wall at Happy Valley referred to elsewhere. This was a wall used in connection with dumping from Stubbs Road being between it and the Wongneichong end of Happy Valley. The force of the water pouring over it eventually carried away the huge boulders of which it was composed and hurled them down the precipitous slope to the corner of Happy Valley.

There are no houses immediately below the wall but two cars (believed to have been unattended at the time) were outside the Young Wo Nursing Home which itself just escaped the main fall. Of these there is nothing left but twisted body work. Yet more telling evidence of the force of the fall is the condition of a P.W.D. steam roller which together with the cars bore the brunt of the landslide. Hugo granite boulders have battered the upper part of it almost to pieces and the watchman who was in charge of it is one of the two whose bodies were recovered this morning by the Fire Brigade.

The main body of water in the Valley itself has found an outlet to the canal, although it is still feet deep at the western end. Most of the posts and railings have stood the strain, however.

headline: Search In Dark
text:
A police officer who was on the spot shortly after the disaster was reported (between one and two this morning) spoke with admiration to a "China Mail" representative of the work of the firemen. "Happy Valley at the time was, in his view, " like a millpond" and in addition at the spot where they were searching for any vestiges of life the water was still pouring down the hillside like a cataract. Roped together and held by others from points of greater degree of safety they worked in the dark waist deep in water. The bodies of the steam roller watchman and a hawker whose pitch had been carried away were the only ones recovered but digging operations continue.

The spot where the disaster occurred, indeed the whole of Happy Valley, presented scenes of indescribable confusion this morning, huge boulders sticking up from piles of sand and slush.

Mr. Edward Johnson, Canadian tenor, the pupil of Lombardi, Caruso's teacher, appears at the Theatre Royal for one night only on June 22.

Edward Johnson is considered the Royal tenor of Italy, for during his seven years unique success all over Europe. His Majesty the King of Italy watched with keen interest this tenor's brilliant career, and in 1920 conferred upon him the Cross of Officer of the Order of the Crown of Italy.

In Rome when His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales was the guest of the King of Italy, he expressed a desire that this gifted tenor should be presented to him after a Command Performance, and a few weeks later, when His Royal Highness was in Guelph, Canada, the birth-place of the tenor, he expressed publicly in his speech the glories of Johnson's divine voice, and urged his townspeople to turn out to the last man to do Johnson due honour on his return home...

Johnson, has also sung before Her Majesty the Queen of Roumania, one of the greatest operatic critics in Europe, who expressed the view that Johnson has one of the most glorious voices she has ever heard.

Johnson's success in New York as the leading tenor, of the Metropolitan Opera Co. is known all the world over.

He has sung in every famous Opera House in the World and everywhere he has obtained great success.

Such a great tenor is to be heard at the Theatre Royal on Monday, June 22, and the residents of the Colony are earnestly urged to be present at the Theatre and give him his due honour by a most enthusiastic reception, for he comes here at the express invitation of some of the music lovers of Hongkong.

In the East we are cut off for years at a time from contact with great mulicarand opportunities of hearing artists of such a high standard are very rare, and in order to induce other great artists to visit this Colony, it is but natural that the only encouragement that they need is the hearty support of the public.

The plan is at Moutries and the charges are $4.00, $2.00 and $1.00.

headline: Trams Held Up.
text:
The Happy Valley tram car got no further than the scene of the disaster but little inconvenience is experienced as the circuit can almost be completed and when the tram gets as far as possible, it returns on its own track. To keep the track clear here and in the region of Morrison Hill, Broadwood and Wong-nei-chong Gap roads it was necessary to keep gangs of coolies working all night, for as fast as it was cleared, more earth and rock would be carried down. The City and the Western district were served with trams as usual last night but it was found necessary to discontinue those to the Eastern districts about 10 30. A start was able to be made this morning, through the good work already mentioned, Motor Cars' Escapes.

About eight cars are imprisoned at various points along Stubbs Road through landslides having occurred before and behind them whilst in motion. The occupants must have had marvellous escapes but beyond having to abandon their cars they appear to have escaped unhurt. Two of them were cars of the Hotels Company. The Hon. Mr. C. McI. Messer was among the “captives.” A night walk up the Peak soaked to the skin seems to have been the only hardship suffered by Mr. McI. Messer together with others.

Stubbs Road as far as Bowen Road is absolutely impassable but upon enquiry the “China Mail” learned from Mr. H. E. Goldsmith, in charge of the Roads Department, that it was hoped to clear that particular sector in the course of the day. From Bowen Road to the Peak might necessitate an extra day's work before it could be cleared and even longer in the case of the sector of the new road from Bowen Road to Repulse Bay and the round-the-island road from Repulse Bay to Shaukiwan.

headline: Streets' Flooded
text:
The actual City appears to have escaped with mere inconvenience caused by floods although houses in Wanchaf, little more than coolie matsheds, appear to have collapsed. This morning, apart from pools, little remained to indicate what the main roads were like at the height of the storm but any who were on the Praya between two and three a.m. speak of streams of water feet deep sweeping across. Owners of shops in Queen's Road have had an anxious night, many of them having been up all night directing bailing operations. As usual the shops in the neighbourhood of the Tabaqueria Filipina have suffered mainly through their low lying position.

A+ St. Francis Street, Wanchai, a number of houses were in danger of collapsing through the floods and when owners abandoned them last night many of them, were swept away by floods of water racing down the street. There appear to have been no casualties, however. Slight landslides are reported at Magazine Gap Road and Macdonnell Road.

Ten inches of Rain. Official figures of the rainfall, supplied, on application, by Mr. C. W. Jeffries, acting Director, Royal Observatory, show that between 8 p.m. and midnight over 7½ inches fell and by 11:30 this morning the total had become 10.25 inches.

The heaviest rainfall would appear to have been between 10-30 p.m. and 11.30 p.m. when 3.160 inches fell. Other figures are between 8.30 p.m. and 9.30 p.m. 1.015 in.; between 9.30 p.m. and 10.30 p.m., 2.010 in.; between 11.30 p.m. and 12.30 p.m. 1.320 in.

The maximum rainfall on one civil day, Mr. Jeffries informs us, was 20.495 inches on May 30 1889, and the present fall has been exceeded on many occasions since.

The over night rainfall will probably enable the whole City to be put on full supply in a day or so, the "China Mail" was informed upon enquiry.

A Chinese was taken to the Government Civil Hospital with a fractured foot. The injuries were caused by the man hesitating before an Aberdeen motor 'bus at the junction of Queen's Road West and Centre Street.

“Some Difficulties of the Inner Life” will be the subject of this week's Public Lecture of the Hongkong Lodge. The Theological Society, 16 Queen's Road Central, on Wednesday June 17, at 5.45 p.m. The Public are cordially invited.

headline: U. S. INVASION.
text:
WIMBLEDON TENNS PROSPECTS.

At Eastbourne, Britain head America (Wimbledon contingent at lawn tennis by 3 matches to 2 (4 singles and 1 doubles as in Davis Cup tiea).

Hennessey (America) beat J.D.P. Wheatley 7-5, 6-2, 4-6, 7-5. Gilbert (Britain) beat Censey 9-7, 9-7, 6-3.

[The Wimbledon championship commence on Monday, June 22.] WHO THEY ARE.

Of America's 1925 Wimbledon team, A. Wallis Myers, C.B.E., writes:—

The six American players who are coming to Wimbledon in June to play an international match against England and to compete in the championships will, with two exceptions, be making their debut in this country. They are a young, post-war team, and their advent in our midst is another proof of the United States Association's desire, by an interchange of players, to strengthen the ties of friendship.

Charles (“Chuck”) S. Garland is the oldest member of the team, and will lead it. He was here in 1920 with the American Davis Cup team which beat England and France. In partnership with R. N. Williams he won the doubles championship at the old Wimbledon, defeating Tilden and Johnston in the semifinal, and Paike and Kingscote in the final. Pressure of business in Pittsburgh kept Garland out of the game for two years after his return to America, but he is now resident in New York, and has made a welcome reappearance on court. John Henmessey, hailing from Chicago, is one of the Middle West players, trained on "dirt" courts, who have sprung to the front in the last year or two. He beat G. L. Patterson and B. I. C. Norton in his own district last summer, and at Forest Hills in September was responsible for Jean Borotra's defeat in the America championship. He is ranked No. 7 in his own country.

Ray - Casey, like Johnston and McLoughlin, has emerged from the golden gate of the West. He is ranked No. 2. in California, and won the doubles championship of Mexico with Vincent Richards last year, the pair defeating the brothers Kinsey; the present doubles champions of America. He has a powerful service and a smash almost as violent. Lucien Williams, a former captain of Yale, and ranked No. 11 in the national list, visited England with the Yale and Harvard University team in 1922. He is now the third best player in the Middle West, coming next to Hennessy and George Lott, the U.S.A. junior champion. Of Lawrence B. Rice, the New England player, Tilden has always held a high opinion. He was No. 9 in America in 1921 and No. 11 in 1922. At present he is No. 15, but his opportunities for play have been restricted by business ties, and he may very well shine over here as brightly as any of his fellows.

The American team will probably compete in the French national championships at St. Cloud before coming to Wimbledon. The majority of them have learnt and developed their game on non-turf courts; they will indeed, be more at home on the Paris courts than at Wimbledon. They may not contain a Wimbledon winner among them, yet they are all products of the modern, aggressive, quickfooted school, and their presence at Wimbledon is sure to provide a stimulus—and possibly a surprise.

headline: LAWN BOWLS. / LATEST LEAGUE PROSPECTS.
text:
NOTES AND COMMENT.

The following is the league rogramme for to-morrow:

Civil Service C.C. v. Taikbo R. C. Kowloon Dock R.C. v. Kowloon

Kowloon's Dock R.C. v. Kowloon B. G. Club.

Kowloon C.C. v. Craigengower C.C.

SECOND DIVISION. Taikoo R.C. v. East Point R.C. Indian R.C. v. Police R.C. R.H.K. Yacht Club v. Kowloon C.C.

Last week's results were about as expected, although. Taikoo managed a wonderful victory against the Dock Club, I understand that with two rinks finished and the third rink only two heads to go, Taikoo wanted nine to win. They laid a five and a four and thus pulled the game out of the fire, scoring an almost impossible victory.

.The Bowling Green Club decisively defeated〉the Cricket Club, whilst Craigengower retain their position at the head of the league by a fine victory over the Civil Service on the latter's green.

The Police, by defeating the Taikoo second string by a substantial margin, retain their unbeaten record in the second division. They seem almost certain to gain promotion at the end of the season. Playing with a very weakened team at Sookumpoo, the Kowloon Cricket Club were overwhelmed by the Indians, whilst at East Point the home team secured their first win at the expense of the Yacht Club.

From a visit paid to the various greens in the Coolny it seems that none has suffered any special damage from the very heavy rains. The Civil Service green had a marvellous escape, thanks to the high banking around it. The Police-green has a little mud on it but this should be cleared in time for their next home game.

Of the games to be played in the first division, that between the Civil Service and Taikoo would appear to be the most interesting, for the home team will need to win to save themselves from relegation, whilst the visitors will try hard for the two points to keep them in the running for the championship.

Having previously drawn their game, both sides scoring 57 points, the return. Kowloon "Derby" between the Dock and the Bowling Green should also be very-interesting. With the advantage of playing at home, the Dock should win.

Judging from the Cricket Club's recent form, Craigen-gower, although playing away, should secure the two points.

In the second division, Taikoo should dispose of the East Point team. I understand the K.C.C. team will be considerably weakened by the absence of some of their best players to-morrow and the Yacht Club might, with a slice of luck, pick up two valuable points.

The Police are visiting the Indians' ground with a firm determination to lower the home team's undefeated (home) record. They appear to be the only team who are likely to do it, but they will need to play all they know to accomplish this. Should they do so, their chances of going through the competition undefeated will be rosy.

headline: PERKING AGITATORS MAKING MISCHIEF.
text:
Despite official statements that every effort would be made to prevent anti-foreign riots, nothing is being done to hinder dangerous inflammatory agitation.

Thousands of incendiary and provocative posters have been posted up throughout Peking, this morning, depicting British police shooting and bayonetting defenceless students, women and children lying on the ground.

While thus stirring up the masses, students and other educated Chinese refuse to face the real facts.

Mr. Palaret H.B.M. Chargé d'Affaires, unofficially offered to see the student deputation and explain the British point of view, but the offer was refused. The vernacular papers are mostly refusing to print Reuter telegrams. They are inserting an absurdly garbled version of events. For example: The Japanese at Hankow are alleged to have injured each other; the foreign buildings at Kiukiang caught fire themselves; while the Yi Ship Pao asserts that Mr. Mackenzie died of sickness and that the British Consul ordered the doctor to mutilate the remains and then accused the Chinese of murder.

headline: Negotiations Broken Off.
dateline: Shanghai, June 18. Troops for Peking. Peking, June 18.
text:
The diplomatic commission has broken off negotiations, owing to the divergence of Chinese and Foreign views.

The commission, sent to Shanghai by representatives of the interested Powers in order to investigate recent events and endeavour to find an immediate solution of the difficulties which were the direct outcome of those events, met the Chinese delegates to day for the third time, at the office of the Commissioner for Foreign Affairs.

At this meeting, the commission handed to the Chinese delegation certain concrete proposals which in their opinion, constituted a fair basis for settlement.

The Chinese delegation presented, once again to the commission a series of demands, which had no direct connection with the recent regrettable occurrences, although the commission had been careful to emphasise from the very start that it had not been authorised to deal with these points.

The Chinese delegation intimately, moreover, that these points must be dealt with at the same time as the incidents themselves.

It is to be noted that the instructions given to the commission are based on the Note, addressed to the Legations by the Waichiaopu, in which mention only is made of four points, all of which are directly connected with the incidents themselves.

Under the circumstances, these two points of view would seem to be altogether too divergent to admit of any hope of an early solution on the spot; and the commission has, in consequence, decided to leave for Peking tonight.

The previous message was an official translation of the French text of the communiqué on the matter. The commission entrains to night; and the whole question, therefore, goes back to Peking. It is understood the Chinese delegation to-day presented the whole thirteen original demands, including the rendition of the Mixed Court; the dismissal of the Secretary of the Municipal Council and that municipal franchise be given to the Chinese.

The Note sent yesterday, to the Walchiapou by the interested Powers, was discussed at a Cabinet meeting to day. As a result, it is understood that the Walchiapou has been instructed to draft a Note in reply, controlling the statements made: Two brigades of War Minister Wu Kwang-hsin's Fengtien troops have arrived in the vicinity of Peking. In Chinese military circles it is explained that they will act as special guards for the Chief Executive. Marshall Chang Tso-lin has also sent one battalion for special police duty in Peking. headline: PLUCKY WOMEN. / ROBBERS WHO CAUGHT TARTARS. / FIVE YEARS APIEOE.
text:
In each of three cases of robbery or attempted robbery heard yesterday at the Criminal Sessions the prisoners owed their appearance to the plucky conduct of the women of the households whom probably they had looked upon as easy victims.

Escaping from her bonds and ungagging herself a woman at Shanghai Street, Mongkoktsui, pursued one of the robbers who had taken jewellery from the house. Her action led to his arrest and he was sentenced to five years' imprisonment.

One of four women playing dominoes in a house at Chatham Road, Hunghom, when robbers rushed in and presented revolvers had the pluck to defy them and run to the verandah blowing a police whistle. The intending robbers immediately decamped but one was captured by Mr. Fokin, of Alex Ross and Co., who was passing by.

The captured man was sentenced to five years' imprisonment.

The spirited resistance of a woman at Shamshuipo scared other robbers who entered a house in Ki Lung Street, and they decamped without taking anything. A Chinese living on the bottom floor grappled with one of them and managed to detain him until the police arrived and he also was sentenced to five years' imprisonment.

headline: MOTORIST CHARGED. / MR. WERSCHKUL'S EVENING RIDE. / REPULSE HAY INCIDENTS.
text:
The greater part of three hours was taken up at the Central Magistracy yesterday afternoon with the hearing of the case against Mr. Howard T. Werschkul, a young American flour broker, who was charged with causing bodily harm to an Indian watchman in the employ of the Repulse Bay Hotel by wanton and furious driving.

The case for the Crown was that he drove a car in a zigzag course past the entrance to the Hotel on the night of Saturday, June 6, that he had not full control of the car and that as a result he knocked down the watchman who was standing outside the Hotel.

Witnesses called all attributed to the defendant's car a dangerous speed for such a spot. Mr. F. G. H. Haslam, who watched the car's progress from the main flight of steps leading up to the Hotel while he was waiting for his own car, said that the occupants were laughing and singing. The car was zigzagging along the road at a speed of about 20-25 miles an hour. He did not see the watchman but heard the crash. The car did not stop. Mr. M. M. Maas, of the A.P.C. gave corroborative evidence.

Mr. C. Edwards, of the Hongkong and Shanghai Bank, who was waiting at the foot of the steps to the Hotel in the main road said that the car was travelling at considerable speed and cut in on another car in such a manner that it caused simultaneous exclamations of surprise from himself and others who were with him. He should think it was going at 18 miles an hour when it passed the Hotel.

Mr A. Grimmett, of the Revenue Office, who was outside the Hotel at the time at the top of the steps said that he thought the car was going to run over the spot where he and his wife were standing. He pushed his wife out of the way and jumped clear himself. The car swerved and hit the watchman on the opposite side. Witness called to the driver to stop but the latter took no notice. The car was going at about 25 miles an hour in his opinion. He noticed that the number was 175.

Mr. Graham, of the Colonial Secretariat, said that the Indian watchman seeing his danger jumped in an attempt to get clear but was caught and carried for some yards.

The injuries sustained were a fractured thigh bone and abrasions, said Dr. W. L. Paterson.

The case for the Crown having been closed the defendant went into the witness box.

On the night in question he had dinner with some friends, among whom were M. Dupre, the boxer, and after watching the dancers it was suggested that they should go for a ride. They got as far as the Hotel garage in the car when it was found that no one had any cigarettes so they returned. On driving off again witness (who was driving) felt something strike the front of the car but thought they had struck the rail. Later when they stopped for a puncture near Tytam Tuk reservoir they found that the front head light had been broken and that it was no longer functioning. At Shaukiwan they were stopped by a police officer who told them he had been warned to keep a lookout for a car of their number.

Mr. Werschkul said that the first drink of an alcoholic nature he had on the day in question was a cocktail or two before dinner. He was going at a speed of fifteen miles, an hour at the time he passed the Hotel which he admitted was faster than he ought to have been travelling at that spot. When he drove down the hill after returning to procure the cigarettes the car was in first gear and he changed into second at the bottom as he took the turn to approach the hotel for the second time.

Mr. Andre Dupre gave corrosive evidence and said that in his opinion the car was travelling at a speed of about ten miles or fifteen kilometres an hour.

The case was adjourned until this afternoon.

The Coroner's Inquiry into the death of a coolie as the result of a motor car running into the pavement at West Point, which, as stated yesterday, opened at the Central Magistracy, concluded in the afternoon when a verdict of manslaughter against the driver was returned. A warrant is out for the arrest of the driver, Fun Pulang, who is absconded whilst on bail of $5,000.
