headline: Critical Position.
text:
The exasperation of the Cantonese at the arrogance of the hired Yuhnanese and Hunanese troops who were brought to Canton by the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen to enable him to oust General Chen (Chiung-ming (Chan Kwing-ming) has led to an outbreak of fighting.

While still protesting loyalty to the principles of Sun Yat-sen and the Kuomintang (Kuomintang) party, the Yunnanese Generals Yang' Hsi-nin (Yang Hsi-man) and Lau Chun-wan have demanded that the authorities order the cessation of troop movements on the East and North Rivef districts; otherwise, they will take measures to resist.

The authorities have replied denouncing their insubordination, dismissing them, and appointing General Chu Pei-teh (Chu Pui-tak) acting Commander of the Yunnanese forces.

This is virtual to a declaration of war. Yang Hsi-nin has seized the Governor's 'yamen', the telephone and telegraph offices, and the electric light plant.

The Yunnanese and Cantonese are entrenched on opposite sides of the Canton River.

The Yunnanese control the whole of the Canton side, while the gunboats under the Canton authorities command the river. The Canton authorities chiefly depend on the Whampon cadets who are trained by Soviet officers.

The foregoing message needs explanation in certain places.

Explanation in certain places. It is not the Yunnanese and Hunanese who are ranged against the Cantonese Communists. The Hunanese no longer exist as a fighting force, having been scattered while trying to make their way out of the province of Kwangtung when Dr. Sun was still alive. The Kwangsi merciennaries are the allies of the Yunnanese.

Similarly, General Lau Chun-wan (also spelt Lau Tsun-wan) is not Yunnanese; he commands the Kwangsi army.

Chu Pui-tak also commands a Yunnanese following but he is loyal to the Communists and is their main strength in their stronghold at Honam, the island immediately facing Canton city.

No news has been available from Canton since the time of the night-boats leaving yesterday afternoon as telegraphic communication has been suspended.

This morning, it was gathered that no wireless message had come down from the British gunboats off, Shameen, but that a report had been received to the effect that there had been a general lull in the fighting since yesterday afternoon and up to this morning.

So far, no untoward incident to any foreigner has come to light although those resident in the eastern suburb are inconvenienced through martial law being enforced by the Kwangsi mercenaries and the danger of fighting breaking out there, as the eastern approach is an important strategic point.

There are eight foreign men-of-war at Cantón, viz., the British gunboats, Moth, Tarantula and Cicala, an American sloop and the U.S.S. Pampanga, two French boats and a Japanese man-of-war. Our Canton correspondent reports that General Fan Sheksang, formerly the strong man of Canton, has returned to the city from the West River. Hitherto, the Communists have been counting on his help, or at least his neutrality, but now it is stated

that he has "rejoined his old colleagues:

Mr. Sun Fo (Dr. Sun's son and former Mayor of Canton) went up to Canton as a peacemaker but judging by results, he must have failed. He returned to Hongkong last night.

The Sai On, Kinshan and Paul Beau brought down full complements of refugees last night, the ships being full long before the hour of sailing. As a precaution; the river steamers in Canton had steam up all day yesterday.

The general strike is still in existence and not a cargo boat could be seen in the anchorage yesterday. The river steamers are not carrying any cargo for Canton. This strike is part of the Communist attempt to cut off Canton economically and thus drive the mercenaries out.

Feeling between Cantonese and non-Cantonese in Hongkong ran high on the water-front last night when the river-bonds were leaving for Canton.

Two Yunnanese who were being jostled and threatened by a large crowd, mostly of wharf-coolies were happily taken care of by Mr. W. H. Edmonds of the Public Works Department. Mr. Edmonds was passing in his motor-cycle and saw what was happening. To a "China Mail" reporter, the strangers professed in Southern Mandarin that they were not soldiers but were merchants who had fled from Canton. With two Indian constables bringing up the renr. Mr. Edmonds eventually made a way for the two men who walked behind the motor-cycle and made their way home under Mr. Edmonds's protection.

(From Our Own Correspondent.) Carlton, Sunday.

Developments are also reported from the Eastern River and the Canton-Kowloon Railway. The Yunnanese, of course, make out that they have got to grips with General Hsu Shung-chi's. Cantonese vanguards and defeated several hundred of them in the neighbourhood of Shek Pai, a railway station.

I am also informed that the Yunnanese are securing labour for the railway and that their trains will be working.

Interviewed, by the "China Mail" yesterday: a "Cantonese official who has just arrived from Swatow stated that most of General Chan Kwing-ming's former subordinates are joining General Hsu's anti-mercenary army. Their explanation is that Dr. Sun is dead, Chan Kwing-ming is now out of the field, so the Cantonese should unite against the common enemy since the old feud has expired.

General Hsu is reported to be preparing a march on Canton and the danger of a flank or rear attack from pro-Chan forces, has decreased considerably. Commanders Hung Leuk and Yeung Kwan-yu, former subordinates of Chan, are now embodied in Hsu's army. Ngai Bong-ping has returned to the Kuomintang 'fold and has been appointed Defence Commissioner of the West River, stated the official, with the Civil Governorship when the cause is won.

headline: LORD CURZON / CASTLES FOR THE NATION.
text:
The "Daily Mail" understands that the late Marquis Curzon of Kedleston has left two historic ruins. Tattershall Castle; Lincolnshire, and Bodiam Castle, Sussex, to the nation.

Tattershall Castle, near Withm, is thought to have been erected about 1440. In September, 1911 it was feared that the famous fireplaces would be sent to the United States. They were taken to London, but Lord Curzon, who bought the castle a little later “to save it from being knocked to pieces,” recovered them.

In June 1912 they were returned to their home on decorated lorries which passed beneath triumphal arches. Lord Curzon was in the procession, and his carriage was drawn by ropes by the viliagers.

Bodiam Castle, near Hastings built in 1386, has been described as one of the most beautiful and interesting ruins in England.

It was bought by Lord Curzon in 1917.

The ruins consist of round towers at the angles with five square ones between them, and the great gateway is flanked by two square towers.

An automatic revolver found on a heap of sand at the back of the Kowloon Fire Station was handed over to the Police by Mr. M. Murphy, overseer of the Y.M.C.A, building.

A lamp trimmer on the s.s. On Lee was arrested yesterday for the unlawful possession of 100 tins of opium, one revolver, and 50 rounds of ammunition.

headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
The strike is spreading to the French Concession. This morning's estimate of the strikers was 250,000, but a number of staffs resumed work today, including the foreign cable companies and Commercial Pressemployees—also 600 workers at the Japanese Dah Koong Mills, and 500 men at the Riverside power station.

The defence is continually being strengthened, approximately 1,500 marines and blue-jackets have been landed from three British, one French, and one Italian cruiser. Seven American destroyers and ten gunboats (British, Japanese and French), in addition to 400 American marines are due to morrow

The absence of riots and the resumption of the workers' indicate that the students are losing their grip of the situation, while the arrival of the Peking Commissioners, whose mission is only to investigate should help to clear the atmosphere.

The wide nature of the student disturbances is further shown by a Hankow message of Friday, which says that 20,000 students are agitating and distributing anti-Foreign leaflets. The Chinese authorities have so far prevented any big demonstrations; the movement began at Hankow on May 25.

headline: Tientain Parade
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
Tientsin, June 6.—A party of 1,000 students demonstrated in the Native City yesterday afternoon and this morning. There was no incident; the streets are heavily guarded by police, reinforced by Fengtian soldiers.

Professors joined the students who made speeches demanding the restoration of Dairen, boycott of the British and abolition of the Concessions.

Marshall Chang Tsc-lin has assured the Police Chief that he will back every effort to maintain order and assume full responsibility in the event of the Peking Government countermanding police measures.

headline: Widéspread Agitation
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
Numerous student strikes and demonstrations are reported in many cities throughout the country, but no disorder is reported except at Chinkiang where the police station was wrecked. There were no casualties.

Arrangements are being made to despatch a foreign warship to Chinkiang. Chief Executive Tuan Chi-jui's headquarters have issued a circular telegram to the Provinces, stating that Government has lodged strong protests with the Diplomatic Body as regards the Shanghai shootings; and also sent Messrs. Tsai Ting-kan and Tseng Tsung-chien to Shanghai to investigate.

The telegram advises the merchants and students to attend to their own business and await a settlement.

headline: Boycott Urged
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
The Cabinet met this morning. It is unofficially reported that they decided to issue a mandate somewhat similar in terms to the Chief Executive's circular telegram. The students held a large demonstration at Tienan Men this afternoon, at which they decided to march to the headquarters of the Chamber of Commerce, surround the building and compel the Chamber to carry out an Anglo-Japanese boycott.

The students surrounded the Chamber of Commerce this afternoon, but were refused admission. Finally a party of student delegates were admitted who urged the inauguration of a strike, a boycott and other measures.

The Chamber practically refused their demands but promised to give a further reply tomorrow.

headline: Powers' Note.
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
After a lengthy meeting this morning of the Ministers of the Powers interested, Signor Cerruti (Italian Minister and Doyen of the "Corps Diplomatique") this evening handed the following Note to the Chinese Minister of Foreign Affairs:

I have the honour, in the name of my colleagues and myself, to acknowledge receipt of the Note, dated June 4, which Your Excellency addressed to me, relative to the disorders in Shanghai

While remarking that the reports received by the Chinese Government are incomplete, since they do not mention several attacks against foreigners, my comrades and myself prefer to reserve judgment until the arrival of full details.

To this end, the diplomatic representatives concerned have decided to send a delegation to Shanghai without delay, to study the situation on the spot and submit a report.

I wish at all events, to de-

clare, that the Foreign Authorities of the International Concession, far from having assumed the violent attitude which the Chinese Government attribute to them, have preserved the greatest self-control as proved by the fact that during the past four days—despite numerous provocations—no serious incident has occurred in Shanghai.

I wish to renew the assurance, already given verbally, that the Police of the International Concession have always had instructions to use their arms only if attacked and in imminent danger.

headline: Tatsuta" Sails.
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
The Navy Office states that H.I.J.M.S. "Tatsuta" sailed this afternoon for Shanghai. She carried 200 marines.

Four more destroyers have been despatched to Shanghai from Sascho, while two others have been sent from Formosa to Canton.

Signor Cerruti (Italian Minister), this afternoon, handed to the Wachiaооц а second Note, in which it was announced that the Powers are sending a delegation to Shanghai on June 8, to investigate and report.

It is announced that the members of the delegation will be: M. S. Tripier, Counsellor of the French Legation.

Mr G. G. M. Vereker, Secretary of the British Legation.

Mr. E. Gerry Greene, First Secretary of the American Legation.

Mr. Shigemitsu, First Secretary of the Japanese Legation. M. de Schooten, Secretary of the Belgian Legation.

Signor G. Scaduto Menola, Secretary of the Italian Legation.

The Senior Consul this afternoon replied to the Foreign Commissioner's notes of May 31 and June 1, on the subject of the recent disturbances in Shanghai. He recapitulated the main facts of the riots, instancing the deliberate attacks on the police, from which it could be seen that the police action was very different to the Commissioner's version. The question of the propriety of the police action is one which should be raised in the course of legal proceedings; when those arrested are tried. There also will be as a matter of course an investigation by the authorities concerned into the action of the police. Besides which competent courts stand ready to deal with any complaints.

The Settlement authorities naturally assume full responsibility for the action taken for the maintenance of order, but remind the Commissioner of the grave responsibility of the local Chinese authorities in respect to anti-foreign agitation, conducted beyond the limits of the Settlement, to which these regrettable occurrences may largely be attributed.

headline: Chinkiang Outbreak
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
The British Consul-General at Chinkiang, near Nanking, tele-graphed to-day: There are riots

in the Concession; can the Navy send assistance?" To which the following reply was sent: "American Admiral last evening wirelessed to an American warship, proceeding up river to put in at Chinkiang."

Later messages stated that the situation was serious. Rioting students had wrecked three houses in the Concession, the Chinese Police, told off-protect foreigners, proving absolutely useless. The rioters carried on joyfully until the Commanding Chinese brought his own troops to the scene, four hours after the Consul General had asked for assistance.

The General restored order and the foreign women and children returned ashore from the boats on which they had taken refuge but a message to night says that the situation is again serious.

The U.S.S. Paul Jones is now due at Chlnkiang and H.M.S. Woodlark should reach there on Monday.

headline: Home Labour Views
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
The Council of the Independent Labour Party has issued a statement, sympathising with the alleged oppressive conditions introduced by foreign capitalism into the Far East. It asserts that under the British Flag in the Foreign Concession at Shanghai children of five years of age and upwards are working night and day shifts of twelve hours for seven days weekly, for twopence a day.

The Labourites demand the immediate application of labour legislation worthy of European standards; also the withdrawal of armed forces. The Council protests against the foreign occupation of Chinese cities.

LONDON, June 7. Discussing the trouble in the Far East, the "Observer" says that China cannot long be denied fiscal

autonomy, which is already enjoyed by India. A general re-adjustment in the relationship between the

Western Powers and China is imperative.

China is no more proof against the contagion of her national consciousness and self-respect than the other great countries of the East. The task of the Powers is to give the new spirit it's direction and outlet.

headline: End in Sight?
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
The morning papers think that the end of the strike is within sight. There is certainly a remarkable change in the general atmosphere. The Chinese in the streets are beginning to fraternise with the Volunteers.

This is mainly due to the impending departure from Peking of diplomatic representatives, which will lead to the discussions by which the Chinese invariably expect to settle troubles big and small, when momentary excitement has passed.

The situation is still very delicate; however, and little would be required to revive the fires of racial antagonism which the extremists are continually fanning. An outstanding feature of the riots has been the loyalty to the Municipal Council of the Chinese Volunteers, despite the bitter attacks of the vernacular papers, while only 100 out of 1,600 Chinese police failed to withstand the strain of the continual viuperation heaped on them at every point by the strikers.

The arrival at Chinkiang of the U.S.S. Paul Jones last night synchronized with the abatement of the riots, which will apparently not be renewed.

To day's reports state that the situation is quiet. A short wireless message says that students are working up a strike at Kiukiang. There are no details.

That the local student situation is outwardly quiet is largely due to the Tupan of Hsiao-yaonan to day issuing two proclamations, the first to the Chinese and foreign citizens of Wuhan and the second to the educational commissioner and the police. He directed the maintenance of peace. The commissioner also issued a proclamation to the students to the same effect.

headline: Peking Mandate
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
The Government issued a mandate last night stating that patriotic citizens had attempted to demonstrate at Shanghai and some had been killed and others wounded, at which the Chief Executive was greatly afflicted. He had asked the Waichiaopu to protest strongly, and had sent delegates of high standing to Shanghai to carry out negotiations to find who was responsible. The Government always protects the interests of the people. All must follow the right channels and work together at this time of difficulty.

The students did not obtain much satisfaction at the Chamber of Commerce yesterday evening, so they proceeded to the Bankers' Association, where they only found one secretary.

They made the usual demands for a boycott etc., and also demand-ed that funds be sent to assist the Shanghai strikers.

The Bankers' Association are meeting to-morrow to consider the demands. Things were very quiet to-day and there were no demonstrations.

headline: Further Peking Note.
parent_headline: SHANGHAI STRIKE. / FRENCH CONCESSION INVOLVED: / NEWSPAPERS' HOPEFUL
text:
The following is a translation of another Note sent by the Wachiaopu to the Italian Minister, M. Cerruti, as Senior Minister of the Interested. Powers, this evening, "concerning the bloody affair at Shanghai":

I had the honour to address to Your Excellency on the 1st inst. Note in which I begged you to give urgent necessary instructions to the Consular authorities at Shanghai to immediately free those persons who had been arrested and to act in concert with the Special Commissioner for Foreign Affairs, there to hinder the eventual return of similar cases.

Contrary to my expectation, new reports of an inauspicious character continue to reach me, according to which the police of the International Settlement on the 1st inst. again fired on the people, of whom three were killed and eighteen wounded, whilst the persons arrested have not all been freed. Other reports state that most of the victims were shot in the back without any agents of the police having been killed or wounded, which proves that the shooting was quite unjustified.

The violent attitude of the authorities of the International Concession, which has excited the discontent of the general public, creates the gravest consequences, notably the declaration of strikes by the merchants and workers in Shanghai.

From a respect for the elementary principles of humanity, and as the authorities of the International Concession are

entirely responsible, I am forced to address again to Your Excellency the most energetic protests. Moreover, I beg Your Excellency to communicate the above to the Ministers of the interested Powers, and to send without delay the most urgent instructions to the Contular authorities at Shanghai to cease immediately the practice of firing in order to avoid any further effusion of blood.

headline: RULE OF THE WAVES. / BRITAIN'S GREAT EXAMPLE.
text:
Admiral Plunkett, addressing the 93rd. reunion of the New York University, after presenting to the University a 12 inch mortar used by Admiral Faragut in the Civil War as a niemoral to the students of Alumni who died in the great war, hauded Britain's rule of the waves to which he attributed the avoidance of war in the past. He declared that future peace lay in the adoption of this standard of eternal vigilance.

The British consul-general, Sir Harry Armstrong, representing Sir Thomas Lipton, presented the University with the must of Shamrock IV. He made a speech expressing the faith and power of Britain and the United States to establish world peace.

headline: Many Striker
parent_headline: LIGHT SECLUSION." / REPRIEVE FOR WOMAN PLOTTER.
text: Peking, June 6.—Students all over the country are organising strikes and demonstrations but the only disorder is in Chinkiang, where the Police Station was wrecked without casualties. A foreign warship is being despatched thither. Professors have joined in the demonstration at Tientsin, where speeches were made demanding the restoration of Dairen, an anti-British boycott and abolition of concessions.—Reuter.

headline: LUCKY ARREST: / ARMED ROBBERY FOILED. SMART WORK.
text:
A Chinese constable attached No. 7 Police Station (West Point effected a smart arrest on Friday night and thus foiled the well-law plans of a gang of men to rob Chinese house at the junction of Sassoon Road and Pokfulam Road. The raid was timed to take place after the street traffic had stopped. The movements of one member the gang, who was on his way, meet his confederates, called investigation from the constable patrol duty, and a search result in a dagger and some wire bear found on him. The arrested ms subsequently made a statement the police in which he alleged the the dagger was given to him by other man and that they were go to Pokfulam to commit an arn robbery. Soon afterwards the others were also arrested.

The same night another Club was arrested at Queen's Road TV following the discovery of a dog hidden in his shoe. This man made an admission to the Ed that he was proceeding on an awful mission.

The two principal figures these arrests are being charged the Central Magistracy by R sional Inspector Peter Grant.

headline: CANTON BATTLE.
text:
(Continued from Page 1, J. J.

Meanwhile active war is break-ing out in other parts of the province.

General Fan Shok-sang, erstwhile, the strong man of Canton, is reported to be withdrawing his troops, from the upper reaches of the West River and a statement has been made that he has declared neutrality. His non-participation will mean a big difference to the Cantonese cause.

Field telephones have enabled the Yunnanese to maintain communication with exposed stations on the "Canton-Kowloon Railway and a little transport can be moved along a short part of the Canton-Shiukwan Railway up the North River.

Allies of the Reds are reported to be concentrating at Suimshui junction where they will combine with the Cantonese detachment from Kongmoon district, now murching to their colleagues' aid. This fore interests to take Fatshan as a jumping-off point for an onslaught on the west of Canton. If history is repeated, Shameen will be in close proximity to the firing zone. The Yunnanese are shortening their line of defence to the west of Canton and have made Wongsha, the district adjacent to the western suburb, their main line of defence against the Red attack from the West River. No news has come in from the North River.

General Hsu Shung-chi is moving an offensive on Canton by land and sea. His land expedition, numbering about 10,000 layonets, has taken Pingshan with little resistance as the Yunninese fell back on Shektan. General Cheung Kai-shek has dispatched reinforcements in the shape of 2,000 or so eadiets, (in reality actual regular soldiers, but under Russian officers), to the main camp at Whampoa, the naval station below Canton. Another 5,000 of the Cantonese troops are awaiting embarkation for Whampoa.

The Yunnanese headquarters predict that Hsu will make for the middle of the Canton-Kowloon Railway and march up the line. The Whampoo force, they expect will strike at a part of the railway nearer Canton and thus try to break the Yunnanese main force in the east. Once the two Red branches join hands, they will make a combined assault on Canton. However, the mercenaries declare they are prepared and have their counter-moves. Accordingly, the Yunnanese are

Accordingly, the Yunnanese are now banging away at Honam with the object of threatening Whampou, if possible.

No sally across the river from either side has been reported. To-morrow, I am told, the Yunnanese will make an attempt on Honam and heavy fighting is expected with a wider range of possibilities. To date, neither side has secured any military advantage since war actually broke out on Saturday. The mrechants in the city are bearing up well.

headline: STOLEN LEAD. / THIEF JUMPS INTO THE HARBOUR
text:
At the Kowloon Magistracy this morning," a Chinese youth was sentenced to three months' hard labour for stealing a quantity of lead solder from the Kowloon Docks on Saturday.

It transpired in evidence that on being intercepted by a watchman, the accused jumped into the harbour with the object of swimming to the opposite shore, but was obliged to come back.

headline: BITES BY DOGS.
text:
Three cases of attacks by dogs were reported to the Police yesterday, the victims in each case being given medical treatment and the animals being sent to Kennedy Town for observation.

At Kowloon, a dog belonging to Mr. M. A. Johnson, of 10 Chatham Road, bit a Chinese living at 5 Torres Building.

Another dog attacked a Chinese in Queen's Road East near the military quarters.

A servant boy was bitten by a white mongrel owned by Mr. L. Gutierrez, of 39 Bonham Road.

headline: LASH FOR THIEF.
text:
SNATCHEID HANDBAG.

EN OFINO BATTERY RATE

The smatching of a hand bag from a European lady at Battery Path had its sequel at the Central Magistracy this morning before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest, when a Chinese youth was charged with the offence. The accused pleaded not guilty.

The complainant, Miss W. Riddle, a nurse at Victoria Hospital, the Peak, slated in evidence that she was walking along buttery Euth at $30 p.m. yesterday when the accused slatched her purse from her hand and ran away. She gave chase as far as the Cathedral Hall. At this point a European boy and Mr. J. M. Shroff kept behind the accused, who ran in the direction of the Government buildings. The purse was loind on the roadside with some of the silver money shrewn on the ground. A sum of about $6 in silver and notes was missing.

Evidence was also given by Mr. Shroff and an Indian consulate. The former stated that he saw the accused running away with the purse in his hand and complainnt following behind. Witness joined in the chase. Near the new P.W.D. building the accused was tripped by in European boy. Pickling himself up and discarding the purse, the accused got behind the building and slid down the drain pipe into Battery Pitch. Witness shouted to an Indian constable on duty at the junction below to arrest the runaway, but the latter evaded the Indian by jumping over the railing into Queen's Road. The accused was later caught by a European.

Sub-Inspector Spour stated that Mr. C. Bowick, of Messrs. Dobwell and Co., Edd, was responsible for the arrest. On being searched at the charge room in the Sub-Inspector's presence the accused had on him $10 in notes, two keys, a police whistle and a pawn ticket. After a statement made by the accused in which he denied the charge, his Worship said that the evidence was quite clear and imposed in sentence of four months' hard labour and life strokes of the birth.

headline: SHIP'S REPAIRS.
text: Repairs done to the S.S. Cochin China, a French ship registered in Saigon but with owners in Hongkong, formed the subject of a claim before Sir Henry Cowper Gollan, in the Supreme Court this morning, the amount involved being $4,181. headline: TEA-POTS IN COURT.
text:
DE ALIERS DISPUTE -AS TO

Strangely out of keeping with the dignified atmosphere of the Courts were three tea-pots ranged in order of size on the barristers' and solicitors' table immediately beneath Mr. Justice Wood in the Summary Court this morning.

Two dealers disputed as to the type which had been ordered, one dealer claiming for the difference in price between those he had bought and those which the defendant said he had ordered and was prepared to pay for.

After arguments as to shape and size of the ordered utensils the case was adjourned for Mr. Turner (appearing for the plaintiffs) to get fresh instructions. Mr. M. W. Lo appeared, for the defendants.

headline: $5,000 BAIL FORFEIT.
text:
MOTOR CAR ACCIDENT SEQUEL

ACCUSED MAN MISSING.

Ball of $5,000 was estreated at the Central Magistracy this morning in the case in which Pun Pul-sang was charged with manslaughter. The case arose out of the motor accident at Pokfulam Road last week when the accused, who was said to have had no licence to drive a car, was alleged to have run on to the pavement and killed a sleeping coolie. Another coolie was seriously injured and is still in hospital. The accused did not put in an appearance and is believed to have absconded.

Pun Luk-chi, the licensed driver of the car, who was alleged to have been seated beside his brother, Pun Pui-sang, at the time of the accident, was charged with unlawfully allowing another man to drive the car. A fine of $100 was imposed.

headline: WRONG TURN.
text:
MOTOR CYCLIST FINEO

Before Mr. E. W. Hamilton, at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning, Mr. F. Munn, a motor cyclist, appeared for the second time recently for a breach of traffic regulations by taking a wrong turning at Hunghom.

After the evidence of a traffic officer, the Magistrate said that the defendant would do well to make himself conversant with the traffic regulations as soon as possible and imposed a fine of $5.

To a remark from the defendant that he understood there was another charge pending against him, the Magistrate said that there were no reductions for taking a quantity, but the effect would rather be the contrary.

headline: FRENCH BANK
text:
EFFECT BEING GIVEN TO AGREEMENT.

In accordance with the interest they have in the Banque Industrielle de Chine creditors will have issued to them in August bonds which will be redeemable by yearly drawing or repurchase.

It will be remembered that in an interview the maringer of the Bank which has taken over the affairs of the Bank Industrielle explained shortly after the announcement of the scheme of settlement that the bonds would be secured on the Boxer indemnity which in itself was secured by the Chinese Maritime Customs and the Salt Tax. "The bonds will be the same as any other bonds," he said, "and the owners will be able to discount them anywhere."

Money for the dividend which is due in July has been deposited by the Chinese Maritime Customs and the warrant for this will be attached to the bonds when issued.

headline: BABY'S LIFE.
text:
CRIPPLED PORTER ON FOOTBOARD.

The prompt action of a young railway porter, Bert Lucas, turned what might have been a domestic tragedy into a comedy at Victoria's Station (South-Eastern Section).

Just before the 8.3 p.m. train to Gillingham left No. 4 platform a woman with a girl, aged 12, and another child, aged 1, had been saying good-bye to relatives leaving by the train. The woman had left her baby in the carriage when the train suddenly started.

Her elder daughter's screamed out: "Grandfather is taking away the baby," and as the train gathered speed the woman in the compartment held the baby out of the carriage window over the platform.

Lucas, thinking that the frantic woman was about to drop the baby from the moving train, ran the length of two carriages, sprang upon the footboard, and worked his way along towards the compartment. He seized the baby from the woman, and, although he is a cripple, having been injured in a shunting accident, regained the platform without losing his balance or dropping the child.

The mother by this time was in a fainting condition, and Lucas held the child until she was restored. He refused to accept any reward, and, without waiting for the thanks of the family, said that he was only doing his duty and walked away.

“These 'ere floods,” said the oldest inhabitant, “remind me of th’ time when th’ old passion prayed fer rain. When th’ rain did come it drowned two of his best cows, an’ washed th’ foundations from under th’ vicarage. Arter that, he went about sayin’ that fer th’ future he’d keep quiet, an’ jest let Providence run-th’ weather ter suit itself!” SNAKE SWALLOWS LIVE

headline: CAUSILWAY DAY INCIDENT.
text:
A snake over twelve feet long, and several inches in diameter was not by a Chinese police officer at a hiking village, near Causeway on Sunday evening.

It is believed that the snake was driven from its home by the recent heat and rain. The story goes that it was in the process of swallowing a cat, whole, when the animal's series drew the policeman's attention. The fired five shots at the reptile with his revolver, two of which lodged in the snake's neck and caused its death.

headline: MOROCCO INCIDENT. / GERMAN TRAWLERS' SEIZED.
text: A message from Fez states that French warships seized two German trawlers in Morroccan waters near Agadir and took them to Mogador where they have been detained.

headline: OUTFLANKED.
text: A bulletin from Fez reports that contingents of rebel tribesmen proceeding in the direction of the Taunat heights were outflanked by French cavalry and friendly tribesman and forced to retreat with heavy losses. The French artillery stopped a fresh enemy attack.

headline: OCCULT PRACTICES. / DRAWING A PICTURE UPSIDE DOWN.
text:
Curious stories of the practice of the occult sciences wore told when the libel-nation brought by Liout-Colonel William Joseph Roskell, of New Cavendish Street, W., against Arthur Ady, of Penton-place, Konnington, was continued. Mr. Ady, who admits the libel, contended that the words were true and fair comment on Col. Roskell's conduct is proprietor of the Delphie Club, for those interested in spiritualism, in Regent Street. One of the alleged libels was that Col. Roskell added and abetted notorious women in obtaining money from the public by fortune telling.

NEW THOUGHT MOVEMENT: Col. Roskell denied that he had permitted fortune-telling in the club.

Questioned about some of the people who had been mentioned in the libels, Col. Roskell said a Mr. Hall Simpson had lectured on the new though movement.

Mr. Justice Sunkey: What is the new thought movement?—I believe it is the sort of idea that if you think right you get everything right. If you want something you have to think it right and you get it. Col' Roskel agreed that symbolic dancing and astral dealing were also subjects of lectures.

Mr. Justice Snukey: What is stroll dealing?—I imagine it is that they now call Conemm. It is nothing to do with the stars.

Mr. Melville (for Mr. Ady): Did you call it the Delphi Club to recall the oracle of Delphi in pre-Christian days when people went to the priest so as to be able to get information about what might happen to them in the future?—It seemed a suitable name.

With regard to Mrs. Susann Harris, Col. Roskell said that Mr. Ady himself had told him that she was not a fortune teller because she used a trumpet, which made it a mechanical experiment. He had never heard that at one demonstration, Mr. Ady put his foot upon the trumpet, closing it up, but "the voices" kept on coming, and it turned out to be Mrs. Harris herself speaking all the time.

Col. Roskell admitted that he allowed Mrs. Bush to come to the club, although he knew she was a convicted swindler. That was viewed as a martyrdom. He agreed that palmistry was practised at the club.

Mr. Melville read an account of a science when Mrs. Harris went under control. "She painted a picture upside down in pastels in five minutes, and at the end threw the chalks about in # violent manner before "subsiding somewhat heavily on the platform."

Col. Roskell explained that a medium might go under control standing or sitting down. Sometimes the voice would change; sometimes the medium would talk in a foreign language.

Mr. Justice Sunkey asked why mediums did such silly things as drawing a picture upside down. (Col. Roskell said it was a much

(Col. Roskell said it was a much more difficult thing to do.

Further cross-examined, Col. Roskell said a lecture was given on "Angels, Their Origin and Work." It was also a custom at the club to have a "ghost evening" just about Christmas time. The members would sit around the fireside and relate the most unusual ghostly experiences that had occurred to them.

Re-examined, Col. Roskell said the members of the club were middle-class people of respectable character.

Mr. Hawke, K.C., (for Col. Roskell), remarked that he saw some of the members were people of title.

Detective-Inspector Albert Kirchner, of New Scotland Yard, said as far as could be ascertained Mr. Ady's real name was Jack Breslau Taylor. He claimed to be an American. When he (the detective) arrested Mr. Ady a large number of libels concerning Col. Roskell were found.

Under the Aliens Act Mr. Ady had been recommended for deportation.

Since serving a term of imprisonment he had been on parole. The American authorities had been unable to establish his identity. Advised he was born in a ship in the Red Sea.

Mr. Justice Sunkey suggested that he should be anchored there. Mr. Justice Sunkey, in summing up, described the libel as one of the most atrocious it was possible to imagine. "I do not think you will think I am using too strong an expression when I say that the defendant is a blackguard," he said. Without retiring, the jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff and gave him £200 damages.

Mr. Hawke, referring to the letter sent to Mr. Justice Sankey by Mrs. Wright, said his client was satisfied that she was a respectable woman.

headline: POOR YEAR / INDO-CHINA
text:
Losses in last year's working of the Indo-China Steam Navigation Co., Ltd., were attributed, at the annual meeting to day, to surplus tonnage in the Far East, unstable political conditions in South China, disturbances in the North, poor rice crops and, indirectly, the Japanese earthquake.

Mr. D. G. M. Bernard presided at the 44th ordinary general meeting held at the offices of Messrs. Jardine, Matheson & Co., Ltd., this morning. He was supported by Mr. A. H. White and the Hon. Mr. A. O. Lang (directors) and Mr. E. F. Aucott. Shareholders present comprised Messrs. Ho, Shal-kit, Ho Kwong, Ho Leung, Li Yun-kun, Ho Tang-ying, Fung Hun, F. C. Hall, A. Murdoch, N. L. H. Railton, Ho Ki, W. Galloway, A. M. da Silva, R. E. Macdougall, J. Fleming, A. Piercy, E. B. C. Hornell and H. Birkett. Addressing the meeting, the chairman said:

Gentlemen,—As it is past the time for which this meeting was called, I will ask Mr. Aucott to read the notice convening the meeting and also the Auditors' Report.

After the notice and auditors' report had been read, the Chairman continued:—The report and statement of accounts have been in your hands for some days, and with your permission I will, as customary, take them as read. Your directors regret that the result of last year's working is again so unsatisfactory. The conditions with which all Shipping Companies operating tonnage in Far Eastern waters have had to contend during recent years have been deplorable, and the year under review has been no exception. From January until March there were welcome signs of activity in the charter trades, and rates were not altogether unfavourable. There was, however, an abundance of tonnage available as in addition to the large number of miscellaneous steamers, usually employed in the Southern charter business, numerous vessels under time charter to Japanese owners found their way into the Shigon and Bangkok trades owing to their inability to find remunerative employment in their own water as a result of the disastrous earthquake in Japan in the latter part of 1923. From April onwards rates began rapidly to decline, and other contributory causes to the severe depression in trade which set in about that time were the poor rice crops in Sain and Indo-China, and the political troubles throughout China. The Civil War, which broke out in North China during the second half of the year, caused a considerable amount of Chinese owned tonnage to come South apparently in order to avoid the possible "risk" of requisition by Chinese military officials, and competition in all directions became still more active

The Bangkok-Hongkong berth rate from April onwards remained almost stationary at 35 cents per piecial inside the bar loading, which is the lowest average figure on record since pre-war days, whilst the Saigon-Hongkong rate, the governing factor in arriving at the condition of Southern charter business, remained during the greater part of the year at a very unremunerative level, falling in November to the ridiculous figure of 8 cents per piecul.

Under these conditions it will be readily understood that the supply of tonnage was greatly in excess of the demand, the consequence being an intrusion of outside steamers into several of our regular berth trades, and in co-operation with other friendly companies, it was unfortunately necessary at times to reduce our tariff rates against these competitors to an unprofitable scale in order to maintain our position in the regular trades.

Although there was a fair movement of cargo in North China during the early months of the year, excessive competition was experienced with a consequent depression of rates in nearly every direction. The tense political situation towards the end of August, which led to the outbreak of hostilities between the Provinces of Jiangsu and Chekiang, and subsequent war between the larger factions in the North, materially affected the usual autumn demand. Every effort was made, however, to maintain, and where possible to increase the level of rates current during the provisions year.

Reference is made in the report to the purchase of the s.a. Barrymore now renamed Kumsang of 5,447 gross tons built in 1920. This vessel arrived from England in November last, and after undergoing necessary alterations to fit her for the Calcutta Line commenced her regular employment thereon in January last, and has so far proved an excellent addition to the Company's Fleet.

The new "stearrier" Liensling, 2,416 gross tons, built by the Hongkong and Whampoa Dock Co., for the Shanghai Tientsin run, was delivered by the builders during the month of May. She is an exceptionally fine conster, being fitted with the very latest cargo handling gear, and having superior passenger accommodation. Since being placed on the run, she has become a very popular vessel.

In view of the steady expansion of shipping business in the Yangtsze River, in which this company is very largely interested, your directors considered it necessary to acquire an additional steamer to operate on the Middle Yangtsze between Hankow and Ichang. The order for the vessel was placed with the Hongkong and Whampoa Dock Co., and it is hoped to have her ready for service about October next. It was also found necessary to purchase another towboat and six lighters to act as feeders to our steamers at Hankow. These have recently been delivered by builders in Shanghai, and are now in commission.

As regards the Upper Yangtze trade, I regret to state we have experienced further trouble with the Fuhwo. After being re-conditioned under the superintendence of an expert sent out from Home by the builders, she resumed her run between Tichang and Chungking. Later in the year, however, she met with a mishap by breaking a shift which necessitated her return to Shanghai. Stronger shafting is now being fitted, and it is hoped she will shortly be in commission again.

Our new steamer Kingwo also running on the Upper Yangtze has I am glad to say proved a decided success and has performed excellent service. Conditions in the Ichang-Chunking trade during the year under review were more favourable. It is satisfactory to note that very little fighting took place on the River itself and there were fewer cases of firing upon steamers, a practice which has been so prevalent in previous years. Your directors regard the development of this line as most important, not only for itself, but as a feeder for our other river boats, and to strengthen our position they decided to augment our tonnage by another steamer. This is being constructed by the Kiangnan Dock and Engineering Works in Shanghai, who built the Kingwo, and the vessel is expected to be completed in July.

The vessel has a double bottom fitted all fore and aft, two large cargo holds and a smaller hold specially fitted "up for the carriage of silk. There are three decks, accommodation being provided on the saloon and boat decks for the 49 first-class passengers and 24 second-class.

Intermediate passengers are berthed aft on saloon deck in a large deck-house while the third-class are carried on the main deck. The first class passengers are accommodated in 23 single-berthed cabins, 10 double-berthed cabins and two family cabins of 3 berths each. Seven pairs of the single-berthed cabins are convertible into double-berthed cabins by means of a communicating door. Four of the state-rooms have been specially fitted up as "cabins de luxe," each having its own decorative scheme; private bathrooms are also attached to these cabins.

The dining saloon, situated forward on "saloon deck, has a height of 11 feet and is entirely free of pillars. Particular care and attention has been given to the design of this room which is about 42 feet square and will form a special feature of the vessel, everything having been carefully studied to give a light and air appearance.

Normally the saloon can accommodate 48 persons at small tables for four persons each, but these tables can be extended so as to accommodate a greater number when required. The floor of the saloon is laid with teak parquety and the corridors in the first-class accommodation have been laid with rubber tiling.

On the boat deck adjoining the main entrance to cabins a smoke-room has been arranged and is designed on the old English style with oak beams and panelling, all the fittings being in keeping. The seats are upholstered in leather, and with the comfortable lounge chairs, card tables and other fittings which are being provided, it is bound to be a very popular room.

The captain, officers, engineers, wireless room and navigating quarters have been placed on a deck somewhat higher than the passenger deck forming a citadel, which meets all the special requirements of the Anti-Piracy Committee.

The firemen and engine room staff are housed convenient to the engine room and grilled off from the main deck, so that they cannot be interfered with in the event of piracy. Electric light is fitted throughout the vessel and numerous fans provided; hot and cold water service is laid on to all wash basins throughout the vessel. The machinery, which consists of 2 sets of four crank balanced engines with 4 boilers, has been constructed by the Taikoo Dockyard and Engineering Co., and is designed to give the vessel a speed of 15 knots on service, but an extra knot is anticipated on trial.

headline: Tribute to Staff.
text:
I am glad to be able to state that no casualty of a serious nature occurred during the year under review, and our thanks are due to the staff, both ashore and afloat, for willing and valuable services rendered.

It is with regret that your directors have to record the death of the Hon. Mr. A. R. Lowe, who has filled the position as auditor to the company for some years past. Also of Captain F. T. Wheeler, the company's late marine superintendent at Hongkong. The benefit of Mr. Lowe's advice in connection with the accounts has always been very keenly appreciated. Captain Wheeler served the Company well and faithfully for a period of 29 years, and showed marked ability in the performance of his duties as marine superintendent, to which post he was appointed in 1919. I feel sure you would wish to express to the relatives of these gentlemen, whose loss is much deplored; the Company's deep sympathy with them in their bereavement.

Turning to the statement of accounts, you will notice that Building Reserve Account has been increased by £12,363.7.2, which represents the gain on the book values on the sale of the Taisang and Wingsang already mentioned.

Securities have been sold during the year to defray the cost of now tonnage and to pay for current expenses. The profit on the sale of these investments amounted to £17,705.12.11, and has been transferred from Investment Fluctuation.

headline: A FAMOUS TENOR.
text:
TREAT IN STORE FOR HONGKONG.

Mr. Edward Johnson, the noted Metropolitan tenor, made his first appearance in the Far East at Tokyo at the Kabuki-za before a large, representative and appreciative audience.

An Italian gentleman who was present at the First Concert in Tokyo sends the following:—

The Kabuki-za was a scene of unprecedented enthusiasm when Giovanni, the gifted young artist, made his debut in Tokyo before a thronged audience. It was an epochal triumph. From the moment his glorious voice intoned the First Number 'Capito M'avete' from Andrea Chemer, the enthusiasm was so great that overwhelming applause followed each and every number on the programme and when he gave Schubert's 'Who is Sylvia,' the eternally popular song, the enthusiasm rose to such a pitch that hats flew all over the theatre and shouts of Brava Giovanni from the foreign element of the audience were continuously audible.

Then followed a series of a few modern English songs so perfectly sung, that the artist and the audience were in one and towards the end when he gave the famous Aria from 'Pagliacci' the spectators got on the chairs and demanded encore after encore and showered overwhelming applause on the young artist who received them with a continuous and magnetic smile. Such enthusiasm has never before been duplicated in any theatre in the Far East for any artist.

Mr. Johnson was born in Canada and was educated in Italy. In 1910 he studied under Caruso's teacher the great Lombardi of Florence.

In 1912 he made his debut and success after success crowned his efforts to such an extent that even the patrons of La Scala took him for an Italian a tribute never before paid to any foreigner. He is as popular in Italy as he is in America.

A real musical treat awaits Hongkong when this talented artist puts in his appearance on June 22 at the City Hall.

headline: UNIQUE EVENT. / STEAMBOAT CO.'S NEW STEAMER
text:
THIS MORNING'S BRAVE ASSEMBLAGE AT TAIKOO.

Unique, in that it was made the occasion of the first double christening that has taken place, at any rate in Hongkong, the launching of the twin screw steamer "Taishan" built to the order of the Hongkong, Canton and Macao Steamboat Company took place at the Taikoo Deckyard this morning.

The actual launching was as pretty a ceremony as could be wished for and everything went off without a hitch. At the appointed time the supports were struck away, the word was given and the Misses Dorothy and Joyce Holyoak simultaneously let go the mechanical release and discharged against the side with the desired effect two bottles containing the time honoured boat christening

The "Taishan" moved forward without a crack gathering just enough momentum to carry her well into the water. Behind, she left a specially erected platform crowded with guests and it would be difficult to express an opinion as to which presented the bravest appearance, the beflagged boat sliding down the ways or the gay assemblage from whose throats issued three hearty cheers as the boat actually took the water. In a specially erected and gaily decorated matshed the occasion was celebrated by hundreds of guests among whom at the head table were His Excellency the Governor, Sir R. E. Stubbs, K.C.M.G. Major General C.C. Luard, C.B. C.M.G., and Mrs. Luard, Sir Claud, Severn, the Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak and Mrs. and the Misses Dorothy and Joyce Holyoak, Commodore and Miss Stirling, Mr. and Mrs. J. Reid, Mr. G. M. Young and Mrs. Hunter.

Prior to proposing long life and prosperity to the "Taishan," M. G. M. Young spoke as follows:

headline: Double Good. Luck.
parent_headline: UNIQUE EVENT. / STEAMBOAT CO.'S NEW STEAMER
text:
Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of the Taikoo Dockyard, I thank you all for coming to see the launch of the latest and most up-to-date vessel yet built for the traffic between this Colony and the famous city of Canton.

We were very gratified, to receive the order from our friends, the Hongkong; Canton and Macao Steamboat Co., and trust that our efforts to give them of our best will prove in every way satisfactory, and that, the vessel will become the favourite one for passengers of all classes, as well as for cargo.

As the fame of "Taishan," the great mountain of China, is known to millions, so I trust will the fame of the steamer, which has just been launched by the Misses "Joyce and Dorothy-Holyoak, spread through every district from which passengers and cargo come for conveyance on these waters, not only as the first steamer that has been christened by two ladies, but that this brought a double portion of good luck to the steamer and those that travel by her.

I shall be very pleased if the young ladies will each accept a memento. (a platinum wrist watch set with diamonds) from the Taikoo Dockyard of this fortunate occurrence and that you will all join in drinking long life and prosperity to the "Taishan." The Hon. Mr. P. H. Holyoak rose after the toast had been honoured with much enthusiasm. Oh behalf of the owners of the new boat he thanked Mr. Young for his good wishes and offered hearty congratulations on the highly successful launching accomplished. He did not doubt from the plans and what he had already seen that the vessel would prove popular with all who used

it and when times became more normal and trade conditions once more settled down to what they used to be like, the record of this boat would surpass the records of any boat in the line.

He thank them for the compliment paid his family in asking his daughters to launch the boat and acknowledged on their behalf the handsome mementoes. In a way the ceremony was unique—a double christening at a launching—at any rate it was in Hongkong. It recalled to him another family record. Several years ago his wife had launched at the Hongkong and Whampoa Dock Company a boat of the same name.—With these remarks he wished to convey thanks to Mr. Young for the sentiments expressed and to wish the Taikoo Dockyard prosperity and success. (Applause). Welcoming the guests and thanking Mr. Holyoak on behalf of the Taikoo Dockyard, Mr. J. Reid said that they had a fine

they could build an even better, perhaps a little faster, ship. The proceedings terminated, the guests made their way back to Hongkong by special launches placed at their disposal.

headline: CHINA'S DEFAULT.
text:
A. deputation representing the British holders of the Marconi and Vickers eight per cent. Chinese loans waited on the Acting Chinese Minister at the Legation in London yesterday to make representations to the Peking Governments regarding the failure to pay interest thereon.

Dr. Chu replied sympathetically and assured the deputation that it was the intention of the Chinese Government to meet its obligations on these loans at the earliest possible moment.

headline: QUEEN'S THEATRE.
text:
CHARLES RAY REGISTERS NEW TRIUMPH.

Charles Ray has scored another screen triumph in "Two Minutes to Go," a story of college life, which began an engagement at the Queen's Theatre last night.

Ray gives an excellent portrayal of a football hero in this admirable attraction. The charm and virility which has characterised Ray in past screen successes was never better exemplified than in his interpretation of the role of the college lad, who, through financial reverses, is compelled to quit the team and give his spare time to peddling milk as a means of working his way through school.

Because he is ashamed of the job and offers no explanation of his leaving the team on which he has been the star player, Chet Burnett, portrayed by Ray, gains only the contempt of his classmates and his sweetheart.

The great day comes, however, when Chet saves his team from defent and transforms a combination of misfortunes into happiness. Ray is given excellent support by Mary Anderson, his leading lady.

headline: PLANTS FROM TIBET.
text:
MR. KINGDON WARD'S RE CENT EXPEDITION.

Mr. F. Kingdon Ward, F.R.G.S., the naturalist and explorer, who was just returned to England after a year's travelling in Eastern Tibet, brought back with him the seeds of a number of "fascinating new" hardy plants collected during his journey. Mr. Ward was accompanied on the expedition by Lord Cawdor. They had three permanent Bhutan servants and a number of porters. Exciting adventures were avoided, but the travellers broke new ground by traversing the full length of the tremendous gorge through which the Tsanpo river pierces the Himalayas.

Permission to make the journey was obtained at the beginning of last year from the Indian and Tibetan Governments, and the expedition was in part financed by the Government, Grant Committee of the Royal Society and by the Percy Sladen Memorial Fund. start was made in March, and Tibet was entered from Darjeeling by the ordinary Lhasa route. When the Tsanpo was reached the party followed the river for 22 miles and then begun their botanical work in Eastern Tibet, May, June and July were spent in searching for new plants. Some unknown country was afterwards explored, and in October and November the seeds of the plants which had been specially noted were collected. The return was then made by the gorge of the Tsanpo, the Tibetan plateau, and Assam to Calcutta.

Speaking of the results of the expedition, Mr. Kingdon Ward said that he and all those interested in the venture were perfectly satisfied. The large collection of seeds brought home was now being gone through. Kew and Edinburgh had received a share, and others had been distributed privately throughout the country. Some of the seeds had gone to New Zealand and Africa. The scientific results would, he thought, be interesting. It had long been recognised that Tibet might provide the key to many problems of the distribution of flora. The difficulty was to get to the country and to carry out exploration in a very mountainous region. Much of the work last year was conducted at high altitudes, and at times the party climbed to 17,000 ft.; and 18,000 ft. When the seeds were collected there was a good deal of snow.

Among the discoveries was a magnificent hardy rhododendron with full orange flowers. The bushes grew to a height of about 10 ft. They were beautiful not only for their bloom, but also for their brilliant blue-green foliage, which could be seen miles away in the snow. Dwarf rhododendrons with real scarlet blossoms were another feature. Whole mountain slopes were covered ankle deep with this plant. An ivory-coloured Himalayan poppy was rather startling, and they had found some wonderful primulas. One specimen grew to a height of 4 ft., while 3 ft., was common. The flowers were remarkable not only for their size and colour, but for their fragrance. A golden yellow variety carried 100 flowers on one stem, and it grew so profusely as to clog up streams. A sulphur yellow bloom was extraordinarily fragrant and filled the air with perfume. Astonishing gentians 18 in. to 2 ft. high had each five or six spikes of sea blue trumpet-shaped blooms. They also had some good saxifrages. In addition to the seeds of the plants described they had brought back bulbs of a pink lily of the Martagon type, which bore 12 to 20 flowers on one stem and was delightfully fragrant. The seeds were germinating well now that they were here, and this was very satisfactory, as they had been three or four months on the journey and had passed through extremes of cold and heat. The seeds were kept alive on the way to Calcutta by placing them in thermos flasks and occasionally pumping in carbon dioxide.

Speaking of the exploration of the Tsampo Gorge, Mr. Kingdon Ward said that two Indian officers penetrated part of the gorge 13 years ago, but did not go right through. He and Lord Cawdor were the first Europeans to make the passage. With its windings the gorge would be nearly 100 miles in length. The river contracted from a normal breadth of 600 to 800 yards to a tumultuous torrent 50 to 100 yards wide. Cliffs rose abruptly to a height varying from 1,000 to 2,000 ft., above the water, and the full depth of the gorge would about 10,000 ft., where it cut through the Himalayas. It was only occasionally that the party could get down to the river, and mostly they were climbing up and down the cliffs. The scenery was superb, and at one point a glacier came right down to the water. Rumours had been heard of a great fall of the river somewhere in the gorge, but they discovered only two moderate waterfalls of about 40 ft. to 50 ft. The folings was very dense, and progress had accordingly to be slow. Nineteen days were occupied from entry to exit. Mr. Kingdon Ward said that from the natives they received nothing

headline: NEW BUS CO. / ABERDEBN KAIFONGS' ENTERPRISE.
text:
AMBITIOUS SCHEMES

Four new Dennis' buses with curtain windows and spring seats, each to hold 23 passengers, are being placed on the Hongkong Aberdeen run by the Aberdeen Kalfong Bus Co., who, it is reported, have applied for permission to extend their service to Stanley with which there is now no direct communication.

An interesting history lies behind the placing on service of these new and up-to-date buses. Formerly Aberdeen was connected with the city only by launch. One such vessel was operated by the Kaifongs, i.e., the community of the village, but they ceased running when they failed because of keen competition. Their competitors then put up the rates and the Kaifongs commenced the 'bus service. The first company did not prove a success and the capital has nearly all gone. Now a new company is being floated with a capital of $200,000, in shares of $1 each so that nearly every inhabitant in the village can become a shareholder.

In the new concerns, shareholders will pay special rates, viz., 15 cents instead of 25 cents for first-class, and 12 cents instead of 15 cents for third-class. As there are English schools at Aberdeen, the company will issue monthly tickets at $2 to students proceeding to school in town and special buses will be run for them.

Because the Convent near Aberdeen is rendering good service to the community, it is also proposed to allow the sisters and staff to travel free as will all police officers in uniform or on duty.

headline: AIR MAIL STAMPS. / £4 TO £160 FOR SINGLE SPECIMENS.
text:
RELICS OF EPIC FLIGHTS.

"Since the war the growth of the new collecting cult of air-post material has become phenomenal. Its adherents to-day are numbered in thousands."

So writes Mr. Alan Turlon, airpost specialist, in "Air Posts of the World," which he has just published, and which contains more than 400 illustrations.

In his gallant attempt for the "Daily Mail" £10,000 prize in May 1919, which ended in a compulsory descent, the late Mr. Harry Hawker carried a special bag of letters. These were retrieved afterwards and are marketed now at £40 to £60 each.

Three pounds of mail was carried when the late Sir John Alcock and Sir Arthur Whitten Brown on June 4-15, 1919 made the first direct Transatlantic seroplane flight, winning the "Daily Mail" £10,000 prize. These Alcock covers are now worth £35 apiece.

The Martinsyde machine which had to abandon the Atlantic flight carried a bag containing about 60 letters. A few of these were overprinted in manuscript: "Aerial Atlantic Mail—J. A. R." the initials of the Postmaster-General of Newfoundland. They are priced at £100 each to-day.

An error in a single sheet of stamps in the early days of the American air mail made these stamps worth £160 each.

Letters carried on the return flight of R34 from New York are listed at £88.

In August 1910, at Blackpool, Mr. C. Grhano-White carried a mail-bag by aeroplane in very bad weather conditions for a distance of 7 miles. These ruro pieces change hands at $10.

Air-borne cards in connection with Mr. Graham-White's "Daily Mail" water-plane tour of the south coast in 1912 fetch us much as £12.

During the Lymphe light aero-plane meeting of 1923, Mr. J. H. James carried about 125 letters in his "maching from Lymphe" to Hastingleigh, dropping them in a bag near the post office. These covers, signed by the pilot, are priced at $4.

headline: NO FRIEND IN NEED.
text:
LONELY

STILL COOLING HIS HEELS.

Chang Poh-loong ("Brilliant Chang) is still confined in the House of Detention awaiting the pleasure of the Governor-in-Council as to his destination.

It is two weeks since Chang was placed behind bars on his arrival as a deportee from England after serving a term of imprisonment for being concerned in the dope traffic. He was transferred to the House of Detention after his interview with the Secretary for Chinese Affairs a week ago. Although the authorities are prepared to allow him out on bail of about $500 pending the final decision, so far no friend of "Brilliant" has come forward to give him temporary freedom.

headline: HUTS ON FIRE.
text:
A fire occurred at Au Tin Chung village in the Castlepeak district at 4 o'clock yesterday afternoon and destroyed eleven grass huts. The damage is estimated at $1,140.

The cause of the outbreak has been traced to the act of a small girl in "burning grass" near the doorway of a hut A breeze carried the burning grass inside the hut and set alight a dry heap lying in a corner: The hut was soon ablaze and the fire spread to the others.

headline: TOLSTOY AT HIS DESK / REMINISCENCES OF SURVI- VING. DAUGHTER.
text:
After her previous lectures, Tolstoy's daughter, Tatyan. Lvovna Suchotin-Tolstoy, delivered an interesting lecture in German at the Russian Embassy in Vienna, thereby opening a series to be given within the scope of the Austrian Society for promoting cultural and economic relations with Russia.

She stated that in his will Tolstoy provided that everybody should have the right to print his posthumous work, writings, and letters without paying royalties. He had fallen dangerously ill, and at that time said in a letter to his family: "The fact that my writings were sold for money has been one of the worst reflections for me during the last years." But he did not definitely dispose of his work before the year of his death. He then wanted his literary work to belong to the whole of mankind. Only when his legal adviser pointed out to him that that course was impossible according to the law did Tolstoy resolve to leave all his writings to his daughter Alexandra. In consideration of her illness, however, he ordered that, in the event of her demise, his posthumous work should pass over to his eldest daughter Tatyana. During his last years he could not be prevailed upon to publish anything, since he might give way to the desire for fame

Toitoy used to write until late at night. Every morning he would give the MS. to the members of his family to copy out; on the following morning the fair copy had to lie on his writing table. Then he would begin to alter, correct, I've done, and complete, which process he repeated on the next day. Thus a large number of chapters hitherto unknown, belonging to "My Childhood," "Resurrection," and the "Kreuzer-Sonata," and many versions of short stories and ideas, were found among his posthumous papers. It frequently occurred that he put some work aside and did not resume it a long time after; often he worked at the same M. S. for years before allowing it to be printed. As he was very economical in the use of writing paper, he would note alterations on old alps or on welopes dragged out of the waste paper basket, or he would conceive the margin of his abets with corrections and completions; so that the setting of his work in order after his death was rendered extremely difficult.

headline: MR. R. MACDONALD AND HIS TROUSERS.
text:
SHOULD THEY BE CREASED?

Mr. Ramsay MacDonald addressed a series of May Day demonstrations in his own constituency and in the adjoining division of Neath. Having been overnight the guest of Mr. J. D. Morgan at his villa near Cardiff, the ex-Prime Minister motored in the early morning to an old farmhouse, Plas Watford, near Cuerphilly, where he breakfasted at eight o'clock. A thirty-miles drive brought Mr. MacDonald to Cynmer, where he addressed a meeting of miners. "I have just come over the mountains," he replied to their greeting, "and everything is beautiful and inspiring except the slate roofs of the habitation of man."

Some people imagined, he said, that the Labour Movement was a sordid affair, but it was nothing of the kind. The significance of their May Day festivals was that the Labour Movement was filled with the spirit of spring. It represented the happy unison at which they were aiming among the workers of the world. Not the miner alone, not the engineer alone, not the Britisher alone, but the Frenchman, German, Czecho-Slovakian, Russian—all must be banded together in one constructive purpose if they were to win the workers' battle completely.

Newspapers were doing their best once again to raise the old Russian bogey. We had had our revolutions here; France had had them; blood had run; wickedness had been done. Where there were tyranny and oppression, revolution was inevitable, and instead of calm-minded men dispensing justice, they had ruthless men going straight to their goal not caring about the methods.

"That," he said, "is the nature of the beast. Do not let us deceive ourselves, but understand that when masses of young virile men and women are pressed down by Czars and rulers, then the inevitable consequence is brutality in order to bring freedom more within the practical reach of the people.

That is not justifying anything. Sooner or later we have got to get into relations with Russia. The trade unions here have got to get into relations with trade unions there. The one thing I warn you about is that you must see to it that in getting into friendly relations with Russian trade unions, you do not cut yourselves off from French and German trade unionists.

Speaking of what he described as the present Government's "barren record," he said their international policy was one of negativism. Egypt, if handled properly, he was convinced, could be settled now in a way satisfactory to both.

Referring to the election of Marshall Hindenburg, he asked, "Did anyone expect that anyone else would be returned?" The Allies, he said, had been strengthening Nationalism in Germany by their own policy.

GETTING TOO RESPECTABLE: Prompted by a reference to his improved health, Mr. MacDonald told a story of how on his recent holiday he took out an old pair of trousers and found, when he put them on, they had a beautiful crease. He happened to be photographed in these. It was then said that he had deserted the workers because the crease in his trousers showed that he was getting for too respectable. On Friday he went into most respectable company, and had since read in the newspapers that he had turned up in a hat.

headline: DANGEROUS CYCLISTS.
text:
KOWLOON RESIDENTS' COMPLAINTS.

Acting on complaints received by the Kowloon Residents Association, the Police yesterday kept a watchful eye open for cyclists who by ignorance of the rules of the road and recklessness constitute a danger to themselves and pedestrians and motorists.

As a result, of their observations several penitent lads appeared at the Kowloon Magistracy, this morning and were given a few words of advice by Mr. E. W. Hamilton, the Magistrate. They all got off with a fine of $5.

headline: WONDERS OF PACIFIC. / MESSAGE FROM ARCTURUS EXPEDITION.
text:
Extraordinary good luck is attending the Arcturus expedition in the Pacific. The New York Times prints a copyrighted message from Dr. Beebe, the leader of the expedition, in which he reports the discovery on April 10 of two volcanoes in violent eruption of Albemarle Island, in the Galapagos group. No eruption has ever been witnessed there before. In honour of the two patrons of the expedition, Dr Beebe has named the volcanoes Mounts Williams and Whiton. He expresses the belief there there is some connection between the eruptions, the Japanese earthquakes, and changes in the Humboldt current. The Arcturus is standing by the islands to photograph the eruptions and be ready to give aid, if needed, to the tiny settlement on Albemarle.

Before the discovery of the volcanoes the Arcturus came upon a gigantic tidierip where the Panama and Humboldt currents meet. In the mass of foam which extended for scores of miles wallowed great numbers of whales and porpoises. Wreckage, covered with organisms and fish of all sizes feeding on them, provided the scientists with an unexpected opportunity for observation. For the first time, they found there the eggs of halobates, the only marine insects in the world. The eggs are being hatched in tanks. Ivy credible numbers of jellyfish coloured the water purple for many square miles. The expedition has caught more than 150 species of fish, among them being transparent founders, deep-sea mackerel with blue and yellow lights, many kinds of jellyfish, and fish which live only on jellyfish.

Dr. Beebe reports that while drifting in the neighbourhood of the tide-rip, the Arcturus repeatedly, but vainly, attempted to break through "the saturation of the static" with its powerful wireless apparatus.

headline: MR. E. BROOKS. / ROYAL WARRANTS CANCELLED
text:
DECORATIONS ANNULLED.

The following announcement was issued from Buckingham Palace.

The Warrants of Appointment as Photographer to the King, the Queen, and the Prince of Wales issued to Mr. Ernest Brooks have been cancelled.

The following further notices appeared in the "London Gazette"

The King has directed that the Award of the Medal of the Civil Division of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire to Ernest Brooks, which was gazetted on June 3, 1918, shall be cancelled and annulled, and his name erased from the Register.

The King has directed that the appointment of Ernest Brooks to be an Officer of the Civil Division of the Most Excellent Order of the British Empire, dated January 1, 1920, shall be cancelled and annulled, and his name erased from the Register.

Mr. Brooks, who accompanied the King and Queen to India for the Coronation Durbar, and later the Duke and Duchess of Connaught on their South African tour, was the first of the rich photographers appointed to the Forces by the War Office and the Admiralty during the late war. He held a commission and the rank of Heutenant.

headline: DRASTIC MEASURES
text:
CRUDE, RUBBER TRADE NEEDS.

The directors of the Rubber Association of America held a meeting to discuss the crude rubber situation.

headline: COTTON TRADE.
text:
In an address at the Manchester Chamber of Commerce, Sir Maneckji Dadabhoy, a member of the Council of State of India, and a prominent Indian industrialist, declared that the Japanese cotton trade competition was going to menace the world unless steps were taken in time both in England and in India. Britain must cheapen the cost of production. He suggested that the Indian import duty of 111 per cent. might be increased to 20 or 25 per cent. against foreign manufactures and reduced to say five per cent. in the case of England.

Mr. J. H. Rodier, chairman of the Irwin section of the Chamber declared that if in order to cheapen production the standard of living of the workers in England must be reduced to the standard of Japan. headline: SIR GUY GAUNT / HONGKONG'S DISTINGUISHED VISITOR
text:
An interesting visitor to the Colony who is renewing acquaintance with the Far East after a lapse of many years is Vice-Admiral Sir Guy Gaunt, K.C.M.G., C.B., C.M.G. M.P.

Sir Guy renews an acquaintance with the Far East which in his younger days must have provided him with many thrills. As lieutenant he took part in operations in the Philippines in 1807 and two years later he was in charge of the British Consulate at Apla, Samoa, when that place was attacked by rebel forces. As a result of his good work there (he raised what was known as Gaunt's Brigade) he was promoted to Commander.

In the capacity of Commander on H.M.S. Vengeance he saw service in the Russo-Japanese war being promoted to Captain in 1907. From 1914 to 1918 he acted as Naval Attache to H.B.M. Embassy in Washington and whilst acting as lason officer for United States with the rank of Commodore first class he was again mentioned in despatches in 1917. His promotion to Rear-Admiral in 1918 followed service with the Naval Intelligence Department and at the time of his retirement he was Vice-Admiral.

Since his retirement from the service Sir Guy has represented the Buckrose division of Yorkshire and has figured with distinction in all matters of administration of the Royal Navy and Colonial defence.

A most interesting story of the Moroccan war between the Riffs and the Spaniards has been revealed to the Scotland Yard authorities in London.

Some of the 20,000 Riffan tribesmen, armed, mounted and trained, in the attack under Abd-El-Krim against the French forces near Fez, Morocco, are shown above.

A detective, who was shadowing the Air Force man, then appeared and said: "I know that you for a long time have been gun-running for the Riffs. I want to know the name of your confederate."
