headline: WELSH NOTES. / CRITICISM OF "THE LAND OF SONG."
text:
[BY AP RHYS.]

"Music is being taken much more seriously in Wales today than was the case a few years ago. The Welsh University has awakened to the fact that the Principality was rapidly losing ground and has realised that the legend entwined round the motto 'The Land Of Song' was but the shadow of an empty tradition."

Thus writes William Beeson in an article referring to the work of Sir Walford Davies, Director of Music for Wales, and the progress that has been made under his direction in the musical education of the masses.

Those of us who have had much experience of the Eisteddfods, national and local, of Wales will probably feel inclined to agree that they have not been run on lines ambitious or far seeing enough for them to have contributed greatly to the maintenance of our tradition of song but few will agree with the writer of the article that this tradition was in grave danger of being consigned to oblivion. Eminent musicians may have declined to participate in the Eisteddfod proceedings because of the disinclination of the authorities to depart from the beaten track but the instinctive love of good music which is ingrained in every true Welshmen of however humble a lot has always obtained satisfaction and always will do, quite independent of the Eisteddfod, if necessary.

Take for instance the response there has been to the happily inspired movement by the University of Wales for the provision of facilities for the masses of Wales to hear the compositions of Bach, Beethoven, Mozart, and Wagner by means of "missioners" who play in the most remote hamlets of the Principality. Enthusiastic receptions are accorded these artists wherever they appear and chapels and schoolrooms are crowded with people anxious to hear the works of the masters.

Again, large audiences of quarrymen, coal miners and agricultural labourers have been evincing extraordinary interest in the performances of Parry's "Blodwen" which are being given in the smaller villages in tents under the guidance and supervision of the Portmadoc Operatic Society. Dr. Joseph Parry, the composer of "Blodwin," is perhaps the only successful modern Welsh composer in the more complex forms of music but a new school of composers seems from all accounts to be springing up, the work of which is in no small measure justifying what Mr. Beeson regards as the "legendary" fame of Wales as a land of song.

Of Parry our critic, however, has nothing but praise and referring to the success which has attended the revival of the chief opera work of this most popular composer he regrets the absence of an English translation of it. Judging from its great popularity in Wales it should not prove less profitable than the works of Continental performers which quickly find a place in the programmes of English operatic companies.

headline: RUBBER NEEDS.
text:
AMERICA'S MEASURES.

HOLLAND NOT TO RESTRICT OUTPUT.

Akron, Ohio, June 12. The Netherlands Minister who was present at the early stages of the rubber conference and a number of leaders of the industry stated that the output of rubber in the Dutch possessions would not be restricted while there was proper co-operation on the part of American consumers.

Increased use of reclaimed rubber forms an important part of the relief plan.

The Rubber Association of America has taken definite steps to break the British monopoly on crude rubber as a result of dissatisfaction at the restriction on export and the consequent rise in price of rubber. Temporary relief will be sought through the standardisation of products, particularly in the case of tyres, footwear and mechanical goods, also by postponing for five months the placing of orders for next spring. More permanent measures of relief will take the form of investment of American capital designed to foster the increased production of rubber in Java and other Dutch possessions. A committee has been appointed to confer with the Dutch Government.

headline: SHANGHAI MURDER.
text:
The growing calm of Shanghai was tragically set back last night by the murder and wounding of Britons. Mr. William Mackenzie, of the Municipal Electricity Department, motored with Miss Duncan, of the Amos Bird Co., outside the Settlement Limits, starting at nine o'clock. Entering Great Western Road extension, a naval patrol stopped the car and warned the occupants that a trench had been dug across the road. The car turned back and entered Keswick Road, but had only proceeded two hundred yards when seven Chinese dressed as coolies barred its progress, stopping the car.

Mackenzie got out and asked what the Chinese wanted. The latter turned on flashlights and fired a revolver shot, missing Mackenzie, who rushed back and started the car under a fusilade. Mackenzie was hit in the jugular vein and fell forward, saying "I'm shot; I'm dying."

Miss Duncan though wounded in both arms grasped the steering wheel and drove off, endeavouring to uphold her dying companion.

Though inexperienced, Miss Duncan controlled the car and proceeded for a thousand yards, when in mistake she entered a new road under construction and went head on into a six foot ditch. Miss Duncan shouted and screamed; but failing to attract attention, left the derelict car and ran to a house adjoining the American Columbia Club, which was occupied by two Shanghai Volunteers, who communicated with the police.

Miss Duncan was conveyed to hospital. Her wounds are not serious. Medical men assert that Mr. Mackenzie died a few seconds after the police found him on the roadside with twelve.32 calibre bullets in his body. Municipal coolies guarding the first trench assert that the assassins quickly fled in the direction of Fahwah village in Chinese territory.

The local papers assert that the so-called Chinese Merchant Volunteers dug the Western Road trench yesterday afternoon. This force, which the Chapel authorities previously maintained, consists of ex-soldiers, now principally controlled by the strikers.—Reuter.

Mr. Sidney Barton, the Consul General this morning vigorously protested to the Civil Governor and the Foreign Commissioner against the murder of Mackenzie —Reuter.

Playing football on Sunday. Whatever would your father say? "Well, sir," replied William meekly, "you can go and ask him. He's keeping goal for our side." In the House of Commons Mr. Sandeman (U., Middleton and Prestwich) asked the Under-Secretary for the Home Department, as representing the First Commissioner of Works, whether, on account of its irritating effect on members, he would remove the painting of Alfred inciting the Saxons to prevent the landing of the Danes, from Committee-room No. 10.

The barricading of the lantern and transepts at St. Paul's seriously embarrassed the enormous congregation for one of the Cathedral's most historic services. The corporation of the Sons of the Clergy, instituted in the time of Charles II., has malutained its annual festivals practically without a break, and yesterday's was the 271st. The Lord Mayor and Sheriff's attended in State in the midst of a considerable throng, and were escorted to the temporary altar with the Archbishop of Canterbury by the Bishop of London, the Dean and Chapter, the College of Minor Canons, the Festival Stewards, and members of the Festival Committee. One of the features of a moving and impressive service which has become almost prescriptive by antiquity and repetition was a new authem specially composed by Mr. Stanley Marchant, Mus. D., and performed by an augmented choir of 200 voices, accompanied by organ and orchestra. It consists of a bold and scholarly setting of the hymn "Yo holy angels bright," by Richard Baxter, the seventeenth century divine, who wrote "The Salute' Everlasting Rest," and is rich in proclamatory and exultant passages. For the annual appeal sermon, delivered by Canon Guy Rogers, the Vicar of Birmingham, the proanher took as his text the concluding varies of Corinthians, I, v. whom St Paul speaks of the

Church's sons as “Ambassadors of Christ.” Her difficulty, as this institution showed, was how to reconcile a high spiritual vocation with the uneconomic wage imposed by a vicious competitive system, Public policy and social developments had stripped the clerical offices of many of its older parochial functions, but its spiritual status remained, and the only remedy for its economic problem must have a basis of moral recognition. The corporation was proud of her sons, and was still loyally striving to help many of them to reconcile their high vocation with that of suppliers for a bare living wage, and to retain their courage and resiliency in that spiritual “ambassadorship” which the Apostle had in mind.

The Primate bestowed the blessing, and at the conclusion of the service took farewell of the Lord Mayor and Sheriffs at the western door.

headline: KING ALFRED'S LEGS.
text:
Mr. G. Locker-Lampson (Under-Secretary, Home Office): I am not aware that the picture in question has had such an effect on members as described.

Mr. Sandeman: Will the hon, gentleman contemplate the legs of King Alfred; after having done that, will he try to concentrate on the work that is going on in the Committee-room; and, having come to the same conclusion as I have, will he have the picture put to the other end of the room or elsewhere, or would he like to go down to posterity with legs on him such as those on King Alfred? Mr. Locker-Lampson: I looked at the picture myself this morning. I do not know if the hon. member realises that it is a very fine example of the early work of Watts, one of our most distinguished artists.

headline: THE CHINA MAIL. / MUSIC OF SANDS. / RACE ON A RUNAWAY CAMEL
text: Reference to the curious sound of desert lands known as the "Music of the Sands" was made Major-General Sir Percy Cox in a lecture on "Some Excursions in Oman," which he delivered before the Royal Geographical Society. Sir Percy made two journeys in Oman while serving as Political Agent of the Government of India, and he was the first European to traverse some of the ground he covered. He first heard the music of the sands, he said, while the caravan toiled up and down the sand dunes. It was like the booming of a great organ in the distance and to one hearing it for the first time an extraordinary phenomenon. Sir Percy described an exciting camel race he had with the pilot of his party. "My came," he said, "was fresh, and in trying to pull her up the headstring came away in my hand, and she went away with me into the blue. Sitting as I was behind the hump, according to the apporoved method of riding in Oman, I could do nothing to stop her, and I was fully occupied in keeping my seat and holding on to my sketching case, compass, etc., and trying to ward off mimosa thorns. The direction she was taking was at right angles to our line of route, and if in my wild career I had happened upon a strange bedouin encampment it might have gone hard with me. I could only just reach the camel's cheek or neck with the end of my riding cane, and the best I could do was to keep her more or less on a wide circular course by poking at her neck and endeavouring to guide her gradually back towards our starting point. At last, in the course of half an hour, I had gradually got her head in the right direction, and my pilot Hamud and another were able to cut in in front of me and head her off. I was somewhat exhausted my clothes torn, and face and hands badly scratched with thorns, but I was otherwise none the worse. I did not offer to race any more, however."

headline: EMPRESS RECORD.
text: After going into dry-dock in Hongkong where two new propellors were put in, the Empress of Australia broke her own speed record across the Pacific. From the Yokohama breakwater to William Head quarantine station on the other side, the giant liner averaged 167 knots, the total distance being 4,300 miles. It is possible that other Empress Pacific liners will have new propellers put in similar to those on the Australia which has given proof of the benefit of the overhaul here.

headline: MAKING MISCHIEEF. / STUDENT AGITATORS URGE BOYCOTT. HANKOW HOTBED.
text:
Student agitators are still making mischief in the North, several of them having now gone to Hankow to attempt to promote a boycott, presumably against British goods.

A few hours later, a breadman employed by Hall and Holtz was stopped at the same place, and relieved of 12 loaves of bread.

Although the thieves in both these cases took the articles to the Chinese Fire Station, officers on duty there, who were interviewed by members of the Municipal Police, denied all knowledge of the incidents.

A number of students tried to seize 20 cattle which were on their way to the French Slaughter House, but desisted on the approach of a party of naval men who escorted the cattle to the settlement.

A Reuter telegram from Peking of June 14. says:—

"General Feng Yu-hsiang, interviewed by the "Ching Pao," declared that in case of hostilities against Britain he would be the first in the field. He said that China need not fear England, which had a big Navy but only a small Army."

We do not for a moment suppose General Feng ever said such a thing, but the invention is interesting, remarks the "North China Daily News."

A “North China Daily News” correspondent writing from Chetoo on June 8 says: — I will just mention that the situation is not so pleasant. The Chinese are demonstrating. They are marching through the streets by hundreds, carrying banners and shouting: “Kill the foreigner,” etc. So far no damage has been done to foreign property but no one knows what the situation will be to-morrow. I did my work all day among some Chinese firms and did some fairly good business. I called on a few foreign firms but had very few results. They seem to be worried about the present disturbance and it is indeed difficult to talk business to men when their attention is attracted by shouting mobs in the street: There has been no violence to foreigners as yet but the police told me to go inside when a mob of ruffians passed by. I think that patrols may be sent ashore from the American men-of-war to-night and if so perhaps the day will be quiet.

A feature of the local situation, which remains quiet, is the unchecked publication of grossly misrepresented reports regarding Shanghai and other places by the Chinese papers.

Two students have arrived here from Shanghai. Their intentions include an attempt to promote a boycott.

About ten student agitators have also arrived from Peking.

An interview between the Consular Body and Tupan Esaio Yao-nun is being held this afternoon.

The breakdown of the negotiations between the Commission sent by the interested Powers and the Chinese delegates is explained by a subsequent communiqué shewing that the Chinese insisted on dealing with a series of demands not directly connected with the recent outbreaks at the same time as the incidents themselves with which the Commission is only authorised to deal. The Commission consequently decided to return to Peking, whither the whole question now goes back.

"Since there has been a considerable easing of the local situation during the past three days, instructions have been given for the withdrawal from duty of a portion of the defence forces and these instructions have already been carried out."

[Of course this means no relaxation of the defence and watchfulness.]

Shanghai presented an almost normal appearance on Saturday in that most of the shops in various parts of the Settlement, including Nanking Road were open to some extent, if not entirely, for business. The markets, which have been a point of attack on the part of the agitators and students, were open, with the exception of the meat shops—flowers and garden produce could be seen everywhere, at Hongkew also.

At Arts and Craft all workmen, 450 in number, have resumed their labours, while at Kelly & Walsh's western plant none have returned. Of the Settlement laundrymen, no less than 1,500 refuse to work.

Numerous instances of thieving and rice snatching took place during the week end. On Saturday a gang of coolies assailed two wheelbarrows on Dalny Road and made off with 30 bags of rice. In the Wayside district another gang made off with one sack.

headline: STAR THEATRE. / TREAT FOR MUSIC LOVERS.
text:
The enterprisag management of the Star Theatre has engaged two artistes of world-wide repute who will appear for one night only—on Sunday next. These are Modle Lena Ambiose, soprano and Senor Scamuzzi, late of the Italian Grand opera company. Both are well known in the Colony. Middle Ambiose has a Soprano voice of delightful sweetness, range, and clarity. Scamuzzi—is Scamuzzi! This artist caused a furore on each of his appearances. He has not only a voice but a personality. The mind wanders to "The Barber of Seville," "Carmen," and "Rigoletto" when thinking of Scamuzzi. Both artistes will render selections from Grand opera. There is sure to be a great welcome awaiting these two incomparable artistes.

According to this morning's Chinese papers, the "China News," (the vernacular paper which was raided by the Police some days ago and has since suspended publication) is to be republished by permission of the authorities.

Three Chinese were remanded for one week when charged before Mr. R. A. D. Forrest at the Central Magistracy yesterday with the alleged murder of another Chinese at Wongneichong village. The body of the murdered man was discovered by some coolies below the filter beds on June 1.

headline: FLASH OF FLAME. / STRANGE STORM HEAR CANTON.
text:
TWO LIVES LOST.

FOREIGNERS' NARROW ESCAPE

A whirlwind of intense velocity lasting only two minutes or so struck Tungshan and Taishatau (to the ef the Canton) about 10 45 last night, causing considerable damage and the death of two men by electrocution.

Huts and matsheds were carried away and a part of the German Consulate roof was torn off. Trees were uprooted and the sky was suddenly illuminated by a big red flare. Electric wires snapped, causing the two men's deaths. Foreign residents who had just got back to their homes in this district were reading about the Hongkong storm when many were thrown violently about while windows came tumbling down. It is felt that if the phenomenon had lasted longer much havoc would have been wrought. The strange part about it is that Canton proper were entirely unaware of the sudden storm.

Canton is generally quiet although rumours of a general strike on Monday are in the air. Minor fighting is reported from Fatshan and the North River.

Ngai Bong-ping's resignation is attributed to disagreement with General Hsu Shung-chi and, so the story goes, to some troops lent him by General Leung Hung kai having been disarmed at the hour of victory; by Cantonese colleagues. The latter report is totally unconfirmed.

H. E. the Governor (Sir R. E. Stubbs) will inaugurate the new building of St. Joseph's College on June 24 at 5.30 p.m.

Tokyo, June 18.—The Nichl Nichi reports that the Japanese Construction Company started work on the Taonan Taitahbar� fallway last month and expected to complete it in October—Rentor.

headline: THE RIGHT WAY.
text:
CRITICAL SITUATION CONTROLLED.

GOVERNOR'S FIRM DEALING

On the morning of June 1, just as the students and labour unions of Changsha were preparing for their annual demonstration connection with the "Six-One" (June 1) movement, when it was proposed to commemorate and make demands in connection with the anniversary of the unfortunate affair on the Bund here in 1923 when marines from a Japanese gunboat, in their effort to clear the dock of a violent mob and permit the landing of passengers and freight from a steamer of the Nisshin Kaisha, shot into the crowd and killed a man, the news came to hand of the serious rioting on May 30, in Shanghai, writes a "North China Daily News" correspondent. News that the police had fired into the crowd and that nine students had died caused tremendous consternation and a great outburst of nationalistic feeling. Processions were started at once and for a day or two Governor Chao made no attempt to repress them.

headline: EXCITEMENT HIGH.
text:
By June 4, when word had come of later disturbances in Shanghai and of further shooting, the excitement was running fairly high. Schools that had been parading the streets in connection with the June first celebration now held meetings—that is, the Student Unions did—and other meetings of a violent sort were called in the hall of the Educational Association.

The leaders of the movement calling for retaliation soon organized what is to be called "The Tsing-Hu. (Tsingtao-Shanghai) Cruel Killing Snow Shame (Vengeance) Association." Included in the leadership of this organization are students and labour leaders as well. Every sort of radical proposition has been made, most of them copying the proposals made in Shanghai, for death penalties on the officers that did the shooting in Shanghai on May 30, for the removal of British consular officers; for a complete boycott against the British and Japanese; etc. In many of the schools agitated meetings have been held, usually ending in the taking of a solemn oath by the students body to work here after body, soul and spirit, for the sake of China; and for the enforcement of a complete and permanent economic boycott against Britain and Japan.

headline: AMERICA DRAGGED IN.
text:
Those who watched these developments in school after school came to believe that it would not be long before other countries would be mentioned by name and included in the attack. By the morning of June 6, when word came of an incident in Shanghai on June 3, when American volunteers were fired upon near the New World Theatre, and police action had again become necessary America was also proclaimed as one of the nations to be found guilty. The telegrams here all said that the American Troop had opened fire with a machine gun and had "killed numberless persons." All sors of rumours of impending violence then spread over the city. The governor had already, on June 4, put up a strong proclamation, condemning the shooting in Shanghai on May 30, as unhumanitarian, but urging students and all others to refrain from acts of violence, so as not to give the foreigners any opportunity for incrimination and for retaliatory acts. He proposed severe measures for those who should be found disturbing law and order. This proclamation had had a decided effect until the afternoon of June 6, when the news of the American volunteers reached Changsha.

Before long a girl was found at the gate of the Educational Association, weeping and calling attention to a printed poster on the walls, soon put up all over the city to the effect that an engineer, a foreigner, in the employ of the Canton-Hankow railway, had beaten a Chinese to death. Later in the evening a new rumour was started to the effect that another foreigner had killed a Chinese to the west of the city.

The Governor, Incensed at these fabrications of disturbing rumours came out early on the morning of June 9, with a strong proclamation, showing that such statements were false and urging the populace to become quiet. The entire city was in a state of siege on Saturday night, with groups of armed soldiers guarding all the roads, in and out of the city. Word has come that on the night of Saturday. June 6, a mass meeting of labourers was held in the cotton mill on the opposite bank of the river from Changsha city. They have tried to stand by and keep order and to refrain from joining in noisy demonstrations.

If the officials continue to keep a grip on things, the situation will surely quiet down soon. The Governor, usually giving the impression of being a watchful waiter, has been aggressive and definite, both in statement and action.

After a week of increasing tension in Changsha, ending with a very serious threatening of evil and the fabrication of numberless rumours on the 6th of June, Governor Chao Heng-ti showed himself to be thoroughly master of the situation. He has been governor for several years and has usually been deemed a mild man. Two years ago he caused commotion among the ranks of labour agitators by executing two student leaders, famed for their violence in speech and manner, who were found to be inciting the workers of the cotton mill to revolution.

His next vigorous display of power came late on Saturday evening the sixth. Learning of a vast mob that had gone out to surround the railway yards, apparently to get even with an engineer about whom a false rumour has, been started during the afternoon, he sent out a large detachment of soldiers to cut off the mob. As they met, the mob taunted them and there was some bandying of words until the soldiers slipped cartridge clips into their rifles and told the crowd to go. This shut down the trouble.

On Sunday the sixth, Governor Chao called together a large and representative group to the yamen and made them a long address. First gaining the car of the company by expressing deep sympathy for those who had lost their lives in Shanghai, he went on to speak of the disturbances here in Changsha. "What influence," he asked, "can we have in telegraphing counsel to other provinces if we are unable to keep order here in Hunan? When people know that in the west of Hunan, at Shenchow, at Hungkiang and elsewhere bandits over-run the country, how can they pay attention to our words? How can we help others when such a situation arises as arose yesterday (June 6) when the fabricat on of rumours and threats of evil. compelled Yali College (the college of Yale in China) and the Fu Hsiang School (a Union Mission Girls' Middle School) to shut down? The interference with order reached such a pitch yesterday that if I had not put on the severest martial law orders, no one knows what would have happened later on at that time."

At a later point in his speech the Governor said, "We must watch and keep order lest, as a lesser ro-sult, we have another outburst, similar to what occurred in Boxer year; and lest, as a major result, we find China broken up and her integrity destroyed"

Such words from a Governor of Hunan are strong. Usually pride does not permit the criticism of local conditions. But Governor Chao came forward at the emergency and saved what was a very ugly threat from maturing.

headline: CITY WELL CONTROLLED.
text: As I write today, June 8, things seem calm and the city is well in hand. As the Governor intimated so many student agitators were calling for strikes and for leaving class duty, that the authorities of the College of Yale in China felt their only course to be to close the institution promptly. The annual Commencement exercises which were set for June 23 will be of a simple form, it is said, with less of the academic formality than usual. Other schools which were closed up during most of the week between June 1 and 6 got under way again today, the Bin. They should be able to keep going till the end of the term if no new word of trouble comes from Shanghai.

headline: THEOSOPHICAL SOCIETY.
text:
Meeting of the Hongkong Lodge. The Theosophical Society a lecture was given on "Some Difficulties of the Inner Life." The Lecturer said in part: "The difficulty one experiences in the inner life is that there seems to be a want of attractiveness in our ideals, even though one may have intellectually decided that their realization is desirable. There arise. Two questions, why do we not want that which we see is desirable and productive of happiness, and what can we do to make ourselves want that which we know to be the best for ourselves and the world? When we turn our attention inwards, we see a bewildering multiplicity of "I's" and are stunned by the clamour of opposing voices, all coming apparently from ourselves. But consciousness is a unit, and it appears in the outer world as many simply because it presents itself there through different media, as an electric current in platinum wire may appear as light, in iron as heat, round a bar of soft iron as magnetic energy, or in a solution as a power to decompose and recombine. As consciousness works through the intuitional, mental, astral or physical body, it becomes blinded by the material that enwraps it, and by illusion identifies itself with the craving of the senses, the reasoning of the intellect, and cries "I think," "I feel," "I want." As evolution proceeds, man learns to know himself to be life, not forms, bliss not desire, knowledge not thought, and then first he becomes conscious of unity, then alone he finds peace. Consciousness, at the present stage of evolution, has its centre normally in the astral (emotional and desire) body. The first thing then to realise is that the desire nature is not our Self, but its instrument, a most valuable instrument which is only badly used. Desire, emotion, is the motive power in us, and stands ever between the thought and the action. Intellect sees, but it does not move, and a man without desires and emotions would be a more spectator of life. The Self must have evolved some of its loftiest powers are it can forego the use of desires and emotions; the question is how to use them instead of being used by them, how to discipline them not how to crush them out. We are held back by wanting to unite ourselves with objects transitory, mean and narrow; can we not, then, push ourselves forward by wanting to unite ourselves with the permanent, the noble and the wide? What we need is to cultivate the emotions and to direct them in a way that will purify and enable the character. The basis of all emotions on the side of progress is love, and that is the power which we must cultivate. The first condition of human goodness is something to love, something to reverence. To stimulate the desire nature as a lifting force we should seek the company of any who are more advanced in the spiritual life than we ourselves. Their very presence will be to us a benefidiction, harmonising, raising and inspiring. Happy the man who can find one more advanced to whom he could direct his love and reverence, for such finding will give him the most important condition for turning emotion from a rewarding force into a lifting one and for gaining the needed power " to want" that which he knows to be best. We cannot love without seeking to please, or reverence without taking joy in the approval of the one we were. Hence comes a constant alminulus to improve ourselves, to build up character, to purify the nature, to conquer all is us that is base, to strive after all that is worthy and thus we find ourselves quite suddenly " wanting " to reach a high ideal, and the great motivation power of the emotional nature for

making such a tie of a noble love, of deep reverence. It is a useful habit to read every morning a few sentences from such books as the Bhagavad Gita. The Voice of the Silence, Light of the Path, The Imitation of Christ, which are most powerful aids to the desire nature, and to carry these sentences with us through the day, thus creating around us an atmosphere that is protective to ourselves and beneficial to all those with whom we come in contact. Another absolutely essential thing is daily meditation—a quiet half an hour in the morning during which we deliberately draw ourselves away from the lower nature, recognise it as an instrument and not the Self, and centre ourselves in the highest consciousness we can reach, and feel that as our real Self. That which is Being, Bliss and Knowledge, that am I. Life, Love and Light, that am I. For our essential nature is divine, and the effort to realise it helps its growth and manifestation. Our moods do not matter. There is no constant relation between our progress and our feelings. We are not necessarily advancing when the flow of emotion rejoices us or retrograding when its ebb distresses us. The Self changes not, that which changes is not our Self but part of the transitory surroundings in which the Self is clothed, and withdrawing from the emotions, we no longer feel them as part of ourselves. Ceasing to pour life into them as a self-expression, we break off the connection which enabled it to become a channel of pain, and thus at least we get rid of some of the helplessness and perplexity which are due to ignorance of our true nature. To the enabling and peacegiving contemplation of our divine nature and glorious destiny of ultimate perfection we may fully rise by worshipping with the most fervent devotion of which we are capable—the Father of the Worlds and the Divine Man whom we revenence as Master. Resting on that Divine Man as the Helper and Lover of all who seek to rise—call Him

Buddha, Christ, ShrI Krishna, Master, what we will—we may, dare to raise our eyes to the one, from Whom we come, to Whom we go, and in the confidence of realised sonship murmur: "I and the Father are One." headline: STRIKE EXTENDS.
text: It should be noted that for convenience sake all meals at the Hotel are being served in the grill room and that they are of the very best. To-day, at tiffin an air of cheerfulness pervaded the room, aided at times by the band. Mrs. Taggart and others were prominent and the Hotel is to be complimented on what it is doing.

headline: Exodus: Continues.
text:
Long before sunrise, in fact within a short time of the incoming river steamers discharging their passengers, hundreds of Chinese had swarmed on to the wharves determined to obtain a passage for Canton or the native village. At daylight this morning the vessels due to leave this evening were absolutely full of passengers. Little or no cargo was worked, but a constant stream of men and women, all carrying luggage, were turned back. A conservative estimate places the number shut-out at 10,000. Many of those going down were domestic' servants, ostensibly from foreign households.

This morning some households still had their servants and were able to get their meals, but the majority of the more fortunate employers were informed that their employees would, reluctantly, as in nearly every case, have to leave about tiffin time.

headline: Scouts Helping
text: The Hongkong Boy Scout's Association is doing its "bit" and arrangements in hand by which this help will be considerably extended if necessary. At present there are several qualified Scouts working in hospitals and many others are holding themselves in readiness for all sorts of other work, down to working in lifts if necessary. The Rev. G. T. Waldegrave, Commissioner, informed us on enquiry that all Scouts had been asked to report to Headquarters. The parade arranged to take place at Government House on Wednesday had been cancelled.

headline: Rumours About To-morrow.
text:
Many are the rumours about tomorrow. Those who correctly predicted on Saturday night that the trams would stop on Sunday now say that the beef and other stalls at the market may have to shut down tomorrow and that the engineeringers and firemen on harbour ferries may stay away.

Vernacular papers suspended publication this morning but extras were issued.

Hundreds of workers are crossing the Territories to travel by train to Canton, A China Mail reporter was informed that had it not been for the rain yesterday and to-day, a much larger number would have trekked miles but refrained for fear of weiting their personal effects.

headline: Earlier Developments.
text:
The strike which commenced on Friday has now developed considerably and affects all classes and almost all industries and businesses.

The boys at the Peak Hotel began to leave shortly before tiffin on Saturday and the remainder went after tiffin. The exodus, from the Peak Club took place on Saturday afternoon, but this did not interfere with the dance in the evening, refreshments being served and the necessary washing-up done with skill and dexterity, by the members themselves.

The Chinese staff at Repulse Bay did not leave until tiffin on Sunday. It was stated that between four and five hundred Chinese engaged in the two hotels—the Peak Hotel and the Repulse Bay Hotel—had gone. A few of the boys from the Hongkong Hotel left during the course of yesterday morning, and last night all but one or two had left. At all the hotels, however, careful and well-planned arrangements have been made to "carry on" as well as is possible in the circumstances.

The boys began to leave the houses in the Peak district on Sunday morning. Previously there had been no suggestion of a strike.

During the night, however, the following notice, in Chinese, was stated to have been left at a considerable number of residences:—

Gentlemen,— I his is to inform you that in consequence of the recent incidents in Shanghai, causing workers and students to suffer cruel deaths, our corps has determined to carry out a general strike on and from Sunday next. Anybody who fails to join the strike will get from our corps extraordinary treatment.

This precious document is said to have been found on the doorsteps of the houses early in the morning. Its effect was extraordinary.

When the employees of the Tramway Company finished their work at Saturday mid-night, there was no reference to any possibility of a strike. The drivers and conductors, however, failed to put in an appearance on Sunday morning and consequently yesterday no trams were running.

At the tiffin given in honour of H.E. the Governor at the Hongkong Club on Saturday, His Excellency made a passing reference to the possibility of his approaching departure being postponed on account of the strike. "If this nonsense continues," H.E. declared, "I am going to see it through, and I do not think the arrangement will be a comfortable one for those responsible for my delay." In view of the developments, since this speech was delivered it seems highly improbable that H.E. the Governor will leave on Saturday as arranged.

headline: Further Details.
text:
About 11.30 a.m. to-day, a Japanese was shot near the French Bridge by an unknown person who is said to be a Chinese. Two shots were heard. One bullet went through the man's left arm into his body and the other struck his leg. He was carried into the Concession by French sailors and Dr. Reynolds of Shameen. Later on I was informed that the man had succumbed and that he was connected with the Japanese hospital at Nam Kwan.

All the Hongkong and Macao boats to-day were anchored off Shameen with the exception of the s.s. Charles Hardouin. The Honam did not sail for Hongkong this morning and is anchored in the same place.

The Canton Government has issued an order that all former gambling houses and Yunnanese holdings are to be used as strike quarters and that the merchants are to contribute to strike funds.

Although the Chinese employees on Shameen have declared that they do not wish to strike but it seems that they will ultimately yield to the inevitable.

What the World is Being Told. Below will be found the Reuter messages broadcast from Hong- kong:—

The motormen and conductors of the electric Tramway Company have struck. The service is temporarily suspended. The strike of Chinese servants is spreading. Many boarding houses, some hospitals and hotels are affected. Boy Scouts are mobilising for the purpose of assisting the hospital. The Government has offered a reward of $250 for information leading to arrest and conviction of persons endeavouring to disturb the peace of the Colony. Numbers of Chinese are leaving the city for Canton. Chinese crews on several more British steamers have deserted.

The Volunteers have been mobilised. Boy Scouts have replaced the striking Chinese attendants at Hospital. Six steamers of the Indo-China Navigation Company are tied up.

Later.

A number of British and other foreign women and children have arrived from Shameen whence they were advised to leave. Police re patrolling the business quarters of Shameen precautionarily.

headline: Canton Shooting.
text:
An unknown Chinese shot dead Mr. Nakadai, the Japanese treasurer of the Japanese Hospital, just outside Shameen, and carried off a bag with five thousand dollars with which Mr. Nakadai was returning from the Bank of Taiwan.

The Japanese Consul has strongly protested to the local authorities, reserving the right to claim indemnity, and asking for police to be posted outside Shameen. He advised Japanese subjects in Canton to come to Shameen.

Many foreigners are going to Hongkong.—Most of the others residing outside the European quarter are now coming to Shameen.

The strike at Shameen began this morning. The Chinese are (ielty leaving the Concession.

There are no disturbances. British Marines are operating the ice-plant and are ready to operate the waterworks.

Later.

The Civil Governor of Canton has requested the merchants to contribute to strike funds. Gambling houses closed before the war have been taken over as quarters for strikers who number approximately 1,500. Shameen has an extra supply of food. Another Japanese destroyer has arrived.

headline: WHAT IS ART? / LORD SUMMER'S APHORISMS
text:
The outstanding feature of the annual dinner of the Royal Institute of British Architects, held at the Trocadero Restaurant, was the happy wit of the speech in which Lord Sumner proposed the toast of "The Arts."

What, he asked, is an artist? He had written it down, for this reason: there was a minor art, unworthy of being included in the arts, which was called the art of dialectic, or argument, and the secret of that art was wisely to choose your axiom, to proceed rapidly and unexpectedly to conclusions drawn from the question, and to know the precise moment when to beg the question. (Laughter.) That was the true secret of political reasoning. "An artist," proceeded Lord Summer, "is one who creates beauty by the outward expression of his inmost self through a medium which he has selected. What follows from that? First of all, by very definition, an artist is a monstrous egotist. He wishes to express his inmost self and stamp himself on the world. It follows that his highest pleasure is to do so, and, like the blossoming aloe, when once in a hundred years he has achieved that object, the time has come for him to pass away. (Laughter) I think another thing follows from that. His sole pleasure is the creation of beauty. Beauty when created is property of no one; it belongs to the world; it is the artist's gift to his fellow, but inferior, men. (Laughter.) The opposite of it is utility. In proportion as the artist makes anything that is useful he ceases to be an artist. (Laughter) "But that which is the property of all the world," continued Lord Summer, "ought not to be sold for a great or even a small price; it is like pure air or pure water, and on the other hand it is only that which is useful which mankind can reasonably be called upon to pay for. It follows if an artist should sink to such a depth that he can sell his work he is ceasing to be an artist. (Laughter). He is entering the ranks of the profession (Laughter.) "Art is the presentation of the ideal by the manifestation of the impossible. It is a production of poetic illusion for prosaic material; it is the achievement of the subjective reality in the objective garb of plastic constructive materials. I thought that covered the ground until I came across another aphorism: 'Art is a subject on which all mankind talks the most absolute bosh.' (Laughter.)

What is the democratic view of art? I think it is summed up in this proportion: 'Art is what gives me pleasure, great art is what gives me great pleasure. Provided I enjoy it, it doesn't matter whether it gives other fellows pain or not. (Laughter.) That is why the cubist, futurist, or vorticist painter is so truly democratic. (Laughter.) The agony he inflicts on those who are rash enough to cast an eye over his deathless works is pleasure to him. There are similar successes in architecture. (Laughter.) I have seen in the Press a large number of most interesting pictures of houses that are being built in this country to make homes for heroes. All appear to me to have the one great element of utility that they enable tenants to get houses which can never by any possibility pay the owners of them; but there are some of them, I grieve to say, which appear to have been built for blinded heroes — (laughter)—and which it would be inhuman to call upon anybody else to occupy. (Laughter.)

"Is it not true to say that the Arts are a civilised nation's pride? The Arts, however, we may understand, or misunderstand them, are the things, each in its different way, to which all of us send out our hearts. They are the soul of life; they are things without which we would rather die—and without the Arts the nations will die. (Cheers)"

Sir Frank Dicksee (President of the Royal Academy) and Sir Lionel Earle (Permanent Secretary to his Majesty's Office of Works) responded.

Earlier in the evening Viscount Peel (First Commissioner of Works), submitting the toast of "The Royal Institution of British Architects and its Allied Societies," said he thought the Government had shown in a very practical way its sense of importance of architecture by including for the last three or four Governments the First Commissioner of Works in the Cabinet. He regretted to think that there were no architects in the Cabinet; they had artists—(laughter) literary men, and even poets, but no architect, and he doubted if there were many, if any, architectural either in the House of Commons or the House of Lords. But he did not think anybody could attack the present or any other Government for being other than generous in its architectural tastes. The House of Commons carried on business under what he might call British Gothic; the judicial limb of the Government undoubtedly had some connection with the French Gothic of the fourteenth century; but our administrative offices were very curious lot indeed.

headline: PRINCIPAL TENANTS:
text:
An important judgment was given in the Summary Court this morning, the effect of which is that a principal tenant cannot terminate the tenancy of a sub-tenant for any illegal act on his part.

The Rents Ordinance empowers the lessor to do this if "any person residing with a tenant" shall have been convicted of using the premises for an unlawful purpose, but Mr. Justice Wood held that this definition could not be applied to a sub-tenant of a lessee residing on the premises.

Under the Ordinance, Mr. Justice Wood pointed out, an application for possession could succeed if the domestic tenement was reasonably required for occupation as a residence for the lessor or "any person residing with him," but it could scarcely be held that the lessor could claim this privilege in respect of any sub-tenant of his own.

His Honour said that it might quite rightly be held that his construction meant that any attempts of the owners to suppress illegal use of their property might be rendered abortive, but nevertheless it seemed clear that the legislation purported to regulate only the relations of the lessee with the immediate lessor and peersons under his control.

headline: DEFECTIVE BRAKES
text:
CAR DRIVER WARNED BY THE MAGISTRATE.

A licensed motor car driver named Chan Kwai was charged at the Central Magistracy this morning with a breach of traffic regulations and driving a car with defective brukes. The prosecution was a sequel to an accident in which a small boy, a woman, and an old man were injured.

The case was settled by the accused undertaking to pay a total of $30 as compensation to the injured persons. The accused received a warning from the Bench to be more careful in future.

headline: ARMS SEIZURE / TWO CHINESE REMANDED.
text:
An arms seizure of considerable size was effected by the Police on a search of the s.s. Benvrackie. The haul comprised ten Mauser pistols and stocks; two automatics, 22 revolvers and 5,402 rounds of ammunition.

Two Chinese members of the crew were charged at the Kowloon Magistracy this morning with the unlawful possession of the arms and remanded.

The Water Police executed a search warrant at the Kowloon Hotel yesterday and arrested a Chinese, who had in his possession a revolver and five rounds of ammunition.

The President of the Institute (Mr. J. Alfred Goich) and Mr. Percy Thomas responded. Lord Riddell and Mr. R. C. Norman replied for the guests, whose health was pledged at the call of Major Harry Barnes. SATURDAY'S ENJOYABLE FUNCTION.

If the term "a crowded house" can be applied to an open-air entertainment, that describes the audience at the first of the Kowloon-Cricket Club's al fresco entertainments on Saturday evening. Conditions were ideal for sitting out of doors whilst the programme submitted by The Pharies of the 4th submarine flotilla was up-to-date and full of amazingly humorous items as well as things by an accomplished singer to say nothing of a female imperator and the "Titania's" orchestra. Those mainly responsible for the good things provided were Piano Pinkie, E. F. Sayer; Moth-Eaten Monty, R. Genes; Cumhither Cumshaw, A. Probert; Melodious Marazion, A. W. Wade; Villianous Victor, A. S. Peacock; Diaphanous Daphne, H. Guard.

The grounds were nicely illuminated and the refreshment tents received a full measure of patronage. The K.C.C. is to be heartily congratulated on the success of the evening which should encourage it to similar efforts.

headline: COLLEGE BAZAAR.
text:
In spite of adverse circumstances the faith of the promoters of St. Stephen's College Bazaar in carrying on with the arrangements was justified and the Building fund will benefit considerably as a result. The Bazaar concluded on Saturday afternoon and evening. At three o'clock Sir Henry Pollock, K.O., who was accompanied by Lady Pollock and Miss Middleton Smith, introduced in the Great Hall Mrs. Chow Shou-son and spoke of the keen interest she had always taken in the welfare of St. Stephen's. Mrs. Chow Shou-son acknowledged through Mr. Li Chor-chi and in opening the Bazaar wished it and the Building Fund every success. Mrs. Chow Shou-son was then presented with a memento of the occasion by Mr. Chan Cheung-nin, who has been largely responsible for the general arrangements of the Bazaar. The Rev. H. W. Hewitt, Principal of the College, thanked Mrs. Chow Shou-son both for her presence and the interest she had always taken in St. Stephen's. He would also take the opportunity of thanking all who had worked toward the success of the undertaking and had given unsparingly of their time and labour.

The outdoor entertainments were the same as had proved such an attraction the day previously and they drew another large crowd in spite of the heat. The stalls in the Great Hall were also extensively patronised and the appearance of the Colony's champion ping pong players in a specially arranged tournament for a cup was the signal for a general rush to the room in which it was held.

In the evening a variety entertainment and cinema show were given to a large "house."

A well-dressed clerk of the Eastern Telegraph Co., delivering cables during the messenger boys' strike went to a London hotel. A porter took his hat and umbrella and showed him into a room. Then a woman came in, exclaiming, "It's so nice of you to have called. Will you come up and see the wedding presents!" In spite of the fact, a considerable number of farm hands from Great Britain and European countries are being distributed on western Canadian farms, the supply is not equal to the demand and shortage is becoming more pronounced as spring work develops more extensively. Wages are averaging from $30 to $40 (gold) per month and board.

A small army of Paris shop girls are wearing wigs, which they discard on leaving, the premises where they work. Shingled heads have been banned by their directors, under threat of immediate dismissal, and there was nothing left to do but to make the best of a bad job—which the pretty wigs they wear show they have done.

Contests for the Canadian typewriting championships were held simultaneously in five cities of Canada. Miss Irma Wright, of Toronto, won the one-minute contest with a speed of 117 words a minute. This says the "Daily Mail," is far behind the feat of the 29-year-old Miss Millicent Woodward, of Mansfield, England, champion typist of Europe, who, in December, 1922, typed 276 (memorised) words in one minute. She was credited then with receiving £1,000 a year as chief demonstrator for a firm of typewriter manufacturers.

Teachers are wanted for French, Spanish and shorthand classes in Maidstone Prison.

Now celebrating its 100th birthday, the Wesleyan Chapel, St. Germans, Cornwall, owes its origin to a false pair of butcher's scales. By means of the scale a servant to the Earl of St. Germans unjustly accused the butcher of fraud. The Earl, in reparation, offered the man anything he liked to select. He chose a site for a chapel.

I'll taste the luxury of woe, —THOMAS MOORE All for a shilling, a London police-woman was informed that Her life would be full of trouble. Her home would be broken up. Her mother was on a bed of sickness, and

Her sister was mentally afflicted. For making these gloomy prophecies Mrs Charlotte Gentle, a fortune-teller, of Liver-road, Parsons Green, was summoned at West London Police Court. "To me, the astonishing thing is that she should have so many customers, considering she tells such a gloomy tale to them," said the magistrate. Mrs Gentle was fined £3.

A rabbit in flight near Elm Spring, Arkansas, led to the discovery by a shpoting party of a man's skeleton in the hollow of a giant oak (says the "Central News"). When the rabbit took refuge in the hollow, whose opening was only a few inches wide, the "hunters" enlarged the entrance and found the skeleton, also an old flintlock rifle and a buckskin pouch of gunpowder, Foresters judge that it must be over 60 years since the opening was large enough for the man to creep through. Perhaps he took refuge when pursued by Indians. Perhaps he could not so turn as to get out again. Or he may have been wounded and died in the tree, which has since grown up around him. James's Payn's story of the "Lost Sir Massing-berd" is recalled by the discovery.

headline: Mongomery.
text:
Since the Duke and Duchess of York returned from East Africa Her Royal Highness has been kept very busily engaged at her home at White Lodge in arranging the large number of interesting souvenirs of almost every description that they have brought back with them. In due course several of the sporting trophies that fell to the rife of the Duke of York are to be placed in position. White Lodge, with its many windows and light and airy appearance, lends itself admirably to a display of this description. The Duchess of York has also brought home a large collection of specimens of native workmanship, some of which are quite unique of their kind. Some of these are destined as presents for the intimate friends of the Duke and Duchess.

The home-c ming of Lord Reading is deeply saddened for him by the untimely death of Godfrey Isaacs. The affection was particularly strong between these brothers, each so brilliant a leader in his chosen walk of life. Though the elder by six years, and in his way quite as hard a worker as his brother, Lord Reading happens to have been blessed with by far the more versatile mind, and has always understood the art of cultivating varied interests and the necessity for hard brain-workers, of mental recreation. On the other hand, Godfrey Isaacs was always so utterly possessed and obsessed by his job that it was no easy matter to get him to take even a passing interest in anything else. For the last fifteen years the Maronji Company and its affairs had been his life, and what he was forced by the doctor to retire from the ago worn out with overwork and want of rest he had the appearance of a man who had nothing to live.

One hundred families of Hebridean settlers for the Vermillion district of the Province of Albert were expected to arrive during the latter part of May. In the past three years hundreds of settlers from the Hebrides Islands of Scotland have come to Canada under the auspices of the Scottish Immigrant Aid Society, most of whom have been successfully established in Alberta.

Mr. Tom Johnston, the Socialist M.P. for Dundee, is to ask the Premier whether Government accepts the rule that members of the Cabinet, during their tenure of office, should refrain from contributing articles to the Press upon public affairs and whether he is aware that Lord Birkenhead is a voluminous contributor to newspapers upon matters affecting public policy, and as to what steps, if any, he proposes to take. It may be noted that Lord Birkenhead is at present contributing a series of articles to the "Evening Standard" upon the divorce laws.

Mr. Henry Arthur Jones, the dramatist, at a Shakespeare celebration alluded to the fact that he was born in a farm house in Buckinghamshire under conditions rather similar to those of Shake. Spears. "I told this fact to my granddaughter the other day," he said, and she replied. "If you were born in the next county but one to Shakespeare, why don't you write better plays?" (Laughter.)

headline: 一
text:
The King's early return from his holiday did not surprise anybody in the Court circle. It was an open secret that His Majesty went abroad most unwillingly, and only upon the urgent representations of his doctors. The effect of the change has entirely justified the medical advice. But the King was anxious to be back for the resassembling of Parliament after the Easter recess. Two couriers a week have kept him in close touch with affairs, but when Parliament is sitting the King likes to be on the spot.

An estimate of the life-work of Sun Yat-sen leads a writer in "Asia" (New York) to compare the three men who, by common consent, are estocried the greatest men of modern Asia. They are Gaudhi, Mustapha Kemal Pasha, and Sun Yat-sen. But between Sun and the other two, he any, there is this unlikeness: Gandhi has the respect, the worship even, of the Indians, and Kemal the power over the Turks; but Sun Yat-sen is regarded by the Chinese with indifference and sometimes with mockery. Yet Sun Yat-sen no less than the other two is entitled to his place in the triumpeate that may truly be said to have fired with new spirit in the aged soul of the East. Indeed he was the first of the three and made the talk of the other two to the other. Though pressure has been brought upon her by her friends, Lady Astor declares she has no intention of retiring from Parliament.

Mr. Eina V. Schou, the millionaire margarine king, has died in Denmark. In 1889 he began business with one ton of margarine which he invented, and was soon manufacturing 1,000 tons a week.

headline: Hongkong, Tuesday, June 2, 1925.
text:
To-day's news from Shanghai is only reassuring to the extent that it emphasises the determination of the Police and the Municipal authorities to subdue the disturbances at all costs. Within a few hours the vapourings of a few students of Communist tendencies have been responsible for the creation of an international crisis which may drift along a course diametrically opposite to that intended by the first few demonstrations.

Not even the best friend of China would desire a replica of the Boxer Riots and of the humiliation that these eventually brought in their wake for China. But hot-headed youth inspired by sources that know not lav and order—and in fact are "up against" it—cannot be expected to stop and think of the consequences. But at the same time they themselves must share the suffering of these consequences. They cannot expect sympathy. They cannot be raised to the status of martyrs. Law and order must prevail even in China when the lives and the interests of foreigners are menaced.

It matters not at this distance from the scene of conflict whether the riots originated in the killing of a Chinese workman by a Japanese during the recent-cotton strike, or whether the primary cause was a desire on the part of Chinese students to escape examinations and get promotion without them. What does matter, and matter very much, is the fact that the rioters have shown their hands by the inflammatory posters they have issued broadcast over the city denouncing Imperialism and foreigners. That is proof positive that they have only been waiting for the flimiest excuse to break out of bounds and foment what really is tantamount to an anti-foreign rebellion. That is both a stupid and a dangerous policy to pursue. It must recoil on the heads of the Chinese themselves and on the Chinese as a nation.

If those who have the authority and the influence do not step into the breach and assist the Municipal authorities and the Police in Shanghai in the speedy restoration of order, they will assuredly regret it. There must be no weak-kneed measures or sentiment. The riots must be quelled and the originators and participants severely punished. And if that is not done within a reasonable space of time the duty of the British and the other foreigners whose interests are menaced is obvious.

The growing amount of motor traffic is revealed by the amendment of traffic regulations published in the last number of the Government Gazette. Seldom, if ever, does one see a truck in charge of a number of screeching men. The Government has wisely initiated or encouraged a system of motor haulage in keeping with modern conditions. This is all to the good and a further aid to safety, for it is admitted that proffemoving vehicles are less a danger to traffic than the slow moving kind. The speed of 15 miles and 12 miles per hour assigned to various trucks is reasonable. What is of vast importance to the efficiency with which the road haulage is used. The additions covering ordinary vehicles are sane. A licensed driver is not to allow his vehicle to be driven by one who is unlicensed; whilst public motor vehicles are to carry a spare wheel and a serviceable kit of tools to the satisfaction of the head of the police. There should, it appears to us, be some rule covering those roads where there is either no sidewalk for pedestrians, or one of narrow dimensions making it almost impossible for it to be used. In this class of thoroughfare the pedestrian is in extreme danger of injury. A word of caution to drivers should not be out of place.

headline: How to Control Oplum.
text: One suggestion for the control of opium emanates from America. The physician attached to the Tombs Prison, New York, who has thousands of addicts under his care, proposes that the United States should solve the opium problem by prohibiting the importation of opium altogether, growing in the U.S. all the poppies necessary for the manufacture of poppies for medicinal purposes, and keeping the manufacture under Government control. He indicates where, in America, the poppies could be grown. The suggestion is a practical one. It is that of the putting your own house in order type, and on this ground alone commends itself. It has to be remembered that the Westerner has quickly come to the use of what may be termed oriental drugs and narcotics. Rightly used and under qualified medical control the moderate use of such for medicinal purposes is in order. It is the abuse that is causing so much harm—moral and physical—in those who have become addicts. Adopt this eminently sound, simple and sane question amongst Western nations, and those who are primarily responsible for the growth of the poppy will have profitable channels closed to them. It will enable those in real earnest in Eastern countries the better to grapple with an evil which has done much to sap the moral, and physical fibre of great peoples.

headline: China's Chaos.
text: Straws show which way the wind blows. A "Times" leader also shows which way thought is trending in Europe regarding things Chinese. This great paper pleads that Britain takes the lead in devising a plan for delivering China from the incubus of Civil War. Easier said than done. Any nation that takes such a lead is bound to become unpopular and misunderstood. But that must be risked where a great gain is likely to ensue. It seems remarkable that the question of China has not, so far engaged the attention of the League of Nations. Those of China's leaders who profess a wish for the country's release from all her troubles, should have no hesitation in letting such an impartial tribunal as the League of Nations attempt to devise some plan of salvation before disruption takes place, or armed interference becomes an absolute necessity. There seems no immediate prospect of peace plans coming from those who profess and call themselves leaders. There is no one to follow the example of Sir Robert Ho Tung—not even from the safe vantage ground of Hongkong—and the situation, all over the country goes daily from bad to worse.

headline: CORNWALL
text: of the young people going in droves into the country to partake of milk and cream. Carew in his Survey of Cornwall (p. 68), speaking of the church ale, says that "two young men of the parish are yersly chosen by their last foregoers to be wardens, who, dividing the task, make collection among the parishioners of whatsoever provision it pleaseth them voluntarily to bestow. This they employ in brewing, baking, and other acates (provisions) against Whitsuntide; upon which holy, days the neighbours meet at the church-house, and there merrily feed on their own victims, contributing some petty portion to the stock, which, by many smalls, growth to a meetly greatness; for there is entertained a kind of emulation between these wardens, who, by his graciousness in gathering and good husbandry in expending, can best advance the church's profit. Besides, the neighbour parishes at those times lovingly visit each one another and this way frankly spend their money together. The afternoons are consumed in such exercises as old and young folk (having leisure) do accountably wear out the time withall. When the feast is ended, the wardens yield in their account to the parishioners, and such money as exceed the disbursement is layd up in store, to defray any extraordinary charges arising in the parish or imposed on them for the good of the country or the prince's service, neither of which commonly grips so much but that somewhat still remayneth to cover the purse's bottom. This custom is falling into desuetude, if it be not already discontinued.

headline: HONGKONG AND THE CHATER COLLECTION.
text:
Reviewing the Chatter Collection: A Catalogue of Pictures Relating to China, Hongkong, and Macao, 1655-1860," with descriptive letterpress by James Orange (Thornton Butterworth. £7.7s.), Mr. J. O. P. Bland writes as follows in the "Sunday Times," (London): Of the many benefits conferred by Sir Paul Chatter on his fellow-citizens of the Crown Colony of Hongkong, assuredly none will rank higher in times to come than his gift of this collection of pictures and books descriptive of the early days of the Colony and commemorative of the events which led, and the men who contributed, to its making. This handsome volume, with its eighteen plates in colour and 243 in half-tone, constitutes a very fitting and felicitous monument, not only to the public-spirited munificence of "Sir Paul," but to the memory of the stout-hearted mariners, pro-Consuls, and merchant adventurers of England who, against heavy odds, opened up new and great highways of commerce in the Far East. It contains, moreover, much more than the customary catalogue of an art collection, for Mr. Orange has done his work as editor and commentator with a through knowledge and enjoyment of his subject and much scholarly discrimination. The arrangement of the work, in appropriate sections provided with exhaustive indices, should make it of real and permanent value to students, while the numerous quotations from contemporary authors, which accompany each section, enable the casual reader to form a very vivid and accurate impression of the events and scenes they describe.

It is a wonderful pageant of stirring days and captains courageous which these pictures present, beginning with the earliest attempts of the Portuguese Spaniards, British, and Dutch in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries to secure a footing for trude on the coasts of southern China, and to penetrate beyond the barriers of the Celestial Empire's splendid isolation. After the entry upon the scene of the stately orgosies of the Honourable East India Company, at the beginning of the seventeenth century, the European figures in the pageant become conspicuously British. This was to be expected, for, from 1678 onwards, when the Company established its direct and regular trade with Canton, Amoy, and (Later) Chusan, the long and often disbearing task of opening up commercial relations between China and the rest of the world—of sowing, where others have since helped fall almost entirely upon England.

headline: EVOLUTION OF THE CLIPTERR SHIP.
text: The series of paintings and drawing by W. Alexander (droughtsman attached to Lord Macartney's Embassy, 1793), by Chinnery, A. Borgel, T. Allom, and other artists, beautifully reproduced in this volume, conveys a very clear impression of the times and scenes in which these venturesme' exciles lived, moved, and had their being, up to the end of the "period of conflict" in 1860. The story which they tell is admirably annotated by well-chosen quotations from Ellis's Journal of Lord Amherst's Embassy," Bernard's "Voyages of the Nemesis," Chatterton's "Mercunile Marine," "McLeod's 'Voyage in H.M.S. Alceste,' William Hickey's "Memoirs," and the writings of Fortune, Hunter, and other authors. One of the most interesting sections of the work is that which describes the evolution of the tea and opium clipperships, things of beauty that moved in an atmosphere of poetry and romance, now lost to our machine-driven world. Their brief history of forty years was, as Chatterton says, "the golden age of the Mercantile Marine, a period when it rose to such a standard of scamanship as was never, seen before nor will ever be witnessed again." It is very fitting that this graceful monument to their memory should find its home in a Crown Colony which largely as the result of their traffic and discoveries has grown within the memory of living men from a barren island of the Ladrones to become one of the greatest seaports of the world. It is well that it should not be left to the India Home Club of New York to possess the only representative collection of paintings relating to the lives and achievements of these moneyers and acquire builders in East India.
