headline: “CHINA MAIL” SPORTS PAGE. / LAWN BOWLS. / LOCAL NOTES AND COMMENT. / LEAGUE PROSPECTS.
text:
The following are the league games down for decision tomorrow:—

Tnikoo R.C. v. Kowloon Dock R.C.

Kowloon C.C. v. Kowloon B.G.C.

Civil Service C.C. v. Craigen- gower C.C.

SECOND DIVISION. Police R.C. v. Taikoo R.C. Indian R.C. v. Kówloon C.C. East Point R.C. v. R.H.K. Yacht Club.

The games are down to start at 3.30 p.m. sharp on the ground of the first-named and the results in the first division will be awaited with interest.

Taikoo are at home to the Kowloon Dock team and they will be anxious to average their defeat at Kowloon. Playing at home they will have an advantage and are likely to turn the tables on their opponents to-morrow. They still have a chance to become league champions, but they will need to win all their remaining engagements.

With such a creditable win in their favour, over Taikoo last week, it is evident the Bowling Green Club have found their form; although they will be playing away from home, I rather think they will be too good for the Cricket Club and may return home with the points.

Craigengower had a splendid victory away from home last week and to-morrow they visit the Civil Service who have yet to be beaten on their own ground. It will be necessary for the former to win to-morrow if they wish to retain their position at the head of the league.

In the second division the Police receive Taikoo and as they succeeded against this team away from home earlier in the season, it hardly seems possible for them to fail at home. However, the Police Green is one that any bowler can play on and the result seems open. Should they win to-morrow, the Police are pretty certain of the junior league championship and an immediate return to senior circles.

The Indians are at home to the Kowloon Cricket Club and I do not think the latter are strong enough to take the unbeaten home record away from the Indians. They had very hard luck at Taikoo last week for after being five up on the eighteenth head they lost by one.

The East Point Club—have as their guests the Yacht Club. Both Clubs have yet to register a win and the losers to-morrow seem doomed to be the “wonder spoonists” for this season.

Nothing seems to have been done since the decision to run the open championship singles on the new lines. I have not heard of any club starting their preliminary rounds yet. There does not seem to be much enthusiasm in the competition this year.

Now it is definitely known that Shanghai are sending down an Interport team towards the end of September, it behaves the selection committee to get busy. A few trial games, "probables v. "Possibles," should be arranged, and every player of reasonable ability should be given a chance.

It will also be necessary for the team that is picked to represent the Colony to get some practice together, and they should play against a team chosen from "The Rest."

Both the above suggestions I commend to the consideration of those responsible for the arrangements that are to be made.

headline: RIFLE CONTEST. / SINGAPORE WITHDRAWS FROM INTERPORT. / SHANGHAI WIN.
text:
Confirmation of the interport rifle news from Singapore has been received by Mr. C. H. Summers, the honorary secretary.

The following cable was published in the "China Mail" on June 2:

Singapore fired-off yesterday in the interport contest but protesting on account of faulty ammunition.

In a letter to Mr. Summers, the Singapore secretary stated that their team intended to shoot on May 31. After doing the 200-yards, the team withdrew because they had bad ammunition.

Last year Penang did not shoot in the contest. As no word has been received it is presumed that Penang did not enter again this year. However, the honours have been wrested from Hongkong. Hongkong put up a score of 875 but Shanghai made 921. It would now be safe to assume that Shanghai are the winners.

A Reuter cable received last night says that Tilden, the best lawn tennis player in the world, has been released from his contract to report championship matches for a newspaper. He will thus be eligible for the U.S. team.

headline: GOLF CHAMPION. / NOTES ABOUT ROBERT HARRIS. / HOW HE PLAYS.
text:
Robert Harris, who has won the Amateur Championship by the biggest margin that it has ever been won by learnt-his-golf as a boy at Carnoustie, which has been the training ground of many fine players. He went to live in London in 1902, and since then has taken a leading place in the Championship but never before won it. He has played every year for Scotland in the international match which always takes place before the championship. He reached the final round two years ago against Wethered, but was beaten by 7 and 6. Wethered producing some of the finest golf that has ever been seen in the final.

Harris plays for a golfer of his class with his foot very close together, and with rather an open stance, that is with his right foot slightly in front of his left. He is a very long hitter with both his wooden, and iron clubs, and has an excellent temperament, never getting worried by the big crowds that follow round. He is what one might call getting on for the veteran stage, being about 46. He plays most of his shots with natural pull on the ball, which gives the player that extra bit of run, and no doubt on Long course like Westward Ho! this was most useful. Harris is on the London Stock Exchange, so most of his Golf consists of week-end play, which is more to his credit, as he is unable to get so much practice as some other players.

His opponent, Kenneth Fradgley, who has never previously gone so far in the Championship, was evidently the victim of nerves in the final.

headline: Students' Trial
parent_headline: THE CHINA MAIL. / SHANGHAI TROUBLE. / CABLES
text:
The students trial was concluded to-day, the accused men being ordered to furnish a bond guaranteeing their good behaviour. The American Assessor, Mr. Jacobs, said that he deeply regretted the case which had much embittered the Sino-Foreign relations.

There was no demonstration by the big crowd. The Court was heavily guarded by police and an armoured car.

Following a coolie dispute, last night of Messrs. Butterfield and Swire's upper wharf in which a good deal of stone-throwing took place, a liquid of Chinese Police fired over the crowd, which scattered. A dozen arrests were made. The trouble apparently was purely Chinese, but this morning, when the upper wharf coolies attempted to resume work, they were mobbed and prevented from doing so.

A strike has been declared, and students are at present haranguing the coolies.

Fengtian Troops Arrive. Special trains are conveying to Shanghai upwards of a thousand Fengtian troops from Nanking this evening. Chang Hsueh-Jiang, Chang Tao-lin's "star" commands these troops whose mission is ostensibly to maintain order on the borders of the Settlement.

The movement derives an extra importance from the identity of the commander, who will doubtless personally report the Shanghai situation to his father. It is also believed that Chang Tso-lin is taking advantage of the situation to strengthen his grip on the Shanghai region.

It is reported that 600 students led by Peking aglintors demonstrated at Mukdan, whereupon the Education Bureau warned the students not to harm foreigners or cause disorders.

The students' efforts to cause general strike failed owing to official precautions

Pelong Students

The students, on reaching the Walchiaopu, sent in a, deputation. It is reliably reported that the deputation demanded the despatch of troops to Shanghai, and similar steps.

Not being satisfied with the Minister's replies, the students, on his departure, smashed a large mirror and several windows, and did other damage before leaving the building.

The students make the same demands to Tuan Chijul, who saw the deputation personally, and he promised to bring up the demands at a Cabinet meeting to be held tomorrow.

As far as can be ascertained, no attempt was made to molest any foreigner throughout the demonstration.

headline: INCIDENT OF THE FLAGS.
text:
A circular has been issued by Mr. E. C. Lobenstine, Secretary of the Council of Higher Education of the Chinese Christian Educational Association, reviewing the outbreak from the Christian viewpoint, containing a warning against coming to erroneous conclusions before the result of the enquiry is known, and enclosing a statement by Dr. Potts on the closing of St. John's University.

The students who took the chief part in the demonstration of Saturday, May 30, came from four radical colleges, two of these were the Shanghai University control of the student movement. Within the last two or three days, largely owing to the valuable work done by the Young Men's Christian Association, a change has taken place within the Student Union and every effort is being made to keep the more conservative element in control of the Union's activities. The Union is coming out in opposition to the use of force, although still active in the promotion of a general strike. The strike situation is serious and is growing. Foreign nations have brought in marines who are assisting the regular volunteers and those who have volunteered for temporary service.

The students are still in Shanghai College although they are not attending classes. The faculty of the College passed two resolutions the day before yesterday; one lamenting the events of May 30 and the other calling for a thorough investigation of the entire situation.

It seems to us here that the present is a time when all in Church and Christian institutions need to exercise the utmost caution when careless remarks may, because of the present tense feelings, be unduly magnified and receive wide publicity. One incident from an institution in another city is being widely circulated here, namely, that a foreign professor said the institution was supported by foreigners and therefore was a foreign institution and that if students did not like the way the institution was run the thing to do was for them to leave it.

The issues at stake in this incident are very far-reaching indeed, and raise for us, as Christian workers in China, fundamental questions both to our own Christian attitude toward justice and fair dealing and our methods of working in a country where there may justly be differences of opinion as to what course of action a Christian should choose.

We trust that the information that a thorough investigation is assured will be helpful to you in dealing with your own students and will help to convince them that the best thing for them to do is to continue with their studies, believing that the solution of the questions at issue can best be worked out by those who have access to all the facts, and that the publication of the exact facts is the surest first step toward securing strict justice.

President's Statement.

The President of the St. John's University, in his statement in regard to the sudden closing of the term; gives a brief chronicle of the events leading up to the present situation, in which he says:—

Owing to the excitement caused by the killing of some students by the municipal police in the riot on Saturday afternoon, May 30, an organization called the Students Union was formed by the student body at St. John's. A communication was received from this organization asking that the students might be allowed to suspend their studies indefinitely and also containing the following clause:—

"During the period of suspension, it is our express desire to make sure that no student is unnecessarily absent from the campus. For this reason, we beg to request you to refer all letters to us that are from the students parents or guardians asking for leave. We have a special committee to attend to this matter."

A joint faculty meeting of the College and the Middle School was held on Monday evening, June 1, and it was decided to appoint six members of the faculty (three Chinese and three foreign) to meet with six members of the student body (four elected from the College and two elected from the Middle School) for a conference. This conference was held on Tuesday morning, and an endeavour was made to get the students' point of view. Another joint faculty meeting of the College and the Middle School was held at seven o'clock (Tuesday). The faculty then adopted the following regulation:

The University has decided to allow the students to suspend their studies until next Monday morning 7.40 a.m. If at the end of that period, they are not ready to resume their regular duties, the University will be closed and all students will be requested to return to their homes. Students living in the vicinity are allowed to return to their homes now. “Letters will be sent to parents and guardians informing them that the University disclaims any responsibility for the students' welfare or safety while they are off the premises.” Students remaining on the grounds and occupying the College dormitories will be expected to observe the regulations put on by the administration.

Chinese flag could be flown at half mast. As it was late, the President had no time to confer with anyone and gave the permission. On Wednesday morning two flags were raised on the flag poles, the Chinese flag at half mast on one pole and the American flag at the top of the other pole. Bishop Graves requested that the flags be taken down, giving his reason that the flying of the Chinese flag at half mast indicated that as an institution we considered the action of the municipal police to have been wrong, which we were not prepared to do. The President promised to comply with his request and sent for the Assistant Scoutmaster. Owing to the fact that the Assistant Scoutmaster did not come immediately, the President decided to take down the flags himself which he proceeded to do. Both flags were taken down at the same time. When the students came out from their mass meeting which they were holding in the Assembly Hall they were surprised to find that the flags were down and sent a deputation to wait on the President to ask why they had been lowered. The President informed them that he himself had lowered them and that owing to the objection made to their being raised, he thought it was better to follow the rule which had been made by the Administration that flags would only be raised when the College was in session. A short time afterwards, hearing a commotion he went out from his office and found some of the students about to raise another Chinese flag. No permission had been asked for doing this and no expiration had been given to him. It seemed to him that it implied that the student body was in such a state of excitement that it was unwilling to abide by the regulations. One of the conditions upon which they were allowed to remain in residence while suspending their studies was that they would observe the regulations put out by the administration.

The President came to the conclusion that the only way to avoid conflict with the students was to close the institution for the term, and it will not be re-opened until next September. The students were not expelled. No threats were used, but they were requested to return to their homes.

headline: Faithful Servants.
text:
On Saturday morning a full shift of workmen returned to the Wing On Cotton Mill on Seoul Road after three days' holiday. They were permitted to work throughout the day and at six o'clock the management paid them off—not to return until further notice.

The tramway company is still getting a full quota of men, all but half-a-dozen returning daily to their labour. An attempt was made yesterday to resume the service on Chekiang Road which was discontinued after last Monday's riots, but the threatening crowds forced Chinese passengers to descend and the service has since been cut out. The busses are maintaining a curtailed service.

Sixty coolies among 250 employed on the Shanghai Building Co. new project on Thorne Road appeared for duty yesterday. The ehauffeurs of the Park Garage, as well as the Eastern and Star Garages, have resumed work.

More house-boys in the Western district have informed their masters that though wishing to continue with their domestic duties, they have been forced to quiet. Others are holding out, faithful to their trust. Although many shops are not doing business in outlying districts, the police report that hawkers are still thriving. The police arrested one for distributing leaflets.

headline: Strike at Nanking.
text:
Following the two mass parades of last week, the students have been spending their time in meetings or in speechmaking on the streets. Schools are combed for contributions and a house-to-house canvass on the streets is being conducted for the aid of the striking workers.

On Friday, 5,000 workers of the International Export Company struck and formed a huge parade. The students are working sympathetically with them. Servants in British homes and employees of British Companies have also struck. The agitation in Nanking is centering against the British and Japanese, and the student leaders are advocating no violent measures but the weapon of boycott. Even richness are placarded with the sign "We do not carry British or Japanese."

Purvis, acting Water Authority, told a "China Mail" reporter this morning were in the reservoir, may seem a lot, but the quantity is below the average for the year, hence the restrictions which are announced this morning. Districts west of Garden Road have experienced "modified restriction" for some time and now these are being extended to districts east of Garden Road.

In order to ensure a full supply for the two consecutive hours allotted to the different districts the times will vary, but as will be seen from the advertisement, information as to the hours of supply to any particular property may be obtained on application at the offices of the Water Authority, the Secretariat for Chinese Affairs, or at the Tung-Wah Hospital.

Mr. Purvis informed the “China Mail” upon enquiry that it was quite possible that this might prove a low rain year and if the Tytam Tuk reservoir supply fell off it might leave them in a bad position for next year. Kowloon would have to be restricted next month unless beneficial rains set in this month, but that was a step not to be lightly undertaken because of the lack of the facilities for getting water in Kowloon.

headline: GANG—WITH KNIVES. IOLD CUSTOMS PASS ROBBERY.
text: A gang of men armed with knives held up five Chinese woman returning to Nam Wai in the Salkung district from Kowloon City yesterday afternoon. Rome has for long been recognized as the city of fountains. These are always playing, and give the city a gay and lively aspect. At almost every corner, especially in the ancient part of the town, you are bound to find one, and their number has increased to such an extent that the claim that modern Rome has surpassed imperial Rome, at least where fountains are concerned, is fully justified. Besides the large and well-known fountains, such as the Trevi Fountain, or the Fontana delle Naiadi, or the one at the Janiculum, there are numberless smaller fountains in various parts of the city which are scarcely ever visited by foreigners and the very existence of which is even ignored by many Romans. Many of these are really gems of art, hidden in remote and obscure corners in zones now mostly inhabited by people of the poorer classes.

headline: GENERAL.
text:
Says an Australian paper:—An unprecedentedly long record of service in the overseas trade with Australia is shared by the steamers Taiyuan and Changsha, which have been voyaging continuously between China and Japan and Melbourne via Sydney for close on 40 years. The first worn-out cable in the Melbourne Tramway system was taken by the Taiyuan to Hongkong at an early stage of her career, the broken strands being converted by Chinese into nails for use in tea chests.

What must have been an amusing spectacle, though productive of a certain amount of anxiety, occurred recently in the Mersey River. A hopper with a crew of nine men was blown on to a sandbank during a high gale. A lifeboat put out and stood by the hopper till the crew decided that it was no place for them. They were taken off and tugs remained by the hopper to take her off at high tide. But this hopper was of an independent turn of mind and slipping off the sandbank she made for home—which was the Sandon Dock. On her way she passed no fewer than fifteen ships, wending her way across the bows of one and under the stern of another. The tugs which had been ready to tow her off had nothing to do but follow her. As she arrived opposite her dock gates, which were open at high water, onlookers thought she was going to bump into the dock wall, but avoiding this she sailed serenely into her own dock, where human beings once more took charge of her and tied her up at her berth.

headline: DRAMATIC CRIME. / BALKAN LEADER SHOT DEAD.
text:
WOMAN'S VENGEANCE.

The Correspondent of the "Chicago Tribune" writes: Vienna is discussing the most dramatic sensation it has had in recent years. There is only one topic amongst the Viennese, that is the extraordinarily dramatic murder in the Vienna Municipal Theatre. Before hundreds of spectators gathered to witness Ibsen's tragedy, "Peer Gynt," Balkan hatred suddenly blazed out from the darkness of a private box. At the very moment that Ibsen's Peer Gynt was simulating death on the stage a beautiful young Macedonian woman, Mencia Carniciu, rose from her chair in a private box where she was sitting with a party, drew an automatic pistol, and fired six shots into the dress circle a few feet below.

When the lights were turned up, Todor Dimitroff, a Macedonian secret agent, was found shot dead, his wife mortally wounded, and another person badly hurt. After a breathless moment the audience stamped for the exit. Police rushed to the woman's box and arrested her. She declared she had avenged treason against her countrymen by the act.

According to the story of Mencia Carniciu as hastily told to the police, the man she killed, Todor Dimitroff, betrayed two Macedonian comrades in Sofia several years ago. They were both executed, and she was appointed to avenge their death.

Upon searching the clothing of the dead man's wife and her companions in the theatre who were also wounded, it was found the wife was carrying a small revolver, and the men were all armed and well provided with ammunition.

Name. Dimitroff received a bullet through the back of her skull, penetrating through to the throat. She is in a desperate condition.

headline: PRISONER'S STORY.
text:
Mencia Carniciu presented a striking figure when she appeared before the Chief of Police to be examined. She is 26 years old and is the daughter of one of the richest families in Macedonia. She is a young woman of extraordinary beauty, tall and svelte, with jet back hair and blazing black eyes. She was utterly defiant in face of the murder charge. She told the examining magistrate she vowed two years ago to take the life of Todor Dimitroff as retribution for the lives of two Macedonian patriots whom, she declared. Dimitroff betrayed to their death, Telling the story quietly and proudly, she related how she came to Vienna and contrived, through a woman who knew the Dimitroff's, to arrange the exact seating for both parties in the Municipal Theatre for the performance of Ibsen's "Peer Gynt." Deliberately she told how she had visited the theatre and witnessed the performance earlier in order to judge the best moment to open fire.

"I knew he was always expecting attack, and always ready to attack, Mencis Carniciu declared," So I schemed to sit behind him, and as soon as the chance was right I fired"

Apparently Madame Dimitroff threw herself between her husband and the line of fire at the crack of the revolver, which explained how the second bullet found its mark in the skull of the dead man's wife. Dimitroff's companion, a man named Bagatinoff, had just been able to get his pistol from his pocket when Mencia fired again, killing Dimitroff.

The murder occurred at the moment when Peer Gynt was supposed to be drowned in the Sea. The Viennese actor, Herr Tressler, who was playing the part, emerged from the waves and came back to life, and addressed the audience from the stage, urging them to remain in their seats.

Police investigation establishes the political character of the dramatic murder. From the history of his past activities in Balkan politics the police have confirmed that Dimitroff was responsible for the death of two Macedonian leaders, Boris Sarafoff and Ivan Garbanoff, in Sofia seventeen years ago. Dimitroff, who was 50 years old, had been living in Vienna during the past few months at the apartments of a prominent Macedonian patriot, Philip Attanasoff, but the latter was recently driven from Vienna by the police. Recognised as a sworn enemy of the present Bulgarian Prime Minister, M. Zankoff, Dimitroff went in fear of his life. He was always accompanied by three or four Macedonians armed with automatic pistols, ready to protect him from assassins.

According to a number of Mencia Carnici's friends, an element of mystery in the case is now presenting itself. Her intimate friends declare she was madly in love with the man she killed. When the police arrested her immediately after the tragic murder she had a smoking pistol in one hand and a razor in the other. She admitted that she intended to commit suicide, but she was either too stunned or had no time in which to do it.

In the files of the Vienna police head-quarters officials have found an old Bulgarian extradition paper drawn up against Dimitroff, charging him with being a member of the Macedonian Revolutionary Committee.

The victim of the tragedy in the Burgtheater has now been ascertained to be the notorious Todor Panitza, the founder and leader of the Macedonian Federalist organisation, who twenty years ago murdered two leaders of the Macedonian movement, Sarafoff and Garbanoff in the streets of Sofia. Panitza then fled to the mountains in the Macedonian regions of Bulgaria, where he organised revolutionary bands and lived like a prince, though he was always in dread of assassination. He came to Vienna a few days before to adjust differences which had arisen between Bulgarian emigrants there. He was always attended by heavily armed companions to guard him against attack and murder, and his presence occasioned much irritation in Austrian political circles, which represent such abuse of the rights of asylum being extended to Bulgarian emigrants.

headline: KIDNAPPING CASE
text:
The sequel to the alleged kid- napping of Mr. Harry Pollitt, secretary of the Communist or- ganisation known as the National Minority Movement, was heard at Liverpool. Assizes before Mr. Justice Fraser. Five local men, William P. Cochrane, 30, garage proprietor; George F. McGachen, 30, cotton salesman; James B. Owen, 30, commercial traveller; James H. Browner, 35, tailor; and John H. Rowlandson, 26, commercial traveller, were charged with con- spiring to assault and unlawfully imprison. Pollitt.

Mr. A. E. Griffith, who prosecuted, said that Mr. Pollitt, a boilermaker by trade and a trade union speaker, professing Communist beliefs and opinions, was to have addressed a meeting in Liverpool on Sunday, March 15. On the Saturday he was met at Edgehill Station, Liverpool, put into a motor care, and taken to the Liver Hotel, Rhyddalog, a village on the Flintshire moors.

Mr. Pollitt stated that at Edge-hill Station Rowlandson and Owen entered the railway compartment where he was and asked him to address a meeting at Marnaduke-street at the Communistist headquarters. He refused, but was pulled out of the train.

He was, he said, bustled through the barrier into a waiting motorcar. He made no protest at the hotel. He was asked what his financial loss had been, and he replied that he had suffered none. He did not accept any payment.

headline: FAME AND ADVERTISEMENT.
text:
Cross-examined by Sir Henry Curtis Bennett, K.C. (defending), Mr. Pollitt said he was a Communist speaker and had been convicted in 1921 for making alleged seritious speeches.

Sir Henry: "In fact, I might describe you as the famous Mr. Politt -Yes, and I am only quite young."

Do you find advertisement is something which is apt to make you become famous?—No. I find one becomes famous and then gets advertisement.

When Mr. Pollitt described how he was pushed into the motor-car with five other men and said one of them sat on his knee, Sir Henry Curtis Bennett asked: "In an ordinary Ford car, with six persons, somebody had to sit on somebody's knee?" "Yes," replied Mr. Pollitt, "but I don't see why it should have been my knee."

How did you recognise that these gentlemen were not comrades directly they came into the compartment at Edgehill?—First, because I had a definite understanding with my comrades to meet me at Lime street; and, second, my comrades never meet me dressed as hooligans with their caps down over their eyes, mufflers on, and their coat collars turned up. (Laughier.)

Regarding a bottle of mustard oil with which Mr. Pollitt's chest was rubbed at the inn because he had a cough, Sir Henry asked: "Was it famous because some of it got on your chest?"

Mr. Pollitt: Rowlandson rubbed my chest with it—and did it very well.

headline: DIPLOMACY.
text:
You were quite friendly with the defendants?—No, I was diplomatic. Did you toss for drinks with them and lose?—No.

Did you have everything you wanted, a glass of beer with your launch and so on?—Everything was quite proper.

Sir Henry suggested that far from declining financial assistance to recoup him for any loss, Mr. Pollitt received five £1 notes from the defendants.

Mr. Pollitt: I say it is a deliberate and dastardly lie. I had only $35s_{1}$ If I had had more I should have gone straight to Liverpool and exposed the whole business.

Mr. Bold, proprietor of the Liver Inn, said they appeared to be a happy party, and there was no sign that anyone was being detained against his will; and another witness said they behaved as if they were "all pals together."

Rowlandson stated in evidence that what took place was not ordered from the London headquarters of the British-Fascisti. At Edge-hill Station Mr. Pollitt made no protest. When the car broke down on the way to Shrewsbury, he gave Mr. Pollitt five £1 notes.

headline: LESSER KNOWN PARIS.
text:
Paris, to the majority of holiday makers, is only synonymous with Montmarre restaurants and the grey-upholstered Louis. Selze salons of the couturier, says the Paris correspondent of the "Morning Port." The shopping facilities of the Bon Marche will be the only reason for crossing the Selne, so they may even miss the Tuileries Gardens, not yet in the full splendour of their summertime herbaceous borders, or the Luxembourg terrace, where the pink and white hawthorn trees coquet with the grey stone statues of the long dead queens.

Will any one of the Easter visitors, I wonder, go so far away from such "dancings" as the "Garden of my sister" as to stroll through that old-world country town in the very heart of Paris called the Ile St Louis, and lean on the sunny stone coping of the qual to admire the house with gilt dolphin drainpipes to which perf little de Lauzun is said to have taken Le Grande Mademoiselle after their ill-assorted marriage.

The island takes its name from the saintly king who was the central figure of Thirteenth Century life in France. Paris, having been spared a great fire like the one that made Evelyn mourn "London was, but is no more," preserves an astonishing number of mediaevel buildings that few tourists ever see. Of these the best known is the most beautiful, the Sainte Chappelle, that "Most perfect monument of pure Gothic in Europe."

headline: CRUCIFIXION RELICS.
text:
Louis IX. commissioned Pierre de Montorcau to build him this jewelled casket as a shrine to hold the crown of thorns, the fragment of the Cross, and the metal of the lance that pierced the side of Christ, that he had bought for 100,000 francs from the needy Oriental Emperor Baudoin.

Another great monument to St. Louis is the Sorbonne, the great centre of French University life, in the rue de la Sorbonne, a street that has changed its name many times in the elastic French fashion since it was called the "Street of the Two Doors," in 1250.

The name of the college is always associated with that of Robert de Sorbonne, the almonter of St. Louis, whose disputes with that faithful Boswell, the Sire de Joinville, were among the monarch's few diversions. But it was Robert de Duai, the doctor of Queen Marguerite de Provence, who was the real founder of the Sorbonne.

He left a legacy with which Robert de Sorbonne started the little theological college that later, under the fostering care of Richelieu, grew into the vast building of to-day.

There is yet another institution, still existing in Paris, and more directly due to St. Louis's benign, violence, with a history so curious and interesting that its neglect by the majority of guide-books is "all the more inexplicable".

headline: 300 ULIND BEGGARS
text:
There is no trace now left in the rue St. Honore of the original Hospice of the Quinze-Vingts, the huge caravanseral where St. Louis, lodged his three hundred blind beggars with the double object of giving them shelter and riding the streets of them. The tobacco shop of L. Civette is just where the old gateway stood till Cardinal de Rohan realised in 1779 how valuable the site had become, and how much money he could realise by its sale.

Six years before the tragic folly of the necklace affair was to shake the throne of France, the Cardinal moved the blind beggars to the old hotel of the Black Mosquitaires, a corps that had been disbanded four years previously, and in this second home, built by de Coite in 1609, their bret ren live to this day in the rue de Charenton, far from the path of the tourist.

St. Louis's dry much nearer the Grands Boulevards, but its days are doubtless numbered. Almost from the windows of that most dingy of little restaurants, on the corner of the rue Canbon and the rue St. Honore, where you may be served with food that might be equalled, but never surpassed, may be seen a deserted building that looks as if it had not been entered for many a day. Few people could tell more than that it formed part of the convent of the Dames de l'Assomption, that once stood where the big new building of the Cour des Comptes is now, but the old house is, or was a few months ago, a link with the Thirteenth Century in modern Paris. ULYSSES RETURNS. The story goes back to the day of Jean Haudri, the King's secretary, who started on the Crusade with St. Louis when all the inshits of the good city of Paris accompanied their beloved king as far as St. Marcel to wish him God speed. On the way back from Palestine Haudri, loitered on his way in Gallic. His wife, despating of his return, made a vow never to reenter the married state, and

shut herself up with one or two widows to bear her company. After many years this dilatory Ulysses came back; and in order to get a dispensation for his wife to free her from her vow, he offered to pay the expenses of a religious community of twelve poor women.

After the death of this plous couple the Haudricites, as the nuns they had sheltered were called, were transferred to another home. Four centuries later the Cardinal de la Rochefoucauld gave the commission, now called de' Assomption, his own house for their convent. The huge dome, that for so many years has been left, and used for the past in the very centre of New York, was once the convent chapel, and it was here that the funeral ceremonies of the Marble de Lafayette were held. headline: Hongkong Education.
text:
(To the Editor of the China Mail).

Sir,—I have wondered, since local education has become a topic for discussion, how European ladies, diploma-ed or not, can ever hope to appreciate Chinese characteristics.

Now and then, I read of the number of qualified school-mistresses coming out to the Education Department. Some of the experts tell us that even an Oxford honours man has not got it in him to be able to adapt himself to understanding our traits and thereby making himself the most appropriate teacher. If so, how can the average diploma-ed schoolmistress do any better. Better it would be for all Hong Kong were to stick to the old system of a normal school for local Chinese youths and the University product but "and, this is a very great but, no difference in the status or salary of the two.

headline: Plague of Bees.
text:
Sir,—Through the courtesy of your columns I would like to ask whether the rearing of domestic bees comes under the Sanitary Department as an offensive trade or under the Police Department as a common nuisance? At any rate, this is the hiving season of bees and my house has been invaded by swarms of bees who are a great nuisance. Will those responsible take note that anybody keeping a domestic animal (in law, anything from a prehistoric monster to a mosquito) to the annoyance and/or danger of a neighbour is liable under an old Ordinance of the Colony?

Thanking you for the insertion of the above and enclosing my card,

Yours, etc., CONDUIT ROAD. Hongkong, June 2.

headline: FATAL LEAP. / SUNDAY AFTERNOON'S TRAGEDY.
text:
Pathetic circumstances attended the death of one of Messrs. A. S. Watson & Co.'s mineral water agents on Sunday afternoon when Mr. Mak Kip (35) of Macao jumped from a verandah and met his death. Mr. Mak, in addition to being agents for Messrs. Watson's, was employed by the Macao Electric Light Co. He had been ill for several months and had lately stayed with Mr. Peter Wong at No. 38a, Bonham Road, Breezy Point. On Sunday afternoon, while, it is believed; his mind was temporarily deranged, deceased either jumped or threw himself from the verandah.

Deceased was a very popular young man and leaves a wife and two children to mourn his loss. He had only been with Mr. and Mrs. Peter Wong for four days, for the benefit of his health, when the untimely event occurred to disturb the peace of mind of those who had his welfare at heart.

headline: FAREWELL / R. N. Y. POLICE MESS CONCERT.
text: A very happy function took place at the R. N.Y. Police Mission Saturday night when a Dinner was given to a few of the Naval friends who are about to leave the Colony. Fitting toasts were given and responded to. Following the dinner a Smoking Concert was held under the Chairmanship of Mr. D. H. G. Smith. Petty Officer Probart proved an efficient entertainer in monologues and humorous songs. Ldg. Sea. Jack Mitchell upheld his reputation in some very catchy songs: Mr. T. Edwards contributed renderings of old time songs. Fresh talent was discovered in Sgt. Eddie McNay who, with his sweet mellow voice rendered "What God Made Mother For" but failed to respond to the call for an encore. Mr. J. Collins contributed to the programme and the chorus party in fine form. Mr. J. Callaghan assisted ably at the plano in accompanying many of the items.

headline: FALSE NAMES. / SAILORS WHO CREATED TROUBLE.
text:
Before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry, at the Central Magistracy this morning, three "American seamen were charged on two counts of evading payment of tramway fare and obstruction.

There was some delay in the accused being brought into Court after they had been removed this morning from the custody of the Police by an escort from the U.S.S. Sacramento as it was found that they had given false names and stated that they belonged to the U.S.S. Pampanga. Their proper names were Jeff Cantrill, Harry A. Thorne and Irvine Coulter, all of the U.S.S. Helena. A traffic officer of the Tramway Company giving evidence stated that he first saw the three accused in a car near the Ming Yuen gardens. They refused to pay the fare when called upon and gave him and the conductors considerable trouble, as well as causing inconvenience to the passengers by changing cars at Causeway Bay and again at Tin Lok Lane. Witness stated that at Bowrington bridge the third accused threatened to strike him. Witness and a Chinese constable kept up with the men after they had alighted near the bridge, and the latter went ahead later and laid information at No. 2 Police Station which resulted in the accused being taken into custody when they reached that point.

The third accused denied that he threatened to assault witness. Asked by His Worship why they gave false names, all three said that they did it in order to hide their movements from the ship. His Worship said that the evidence he had taken was sufficient to prove their guilt and fined each of the accused $10 and $25 on the two counts respectively.

headline: MOTOR TOUTS. / PRIVATE LICENCES ABUSED.
text:
REAPING A HARVEST.

According to the "Wah Tsz Yat " Po," "tramp" motor-cars which now/ply for hire on the streets will soon be forbidden. The vernacular paper explains that there are a number of motor-cars, each bought by a few adventurous spirits who run about town for hire by trips. These cars are registered under "private" licences and, as they have practically no overhead charges can operate at great profit.

Many a local resident has been accosted by youthful touts in the streets. Yesterday, a “China Mail” man who was given a “lift” in one such car, was told by the driver's assistant that they made over $25 a day and on Sunday night had to stop running because their petrol had given out. They had just bought a Dodge car for $2,550 and were confident of reaping a harvest. One advantage which the assistant pointed out was that they were no hours of restriction for cars with private licences and that the fees were much lower.

headline: NEW RENTS LAW.
text:

A resolution to be put to the Council is to the effect that the percentages on the valuation of tenements on the Kowloon Bay Reclamation, payable as rates, shall be 13 per cent on the following New Kowloon Inland Lot numbers: 132, 226, 227, 238, 239 and 251.

headline: SANDAKAN NOTES.
text:
Sandakan has been gripped in a somewhat mild form of 'Flu' epidemic, for the last month or so. Padres, Teachers, and many Europeans as well as Native and Chinese including your correspondent were laid hors de combat for a number of days, but the sickness is gradually disappearing.

It is with regret I learn that on account of ill health His Excellence Major General Sir William Rycroft, K.C.B., K.C.M.G., had to tender his resignation as Governor of the State of British North Borneo. Sir William first arrived in this country to take up the appointment of Governor on November 21, 1922.

The following letter from His Excellency, Major General Sir William Rycroft, K.O.B., K.O.M.G., appears in the "Official Gazette" Extraordinary of May 13.

After a little more than two and a half years in Borneo I am forced to relinquish my post under the highest medical orders. It is with the greatest regret that I sever my connection with the State. On doing so I must tender my deepest thanks to the whole of the officials, European and Asiatic including Native Chiefs, who were responsible for having given me the happiest recollections of my period as Governor.

I am confident that there is a great future for the country, but patience is necessary.

I understand that Mr. A. G. Pearson, C.M.G., the former Governor, who is at present the Secretary, to the Chartered Company in London, will resume office as Governor temporarily. He is expected out towards the end of August; meantime the Honourable the Government Secretary Mr. F. W. Fraser, O.B.E., will act as Officer Administering the Govern

The Honourable the Resident of Sandakan Mr. H. N. L. Bumbury and Mrs. Bumbury left on the 21st by the s.s. Mau Sang via Hongkong on furlough for England and Mr. D. R. Maxwell will act as Acting President.

By the same boat Mr. Koh Peckpin, the Managing Partner of Chop Kim Eng Watt Bros.: the pioneer timber Merchant of Borneo, left to relieve his brother as Manager in the Hongkong branch of the same firm; he was accompanied by Mrs. Koh Peck-pin. Mr. S. A. Rahman, is temporarily in charge of Sandukan firm, until the arrival of Mr. Koh Peck-chick from Hong Kong.

Mr. J. George, Manager of Bakau Company and Mrs. George, left for the United Kingdom on

Mr. C. M. Stanhope returned from furlough and has taken over the Managership of the State Bank, Sandakan branch, from Mr. S. W. Matthews, who proceeded to England on leave.

The many friends of Rev. T. C. Alexander will be pleased to learn of his excellent recovery from a bad stroke of Flu. He has now been discharged from the Hospital.

Capt. Pearson, Superintendent of Sandakan Police, Mr. S. W. Matthews of the State Bank and Capt. Campbell of the U.S. Kinabalu have all been in the Hospital recently, but I am pleased to learn they are all out again.

Another old Borneo landmark Mr. Chan, late, on the China of Sandakan has crossed the world of mist, he died in his native home in Swatow. Mr. Chan, to-pin, was one of the pioneer settlers in Borneo. At one time and before coming South to make his fortune, he was an Assistant in the late Indian firm of Messrs. Taria-Topan, Opium and yarn merchants in Hongkong, whose Manager was the late Md. Khetsey. As Capitan China and a Chinese gentleman, he was well liked and respected by Government Officials, European Merchants as well as Chinese and Native. He was kind to all, of a quiet and unassuming disposition and his word as a Chinese merchant was as good as his bond. He passed away in his native home in Swatow at a ripe old age, an octogenarian, in the presence of his wife, sons and grand-sons, who left Sandakan and reached home in time to be present at his death-bed.

headline: HEAD CUT OFF / GRUESOME WONG NEI CHUNG DISCOVERY.
text: A gruesome discovery was made at a garden in Wong Nel Chung village, near the new filter beds, when the Police removed to the mortuary yesterday the body of an unknown Chinese about 24 years old. The head was completely severed from the trunk, and the circumstances point to murder.

headline: THE NEW KISMET. / BEAUTIFUL SCENIC EFFECTS.
text:
一

It was as a spectacle that "Kismet" made its appeal when it was produced at the Garrick Theatre in 1911. It is as a spectacle that it must succeed or fail, as it was revived at the New Oxford Theatre.

But the manner of the revival is entirely different from the manner of the original production. Instead of the old, flamboyant mounting is seen something subtle in lighting effects, something that bears close relationship with that which is connected with the arts of the Cubists and the Futurists.

The story itself is nothing more nor less than a prop for a series of stage pictures.

Yet, after all, Edward Kno-block has a good tale to tell, and it seemed to be followed with in-terest. The scene is laid in the Baghdad of “The Arabian Nights,” and many strange things happen in a very brief period. How Haji, the beggar, is made a prince and sinks again to the depths is told in lines which are at odd moments apparently intended to be pactical, but which do not lift the play above its spectacular appeal.

Mr. Sam Livesay is the new Haji—a part originally played by Mr. Oscar Asche. Mr. Livesay acts with a certain power, but it appears obvious that once upon a time he saw Oscar Asche in the part. All round, the acting is more than adequate—but the scenic effects matter more than the cast.

headline: MYSTIFIED SCIENTISTS. / A MAN WITH SIX SENSES.
text:
一

What is the strange occult power possessed by Louis Kahn, the "Man with the Sixth Sense"?

His case is inexplicable to the foremost French scientists, and a former French Premier. Academicians, High Court judges, and detectives have been mystified by a display of his uncanny power. He is able to read a letter written by another person without seeing or touching it.

Kahn, who is 53 and a German who disarows German nationality, has just demonstrated his powers before an audience including M. Louis Barthou, a French ex-Premier; M. Loucheur, a former Cabinet Minister; and M. Morain, the Prefect of Police.

There were twelve persons in all present and each wrote in an adjoining room a phrase on a slip of paper which was folded eight times and kept in the closed hand.

He left the room while the ships were exchanged, and on returning said: "Though you have been exchanging your slips each one finally came back to its author." This was correct.

Then he told those present what they had written.

With the exception of an error in one word, which did not alter the sense of the phrase, Kahn faithfully rendered the contents of the twelve slips.

Striking proof of his telepathic powers was shown when, at M. Barthou's suggestion, a woman in the company wrote on her slip of paper a declaration of affection for a well known politician.

Madame, please burn your slip, far away from me so that I cannot possibly see it," said Kahn, and when the woman had done so, he pointed to M. Barthou, remarking: "The gentleman there dictated the phrase to you, so he will be able to certify if I renter it correctly." And, amid laughter, he read word for word what the woman had written.

headline: STOP PRESS. / SHANGHAI RIOTING.
text:
The students here held a meeting yesterday afternoon in the Central Park to discuss the Shanghai affair.

The speakers declared that the affair was a national one affecting the whole of the Chinese people.

Further meetings were arranged for to-day at which it is expected resolutions will be passed demanding the restoration of the foreign concessions, the abolition of extra-territoriality and the Mixed Court in Shanghai, also of the foreign police stations in Shanghai, and the punishment of the police who shot the students.

headline: Strike Begins.
text:
Prisoners were taken to the Mixed Court this morning heavily escorted. The route was guarded by Volunteers and police. There were no disturbances.

It was a subdued looking group of 45 rioters who appeared before the Chinese magistrate and American assessor.

Evidence of arrest was given and the case remanded. Light bail was accepted.

There were a few unimportant isturbances in the outlying districts this morning, including the mobbing of a Japanese constable whom the rioters threw into a creek before assistance arrived.

The strike is taking denite form insomuch as the fresh food markets did not open to-day.

headline: THEATRE. / LILLIAN GISH IN "THE WHITE SISTER."
text:
Miss Gish is magnificent! No actress of this generation on stage or screen has carried the flame of sheer genius into her acting as does the frail little star of "The White Sister" now showing at the Queen's Theatre.

In filming F. Marion Crawford's story, the Director took a company to Italy. Studios and laboratories were established, and then began the making of what should prove one of truly great productions in cinema history.

Most persons are familiar with the story and many have undoubtedly longed for its presentation on the screen. The story, offering many thrills in the way of the actual eruption of Vesuvius, and a flood that sweeps away an Italian town has been closely followed. The settings are exquisite, the photography of the highest quality and Miss Gisk's supporting cast shows it was chosen with care, for the members all contribute to the general effectiveness of the film.

headline: BONDS WITH U.S.
text:
MR. BALDWIN RECALLS A WAR SCENE.

Mr. Baldwin, the Prime Minister, at the sixth annual dinner of the members of the British War Missions to the United States in London, said the bond uniting Britain and the United States was a very special bond.

"We are, as it were, romrades in arms," he continued, "because our friendship began and gathered strength, and was cemented almost within sound of the guns of the great war."

THE FIERY FORNALE After describing the deep and profound silence of the crowds in Horse Guards-parade when the first American troons marched through London during the war, he said:

I wondered how the flight looked to them. I thought of the homes from which they had come, the strangeness of the surroundings to them, their feeling of fresh enthusiasm, our feeling of warm but grim determination be gotten of the three years of hell through which we had passed, and I could not help feeling how little in the triumph of that march they could realise what that fiery furnace was towards which they were going, and from which few of those early regiments could ever hope to return.

It seemed to me then as im possible to cheer as I always find it impossible to applaud when I have heard the most beautiful music that stirs the soul rather than the head

We thought then much of our combined and united influence on the world. Possibly the freshness of that feeling, it may be in both countries, has to some extent evaporated in the strenuous years of peace which have followed. But there is just as much need, if not more need, to day, for the understanding, for the co-operation, and for that mutual help, as must need as ever there was in the time of the war.

Friendship at the best of times was fragile. It would not run along of itself. Friendships required care and consideration. He added:

Whatever else may happen, whatever misfortune may befall your country or my own, the peace and friendship which not exist between the two countries will be, as it shall be my desire to make them, perpetual. Those are the words of Abraham Lincoln. (Cheers.)

Since those words were uttered we have passed through Armageddon together. May the friendship between the two nations, based on mutual knowledge and understanding, be perpetual for the benefit of the whole of the world.

headline: 40 YEARS A SPIRITUALIST / SIR A CONAN DOYLE ON HIS RECORD.
text:
"Among the many misstatements I continually have to meet is that it was the death of my son. In war-time that converted me to spiritualism," said Sir Arthur Conan Doyle in a lecture on "Proof of Immortality" before the Practical Psychology Club of London. "Frequently I have seen the same thing alleged concerning Sir Oliver Lodge. Twenty-five years ago I met Sir Oliver, and we had a strong conversation on the subject, and I found that at that time he was actually more advanced than I was. I can only say that I began to study spiritualism in 1885, and in 1887 I wrote about it; and thus put myself on public record. Since then I have lost no opportunity of reading about it and experimenting upon the subject."

When he completed his studies and became a medical man, he said, like most young men of his generation he was an agnostic of an extreme and militant type. The reason was that he was brought up under the influence of Huxley, Darwin, and Herbert Spencer, all of whom were more or less agnostic, and if it were not for spiritualism he thought he would be agnostic still. He was in this state of mind, when a minor spiritualistic phenomenon came his way, and since then he had followed up a close study of the subject. It was his belief that in certain cases of insanity the persons were possessed of an evil spirit. When a perfectly good man goes wrong I think very often it is an obsession," he added, "and our lawyers ought to learn a little by psychic means. headline: CHEAPER JUSTICE
text:
LORD BIRKENHEAD ON FANCY PRICES.

ABLE LAWYERS FOR COWER FEES.

The Earl of Birkenhead, a former Lord Chancellor, discusses in the "Sunday Pictorial" the heavy legal costs stated to have been incurred by parties to recent litigation.

After denling at length with the comparative brevity of the old cases and the extraordinary length of many modern proceedings and the causes of the change, he writes:—

A word or two may be added upon the practical question whether a client having a case in which he believes, need spend, in order to give that case a chance, the very large sums which are undoubtedly paid to any. In my opinion, he need not...

The ordinary client seems to make the mistake that he does not take advantage of the very great competition that exists both among solicitors and burristers. He may, of course, if he chooses, go to an extremely fashionable and successful firm of solicitors. In this case he buys, and rightly buys, for the reputation of the firm: for the rent of its offices, and for the salaries that are paid to many experienced oள்கள்.

But there are countless firms of soldiers, quite honest and quite efficient, who are neither so fashionable as to command very high fees nor so busily occupied as to refuse work for which a reasonable remuneration is offered. Perhaps in such a case the partner will attend to the matter instead of the managing clerk. Perhaps, also, in such a case the client will not be a loser by the substitution.

The same remark is at least equally true off the Bar. There always exists two or three fussligible leaders at the Bar who command very surprising fees, and do not always find it convenient even to make an appearance in court in order to earn them.

Few members of the Bar would go to such men if they became involved in "litigation" themselves. For the plain truth is that there are always at least twenty or thirty members of the Bar who could not advectes in any case—from

—with the most complete efficiency, and whose business engagements emble them to give sustained and continuous attention to the cases in which they are employed.

Personally, if I become involved in litigation, the consequences of which were grave to me: I would infinitely rather be represented by A, a competent and industrious lawyer, who I knew would not leave the court from the moment my case began until the moment it ended, than by B, who would, at ten times, the fee, saunter into court to cross-examine a "witness" whose examination-in-chief he had not heard, or to reply to a speech which had unfortunately been delivered in his absence.

I reach, therefore, the conclusion that in cases where colossal sums are spent upon litigation, the fault is as often as not chargeable upon the clients themselves. You can spend as much as you choose upon surgeons, counsel, dentists, and tailors, but it by no means follows that he's who pays most is best served.

headline: BISHOP DEFIED. / RECTOR.AND BANNED PREACHER..
text:
St. Mark's Church, in New York's tenement district, provided a stage recently for a dramatic climax over religious principles and the authority of episcopal bishops. When the "heretic bishop," the Rev. William Montgomery Brown, of Arkansas, spoke in St. Mark's, that act emphasized a direct challenge by Dr. William Guthrie, a rector to the authority of Bishop William Manning, of the diocese of New York. Bishop Manning, in a letter to Dr. Guthrie, forbade him to allow Bishop Brown to officiate or speak in St. Mark's, and Dr. Guthrie's decision to continue his determination to have Bishop Brown in St. Mark's really brings to an end a long battle waged between Bishop Manning and St. Mark's.

Bishop Brown was found guilty of heresy last autumn at an ecclesiastical trial at Cleveland, Ohio, but has not been deposed. Dr. Guthrie defended Bishop Brown's appearance in St. Mark's on the ground that the sanctuary of the church had been veiled, that the Church virtually became an auditorium," and in that sense a meeting or symposium was "secular" and clearly beyond Bishop Manning's authority, and jurisdiction. Two years ago St. Mark's was excluded from the Episcopal visitation and administration because of "pagan ritual and eurhythmic dances before the altar." Later Dr. Guthrie dropped the dances and substituted "colour music" in his ritual, various limelight effects being introduced to emphasise serious emotions.

headline: THORNE HANGED.
text:
OVER IN THN SECONDS.

一

John Norman Holmes Thorne was executed in Wandsworth at eight o'clock in the morning for the murder of his fiancee, Elsie Emily Cameron, a Cambeltown girl, who latterly lived at Kensal Rise, London.

A special representative of the Press who was present at the execution says it was probably one of the most expeditious on record. From the time that Thorne emerged from his cell door until the moment he passed into eternity only ten seconds elapsed, Thorne had no sooner stepped on to the scaffold than the lever was released and he had disappeared from view.

He was wearing his navy blue suit, and when he came from the condemned cell his face for a brief moment showed that peculiar flicker of a smile that was was observed on the occasion of his many, appearances in the police court at Crowborough and in the dock at the Assize Court at Lewes.

He seemed to be in the best of health, and from his personal appearance one could not detect any trace of the dread or deal that he had gone through or concern as to the terrible experience that was awaiting him.

As he passed from the cell to the scaffold Thorne was preceded by the Wesleyan chaplain, the Rev. Edward Finch. He gave a fleeting glance to one side as he walked, but did not betray the slightest sign of nervousness.

There was just a touch of halting in his footsteps when he first came from the cell, but he recovered his self-possession in a moment, and never required the assistance of the executioners who held him gently by his pinioned arms.

As he approached the threshold of the execution shed there was a sudden bracing of the nerves. But for the one fleeting glance aside Thorne looked straight in front of him, and carried himself with his head slightly raised.

In the execution shed the work of the executioner and his assistant was exceedingly quick. Almost in one moment the white cap was drawn over Thorne's head, his legs pinioned, the lever was pulled, and in an instant Thorne had expiated his crime

The executioner was Pierpont, who was assisted by Phillips and the officials present at the execution were the governor of the prison, the prison surgeon, and the Under-Sheriff, Mr. Walter C.S. Chapman.

headline: " DISGRACE TO YOUR SEX"
text:
At the moment of your husband's death you were away from him, drunk and singing, and you left two grandchildren in the room in which he was dying, to see him die. If you had been no relation to him, your conduct would have been disgraceful, but as you were his wife, your conduct proves you to be a disgrace to your sex.

These words were addressed by Mr. H. J. Webber, the coroner, at Amphill, Bedfordshire, to Mrs. Desborough, of Pulloxhill, a neighbouring village, at the inquest on her husband, Thomas William Desborough, who died from acute gastritis.

The evidence showed that she had done practically nothing for her husband, except give him pills, castor oil, salts, a bottle of beer, and some brandy because he had complained of feeling ill. He had not been given any of the medicine sent by a doctor the day before his death.

The jury returned a verdict of Death from Natural Causes, and said that the wife was deserving of the most severe censure.

headline: IN ACADEMY AT 19 / YOUNG ARTISTS SUCCESS.
text:
To be “hung” at the Royal Academy at the age of 19 is the remarkable achievement of Mr. John R. Pimlott, of Forest Hill, S.E., who has just received news of the acceptance of a water-colour painting which he submitted, together with two other works.

“I am naturally delight I at the news,” the youth said “particularly as this is only the second occasion on which I have submitted pictures to the Academy. The painting accepted is an Autumn Scene.”

Mr. Pimlett has been studying for two years at Goldsmiths' College.

"As other work keeps me occupied most of the day," he said. "I get good practice by sketching people I see in restaurants."

Mr. Pimlott's father, who is an artist, has had several pictures "hung," his first being at the age of twenty-four.

Mr. A. Sherwood Edwards, a young sculptor, of Ashton-on Mersey, Cheshire, has been informed that a landscape in oils, which he painted from a sketch made while in an anti-aircraft battery in France during the war, has been accepted by the Royal Academy. "The actual painting," he said "did not take more than two hours."

headline: DEAD COUNT PUZZLE. / ALLEGED POISONING BY AN UNKNOWN.
text:
"My son was poisoned," is all that the Countess de Beuret, the mother of the young Count Girard de Montfiore can say about the fatal illness that overcame him suddenly when motoring in Paris with his fiancee, Mlle. Yvonne Doux. The court was a young millionaire sportsman and owner of the Castle of Dompierre in the Aube Department.

The countess and her husband, the stepfather of the young man, have laid a formal charge with the police of murder against some person unknown

The post-mortem examination showed no traces of organic disease, but a chemical examination will have to be made for signs of poisoning.

A colt at the castle of Dompierre died under conditions which suggested poisoning some weeks ago.

The police are making inquiries at Dompierre into a report that the count had a violent quarrel with a person intimately known to him.

headline: SEEING MESSAGES: / VISIBLE ONLY THROUGH TINTED GLASSES.
text:
Messages can now be flashed through the air which are visible only to those with glasses tinted in a special way to receive them, said Dr. Robert Wood to the American Chemical Conference at Baltimore.

These messages can be sent in full sunlight by means of red rays, usually invisible to the eye.

They have already been sent as far as eight miles, and the rays can be used in military signal lamps for flashing signals. Apparently this envisages an army of the future, all wearing special goggles, for Dr. Robert suggests the painting of aeroplanes to make them look to the enemy like his own machines, but to appear to their own men, armed with goggles, in their true colours. He also suggested that the use of invisible light might prove valuable in detecting the presence of cancer and other growths now invisible under ordinary light.

headline: CLUBS IN MALAYA / SOME FINANCIAL PROBLEMS.
text:
MORALITY OF THE CHIT SYSTEM.

"Indging by the long reports of its meetings which appear in our Singapore contemporaries," says the "Strat Echo," the members of the Singapore Cricket Club have no objection to discussing their affairs in public, so it is permissible to take a recent meeting as the text for a few comments on club finance. The meeting concerned the vexed and long-standing question of chit. The committee of the S.C.C. had notified the members of the framing of a new bye-law which provides that all members' bills shall be payable on the fifteenth day of the month following the end of the month to which they supply. Twenty-one members, apparently scentings an encroachment on cherished privileges, requested the calling of a meeting to explain the necessity of the new bye-law, which has the effect of shortening by about a month the period of grace previously allowed to a member in which to scollids account. At the meeting the twenty-one were different in expressing an opinion. Only one of them spoke, and his contention was merely that the change should have been affected by an alteration of rule and not by the passing of a bye-law. The large majority of those present supported the committee, who according to the chairman, "had spent many weary hours on the question of the framing of the bye-law as the only solution that they could find."

The Singapore Cricket Club is certainly not the only institution of its kind in Malaya which has trouble regarding accounts. More than one club posts a list of defaulters for amounts running into very respectable amounts, and it is rather melancholy reflection on the spirit of the times that to be posted in a club does not now seem to be thought quite the shame and disgrace that it was in the old days. In some cases the question of defaulters became so serious that it was decided to make an entire sweep of the time-honoured Eastern chit system and institute either cush deposits or payment for drinks as ordered.

Two notable examples are, of course, the Penang Cricket Club and the famous "Spotted Dog," of Kuala Lumpur, where the credit system was abolished several years ago with apparently benefits which outweighed the inconvenience caused to members who pay their duties regularly. Other clubs catering for junior men have hesitated to follow a lead which has, we think, very much to recommend it. They argue that members should not be robbed of their credit privileges, while in some cases it is even urged that a cash system would cause members to spend less and the club would not be able to pay its way. Such an argument is surely not to be taken seriously. A club which depends for its maintenance on members spending more than its good for them at the bar—especially a club which is supposed to exist to promote the interests of sport—has very small claim to the right to exist at all.

There is a good deal to be said for the view that subscriptions and other dues should cover a club's overhead charges and drinks should be sold at its near cost price as possible. The custom of ordering drinks "for the good of the house" as is done in some hotels, is surely not applicable to our clubs. The treating habit and the fatal ease with which bills can be run up is a cause of regret to those who take the time to think of these things, and while no one wants to see a young man become a hermit and a excuse it is generally admitted that "shouting rounds" has been and is a great deal overdone. Most of us know from experience the extraordinary ease with which a club bill of a hundred dollars and more can be accumulated: Is it right for a young man with a salary of three or four hundred dollars a month to be led into habits like these?

headline: A HEALTHY CHECK.
text:
Having to make a cash deposit and to renew, it when the amount is exhausted has a healthy check on undue expenditure. The member benefits and the club, even if its receipts on paper are not so large, profits considerably by having no bad debts.

The problem of chits is a very old and hoary one, of course, but it is always with us and it has not been solved yet. Hotel and store managers say they would like to see chits abolished and we give their stated opinion for what it may be worth; personally, we are not quite sure. There may be something in the assertion that at the prices' charged the honest customers pay for the losses on the others. In any case the custom still goes on. A young man new to the place can give a large order in a store, and if he is known to be in employment and is presumably of good standing he can obtain credit. The same young man can go to a hotel and give a dinner party to half

a-dozen people, complete with champagne and accessories. If he is not on the wrong side of their books already, the obliging management will trust him for the bill. We suppose it works out all right, and we do not presume to teach hotel and store managers their business; but the effect on the young man cannot be other than unhealthy. Unless he is more than usually strong-minded and has a sense of proportion it is very likely to get him into a wrong way. If living and working in the East will be to his detriment instead of to the advantage. He cannot do it at home; why should he have these extraordinary facilities for getting into debt out here?

headline: WHAT EACH GETS.
text:
Mr. Justice M'Cardle delivered his judgment in the Dennistoun case. In brief Colonel Dennistoun wins on the bigger issue, and his former wife wins on the question of money lent (except that barred by the Statute of Limitations). "I am bound to apply the rules of the law as I conceive them to exist," said the Judge.

Damages amounting to £5,000 were awarded to Mrs. Dennistoun by the jury in Mr. Justice M'Cardie's Court as compensation by reason of Colonel Dennistoun's refusal in January, 1924, to support her in case of necessity. This was a pendant to the jury's decision that Colonel Dennistoun had made a verbal agreement—although not the one pleaded—to support her in necessity if she did not claim alimony from the French Courts. In the jury's view this was intended to be a binding contract, and it was not part of a collusive arrangement for divorce.

Below in the substance of the judgment delivered by Mr. Justice M'Cardie:—

A stay of execution was granted until further order, with liberty to the parties to make application.

headline: 一
text:
Dr. Frederick Cook, the New York physician who claimed to have discovered the North Pole and scaled Mount M'Kinley, entered Fort Leavenworth Prison in Kansas to serve 15 years as a penalty for using the mails to defraud.

The man who bluffed the world with his imaginative story of discovery left Fort Worth, Texas, where he was tried and convicted, smiling as genially as when enthusiasts. New York crowds shouldered him and placed garlands of roses about his neck. It was "an revoir, not good-bye," he said, and declared that he was looking forward to employing his time in prison with profit to himself and the State, as he hoped he would be permitted to practise in the prison hospital. When his time is up he will return to Texas, "the scene of his bitterest trouble," to take up life anew.

For some years following Cook's exposure as a fraud by Admiral Peary, the real discoverer of the North Pole, the doctor disappeared in South America, and little was known of his activities. A few years ago he returned and conceived the plan of organising into the Petroleum Producers' Association a number of concerns owning worthless oil lands and selling the stock to gullable "investors." For the past 16 months Cook has been in jail in Texas awaiting the result of his appeal from his sentence, which was based chiefly on Judge Killett's excoriating denunciatory address describing the former explorer as one of the biggest lars in the world's history. Cook still has many friends who intend to petition President Coolidge for his pardon.

headline: AN ELUSIVE MOON
text:
MYSTERY OF SATURN'S TENTH SATELLITE.

The planet Saturn has a mysterious moon which has engaged the attention of many.

The moon is called Themis, and is officially known as the tenth satellite. For 20 years or more controversy has debated whether it really exists.

The late Professor Barnard, who was one of the most skilled of American observers, could not find 'Themis with the 40-inch telescope at Yerkes.

The satellite is described in scientific sources of Information as a body of the 17th magnitude (which is exceedingly faint) and as being placed at a distance from Saturn of over 900,000 miles.

Many astronomers believe the object to have been merely a spurious effect of the photographic plate, an effect which was interpreted as the image of a satellite.

The only observations of it were made by Professor Pickering in 1903, and these were entirely photographic. Since 1903 Themis has persistently refused to reveal itself.

A special train rushed him and his party across France from Marseilles to Boulogne, and another from folkes to London. The Maharaja brought four wives with him, and great privacy was observed when they disembarked. When every body else had left the wives were carried direct to a saloon carriage in closed sedan chairs. Native servants surrounded the sedans; known as "polti," the wives being "purdahnusheen," meaning that no man may see them.

The Maharaja, besides a suite of 20, brought seven polo players. Fifty-one polo ponies and retinos have already arrived in England, and are now being stabled at Minehead. Somerset

Fifteen polo ponies for the Maharaja's team arrived at Plymouth by the British India liner Pomale, making a string of about 70. They travelled well, only once refusing food owing to rough weather. Each pony is worth about £450.
