headline: ODDS AND ENDS
text:
It is a safe rule always to hang pictures at eye level (says the "Manchester Guardian.") Above that height small pictures look out of place, and large pictures reflect so much light that it becomes impossible to see the subject. To keep a picture hanging straight make a twist in the picture cord before having it on the book. Never tilt pictures by propping them on a nail. The large frame that hangs from the rail or cornice will have sufficient title of its own, while the very small picture should rest absolutely flat against the wall and be suspended from neat hooks, hidden behind its own frame. The very heavy oil painting should be suspended upon chains; for no picture cord will sustain the strain of a really heavy frame indefinitely. Use two chains, one, from each side of the picture, and run them up to two separate hooks. A couple of large-headed nails, one at each end, will also minimise the strain. Where the walls of a house are damp, or there is fear of the pictures marking the wallpaper, screw in two large-headed nails so that the picture rests against them and not against the wall. Never allow the backing of a picture to become torn and broken, for the tears will permit dust and damp to do their worst and result in dimmed colours and discoloured mounts. headline: Motley The Only Wear.
text:
Smart clothes in the great world of London are quite, quite done for the daytime, to the distress, I suppose, of the more gaudy dress designers and to the makers of silks and satins and embroideries. Even for a very formal lunch, or for that now rather rare thing, a sea party, people wear glorified golf clothes (writes Viola Tree in the "Evening Standard.") There is limitless field for greys and browns and for accessories like stockings and handkerchiefs and belts to contrast and to harmonise. But gone are my dear black charmeuse and the charming Russian embroiders of yester year. A straight blue serge can be helped out with a frill, but honestly it is not really the way to dress. A helmet hat rammed on the head and a loose coat over a few other knitted coats in the smartest, and tailor-mades, rather severt, are worn by the young with their high-collared sweaters like jolly Jack Tars. They look nice, but so very, very hot, one tight sleeve over another. Extravagant lingerie is not barred, but it must never show with sports clothes—a shoulder strap or a piece of creeping filet would be absolutely fatal to the ensemble. Everyone to her taste, but where is the fun of the moors and marshes country if one goes about London just the same, looking as if one had a gun concealed under the elbow? Love Romance of a Nm.

A romantic love affair of a nun is reported from Bergamo, on the Swiss-Italian frontier. An old and wealthy Italian woman who was suffering from an incurable disease, and knew that she had not long to live, asked the Mother Superior of a neighbouring Catholic convent to send her a nun daily in order to read the Bible and pray with her. A pretty nun twenty-three years of age was chosen for the purpose, and during her daily visits frequently met the woman's sob, an officer in the Navy, and the couple fell in love with each other. The officer proposed marriage, and was supported by his mother. The nun, who was in a terrible dilemma, as she had to choose between her love and vows, recently confessed her "crime" to the Mother Superior, who took a lenient view of the affair. "Child," she said, "remain in your cell as a week and carefully examine her demands of your heart and con science, some vows, and then tell me your decision." The marriage will take place shortly.

headline: G.B.S. And Stage Licences
text: Mr. George Bernard Shaw, in an interview published in the London. "Evening Standard," suggests a remedy for the cleansing of the "decadent" stage. The public can and inevitably will decide, he says, whether plays are really shocking or disgusting. They may go to see plays that make current morality ridiculous and hold up something better. But they won't consent to be shocked or disgusted or take their families to see disgusting plays. The theatrical manager who produces pieces that are merely vicious will be ruined in no time. It might be well if theatres were licensed exactly as our public-houses are. Such a system need involve no interference with plays as such. Similarly, the licensing of theatres should be in the hands of some public body, with plenty of access for anyone desiring to lodge a legitimate complaint. And a theatre licence should be revoked only for some judicial reason; not for any puritan reason, such as that the theatre is a gate of hell. The question of revoking a licence should be settled by a vote of the whole council. Though I have been attacking the British stage censorship for years, I have never suggested that impunity was the alternative to a censorship. There can never be absolute freedom for the stage so long as you have the police.

headline: 'The Human Walk.'
text: Lecturing on Wednesday at 74 Grosvenor Street, W., on "The Human Walk," Mr. Clement Jeffery, the well-known spinal specialist, said that the cultivation of the walking pillar-box was as absurd as that of the Victorian hour-glass. "The lines of the human figure are exquisitely curved," continued Mr. Jeffery, "and present feminine fashions in shape as well as in walk are physiologically wrong." Mr. Jeffery added that the upright position was achieved by man only after countless ages of striving; it had enabled him to dominate all other living beings by affording him time to use his fore-limbs for the handling of weapons and tools. "The erect position," said Mr. Jeffery, "has a powerful influence on the intellect, and it has been observed that children paralysed in the trunk and lower limbs show an immediate improvement in their mental life when placed erect."

headline: Clock Sota.
text:
A little clock in a black china case decorated with roses and with two tall vases to match, describes one of the many clock-sets that are now shown: (points out the "Manchester Guardian.") Generally speaking, these sets are cheap, of no particular value, but they are well designed and do not look out of place in a room. Once upon a time the marble mantelpiece carried a heavy clock, and usually two plunging horses as well, but there is no place, perhaps fortunately, for such things on the modern wopden mantelpiece; so the clock-set has been designed to fill the gap. To some extent, the china clock is a revival of an old fashion. Fifty years ago many of them rivalled the gilt figure clocks made in France, but the new clock sets have little in common with these elaborate old-fashioned timepieces, being quite simple in design and colouring, and, of course, very much smaller.

Sargent must have died a very rich man, for he commanded higher prices for his portraits than any of his rivals. To be painted by Sargent soon became the fashion, but not all his sitters were pleased. He painted people as he saw them, certainly not with malice, as some declared, but without that flattering touch that many sitters desired. Even Robert Louis Stevenson, whom he painted with his wife, remarked that in spite of its high qualities the portrait looked "dam queer" and was not suited for exhibition. As a technician Sargent was unrivalled. In order to preserve his marvellous touch he practised four hours a day almost every day of his life. Keenly self-critical, he was sometimes known to repaint a canvas twenty separate times to secure the effect he wanted. The highest compliment an artist could receive fell to Sargent two years ago, when his series of nine portraits and portrait groups of the Wertheimer family were exhibited at the National Gallery. For the first time in history the rule that no pictures by living artists should be included among the treasures of the national collection in Trafalgar Square were relaxed. Since an American jazz operetta appeared in Glasgow prior to opening in London, musical Glasgow has been humming and whistling all the jazzy tunes with all the saxophone variations—Associated Press. A nation's music is an index of its character (the Chronicle of Sin Francisco says to reference to the above statement.) Like its architecture, it reflects the pale cast of its thought. " Let me make the songs of the country," said old Andrew Fletcher, " and I care not who makes its laws." Now comes the disquieting news from Glasgow that the plaided and sporraned Scot is about to abandon his p broch and his strathspey. The bag-pipe faces the almost oblivion of the harp. And drab as we are a nation of business men without national picturesqueness, we would not lose the colour of the stranger's giving. We feel a certain agonising responsibility for this defection from national ideals. For it is the introduction of a modern America jazz opera that has turned the Scottish mind from its animated sharps and buzzing drones to the ribald pleasing of the sixophone. Tinpan alley has laid the minstrel low. Imitation is the sincerest form of flairtery, but our self-respect will plead trumpet-tongued against the insinuation that the saxophone represents our supreme contribution to the culture of nations. Its woody cacophonics are really not to be listened to in patience. It is a plague on all our houses. So we would assure the Scot. We would warn him against the insidiousness of the saxophone as we do our own against the balefulness of his distilled Highland Dew. We would extend the prohibition amendment to include the silencing of this ready nailsance. We cannot, in faith, behold him woo this bedizened hurry of the music hails without reciting to him his certain peril. Let no Gordon, or Argyle, or Sutherland, or Douglas be taken in. But, perhaps, we are too severe on ourselves. The saxophone is not of our creation. We have it, but we did not create it. Luy that crime to Antipole Joseph Six of Belgium. We merely sorrowout from Paris. We could give us our strain with pressure. And we must be in stock on the same time.

headline: ODDS AND ENDS
text: Mme. Sarah Grand. Mmo. Sarah Grand, otherwise Mrs. M'Fall, has been staying at Folkstone for a change after illness, but has now returned to her residence at Bath (observes the "Star.") She writes steadily, mostly in the morning, as she thinks this is the best time, and she takes a keen interest in social work. The author of "The Heavenly Twins" and other novels, which attained fame about a quarter of a century ago, is also fond of travelling, and she knows the East well. But apart from these interests, Sarah Grand has no special hobbies, except a great love for all things Irish, Ireland being the land of her birth though her father was an English naval officer. As a young girl in her middle teens she became the wife of Colonel M'Fall, an Army doctor over twice her age, who left her a widow many years ago.

headline: Trains Without Drivers.
text: A "manless" passenger train, run and controlled entirely by wireless, is announced by Mr. G. Y. Allen, of the American Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Co., says a message to the Paris edition of the "New York Herald." It is now entirely feasible, by a combination of automatic and radio supervisory control from a central office, said Mr. Allen, to start a train without a crew, run it at full speed over clear tracks, slow it down or stop it in accordance with the signals of an automatic block-signalling system, start it up again, and open its doors. The wireless features of this system, according to Mr. Allen, are of the "carrier current" type—radio waves which travel along the power lines of the railway instead of spreading out through the ether, as in ordinary broadcasting. The waves, using this system, can be directed to any desired point, and can be utilised to operate switches and other devices, as well as to carry on conversations.—"Daily Express."

headline: Why We Need Iodine.
text: The thyroid gland in the neck, consisting of two lobes and an isthmus, joining them across the windpipe, creates a unique substance, mostly consisting of iodine. Without it none can live. Without enough of it in the blood of an expectant mother, not only is she imperilled, but her baby cannot be born normal. The thyroid gland, if starved of iodine, tries to make bricks without straw, enlarges and nearly dies in consequence. We call that result goitre; astonishing evidence has come from University College, London, suggesting that there is a relation between goitre and cancer. The right course for us is to restore the missing iodine to our own food, so that our thyroids can live and work for us as they should. In my view, the State and the municipalities, notably through education authorities and maternity centres, should see that we are all supplied with iodine at almost costless rates. This will undoubtedly save a vast amount of uglines, idiocy, deaf mutism, and, possibly, cancer.—Dr. G. W. Saleeby, in the "Daily Herald," Air Navigation.

The subject of practical navigation of aircraft was dealt with in a paper prepared by Captain F. Tymms and read at a meeting of the Royal Aeronautical Society. He was impelled by his own experience, he said, and that of others to the conclusion that the air must follow the sea and the aeroplane the ship rather than the iron-bound train, that these questions were of vital importance in the future of aviation. In discussing the question of maps, it was pointed out that there was a fairly general view that a map for aerial navigation should be a picture of the earth as seen from an aeroplane. That was an eminently sound principle, but if carried too far that particular principle would result in a map which would be very difficult to read because of the crowded nature of the information and the diverse appearance of similar things. One was forced to the conclusion, said Captain Tymms, that a map for aerial navigation must follow in general the principles on which all maps were produced—that surface features must be shown by conventional signs.—"Daily Telegraph." A New Substitute for Glass.

The latest chemical discovery is a substitute for glass, made from purely organic materials. It seems to have many attractive properties, being much softer than glass, so that it can be worked on a latho into all sorts of required shapes. It can be coloured for decorative purposes, but the most interesting thing about it is that its "refractive index" can be varied over a wide range, making it very suitable for optical instruments and capable of replacing very expensive kinds of glass in telescopes and microscopes. Another interesting optical point is that it appears to be much more transparent than glass to the invisible rays—ultra-violet and infrared light. It may be a surprise to those who have not heard of synthetic resins to hear that this glassy substance is made by condensing formaldehyde and urea. At first a kind of soft, transparent jelly is obtained which with the aid of a little heat and addition of traces of some sodium salts is converted to a hard glassy material which has the properties already described. It will probably cheapen optical appliances to an unheard-of degree and supersede the expensive fluorite lenses of apochromatic objectives and may find therapeutic application as a substitute for glazing in hospitals.

headline: Cafeteria.
text: Although cafeterian are used by everyone in America, rich and poor, alike, it is to the business girl that they are of special benefit (says a "Daily Telegraph" writer.) The time she spends over her meals is entirely within her own control, so that she has often more than half her free hour to herself, and, in addition to this, the fact that very little service is needed in a cafeteria reduces the cost of food considerably. In nearly every one the process is the same, and the visiting Englishwoman soon slips into the habit, so simple it is, and so practical. When you enter the room you are faced with a long counter-piled with plates of food, and presided over by about half a dozen attendants, whose duty it is to replenish the dishes as required. Generally there is a railing about four feet away from the counter, so that you cannot stray out into the room until you have been given an account of your just debts, and immediately in front of the counter is another railing along which you slide your tray. You pick this up at the door where you find it all ready waiting for you, complete with a table napkin folded round two forks a spoon, and a knife. Once you have secured this, you embark on the rapturous process of sliding your tray along and choosing your lunch from the goodly selection before you. At the very end of the counter you will come to the coffee and tea urns, and here, too, if you are in a very-up-to-date cafeteria, you will find yourself faced with a selection of hot dishes. As you leave the counter you submit your well-laden tray to the inspection of the girl at the cash desk, who adds up the cost of your dishes, and gives you a check for the amount, which you pay at the door on leaving. You are then free to choose a table and settle yourself down to your meal. It is all done very quickly. At the most it is five minutes from the time you enter the door until you are seated at your table, and you may leave the minute you finish. There is none of that process so well known in England of "catching the waitress's eye." By the cafeteria system, too, labour is reduced to a minimum, for, in addition to the attendants behind the food counter there are only about four waiters in the room itself, who gather up your tray and used dishes when you have finished, and refill the water jugs on every table. Even this is often unnecessary, for the newest cafeterias are generally supplied with a fountain of iced water in the middle of the room, and beside it will be more often than not, a glass holder for cardboard cups, which you fill yourself, thus achieving a nice sense of independence, which adds materially to the flavour of your meal.

headline: "PAT" HENDREN MAKES DOUBLE CENTURY.
text:
Although the stronger counties were not meeting one another, the results of the county cricket matches at Home have been very interesting. Derby's defeats of Essex at Leyton is the only surprise.

Some big scores were made but most pleasing of all is the proportion of comparatively new names—a factor auguring well for the future.

The Rose counties remain at the head of affairs. Changes in the table are:—Kent go above Essex, Gloucester drop below Northants, Sussex and Derby each move up two places. Details follow:—

headline: HOME SPORT
text:
NEWS BEFORE THE MAIL : "ARRIVES.

BITS HERE AND THERE.

Light is thrown on various branches of Home sport by the following messages. Some of the main facts have already been published but interesting details are now available.

headline: THE DERBY.
text:
(Times of Ceylon.

Mr. Carew, the Liverpool man, who has won the Calcutta Sweep, in an interview to-day said he believed the Manna ticket had won £100,000.

“After luncheon yesterday,” he stated, “I lay down, said a few prayers, then smoked peacefully till the telephone told me that Manna had won.”

Immediately afterwards—Mr. Carew motored to the Roman Catholic Girls' Orphanage and donated £1,000.

Other Lucky Ones. London May

It has been announced that Mrs. Barclay, wife of a Customs or Post Office official, Calcutta, has drawn Cross Bow in the Calcutta Sweep. A young assistant, named Anderson Wright, has drawn Ptolemy.

A Liverpool resident has drawn Manna

Mr. James Carew, partner of a shipping firm in Liverpool, has drawn Manna in the Calcutta Sweep. He refused £5,000 for the ticket, but sold a quarter share for £2,000 to a London Syndicate.

headline: LADIES' TENNIS.
text:
In the Surrey Tennis Championship the final of the Ladies' Singles resulted in a win for Miss K. McKane, who beat Miss Ryan, 7-9, 6-1, 6-3.

In the final of the Ladies' Doubles, Mrs. Lambert Chambers and Miss Ryan beat Miss McKane and Miss Saunders, 3-1, 6-4.
Miss McKane.

headline: M. C. C. TOUR
text:
Mr. Lacey, the M.C.C. Secretary, states that he is unable to say anything at present regarding the projected M.C.C. cricket team tour of India in the coming cold season. The matter is to be further considered by the M.C.C. Committee at an early date.

It is otherwise gathered that, while the invitation is welcomed and there is a keen desire to acceed to it, there are difficulties in the way particularly owing to the fact that there is a danger of leading players going stale with too much continual cricket. It may be recalled that cricket teams recently toured Australia and South Africa, and that an Australian team is visiting Great Britain in 1926.

headline: Task of Finance
text:
Bombay, May 23.—The local Indian Gymkhana Clubs have shouldered the task of financing to the extent of Rs. 44,000 the visit of the M.C.C. team, which is expected to arrive in India in the Autumn.

The M.C.C. will partake in the annual quadrangular tournament

headline: HARD COURTS.
text:
SPENCE WINS AT SURREY.

P. D. B. Spence, the South African international and hard court champion of Great Britain won the men's singles in the Surrey Hard Court Championships at Roehampton when he beat Randolph Lyceet in the final by 6-4, 6-3, 6-1.

Spence, after the first two games, struck his very best form, and was a long way too good for Lyett, who was by no means off colour. Indeed, Lyett played just as well as Spence allowed him to, and was good enough to crowd the match with interest because of the high standard of lawn tennis which was its feature.

Spence has not played so well for a long time as he did previously. He was both accurate and animated; was forceful off the ground and decisive on the volley. There was hardly a flaw discernible in his play, and he attacked his opponent with such intense vigour that Iyccett had to resort for the greater part of the time to defensive measures, occasionally, but not often, delighting the "gallery" by passing Spence at the net with a superb cross-court drive.

Lyett was soon in difficulties. He did not like Spence's fast break service, and the pace and low trajectory of the South African's driven often caused him to lose that fraction of a second which makes the difference between a winner and an error.

Mrs. Lweett easily defeated Miss Joan Ridley in the final of the Ladies' Singles by 6—0, 6—3.

Mrs. Lycett drove much harder, and volleved exquisitely. Miss Ridley, who had a nasty blister on her right hand, was unable to hit with anything like her usual force, and could do little but scoop up the ball for Mrs. Lycett to kill.

Lyceum and H. W. Austin won the men's doubles, and Mrs. Lambert Chambers and Miss E. H. Harvey were successful in the ladies' doubles.

headline: HOME CRICKET. / THIS SEASON'S NEW FEATURES.
text:
GOSSIP BY MAIL

Summing up new features at the opening of the Home Cricket season, a critic writes:—

Yorkshire hope to equal the Notts record by winning the championship for the fourth year in succession, and think that Major Lupton, the new captain—he's an all-sounder—will prove the forcing bat the county have so long needed.

Worcestershire have had it brought home to them that team chopping and changing spells disaster. This year they hope to pick "the team" and keep it. Middlesex will be met for the first time since the war, and, unlike last year, games have been arranged with Yorkshire.

If their batting was only equal to their bowling—and there certainly is much in an attack that includes Geary, Astill, Skilding, Shipman and Bale—Leicestershire would be a force to be feared. N.F. Armstrong (bat and bowler) and N. Dowen (left-hand bat) may be just the men required. A North and Scottish tour has been arranged. The club have an adverse balance of close on £1,000.

G. W. Stephens, owing to business calls, will not be able to regularly assist Warwickshire. B. W. Qualife, son of "W. G," and a batsman of much the same solid stamp, may be given a further trial; and occasional assistance is expected from N. E. Partridge (always a valuable addition to the bowling strength), and C. A. Fiddian-Green, the old Cambridge "Blue"; from the Oxford "Blue," E. P. Hewetson, and G. W. Stephens.

Hampshire's chief need is a fast bowler. Perhaps one will be unearthed at the Southampton nursery, just established. We are again to see A.L. Hosie, home on leave from India, and possibly Capt. E. I. M. Barrett, now Deputy-Commissioner of Police at Shanghai.

Lancashire needed a reliable bowler to back up Parkin and Dick Tyidesley. They will now have the regular assistance of Macdonald. The battling needed stiffening. J. R. Barnes is expected to appear more frequently. Novelties this season are a match at Nelson (v. Derbyshire), in August. This is one of the conditions on which the local club consented to part with Macdonald, and a game with Scotland (at Old Trafford, May 13, 14 and 15).

M. D. Lyon, T. C. Lowry and H. Critchley. Silmons on will not be seen out for Somerset. A further blow—J. C. W. MacBryan may not be able to spare as much time for cricket. What makes the outlook a little less gloomy is that W. T. Greswell is to be home from Ceylon in June, and has promised to turn out when required. Then there's that youngster from Rugby School. E. F. Longrigg, whom an experienced judge has described as a stylish left-hander. Three professionals now qualifying are Leach, a punishing bit, from Lincashire; Lee, the tall brother of the Middlesex cricketer, a bowler; Warrington, a break bowler from the ground staff at Lord's; and M. L. Hill, wicketkeeper, down from Cambridge. Lincashire are included in the fixtures for the first time since the war.

Little change is anticipated in the constitution of Gloucestershire's team. Games with Notts have been added to the fixture list. Dennett is now coach at Cheltenham College, but is to be available when required.

Only Arthur Staples (right-arm, medium-paced bowler) and Wheat (wicketkeeper) of the Notts ground staff, have any real pretensions to class, which is rather surprising, for James Iremonger has done a lot of coaching there. Several members of the county team are now reaching the veteran stage, and so Notts must indeed look ahead. Warwick and Essex are omitted from the fixtures.

Remembering what happened to V. W. C. Jupp and Clark last year motor-cycling, so far as Northamptonshire crickets are concerned, should be forbidden. M. Fitzroy, an unknown quantity, will skipper the side.

Chelmsford is for the first time favoured with a first-class fixture. Easex meeting Oxford University there.

If you are a Middlesex man and fancy yourself as a left-hand bowler, they've got practice nets up at Lord's especially for your benefit. Middlesex are to give the new wicket-covering regulation—from 11 a.m. the preceding day till the match begins—a full trial.

The only change at the Oval concerns a player's status, S. Fenley, the slow bowler, having joined the ground staff.

We may soon hear of county cricket being played at Chatham. To test the quality of the wickets on the R.N. and R.M. ground, Kent are sending their second eleven. Amos, of Canterbury, and Hubble, a nephew of Jack, have joined the "colts."

headline: GRAT GÀME. / J. O. ANDERSON PLAYS IN COLOMBO.
text:
TENNIS, WONDER.

Seldom has Colombo had the opportunity of witnessing such a brilliant display of tennis, as that given by J. O. Anderson, the Australian Club. His opponent was F. de Saram. the local champion

Although Anderson was visibly affected by the heat he gave more than a glimpse of his greatness as a player. Either at the back of the court or close up at the net; Anderson brought off some drives which would have beaten anybody. He possesses a vast repertoire of strokes," which he executes with grace and accuracy. His service, although perhaps not as fast as Patterson's has a lot of spin in it, and his first particularly wants a lot of watching. He double-faulted on four or five occasions during his game with de Saram, but he did not find it difficult to beat the local champion with his service.

His back-hand and forearm drives were executed. with remarkable speed, and he left de Saram standing with hurricane shots which he effected by meeting the ball sideways; waist high. His overhead work, too, was very good.

headline: QUEEN'S THEATRE. / JACKIE COGAN IN CIRCUS PICTURE.
text:
Jackie Cognis is with us again and best of all he returns in what may truly be called the most delightful vehicle of his screen career a rollicking circus picture.

The wistful little figure is given a part in the "Circus, Dys," that seems better suited to his talent than anything else he has done.

Proof of this was amply man瘋tested by the tremendous enthusiasm with which the audience greeted the picture on its opening last night at the Queen's Theatre.

Jackie plays the role of Toby Tyler, a youngster who, with his widowed mother is forced to live on the farm of a hard-hearted uncle. Driven to desperation. Toby runs away from home to join a circus. How he rises from a peanut merchant of the "big top" to be a star of the sawdust ring, bringing happiness and prosperity to his mother is one of the most refreshing tales ever unfolded on the screen.

And the whimsical humour and touching flashes of pathbos that have distinguished past screen performances of this big-eyed little star are stronger than ever in "Circus Days"

headline: SQUEEZE 7
text:
CHARGE AGAINST CONSTABLE

THREE MARKED COINS.

A cooked food hawker of Stuninton Street came before Mr. Burlingham (Assistant Superintendent of Police) yesterday with a complaint that an Indian constable had been in the habit of receiving 30 cents as "squares" every morning for about one week. To ascertain the truth of the man's story, Mr. Burlingham handed him three marked ten-cent pieces and detailed Sergeant Nolloth to watch proceedings by hiding himself in a house near the stall this morning. The policeman was taken into custody after he had received the money and was searched in the presence of Mr. Burlingham at the charge room when the tell-tale coins were found in his pocket.

The Indian policeman was subsequently charged before Mr. S. B. B. McElderry at the Central Magistracy. The case is proceeding.

headline: FREAK DINNER / ELEPHANTS AND CAMELS IN BALLROOM.
text:
One of those freak dinners by which American millionaries love to display their capacity for “hanging the expense,” has taken place at the Waldorf Astoria, New York.

As the guests entered they suddenly found themselves lost in a grove of palm trees with monkeys swinging on the branches.

Arab guides received the guests and conducted them to a large ballroom arranged to imitate the desert.

Sand four inches deep covered the floor and appropriate scenery hid the walls.

Two hundred guests were served by waiters, genuine and imitation natives, but all were in costume. During the dinner dervishes, sword jugglers and dances performed on the sand. Many guests were alarmed for a moment when Arabs on horseback dashed in and gave their performance.

The finale was a procession of elephants, camels and other animals. This was somewhat spoiled by the behaviour of the camels. As soon as they smelled the sand they rushed in snorting, lunging about, and finally threw themselves down and rolled delightedly on the floor.

Mathew Brush, the banker host, was delighted with the success of his effort. Incidentally, he is a large shareholder in the hotel, which naturally will not lack publicity.

headline: A WAR DISCLOSURE.
text:
GERMAN THREAT TO INVADE AUSTRIA.

How Germany nearly added one of its own Allies to the countries already bringing against it in the World War is revealed by Dr. Otto Elover, the Austrian Socialist leader and Foreign Secretary in the first Republican Government, in his just-published book, "The Austrian Revolution" (Teomird Pursons, 10s. 6d.).

On the thesis that the whole modern history of German Austria is coloured by the opposition between German and Austrian mentalities, Dr. Bauer argues that this antagonism was only neutralised by the fact that, from 1897 onwards, Austrian patriotism saw its Empire threatened by the financing agitation of the Slav races within its frontiers.

How artificial was the apparent resulting unity, and how fundamentally different the outlook of German and Austrian, was clearly shown in January 1918, when, following the Brest-Litovsk Treaty, the Austrian people demonstrated against the continuance of the war against Russia to fulfil that Treaty, and, by a great general strike in Vienna, presaged a revolution that would enforce peace.

headline: A SPARATU PEACH
text:
Dr. Bauer discloses how this movement was quenched mainly by the knowledge that the Germans were actually ready to invade their Ally's country and suppress the threatened rebellion by armed force.

The military authorities managed to throw forces into the strike areas very quickly. Even if Austrian militarism no longer had at its command sufficient force to repel a revolutionary, insurrection, at the moment when German Imperialism disposed of a larger reserve army than at any other time during the whole war, an Austrian revolution could have had no other result than an invasion of Austria by the German armies. headline: THE "STUDIO:"
text:
The "Studio" for April maintains the usual standard of cautious excellence, avoiding carefully anything that might give offence as being too "modern." However it makes one departure that is of considerable general interest: it comments favourably on the settings for Mr. Douglas Fairbanks' production of "The Thief of Highdad." This is very encouraging for those who see in the cinema means of raising the artistic standards of millions to whom the higher arts make little appeal.

Perhaps the most remarkable reproduction is that of a drawing by Miss Stella Langdale—a virile work reminiscent of William Blake. Those interested in Japanese scenery will read with delight the article which accompanies reproductions from the watercolour work of Sir H. Hughes Stanton.

headline: — EDW ARD MARSN. / EXTRACTS.
text:
ON THE WEDDING MOON.

At eight or thereabouts Lindsay Mountford buffet into the room. He said it was a glorious morning, and I must come for a swim! Swim, indeed! I had hardly the strength to shave, let alone swim!

'What's the matter?' he asked brutally. 'You look rotten!'

My dear Lindsay, I retorted, when you are married, if you over are, you will feel on the morning of your wedding exactly like a man who is going to be hanged.

That's not very complimentary to the girl," commented Lindsey. "Oh, yes, it is." When a man is to be hanged at eight o'clock he knows that he will be in Heaven about five minutes past. Does that make him any jolier? No, Lindsey. You know nothing at all about being married. "The Fast Lady," by Keble Howard. (Fisher Unwin). 7s. 6d.

She's nice,' said Angela, judicially. 'But I don't feel there's anything in her.'

headline: "THE TWO PINS CLUB" / LAST FURNISS BOOK.
text:
Stories of leading characters in the sporting and dramatic world in the last half-century are told by the late Mr. Harry Furniss in

"The Two Pins Club," which, illustrated by the famous artist himself is published by Mr. John Murray, at 10s. Gd.

"The Two Pins Club" was a riding club, whose members were the famous Lord Chief Justice,

Lord Russell of Killowen; Sir Frank Lockwood, K.O., Solicitor-General; Lord Burnham; Sir Charles Mathews, Director of Public Prosecutions; Sir John Hare; Sir Frank Burnand, editor of "Punch"; Sir John Tenniel, the cartoonist; Linley Sambourne, the artist; Rudolph Lehmann, and Mr. Furness.

The club was named by Sir Frank Burnand after "the two knights of the road, of course," John Gilpin and Dick Turpin, and members rode out of town each Sunday possible to lunch in some attractive place near London.

Mr. Burniss reveals in this book "a little mystery that puzzled the Pressmen of the time, and was known to very few members of the Garrick." At a critical period, "a short" while before the Balfour Government died of ennui," the Turner Councils within the Cabinet Council were held in the strangers' room of the Garrick Club. Nobody knew where the discussions took place, and so little known was Balfour at the club that his presence there passed unnoticed.

The story of a sedate housekeeper who became a "bookie" is told by Mr. Furniss. A doctor in a provincial town died and left his house to his faithful housekeeper, so that she might take in lodgers. But the doctor had been an ardent sportsman and keen racing man, and the quiet, uncommunicative housekeeper had learned more than her employer would ever have believed. After his death she used her knowledge to set up to business as a bookmaker, and in time built up a prosperous concern.

Mr. Furniss died as this, the last book he wrote, was passing through the press.

headline: RED LIGHTS."
text:
Carriso Gorge, one of the most desolately beautiful spots in the wild, fastness of the Mexican border, was the location Clarence G. Badger selected for filming exterior scenes for the Goldwyn picture, "Red Lights" which is showing at the World Theatre for the last time to-day. The story was adapted to the screen by Carey Wilson from the stage play, "The Rear Car." 123d Field Artillery band gave its first dance in 1911. Marie Prevost and Alice Lake were the popular belles of the evening. The mayor and sheriff centred their attentions on the two actresses.

A special train of ten coaches, carrying a radio, an airplane, a five piece orchestra and a special car on which was mounted an electric generator left Los Angeles for the border with seventy-five members of the company including carpenters, electricians, property men, cameramen, extras, mechanics and technical men. Two immigration officers accompanied the party as representatives of the United States Government, for the greater portion of the railroad runs through Mexico. The little town of Jacumba Hot Springs was the destination of the Goldwyn special. With the arrival of the Goldwyn company the citizens of the town hailed a new era of prosperity. There had not been much excitement since the Mexican revolution, when Uncle Sam's soldiers camped about the town. The few little dilapidated shacks and stores with sand drifted around the doorways did not present a very lively appearance to the movie crew. A company of gypsies had encamped just off the main street. Several fat, black Mexicans with stuffed black beards dozed on the steps of the pool hall. A limp cigarette dangled from the fat cheek of one of the idlers. Johnnie Walker slapped him on the back the cigarette dropped. He did not open his eyes but moved one foot to a more comfortable position. For five weeks the "Red Lights" company lived in their train side tracked at this little village. The town was enlivened Saturday nights with a dance on the floor above the pool hall. The orchestra, which accompanied the "Red Lights" company, played the latest jazz strains and was voted the best orchestra that had appeared in the town since the

Several thrilling and laughable incidents marked the visit of the movie troupe.

One of these was provided, by Raymond Griffith. Along the route taken by the train are seventeen tunnels. The country is wild and infested with mountain lions and bobcats. Griffith was walking alone through one of these tunnels with a.32 automatic in his hand. A large boulder dropped with a thud from the top of the tunnel. In the black darkness of the tunnel this was very perturbing, to say the least. Griffith in his terror opened fire with his pistol, and emptied it in the direction of the rock which he had mistaken for a wildcat. Other members of the company rushed into the tunnel and found Ray sitting on the rock wiping his brow.

Not being able to cash cheques, the actors were forced to beg credit at the stores. Many left town without their watches or other jewellery. When they arrived home they mailed money to pay their bills, and received their valuables in the next mail. Clarence G. Badger worked night and day directing the railroad scenes for the picture. A special developing room aided the cameramen in making their tests. Some of the most successful and unusual night scenes were taken on the train.

headline: WORLD THEATRE
text:
1889 and the Galveston flood of 1900, with their toll of thousands of lives, are but passing incidents in the list of such disasters recorded in history.

All of which is recalled by a motion picture on view at the World Theatre to-morrow. It is William Fox's super special production, "The Last Trail," adapted from the novel of that name by the famous Zane Grey. Toward the close of the story a huge reservoir dam in the mountains is broken by dynamite explosion—the work of the Villian—and the liberated waters sweep down upon a village miles away. To create this startling incident, which constitutes the big climax of the Fox picture, the director, Emmett J. Flynn, under took a singularly formidable task. He built the village in California valley. He constructed a big.com. create dam high up in the hills. It was a costly enterprise, involving much valuable time and high-priced labour. But that the end justified the means will not be denied by anyone who witnesses the explosion and later views the village inhabitants fleeing to the hills, and the place destroyed.

headline: PEAK TRAMS. / COMPANY'S PLANS FOR THE FUTURE. / BIGGER CARS
text:
NO POSSIBILITY OF SLIPPING.

Plans for electrifying the Peak tram and for the construction of new cars to carry more passengers were referred to at the annual meeting of the Peak Tramways Company, Ltd., this morning. In order to meet the capital expenditure involved it was announced that a call of $4 will be made on the $1 paid up shares. Mr. Henry Humphreys presided over the meeting, and was supported by Mr. W. E. L. Shenton, the Hon. Mr. A. O. Lang, and Mr. A. S. Gubbay, directors: Mr. G. Rapp, secretary; and the following shareholders: Messrs. D. E. Clarke, J. A. Tarrant, A. A. Alves, J. P. Braga, D. Cox and W. Morley. The Chairman said:—Gentlemen, I propose with your permission to take the report and statement of accounts and Auditors' report as read. The traffic receipts for the year under review show an increase of $19,787,67 over the corresponding period of last year but the net profits are $1,756,92 less. This is accounted for by the fact that last year we made a non-recurrent profit of $16,765 on investments realized; the difference represents increased running expenses. The item unexpired season tickets no longer figures as a liability in the accounts as we ceased issuing these in June last. Under the heading of "of assets" "Mount Cameron Surrey" $3,000 appears for the first time. This survey cost $6,000 of which the Government agreed to pay half. If nothing eventuates from the projected scheme, this $3,000 will have to be written off the Com

I do not think there is anything else in the accounts which calls for any comment, but I think shareholders and the general public would like to know what improvements have been effected and what will shortly be undertaken.

The improvements to the upper terminus, virtually destroyed in the typhoon of August, 1923, are nearly completed. They comprise increased facilities for passengers in the shape of waiting room and cloak room accommodation also more platform space. They also comprise two up-to-date modern flats in lieu of one that was by no means up-to-date. One of these the Superintendent will occupy, the other will be let.

The Government has approved of the Company's scheme for electrifying the tram. The current will be obtained from the Hongkong Electric Company at a cost which it is estimated will not exceed that of our present steam power. This, of course, entails new machinery and an extension of the existing engine house to accommodate same. Plans of the extension have been approved and tender for same accepted. Our steam haulage plant is practically worn out and whether we continue with steam, or adopt electrical power, new machinery will have to be acquired shortly. Steam plant would cost more and has the disadvantage of being noisier and dirtier. The Government has consented to our having new cars to carry 55 passengers in lieu of 42 passengers as at present. This does not involve any material increase in the load is the cars, though larger and equally strong, are built of lighter material than the old. The Company desired to construct cars to seat 60 passengers but the extra 13 passengers allowed is a great advance and should relieve congestion for many years to come. The cars will be run on the double drum system, with two ropes, instead of by two drums and one endless rope as at present. This will do away with the possibility of slipping which has always been a source of trouble.

text:
All these changes involve a considerable capital expenditure and it has been decided, in order to meet same, to make a call of $4 per share on the $1 paid up shares on November 1 next. Notice of such call will be given in due course both by advertisement and circular.

I have no further remarks to make, gentlemen, and after the accounts have been seconded I shall be pleased to answer any question shareholders may have to ask.

As there were no questions Mr. Tarrant seconded the adoption of the report and accounts and they were carried unanimously.

The Chairman proposed and Mr. Cox seconded the re-election of the following directors to serve for the ensuing year:—Sir Paul Chater, Mr. W. E. L. Shenton, the Hon. Mr. A. O. Lang, Mr. R. M. Austin and Mr. A. S. Gubbay.—Carried.

Messrs. Lowe, Bingham and Matthews and Linstead and Davies were re-elected auditors at a remuneration of $150 each on the proposition of Mr. D. E. Clarke seconded by Mr. Morley.

headline: QUEEN'S THEATRE. / JACKIE COOGAN AS CIRCUS, STAR.
text:
Amid the fanfare of trumpets, the piercing notes of a steam caliope, the prancing of horses, the squealing of monkeys and the roaring of lions, Jackie Coogan runs away and joins a circus in his latest picture, "Circus Days," which comes to the Queen's Theatre to-day for an engagement of five days.

Heralded as the finest picture that the inimitable Jackie has yet made, it is the sort of story that should appeal to every boy or girl—young or old.

Driven from home and his widowed mother, Toby Tyler, the youthful hero played by the star, starts his adventures under the "big top" as a peanut salesman. His vicissitudes are many, but Dame Fortuna finally looks upon him with favour, and through a sudden accident Toby finds himself the star of the circus, and the one big hero of the sawdust

headline: BOOKS
text:
RAMSAY'S RAMBLINGS

EX-PREMIER'S TRAVEL

"The wanderlust is perhaps the most precious of all the troublesome appetites of the soul of man. It makes him keep in his cupboard a friendly old suit of comfortable wear that has paled under the fervent eyes of the sun and been matured by dust and mud and rain, and with that a pair of honest boots, nailed like the oak door of an ancient keep, which of themselves direct one's way of'er moor and fell and bog and by-path away from the offence and clamour of cars and trains."

—MR. RAMSAY MACDONALD. in Wanderings and Excursions. (Jonathan Cape, 68. net.)

"The ex-Prime Minister gets so much colour and gaiety and romance out of a single drop of ink, when describing his journeys—especially those through the countryside where so much of his youth lies buried—that we are glad he has had a selection made and put forth of his travel papers." says the "Morning Post" in a generous tribute of Mr. Ramsay MacDonald's new book, "Wanderings and Excursions."

"The spirit of adventure awakens in him as he passes by Tortuga, the den of the bucaneers, or skirts the coast of Hayti, with its one hero, Toussaint, or sees the unmatched, unearthly blue of the Central American mountains, or enters the decaying, ghost-haunted Halls of Jamaica," adds the "Morning Post." "The past becomes alive again for him as he view the outposts of the Isles of Greece, dim but flushed in the morning light," or visits Constantinople ("The meeting of many waters flowing from the East and the West; the No Man's Land between Europe and Asia, where all men gather"), or reads a Latin epitaph on a gravestone in the museum at Brindisi, or wanders through the Holy Land, every name in which is written on the heart. "But we like him most, he is the best of travel in g-companions, when he roams on shank's nag through his own country and talks with grey-haired derelicts about the wild doings of his boyhood, and surdes uphill to the magic lilt of

'Sure, 'by Tummel and Loch Rannoch and Lochaber I will go, '

y heather trucks wi' heaven their wides.

"As a politician we have no use for him—but as a wayfarer in Broad Scotland we like him fine, and are not afraid to confess it."

"In his sketches, of political activities Mr. MacDonald has a lightness of touch and a humorous outlook which may well surprise the bourgeois reader of this book who has not been accustomed to read his article in Labour publications," says the "Times Literary Supplement."

"His amused contempt for the proceedings of the French Chamber," his racy accounts of the meetings of the Berlin Socialist Conference with its clash between Socialist moderates and Bolshevik extremists, his sober warnings against political violence and legislative over-haste, and his dictum that one of the weakest things in the world is an Act of Parliament which does not embody public opinion, his recognition that in Republican Germany it is the capitalist who has succeeded to the throne of the feudalist and that German capitalism is now more strongly entrenched than ever, will all seem very strange to the average political opponent in this country, who has been apt to judge Mr. MacDonald rather from his own party posters and headlines in his own morning newspaper."

headline: "BARE SOULS." / SOME INTIMATE PEN PORTRAITS. / OBARLES LAMB.
text: Charles Lamb was a creature of whom and frolic fancy, turned life upside down and inside out, sported with it, trifled with it, tossed it in the air like soap bubbles or thistledown, regardless of where it fell or whom it might light upon. In all his mockery and in all his seriousness, in his business and in his leisure, it is clear that what first and always interested him was the human heart. Up to anything; down to anything; whatever supit hominem. A perfect man; is his description of a dear friend; it fits himself. New lives, new thoughts, new habits, new manners stimulated and excited him. Lamb may well be a saint to those who feel that the insoluble mystery of the universe is in no way better solved than by the two delicately related keys of love and daughter.

headline: GUSTAVE FIA BERT
text:
Flanbert was a thorough-going idealist and, as with so many of that type, the idealism sourced into pessimism because it could never be satisfied. The deepest pessimism does not spring from mere negation, still less from a fat and slothful materialism, which is apt to enjoy its senses and let the world go; the sudden pessimist, whether Madame du Deffand or Flaubert, is one who asks too much of life and of the living; one whose ideal is so high, whose conception of what men should be, of what men might be, is so noble that the sordid reality, as it creeps upon the dull and muddy earth, breeds nothing but disappointment and despair. Human souls might be glorious in hope, in aspiration, in love, even in actual achievement, and they are—what they are.

There is one thing about Voltaire that his bitterest enemy cannot dispute and that his friends rejoice in—his enormous vitality. From infancy to age every particle of him seemed to live, to vibrate and quiver with an intense, inexhaustible, irrepressible animation, which entered into all his thoughts and deeds, and extended itself to everything and person that came near him. He snms it up in three words. 'J'aime tout.' 'I like everything.' The things he did not like he hated, and he often liked and hated the same thing as the mood took him. He might be

angry, he might be discouraged, he might be weary, he might be desperate: he was never indolent and never indifferent. Life was a great game, or, if you preferred, a great battle; but while you lived you must make the most of it, must make every nerve and muscle you had tell something and do something.

headline: " FANTOMAS."
text:
Rena Parker, the dark-eyed stage beauty who is playing an important part in the William Fox serial "Fantomas" which will be shown at the World Theatre from Sunday to Wednesday, gives up a very important engagement in a play that was a hit in New York, to become the countess in "Fantomas." This serial is Miss Parker's first attempt in motion pictures. She had had many offers to leave. the stage, but was loath to do this in view of the progress she was making. In these days, however, the silent drama has a pulling power that makes continued resistance very hard for the stage actor or actress. When Edward Sedgwick was seeking a girl for the part of The Countess he happened to see Miss Parker in "Betty Be Good," and made her so flattering an offer that she did not hesitate. She believed she had an opportunity to do some fine acting in "Fantomas," and those who have watched her work know that she fulfilled all demands—her beauty adding to the effectiveness of her acting ability. Miss Parker was born in Chicago and was educated there. When schooling days were over she went to Paris, then to Berlin, and finally to London, studying in each of these capitals music, art and voice culture.

She began her stage career in vandeville, singing and dancing. Soon with her winning ways, her charming voice and her clever dancing she became prima donna in "Nobody Home," and played in that both in New York and on the road. Then she was engaged for "To night's the Night." She was the prima donna in "Flo Flo" in New York and spent a several on the road with it. Then Charles Dillingham engaged her for "Applis Biosoma" in New York. Finally she was featured in "Betty Be Good" in New York and starred in it on the road. Miss Parker has played in London at the Alhambra, opposite George Grusmith. She toured the provinces in Sideville. She has played in Paris and at the Winter Garden in Berlin. Her recollection of her first appearance in Berlin is not altogether pleasant. There was no applause during her act, but she received an ovation when she finished and was bowing herself off. Yet she was not sure she had pleased. She received an invitation to the Royal Box, but, being a modest girl, she declined to go. When she left the theatre a German officer spoke to her on the street. She felt offended and slapped his face. Was the officer arrested? No, but Miss Parker was. The American consul secured her release.

headline: JOHN KEATS.
text:
What is most striking about Keats in all the matters and relations of life is the richness and splendour of imagination with which he transfused and interpenetrated even the commonest things. All readers of his poetry are familiar with this quality, and the poetry would apply suffice to illustrate it. But his letters are at once less known and more personal, and the glow and glamour of imagination, touches them everywhere as it does the poems. Often in the middle of a letter he burst right into verse. Or he brings in his memories of Shakespeare and other poets till it is difficult to tell where they end and he begins. He himself marks this element of his correspondence and enlarges upon its delightfully: "If I scribble long letters I must play my vagaries—I must be too heavy, or too light, for whole pages—I must be quaint and free of tropes and figures—I must play my draughts as I please; and for my advantage and your erudition, crown a white with a black, or a black with a white, and move into black or white, far and near as I please."

"Bare Souls": Critical Portraits, by GAMALIEL BRADFORD, 128. 6d.
Anyone watching Miss Parker's work in "Fantomas" would hardly believe this was her first screen appearance. She is sure to collect quite a "fan" following.

headline: “SLAVE OF DESIRE.”
text:
That the stories conceived and written by Honor de Balzac, held great screen possibilities, was proved at the World Theatre last night, where Gilbert E. Gable's "Slave of Desire," a picturization of Balzac's novel, "The Magic Skin," was shown. This story lends itself admirably to screen treatment and both the producer, Gilbert E. Gable, and the director, George D. Baker, have followed closely the characters and events of the story, as well as its spirit. While necessarily much of the philosophy that Balzac put into his story is missing in the screen version, that loss will be made up for, to the admirers of Balzac, by the truthfulness to life, to manners and customs, and characters of early Nineteenth Century France, which the producer has put into this photoplay.

The characters of "The Magic Skin" take life upon the boreon and in their acting by a great cast, present vividly the basic theme of the novel that whatever we wish and struggle for and get, that we also pay for. Mr. Gable has made most drama to and continuously interesting picture from "The Magic Skin" and has stressed some of the big episodes, such as that of the least in a truly speciacular manner. The big appeal of the picture, however, lies in the human quality of the characters and the story in which they act out their designs. headline: EXTRACTS
text:
People's opinions are often not a part of themselves at all, but a little bag they carry.

“Men often seem to me to want to do by words what can only be done by a look. Women know that by instinct.”

“People don't understand that one must get up an appetite for talk, just as one must for dinner.” “It is wonderful what a very long way a very little talk goes, if it is said with the right glance.”

“The only thing in which all men and women are alike” is in their desire for admiration—large draughts of unqualified admiration—that is what they want—it gives them a restful feeling.

"The only way you can understand people, if you want to, is to take them to bits. Often it isn't worth while; and even when you can do it, you have to remember that there is something else beside the bits."

“Freedom of movement is always beautiful, and I hate to see movement hampered. What ought to be covered up is anything unshapely or corpulent. I should like to put some of my men friends into decent cassocks

—long clothes ought to be the mark of age, not of youth and innocence." — "The House of Menerdue," by A. C. Benson. (These cross-word puzzles have been made by experts but our readers are warned to watch out for occasional phonetic spellings, such as harbor, plow, and altho.)

headline: COMING SOON.
text:
More to Be Pitied Than Scorned will be shown very shortly at the World Theatre.

This player run for many weeks in New York as a spoken play and all of the thrills and throbs of the original have been retained and intensified.

J. Frank Glendon, who plays the leading part, is too well known to need introduction.

He is admirably fitted to the part and his enormous following will ensure crowded houses wherever this picture is shown.

Playing a part where admirable histrionic ability is necessary as well as physical strength, Glendon is perfectly at home in "Moro to Be Pitied Than Scorned" and his handing of the role is exceptionally fine and finished.

Alice Lake, Rosemary Theby, Philo McCollough and Baby Josephine Adair make up the balance of the leading roles and each is perfect in his given part.

Baby Adair, whose future as an actress is all before her, gives a heart-winning performance as Ruth Lorraine.

This tiny, golden-haired sprite bids fair to be the leader among child actresses in a very short time.

Her portrayal of emotion is so absolutely convincing that it required a considerable amount of candy on several occasions to make her stop crying for her stage "mamma" after she had been carried away from her.

headline: WORLD OF SPORT. / IN OXFORD
text:
RUGBY PLAYER'S STORY OF ARREST IN FRANCE

"I suppose my trousers brought suspicion on me," said the member of the Esher Rugby Club, who was the victim of mistaken arrest when the team recently played Havre.

“Though I was knocked about a bit,” he added, “I did not want to complain to the consul as we were returning next day. It was best to treat the matter as a joke.”

The player is one of the forwards in the Esher Fifteen and on the evening when the team landed wore a pair of trousers of Oxford bagginess. He was followed by gendarmes to a café.

Suddenly, he went on, eight gendarmes came round me and, shouting "He is an apache," arrested me, and, putting a chain round my wrists tightly, marched me to the station, searched me, and then knocked me across the room. Neither my passport nor the efforts of my friends, who tried to explain the reason of our visit, made any difference.

I was thrust into a cell that resembled a stable and locked in for the night. They gave me a punch under the jaw in parting.

I was given nothing to eat or drink and was not released till I had been there five hours.

Have won the match by 3 tries to nil.

headline: DERBY SUBSCRIPTION.
text:
NOVEL TERMS OF STOCK EXCHANGE SWEEP.

Novel conditions appear on the tickets of "The Derby 1925 S/E Mutual Subscription Fund," which is the name of this year's Stock Exchange Derby Sweepstake. These are the terms of subscription:

The fund will be distributed by the organisers as to 10 per cent, less all costs and expenses incurred by the organisers, among charities; and as to 90 per cent. in such manner as the organisers in their absolute discretion deem fit. All subscriptions are made and received upon the basis that the organisers shall be under no legal obligation whatsoever, whether directly or indirectly, to the subscribers, but they honourably pledge themselves to distribute the whole of the 90 per cent. of the fund by means of allotments to such of the subscribers as they may determine.

The fund is limited to members of the Stock Exchange and “the list will be closed at the discretion of the organisers.”

Each ticket bears the signature, printed in facsimile, of the two members of the Stock Exchange who are honorary organisers.

headline: AUTO SUGGESTION.
text: At a certain Scottish golf club the whisky is as popular as the game, and as freely indulged in, One day a member became seriously ill and had to be removed to a home after noticing that his niblick had turned a pale blue colour shot with yellow stripes. Months later, when he had returned and was playing in a foursome, an adder moved out of the rough and took its snaky course over one of the greens. The convalescent turned pale and stood stock still for a second, then he observed with a shaky laugh, "I know you fellows all think I saw a snake there, but I didn't."

headline: IDEAL PARTNER
text:
HELPFUL SUTCLIFFE.

THIRD TEST INCIDENT.

Continuing, in the “Daily News” his comments on the last English cricket team's Australian tour; J. B. Hobbs says:—

"No more united band of cricketers ever left England in quest of the ashes. Those members who were left out of the various matches took their disappointment like bricks.

The most consistent batsmen were Sucliffe and myself. Sucliffe's wonderful pe formances justify the expectation that he will be my successor. He possesses the right temperament for a great occasion. Is always a cheerful and encouraging partner, and never suffered from swelled head when Australia was riaging with his praises. I recollect that, in the third test, when we got together later than usual, the wicket was tricky, and Mailey was bowling wonderfully. I felt at sea, but suddenly, at the end of an over. Sucliffe approached and said: Look here, old man; it stands to reason that he cannot bowl like that for long. Just stick to it, Jack! I did, and made another century.

headline: RACING STORIES
text:
"SAUCE FOR THE GOOSE" A certain noble punter having had a very good week and not having received his cheque, on the following Monday, write to his commission agent to ask the reason. The reply came by wire, "Plenty of money; run out of cheques."

Later on, in the season the punter had a very bad week and omitted to put his account in order. On his bookmaker writing to remind him he replied (also by wire), "Plenty of cheques; run out of ink."

headline: HIS CHOICE.
text:
In a public house in Dublin there is an assistant who is very free with his “tips” that are seldom successful. On the morning of a recent Baldoyle meeting a friend called there and on seeing him the assistant exclaimed rather excitedly. “Look here, look here, I have a horse for you!”

Amid general laughter came the reply. Thanks, keep him for yourself. I am going down by train.

headline: YOKOHAMA GOLF.
text:
OPENING OF THE SEASON.

The summer golf programme at the Nippon Race Club links begins to-day, June 6. This is the opening day for the "Nil Desperandum" Cup and the summer "Eclectic" competition. The June medal also will be played for to-day.

"To-morrow," June 7, the first half of the first round of the international matches will take place. The Columbia Society and the St. Andrew's Society are to meet four players a side, with singles in the morning and foursomes in the afternoon. It is proposed to hold the second half of the first round on Sunday, June 28, when players representing the St. George's Society and the St. Patrick's Society will meet. The final is scheduled for Sunday, July 12.

The “Nil Desperandum” Cup has been presented by a member of the Nil Desperandum organisation with “knock out” match play competition, club handicaps to court, for players with a par handicap of 20 and up. The matches will be for 18 holes with 36 holes for the final. Entry lists have been placed in the club house and in the Yokohama United Club. The lists close on May 31. It is hoped to give contestants three weeks for the first round and two weeks for the second but in any event players must complete their matches within the times stipulated. Closing dates for each round will be posted on the notice board in the club house.

Other events to be played in June and July are the inter-club matches with the Tokyo Golf Club, and the play for the G.G.B. Cup 1925, a cup presented by Mr. G. G. Brady, a former resident of Yokohama.

headline: WIMBLEDON.
text:
ANDERSONS CHANCES.

J. O. Anderson, Australian champion, has left for England to take part in the British championships at Wimbledon. As the entries for these events will include all the leading players of Europe and some of the Americans, probably including Richards, Australians will be looking forward to the results with more than ordinary interest. There are many who think that Anderson will not only carry off the British title, but will produce form far superior to anything shown by him in America before. Since he last played in the States his backhand strokes have improved wonderfully, until now he is practically as deadly on a high ball on his backhand as he is on the forehand. His match with Tilden should be worth going miles to see if both are in top form. Anderson is trying to arrange

Anderson is trying to arrange for Lycett to partner him in the Wimbledon doubles again. He was successful with the same partner in 1922, their opponents in the final being Patterson and Wood.

Patterson will pair with Anderson in the national doubles championship of America, which will be played before the final round of the Davis Cup, and it will be interesting to see what sort of a pair they will mould into. There will be no doubt about the severity being there, as in the case of the Tilden-Johnston combination.

headline: ODDS AND ENDS
text:
In England Cabinet Ministers cannot afford to keep motor cars. In America, thanks in the main to the enterprise of Mr. Henry Ford, a car is regarded as an essential perquisite to the normal working household. Professors and students, typlits and bricklayers, the humblest operative as well as the wealthiest millionaire owns, or appears to own, a car. Little children drive about in toy automobiles. In Los Angeles there is a car to every four persons, children included. When winter comes the roads of Florida are black not only with the automobiles of the wealthy in search of change and sunshine, but also with the Ford cars of the working men. American civilisation is on wheels.—The Rt. Hon. H. A. L. Fisher in "Scribner's Magazine."

That old Joko about Scotsmen preferring church services by radio because there is no collection plate attached there, will have to be discarded according to officials of the Canadian National Railways (reports the "Canadian National Railways Magazine.") William Stapleton, district passenger agent at Saskatoon, has wired headquarters, that when the Continental Limited, a radio-equipped train on the Canadian National system, was approaching one Sunday morning recently, the operator received the service from Westminster Presbyterian Church, in that city. The sermon of the Rev. George A. Dixon, of Knox Church, Calgary, so delighted the passengers in the radio observation car that a collection was taken up which was handed to the minister of Westminster Church when the train reached Saskatoon shortly after noon.

headline: "Shock" For Heifers.
text: appearance of a mystery has occurred at Mid-Strathmore, Thornton. About 20 cows belonging to Mr. Thomas Wood, Cottage Dairy, Thornton, were put into the field tenanted by Mr. John Lochhesad, farmer, and sub-let to Mr. Wood for grazing. The cattle included several heifers, and were seen by Mr. Wood to wander to a corner of the field where there is a transformer which reduces the current of the main electric cable that supplies light and driving power for the district from 12,000 to 250 volts. The ground at the corner is somewhat soft, and Mr. Wood was surprised to see five of his animals suddenly in difficulties, kicking and struggling as if they were in pain. Three of the cattle managed to free themselves from the danger zone, but two others were rooted to the spot. Considering the high voltage on the cable and the fact that the ground, with the moisture in it, proved a perfect conductor, it was fortunate that no one made to get to the cows, for a human being must certainly have succumbed to the shock which the beasts experienced. It was found that one heifer was electrocuted.

headline: City Under Sea.
text: Sir E. Derison Ross, Director of the School of Oriental Studies, Finsbury-circus, E.C., who recently returned from North Africa, brings news of the discovery of an unknown Phenician city now beneath the sea near the Isle of the Lotus Eaters, or Jerba, as it is now called. "I cannot vouch for the discovery myself," said Sir Dension to a "Daily Mail" reporter, "but I have no reason to doubt it. A French official in Tunis described to me how the Arab fishermen diving after fish saw this city under the water and dived down, bringing up things which immediately attracted the attention of archaeologists. I must confess that I have never heard of any Phoenician city in that locality; but then the site of Carthagenian Carthage has not yet been discovered. I understand that the French are organising exploration of the city on proper lines." While in Tunis Sir Dension visited the explorations of the combined French, English, and American commission. "They have made some wonderful discoveries just outside the city," he said. "They have found one place on a comparatively small site which was apparently a temple to the Goddess Thanity," but exactly what it is they have not yet been able to determine.

headline: Thỏ Magic Carpet
text: Most of us look upon Turkey carpets and carpets made in the East as things which surpass all European Products (says the "Children's Newspaper.") But there is a magic in our English carpets which the Eastern manufacturers cannot imitate, as was revealed the other day by some British dye experts. Certain of the rich men of Turkey, when they require specially beautiful carpets, the rich colours of which are to stand the test of centuries without fading, have actually sent over the designs to England and have had their "Turkey" carpets made in Lancashire and the materials dyed in Bradford. We are apt to wring our hair ds at German progress in the dye industry, but some of our dyes have never been surpassed, and so it comes about that many of the most beautiful carpets of the East have been woven in England, and coloured with British dyes! English people sometimes buy them back again years afterwards, little knowing that their real Turkey carpets are every bit as English as they are.

headline: Modern “Sameness.”
text: Modern dress may, as its admirers declare, be an indication of its wearer's personality, but though the women guests at Miss Viola Baring's wedding wore different colours they created an impression of "sameness" that was almost tiresome (say an "Evening Standard" writer). Cloche hats and long coats were worn by about 99 per cent. of the feminine guests. It was only at the reception at Rutland Gate that one was able to sort out the colours and note that Lady Louis Mountbatten was in navy blue trimmed with beige fox fur, that pistachio green is a tint that becomes her sister, Miss Mary Ashley, very well, and that Lady Mainwaring, whose small daughter Zara was one of the bridesmaids, wore a cyclamen-pink dress and, a hat to match.

headline: Coffee Stalls de Luxe.
text: One day, perhaps, an epicure will write an exquisite little volume on the novel meals one may obtain in the early hours from London's coffee stalls (writes a "Daily News" writer.) Returning from Fleet Street early one morning, I called at such a stall in a South-East London suburb and enjoyed the proprietor's speciality. This was—hot fried sausage cut into thin slices and placed between pieces of bread and butter. Most intriguing—I had two of these sandwiches and a good cup of coffee for 5d.

headline: Gold Salt for Tuberculosis.
text: A report on the "Gold Treatment" of tuberculosis has been prepared by the Medical Research Council. This treatment depends on the use of a drug called "sanocrysin," and was introduced by Professor Moellgaard, of Copenhagen. The evidence, it is stated, is sufficiently encouraging to demand further clinical study. The Medical Research Council adds that extended observations are imperatively required before it can be clearly stated whether or not the gold salt is of value in the treatment of tuberculosis, and before it should be made available for general use in medical practice in Great Britain.—Times.

headline: The Unknown of London.
text: Everybody ought to carry some form of identification, said Mr. Ingleby Oddie, the Westminster coroner, at an inquest on an unknown man between 50 and 60 who was suddenly taken ill in the street and died in Westminster Hospital. He was in possession of £810s. "He was one of those men who walk about London with no means of identifying themselves," said Mr. Oddie. "No doubt the man lived in London, but we don't know who he is." About 50 unknown people are found dead in London every year, and a score of them at least are buried without a trace of their names or their families ever being found, although months are spent in inquiries. "Of course some people do not want to be identified said a London coroner to a "Daily Mail" reporter. "They belong to a sort of suicide club and they do their work thoroughly."

headline: KIUNGCHOW, May 1
text: The latest development in the Hainan situation is the clan fighting between the Limkos and Hakkas in the western part of the island. The Limkos are a LoI tribe, aborigines and semi-time, and far outnumber the colony of Hakkas, which has its centre south of Namoa, at Namfong. The trouble started about the first of the year when a band of Hakkas and official soldiers burned eight Limko villages which were known to be robber villages. The Limkos, of course, had to retaliate, and to date it is said that over forty villages have been razed. The Hakkas have been the more aggressive. The official soldiers who were in the region have withdrawn, saying that they were few to cope with the situation. But now Gen. Teng. governor of the island, has dispatched three ying of troops under Tang Hoang Tsiang, (regional protective police) to Nodoah which is the most important town of the region, with orders to settle the Limko-Hakka war. An American mission has a station at Nodoah and several of the Limko-Hakka war. headline: The Byers City.
text: "Southern Star," published an official announcement of the settlement of the Byers' case a few days ago. It stated that the American Government had demanded $50,000 indemnity for the murder, but in view of Hainan's poverty, this had been reduced to $20,000. This was paid over a month ago and a receipt for the money was published in the paper. Ho Lih-tsiang, who was in command of the troops at Kachek, at the time of the murder last June, has been deprived of his official titles until he succeeds in arresting the murderers. A good many troops have been dispatched into the mountains to hunt out the bandits, but there has been no report on their success or non-success. Chen Ki-zi, a People's Army leader and Sun's adherent whom some Chinese say was responsible for Mr. Byers' death, is still at large in the mountains engaging in raids. The head-bandit, Lim Si-biau, who is also accused, has not been caught, although there is a large price on his head. Several American missionaries have returned to Kachek and are slowly opening up the work. The compound is being carefully guarded.

headline: PRISONER PLAINTIFF / WINS-ACTION AGAINST LANDLORD.
text:
A prisoner from Victoria Gaol made a successful claim for $500 yesterday in the Summary Court. The action was brought against his former landlord on the grounds that the money had been paid to him as a deposit against rent.

The defendant admitted that the chop on a receipt for the money was his chop but denied that the signature was. He had never had the money and was it likely his solicitor (Mr. Leo d'Almada) asked, that a man would pay such a large sum some months after going into a tenement and without a lease or agreement. His Honour Mr. Justice Wood gave judgment for the plaintiff, however, holding that the onus to prove the signature was not valid was on the defendant. Mr. G. R. Haywood appeared for the plaintiff.

headline: DAZED BY FUMES.
text:
IMPRISONED IN STRONG-ROOM.

While working in a strong-room in a new building in Bath Street, Glasgow, two masons, James McGrory and Thomas Joyce, were imprisoned for a quarter of an hour by the heavy door of the room accidentally closing.

A coke fire had been placed in the room, which is in the basement, to dry the walls, and owing to the fumes from the fire the two men were in a dangerous position. The door, weighing half a ton, being jammed with debris, the workmen outside were unable to effect a speedy rescue of their mates and had to break through the wall and the ventilator above the door so as to pass a crowbar to the imprisoned men.

When the door was forced open, McGrory and Joyce were in a dazed condition. They were taken to the Royal Infirmary and after treatment were allowed to go home.
